para.p: Although spatial intelligence is increasingly discussed as one concept, its meaning varies substantially across academic disciplines. Each field approaches spatial intelligence through its own problem formulations, representational assumptions, and evaluation criteria. As a result, what counts as spatial intelligence in one domain may only capture a partial aspect of what another domain considers essential. This section reviews how spatial intelligence is understood from several major disciplinary perspectives, highlighting both their unique emphases and their limitations.

From the perspective of computer vision, spatial intelligence is primarily associated with the ability to infer geometric structure from visual input. Research in this area focuses on problems such as depth estimation, multi-view geometry, camera pose estimation, and 3D scene reconstruction. The core objective is to recover spatially consistent representations from 2D images or videos, often under strong geometric constraints. These representations provide powerful spatial priors, enabling reasoning about layout, scale, and relative positioning of objects.

Closely related, computer graphics emphasizes the synthesis and rendering of spatial scenes. Modern neural rendering approaches, including NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, prioritize appearance fidelity, view consistency, and continuous scene representation. While these methods excel at producing visually coherent 3D environments, they typically do not model agent-centric interaction, decision-making, or task-driven behavior. As a result, spatial intelligence in vision and graphics is often appearance-centered and offline, rather than action-oriented.

In robotics and embodied AI, spatial intelligence is traditionally defined in terms of an agent’s ability to localize itself, navigate environments, and manipulate objects. This includes spatial perception, motion planning in three-dimensional space, and interaction with representations such as occupancy grids, semantic maps, and volumetric models. Here, spatial intelligence is inseparable from embodiment and control, as spatial reasoning directly informs action execution. The central concern in this discipline is not only representing space, but using spatial representations to support real-time decision-making under physical constraints. Consequently, spatial intelligence is evaluated through task success, robustness, and adaptability in dynamic environments. This action-centric perspective highlights aspects of spatial intelligence that are often absent in purely perceptual or representational frameworks.

paragraph.title: Geographic Information Systems and Large-Scale Spatial Modeling.

para.p: At a larger spatial scale, geographic information systems view spatial intelligence through the lens of structured spatial data, coordinate systems, and topological relations. GIS focuses on modeling, querying, and reasoning over large-scale geographic environments using maps, graphs, and spatial databases. These systems excel at spatial querying, route optimization, and long-term planning across city or regional scales. However, traditional GIS frameworks are rarely coupled with embodied agents or interactive learning. Spatial intelligence in this context is largely static, symbolic, and detached from perception or action. This contrast highlights a scale-dependent interpretation of spatial intelligence, where global consistency and abstraction take precedence over local interaction.

Long before AI adopted the term, differential psychology treated spatial ability as a measurable dimension of human intelligence. Shepard and Metzler’s mental rotation experiments showed that the time needed to compare rotated 3D shapes grows linearly with their angular disparity, providing the first chronometric evidence of analog spatial representation [], and the factor-analytic tradition from Thurstone’s space factor to Carroll’s broad visuospatial factor established spatial ability as a distinct, testable construct []. The term spatial intelligence itself was popularized by Gardner’s Frames of Mind (1983), which listed it among seven human intelligences and defined it as the capacity to perceive the visual world accurately, to perform transformations upon one’s initial perceptions, and to re-create aspects of visual experience even in the absence of the relevant stimuli; the construct, however, predates that label by half a century. Two findings from this literature matter directly for AI. First, spatial skills are malleable: a meta-analysis across hundreds of training studies shows they improve with practice and transfer across tasks [], suggesting spatial competence is acquired rather than fixed. Second, the psychometric task inventory, covering mental rotation, perspective taking, and spatial visualization, has become a direct template for probing spatial understanding in multimodal foundation models, so this measurement tradition now feeds AI benchmarking rather than sitting apart from it [].

In cognitive science and neuroscience, spatial intelligence is studied as an emergent property of interacting neural systems rather than as an engineered representation. Research has identified key brain regions associated with spatial cognition, including the hippocampus for spatial memory and navigation (place cells, and grid cells in entorhinal cortex), the parietal cortex for spatial attention and transformation, and occipito-parietal networks for visuospatial processing []. From this perspective, spatial intelligence arises from neural mechanisms supporting cognitive maps, mental imagery, and spatial reasoning; it is primarily internal and cognitive, centered on perception and imagination rather than external interaction.

A further disciplinary lens comes from linguistics, which asks how language encodes and constrains spatial thought. Talmy’s analysis of how language schematizes space [] and Landau and Jackendoff’s account of the asymmetry between rich object naming and the small closed class of spatial prepositions [] established that linguistic descriptions compress spatial structure into coarse, topology-like relations. Levinson’s cross-linguistic work further showed that languages differ systematically in their spatial frames of reference, distinguishing intrinsic, relative, and absolute systems []. This vocabulary has migrated directly into AI evaluation, where egocentric versus allocentric reference handling is now a standard axis of spatial benchmarks for multimodal models, making the linguistics of space an operative rather than merely historical influence.

Beyond physical geometry, spatial intelligence also carries meaning at the social and mental levels. Human beliefs, emotions, and behaviors are situated within social environments that are themselves spatially structured. From this viewpoint, spatial intelligence encompasses the ability to reason about others in shared spaces, interpret spatial cues in social contexts, and align internal mental states with external environments. This perspective extends spatial intelligence beyond physical navigation toward a unified model of the physical and mental world. It points to broader scientific and societal opportunities, including AI systems that operate in unstructured real-world settings and interact naturally with humans. In this sense, spatial intelligence supports a joint modeling of physical space and human cognition, serving as a bridge between external environments and internal mental states.

For decades, research on spatial reasoning and spatial representation has progressed from markedly different perspectives across multiple subfields. These efforts often evolved in isolation, lacking a shared vocabulary, common research objectives, or directly comparable evaluation benchmarks. As a result, techniques developed in areas such as SLAM, 3D vision, scene modeling, world modeling, and embodied planning frequently addressed overlapping problems without converging toward a unified conceptual framework. Spatial intelligence emerges against this backdrop as a response to fragmentation, offering a higher-level abstraction that can organize and align these historically disjoint research trajectories.

Under the emerging spatial intelligence paradigm, a set of shared demands and core concepts has begun to surface. A central driving force behind this convergence is the growing need for agents that exhibit spatial consistency and physical groundedness, and that can operate continuously within dynamic environments. Such agents must integrate perception, representation, and action in a coherent manner. This requirement has catalyzed the fusion of visual perception with geometry-aware modeling, as seen in navigation-oriented neural rendering approaches and interactive NeRF-based systems. Research at the intersection of neural scene representation and active planning has given rise to a new generation of 3D world models that are not only reconstructive, but also executable and actionable. Similarly, vision-language models are increasingly extended to operate in three-dimensional environments, enabling multimodal agents to localize, describe, and interact with objects within voxelized or volumetric scenes.

At the conceptual level, a set of shared primitives is gradually taking shape. Spatial representations, whether instantiated as voxel grids, signed distance fields, neural feature volumes, or topological graph structures, are becoming central components across domains ranging from autonomous driving and AR/VR to assistive robotics. Fundamental spatial relations, such as containment, adjacency, support, and traversability, are being formalized and embedded into reasoning modules, scene graph systems, and relational neural networks. These abstractions provide a common representational substrate that enables knowledge transfer and system interoperability across tasks and modalities.

We note that the research community has yet to settle on a single taxonomy for this emerging field. Recent surveys and position papers organize spatial intelligence along markedly different axes: by task family and benchmark [], by the cognitive functions that video-based spatial tasks exercise [], by spatial scale from embodied agents through cities to Earth systems [], or, in Li’s position essay, by the capabilities a world model must possess, namely being generative, multimodal, and interactive []. These framings overlap without coinciding, and none has achieved consensus status. This handbook’s representation-centric organization, which follows how spatial representations are built, used, and acted upon, is our deliberate choice among these alternatives: it is the axis along which the historical evolution of Section unfolds most naturally, and the one that lets fragmented communities be compared on common ground.

Taken together, these developments indicate that spatial intelligence is no longer confined to any single domain. It is evolving into a unifying functional substrate that spans perception, reasoning, and interaction; bridges vision, language, and action; and connects symbolic representations with neural models. The unification runs deeper than shared technique. Spatial intelligence aligns and integrates multiple disciplines, including computer vision, robotics, psychology, cognitive science, linguistics, geospatial systems, human-computer interaction, and neuro-inspired AI, and through this alignment it functions as the connective tissue that enables the next generation of generalist AI systems to perceive the world, reason about it, and act within it.

para.p: Given the inherently hybrid and interdisciplinary nature of spatial intelligence, it becomes necessary to revisit and refine what we mean by “spatial intelligence” in a precise and unified manner. Rather than treating spatial intelligence as a loosely defined collection of capabilities, we aim to articulate a coherent conceptual framework that can accommodate its diverse manifestations across systems, tasks, and environments. In this section, we therefore propose an explicit definition of spatial intelligence and analyze its core properties in a structured way.

p.emph: Spatial intelligence is the ability of an AI system to construct, maintain, and manipulate spatial representations of the physical world or environment that support perception, reasoning, prediction, and embodied action, to accomplish tasks within a given environmental context.

para.p: This definition emphasizes several essential aspects. First, spatial intelligence is grounded in representations of the world rather than isolated sensory inputs. Second, it is functional rather than static, supporting perception, reasoning, prediction, and action. Third, it is inherently situated, meaning that spatial intelligence only manifests meaningfully within an environment where tasks are defined and executed. In the following, we unpack this definition by examining its key attributes.
At a minimum, spatial intelligence involves two fundamental parties: an AI system and the physical world or environment in which it operates. Neither can be meaningfully defined without the other.

The AI system refers to any computational entity capable of perception, reasoning, and decision-making. This includes, but is not limited to, large language models, multimodal foundation models, world models, embodied agents, and robotic systems. Crucially, spatial intelligence is not tied to a specific architecture. Instead, it characterizes a class of capabilities that may be realized through different model families, training paradigms, and system designs [].

The environment denotes the external context in which the AI system is situated. This typically refers to the physical world governed by geometric, physical, and causal constraints. In some cases, the environment may also include social or human-centric settings, where spatial structure interacts with social norms, human intent, and collective behavior []. Spatial intelligence arises precisely from the interaction between the AI system and such structured environments.

A core component of spatial intelligence lies in the ability to form, maintain, and manipulate world-centered spatial representations. These representations serve as structured world models that are compositional, generalizable, and reusable across tasks.
Spatial representations may vary along several dimensions:

Granularity. Representations can operate at different spatial scales, including object-centric representations, scene-centric representations, and relational representations capturing relative geometry or topology.

Modality. Spatial information may be derived from heterogeneous sensory channels, including pixels, grid maps, point clouds, voxel grids, language descriptions, audio signals, spectral measurements, radar inputs, as well as tactile and force feedback.

Level of Abstraction. Spatial representations may be geometric, such as metric coordinates and surfaces, topological, such as connectivity graphs, or semantic and symbolic, such as object categories and relational predicates.

Concrete versus Abstract. Representations may directly encode observable properties of the physical world or serve as abstract internal models that summarize, compress, or reinterpret spatial structure for reasoning and planning.

Importantly, spatial intelligence does not require committing to a single representational form. Instead, it demands the ability to align and translate across multiple representational levels in a world-centered manner.

Spatial intelligence is not a static property acquired through passive observation. Rather, it emerges through continuous and dynamic interaction with the environment. This interaction includes navigation, manipulation, exploration, and embodied perception. An intelligent system must ground its spatial understanding in embodied experience, for example by learning the structure of a room through movement, or improving depth perception through active viewpoint selection. Interaction also extends to socially situated behaviors. Maintaining appropriate interpersonal distance, coordinating actions with humans, or navigating shared spaces all require spatial understanding informed by social context. As a result, spatial representations must be executable and continuously updated through perception-action feedback loops. We further decompose dynamic interaction into several functional components.

Perception refers to the extraction of spatial structure from multimodal sensory inputs. This includes recognizing objects and scene elements, estimating distances, identifying spatial layouts, and localizing entities within an environment.

Spatial reasoning involves inference over spatial relations and dynamics. This includes trajectory prediction, path planning, occlusion reasoning, spatial causality, temporal change modeling, relational inference, and logical or commonsense reasoning about space. Such reasoning spans both low-level problems, such as shortest-path computation, and high-level abstractions, such as understanding how rearranging objects alters the affordances of a space.

Prediction in spatial intelligence operates along two axes. One concerns forecasting future spatial states or events in a manner consistent with physical laws and causal structure. The other concerns generative capabilities, such as producing spatially aware images, videos, 3D or 4D scenes, and motion trajectories.

Embodied action denotes the capacity to interact with physical or simulated environments while continuously pursuing goals. This includes pose adjustment, navigation, grasping, and object manipulation. Typical scenarios include domestic robots and autonomous driving systems. Such action requires tight integration of perception, reasoning, planning, and prediction, while aligning internal spatial models with task objectives, human intent, and social context.

quote.p: A well-designed spatially intelligent AI system should satisfy the following criteria:

para.p: High-quality world representation. It must acquire a rich, consistent, and generalizable spatial representation of the world that captures geometry, relations, and structure across scales.
Dynamic interaction capability. It should support accurate perception, reasoning, prediction, and embodied action through continuous interaction with the environment.
Alignment between model, task, and environment. The internal spatial model must remain aligned with external task objectives, environmental constraints, and feedback signals during execution.

To make the definition more precise, we provide a lightweight formalization that captures the core components of spatial intelligence without committing to a specific implementation or learning paradigm.

This formalization clarifies that spatial intelligence is not tied to a specific modality, algorithm, or architecture. Instead, it is defined by the existence of a system-induced, world-centered spatial representation space
R S
and the ability of the AI system

to manipulate, update, and exploit this representation to support perception, reasoning, prediction, and embodied action within an environment.

The proposed framework is intentionally designed to be inclusive rather than prescriptive. Rather than introducing a new task taxonomy or replacing existing formulations, it provides a unifying lens through which a wide range of spatial intelligence-related tasks, domains, and research traditions can be consistently described. From this perspective, most existing work can be understood as instantiating or emphasizing only a subset of the core elements defined in our framework, often driven by domain-specific constraints, data availability, or evaluation protocols.

A large body of research in computer vision, graphics, and extended reality focuses primarily on the representation layer of spatial intelligence. Tasks such as 3D reconstruction, neural rendering, scene synthesis, video generation, and emerging 4D spatiotemporal modeling concentrate on learning expressive spatial representations
R S
, often with little or no emphasis on action, task execution, or long-term interaction. Within our framework, these approaches can be viewed as developing increasingly powerful instantiations of world-centered spatial representations, while largely abstracting away the agent
S
and the functional operators that connect representation to behavior. Their contributions lie in advancing the expressiveness, continuity, and generative capacity of spatial representations, even if they remain largely offline or perception-centric.

Robotics, embodied AI, and embedded systems emphasize a different subset of the framework, placing primary focus on action grounding and closed-loop interaction. Vision-Language-Action models, navigation agents, and manipulation systems operationalize the mapping from internal representations to actions, often under real-time and physical constraints. However, in many cases, the underlying spatial representations remain task-specific, shallow, or tightly coupled to particular embodiments. From the perspective of our framework, these systems instantiate the functional operators and dynamic interaction components, while relying on relatively limited or implicit world representations. This explains why many embodied systems exhibit strong short-horizon competence but struggle with long-term consistency, world editing, or cross-task transfer.

Classical and modern SLAM systems provide a complementary example. SLAM explicitly targets the construction and maintenance of a world-centered spatial representation under uncertainty, typically in the form of metric maps, pose graphs, or hybrid geometric-topological structures. Within our framework, SLAM can be understood as a specialized instantiation of the representation update process, with strong guarantees on geometric consistency and state estimation. At the same time, SLAM systems often remain agnostic to high-level reasoning, semantic abstraction, or task-conditioned decision making, highlighting again that they occupy a specific slice of the broader spatial intelligence spectrum rather than the full stack.

Viewed through this unified lens, existing spatial intelligence research does not fragment into incompatible paradigms, but instead forms a landscape of partial realizations. Different communities emphasize representation learning, perception, reasoning, prediction, or action to varying degrees. Our framework provides a common conceptual structure that makes these emphases explicit, clarifies their limitations, and reveals how advances in one area can be systematically integrated with others. In this sense, the framework is not a replacement for existing approaches, but a scaffold for understanding how they collectively contribute to, and fall short of, world-centered spatial intelligence.

chapter.title: Chapter 3Scope and Structure of This Handbook

para.p: This chapter provides a structural overview of the handbook. We clarify the scope, goals, and organization of the volume, and explain how the different parts jointly form a coherent research landscape for spatial intelligence. Specifically, we introduce the core research pillars covered in this handbook, outline their relationships, and offer guidance on how readers from different backgrounds may navigate the content.

We outline the core research pillars that constitute the structural backbone of this handbook. They traverse the full pipeline from spatial representation and perception to reasoning and generative capabilities, and ultimately extend into concrete real-world applications. Each pillar aligns closely with a corresponding Part or chapter of the handbook, serving as a thematic axis for both foundational methods and emerging challenges in spatial intelligence.

Representation (Part II: Spatially Aware Representation) This pillar investigates how spatial information is encoded and represented across modalities and dimensions. We begin with single-modality representations, including 2D (e.g., , visual frames), 3D (e.g., , point clouds, meshes), and 4D (e.g., , dynamic scenes, spatio-temporal fields), as well as non-visual modalities such as language and audio. Particular attention is given to cross-modal alignment and fusion mechanisms that unify heterogeneous data sources. These representational strategies provide the necessary structural foundation for downstream reasoning, manipulation, and generation.

Perception (Part III, Chapter : Spatial Perception) This pillar focuses on how intelligent systems extract structured knowledge from spatial environments. Topics include object detection, semantic and instance segmentation, depth and surface normal estimation, visual odometry (VO), and ego-motion prediction. These perception modules translate raw sensory inputs into geometric or semantic abstractions, enabling agents to comprehend and navigate the physical world.

Reasoning (Part III, Chapter : Spatial Reasoning) Reasoning in spatial intelligence spans multiple paradigms: symbolic reasoning over geometric primitives or logical propositions; geometric reasoning over shapes, topologies, and configurations; neural reasoning using deep architectures; and LLM-driven spatial inference based on large-scale pretrained priors. These methods enable agents to interpret relations, deduce spatial constraints, and plan in dynamic settings.

Reconstruction and Generation (Part III, Chapter : Spatial Reconstruction and Generation) This pillar examines the generative side of spatial intelligence. It encompasses tasks such as 3D reconstruction from observations, 2D/3D scene synthesis, controllable image and video generation, trajectory and motion prediction, and dynamic world creation. These generative processes are often guided by spatial prompts, semantic layouts, or agent intentions, forming a bridge between structured knowledge and creative capability.

Applications (Part IV: Applications) Finally, the application pillar illustrates how the above methods power real-world systems. Domains include embodied agents and robotics (e.g., , navigation, grasping), autonomous driving and aerial agents, warehouse and wearable AI systems, extended reality (XR), including virtual and augmented reality, geospatial AI (e.g., , urban planning, satellite analysis), biomedical and scientific computing (e.g., , 3D medical reconstruction), intelligent assistants, and further fields such as construction, sports, cultural heritage, marine systems, and retail. These chapters emphasize system-level integration and highlight how spatial AI capabilities translate into societal impact.

section.title: 3.2Goal of the Handbook: Charting a Research Ecosystem

para.p: The primary goal of this handbook is not to present a catalog of isolated techniques, but to chart an emerging research ecosystem centered on spatial intelligence. As established in earlier chapters, spatial intelligence is neither a single method nor a narrowly scoped task. Rather, it is a unifying paradigm that connects representation, perception, reasoning, generation, and action through structured models of the world.

paragraph.title: From Isolated Methods to an Integrated Landscape.

para.p: Much of the existing literature on spatial intelligence is fragmented. Some surveys focus deeply on individual subfields, such as SLAM, neural rendering, or 3D generation, while others adopt a high-level perspective that lacks technical grounding. This handbook aims to bridge this gap by organizing spatial intelligence as an interconnected landscape, where advances in one component are explicitly related to others. Our objective is to reveal how seemingly distinct research threads jointly contribute to world-centered intelligence.

paragraph.title: Spatial Intelligence as a Connective Substrate.

para.p: A central thesis of this handbook is that spatial intelligence functions as a connective substrate for next-generation AI systems. It provides the structural glue that links perception with reasoning, language with geometry, and planning with embodied action. By framing spatial intelligence in this way, the handbook draws connections across computer vision, robotics, simulation, geospatial systems, cognitive science, and neuro-inspired AI. This perspective enables a shared conceptual vocabulary through which contributions from different communities can be meaningfully aligned.

Beyond synthesizing existing work, this handbook deliberately highlights unresolved gaps in the current research landscape. These include the disconnect between symbolic and neural spatial representations, the limited grounding of perception in actionable world models, and the difficulty of integrating spatial reasoning into long-horizon embodied agents. By making these tensions explicit, we aim to clarify where current paradigms fall short and where future breakthroughs are most likely to emerge.

paragraph.title: A Blueprint for an Open Research Program.

para.p: Ultimately, this handbook is intended as a blueprint for an open and evolving research program. Rather than proposing a closed taxonomy or a definitive solution, it offers a structured lens through which spatial intelligence can be studied, extended, and reimagined. We invite readers not only to learn from the systems and methods surveyed here, but also to rethink spatial intelligence as a first-class organizing principle in the design of generalist intelligent agents.

Given the interdisciplinary nature of spatial intelligence, which spans AI, computer vision, robotics, graphics, GIS, and cognitive science, it is crucial to provide tailored reading paths that help each type of reader gain the most value from this handbook.

p.text: (e.g., , undergraduates, junior graduate students, newcomers to spatial AI)

para.p: Begin with Part I: Introduction and Background (Chapters 1–3) to grasp the motivation, historical evolution, and research scope.
Then proceed to Part II: Spatially Aware Representation to build a solid understanding of core representations in 2D, 3D, and 4D, including geometry and topology.
Optionally skim Part IV: Applications to get a glimpse of real-world use cases, such as robotics, autonomous driving, and AR/XR.

p.text: (e.g., , PhD students, postdocs, faculty, or interdisciplinary scholars in AI-related fields)

para.p: Focus on Part III: Spatial Intelligence, from Perception to Generation, which includes chapters on:
Spatial perception, from detection and segmentation to depth and odometry
Symbolic, geometric, neural, and LLM-driven spatial reasoning
Generative spatial models for scenes, videos, and worlds
Also study Part IV: Applications for cross-domain synergies, particularly in GeoAI, healthcare, urban simulation, and embodied cognition.
Consider Part V: Discussions and Futures for open problems, benchmarking gaps, and research directions.

p.text: (e.g., , practitioners building simulation environments, digital twin platforms, or perception pipelines)

para.p: Prioritize chapters in Part III (Generation) and Part IV (Applications) that introduce:
Modular spatial generation frameworks
Multi-agent simulation engines and control loops
Deployed system domains (e.g., , robotic manipulation, warehouse automation, wearable AI, aerial agents)
Use Part V: Discussions and Futures to anticipate where deployment bottlenecks and benchmark gaps lie.

p.text: (e.g., , scholars in architecture, biology, geoscience, or cognitive science)

para.p: Start with Part I (Introduction and Background) to acquire shared conceptual grounding.
Dive into Part IV (Applications) for domain-aligned chapters and illustrative case studies.
Refer to Part II (Representation) to gain a technical foothold in spatial structures and encodings.

Overall, this handbook is modular in structure and can be read either linearly or selectively depending on the reader’s focus. The chapter cross-references are designed to aid flexible navigation and long-term use.

part.title: Part IISpatially Aware Representation: Building Blocks of Space
part.toctitle: IISpatially Aware Representation: Building Blocks of Space

figure.toccaption: 3.1Part II in one view. (1) Encode first: a scene must be encoded before it can be perceived, reasoned about, or acted on. (2) One modality at a time: the same object as pixels, depth, points, meshes, voxels, and Gaussians, and then as language and sound, from explicit geometry to implicit structure (Chapter ). (3) Into a shared space: the separate encodings are aligned in one space without losing the geometry that makes them spatially meaningful (Chapter ).

caption.text: Part II in one view. (1) Encode first: a scene must be encoded before it can be perceived, reasoned about, or acted on. (2) One modality at a time: the same object as pixels, depth, points, meshes, voxels, and Gaussians, and then as language and sound, from explicit geometry to implicit structure (Chapter ). (3) Into a shared space: the separate encodings are aligned in one space without losing the geometry that makes them spatially meaningful (Chapter ).

para.p: Everything a spatially intelligent system does, perceiving a scene, reasoning over it, generating or acting within it, passes through some representation of space. That representation is upstream of the capability: what a system can perceive is bounded by what its encoding can express, and what it can reason about is bounded by what that encoding makes accessible. Before the later parts turn to perception, reasoning, and generation, this part asks the prior question of how spatial structure is captured at all, how the geometry, topology, and semantics of an environment come to be held in a form a machine can compute with.

The question is approached in two movements. The first takes each modality on its own terms, asking how images, video, 3D scenes, language, and sound each encode spatial structure and what each renders explicit or leaves implicit. The second asks how these separate encodings are brought into a shared space, so that signals as different as a pixel grid and a sentence can be aligned without losing the geometry that makes them spatially meaningful. The order is deliberate, since a modality must be understood by itself before its representation can be fused with others, and it is in that fusion that the partial, sensor-bound view offered by any one signal begins to reinforce the rest. Together they form the representational substrate on which the remainder of the handbook is built.

Single-modal spatial representations ask how much of a scene’s spatial structure can be recovered from one modality alone, without recourse to cross-modal correspondence. The question matters because every multimodal system is ultimately built from unimodal encoders, and the spatial content a fused representation can carry is bounded by what each modality already captures on its own.

What separates the modalities is not whether they carry spatial information but how overtly they carry it. Vision presents geometry almost directly, arranging appearance and shape over a spatial grid or the volume a scene occupies. Language and sound hold the same structure only obliquely, the one as symbolic relations among named entities, the other as the physical trace that propagation leaves on a signal. Others still are tied to a particular sensor or task, trading generality for fidelity to the data they were built around. This chapter proceeds along that gradient, from the most explicit geometric encodings of space toward the most implicit, examining each modality on its own terms before the question of how they combine is taken up.

The 2D representations are the most direct and information-dense entry point into spatial intelligence: images and videos provide a regular, discretely sampled grid over the visual field, on top of which a family of structured maps can be defined to expose geometric and semantic properties of the underlying scene. We organize this section around seven such representations (Figure ): the raw image/video tensor itself, and six derived maps: segmentation, depth, surface normal, edge, optical flow, and 2D keypoint representations. All seven share the image grid as their domain, which makes them straightforward to fuse with one another and to consume with convolutional or transformer backbones; what differs is what each representation exposes: appearance, semantics, geometry, boundaries, motion, or sparse structure.

From a computational perspective, images and videos are treated as structured arrays of numerical values that can be efficiently processed using linear algebra operations and convolutional kernels. This regular grid structure enables weight sharing, local receptive fields, and efficient parallel computation, forming the basis of CNNs and their spatiotemporal extensions []. In modern deep learning systems, image and video tensors may undergo normalization, resizing, patch embedding, or tokenization before being fed into neural architectures, including CNNs and vision transformers []. For video inputs, spatiotemporal extensions either inflate 2D kernels into 3D convolutions [] or extend self-attention across space and time, as in the family of video transformers [].

Video panoptic segmentation (VPS) further combines VSS and VIS, producing temporally consistent panoptic outputs, and is commonly evaluated with metrics that account for both segmentation quality and tracking consistency []. Closely related settings include video object segmentation (VOS) [], which segments foreground objects across time under semi-supervised or unsupervised protocols, and referring segmentation, which predicts masks grounded by natural language expressions in images (RIS) [] or videos (RVOS) []. Segmentation maps are typically formed by dense prediction models that produce either hard labels or per-pixel class probabilities

A key advantage of segmentation is its explicit and interpretable structure: it converts low-level pixels into object- and region-level representations that support downstream reasoning and decision-making, and it can be fused naturally with geometry (e.g., , depth, normals) and language in multimodal systems []. Consequently, segmentation maps are central to applications such as autonomous driving, medical image analysis, robotic manipulation, visual editing, and human-computer interaction.

A depth map is a geometric representation that augments a 2D image with per-pixel distance information, describing the spatial layout of a scene from a given viewpoint []. Formally, given an image domain
⊂ Ω

Related representations store inverse depth or disparity, which must be converted to the appropriate metric depth or range before geometric back-projection []. Depth maps can be obtained through multiple mechanisms, including stereo vision via triangulation [], active sensors such as structured-light or time-of-flight cameras [], and learning-based monocular depth estimation []. When combined with known camera intrinsics, a depth map enables the back-projection of image pixels into 3D space, thereby serving as a bridge between 2D image representations and 3D geometry. A key advantage of depth maps lies in their compact, image-aligned structure, which allows them to be processed using standard convolutional architectures and easily fused with the RGB appearance information. Compared to volumetric representations, depth maps are memory-efficient while still encoding meaningful geometric cues. As a result, they are widely used in applications such as 3D reconstruction, novel view synthesis [], robotic navigation, and autonomous driving [].

denotes the unit sphere. Surface normal maps can be derived from depth maps or 3D geometry via local differentiation, or directly estimated from RGB images using learning-based methods []. Classical approaches to normal estimation rely on photometric stereo or geometric reconstruction [], while modern methods employ CNNs to regress surface normals from monocular images []. Regardless of the estimation procedure, surface normal maps remain image-aligned and encode rich local geometric information that complements depth and segmentation cues. Surface normal maps can capture fine-grained shape and orientation details that may be ambiguous or noisy in raw depth estimates. Because surface normals are invariant to absolute depth scale, they provide robust geometric constraints for scene understanding. Consequently, surface normal maps are widely used in applications such as 3D reconstruction, object pose estimation, scene layout analysis, realistic rendering, and as auxiliary supervision in multi-task learning [].

Classical edge detection methods rely on hand-crafted operators such as Sobel, Laplacian of Gaussian, and the Canny detector [], while modern learning-based approaches directly predict the edge probabilities using convolutional neural networks []. Edge maps may be binary, indicating the presence or absence of an edge, or real-valued, encoding edge strength, orientation, or confidence. The primary advantage of edge maps is their ability to significantly reduce visual complexity while preserving essential geometric structure. This abstraction makes them relatively robust to changes in illumination and appearance. Consequently, edge maps are widely used in image segmentation, contour detection, shape analysis, line drawing, and as intermediate cues for higher-level tasks such as object recognition and depth estimation [].

More recently, deep neural networks have been proposed to directly regress dense flow fields from image pairs or short video clips []. Regardless of the estimation method, the resulting optical flow map remains image-aligned, preserving spatial correspondence with the input frames. The main advantage of optical flow maps is their ability to capture rich dynamic information about scene motion, including object motion, camera motion, and motion parallax, while remaining computationally efficient. As a result, optical flow is a core representation in video analysis and robotic perception tasks such as motion segmentation, action recognition, video interpolation, and visual odometry.

A 2D keypoint set is a sparse image representation that encodes the image-plane locations of a finite set of semantically or geometrically meaningful points, such as corners, joints, or landmarks []. Unlike dense maps that assign a value to every pixel, keypoint representations summarize visual content with a small number of salient points, trading pixel-level coverage for compactness and geometric explicitness. Depending on the task, keypoints may represent generic interest points, object-specific landmarks, or articulated structures such as the human body joints. The detection task that produces such a set, including its extension to landmark detection and human pose estimation, is discussed in detail in Section of Chapter . A key advantage of 2D keypoint representations is their sparsity and compactness: they significantly reduce the dimensionality of visual data while preserving critical structural information. This makes keypoints computationally efficient, robust to background clutter, and well-suited for geometric reasoning and correspondence matching. Human pose estimation is a specialized and highly structured instance of 2D keypoint detection that focuses on localizing a predefined set of anatomical landmarks of the human body, such as joints and facial keypoints, in images or videos []. The 3D representations lift the 2D pixel grid into the ambient space the scene actually occupies, replacing image-plane appearance with explicit geometry and topology. They are the substrate on which downstream tasks that require metric reasoning, occlusion handling, viewpoint manipulation, or physical simulation are built, from autonomous driving and robotic manipulation to medical visualization and immersive graphics. Compared with the depth and surface normal maps of Section , which still inhabit the image grid, 3D representations expose geometry directly and can therefore describe parts of the scene that are not visible in any single view.

We organize this section around the eight 3D representations that dominate current practice (Figure , Table ): RGB-D images, voxels, point clouds, meshes, implicit fields, neural radiance fields (NeRF), 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), and hybrids of the above. They differ in what they store (surfaces vs. volumes, explicit primitives vs. neural functions), how they trade off fidelity against memory and rendering speed, and how amenable they are to editing and to gradient-based optimization.
RGB-D Image. Pairs a standard RGB image with a per-pixel depth map; view-dependent and cannot capture occluded surfaces from a single frame.

Voxel. A uniform 3D grid of volumetric elements; conceptually simple and well suited to inherently volumetric data, but memory grows as
⁢ O
(
N 3
)
for
N
cells per axis.
Point Cloud. An unstructured set of 3D points, typically the native output of LiDAR or photogrammetry; faithful to the raw measurement but lacks surface connectivity.
Mesh. Surfaces defined by vertices and faces; the dominant representation in graphics for its GPU-friendliness, at the cost of a fixed connectivity that complicates topology change.
Implicit Representation. Defines surfaces as the level set of a continuous function (e.g., , Signed Distance Functions); resolution-agnostic and topology-flexible, but slow to render.
NeRF (Neural Radiance Field). A neural function over a 5D input domain (3D location + 2D viewing direction) that supports state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis.
3DGS (3D Gaussian Splatting). Represents a scene as anisotropic 3D Gaussian primitives rendered through a differentiable splatting rasteriser, reaching NeRF-level quality at real-time speeds.
Hybrid Methods. Combinations of the above (e.g., , DMTet, Tri-plane) that pair explicit primitives with implicit decoders to balance fidelity, efficiency, and gradient-based optimizability.

para.p:
RGB-D images are a popular 2.5D representation that captures both photometric and geometric information from a single viewpoint. This data format consists of two co-registered images: a standard RGB color image providing appearance and texture details, and a corresponding depth map where each pixel value encodes the camera-space depth of the corresponding scene point. Formally, it can be defined as a function mapping a 2D image grid
Ω
to a 4D space combining color and depth:

Math.text: I _ (r * g * b * d) colon Omega rightarrow R ^ 3 * R _ (absent >= 0)

para.p:
where the first three channels represent RGB color and the fourth channel encodes the depth of the corresponding scene point. In practice, RGB-D data is stored as a tensor
∈ I
R
× H W 4
.

The primary advantage of RGB-D data lies in its efficiency and accessibility. It is captured by low-cost sensors such as Microsoft Kinect or Intel RealSense, and its image-like grid structure enables the direct application of powerful 2D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection []. This fusion of color and depth provides a rich, multi-modal input for scene understanding. However, a significant limitation is its view-dependent nature; an RGB-D image represents only a partial view of the 3D world, suffering from occlusions and providing no information about surfaces hidden from the camera. Despite this, its real-time acquisition and processing capabilities make it indispensable in robotics for navigation [] and grasping [], in augmented reality (AR) for scene interaction, and as a foundational input for 3D reconstruction pipelines that fuse multiple frames into a complete model [].

The voxel grid is a foundational 3D representation that discretizes space into a uniform grid of volumetric elements, or voxels (a portmanteau of “volume” and “pixel”). Analogous to a pixel in 2D, a voxel grid can be modeled as a function mapping discrete 3D coordinates to a set of attributes:

Math.text: G colon set@(1, dots, D) * set@(1, dots, H) * set@(1, dots, W) rightarrow A

para.p:
where
D , H , W
are the grid dimensions and
A
can represent occupancy, color, density, or material properties, thereby enabling a detailed volumetric description of an object.

A key advantage of this representation is its ability to model complex geometries and internal structures, which are often challenging for surface-based methods like polygon meshes to capture. The conceptual simplicity of voxels, which can be seen as the three-dimensional extension of 2D pixels, facilitates straightforward implementation and manipulation. Consequently, voxel grids are natively suited for applications involving inherently volumetric data, such as medical imaging (e.g., , MRI and CT scans) [], where biological tissues are naturally captured as a 3D array of values. They are also widely adopted in computer graphics and gaming for tasks like procedural generation and creating destructible environments, as popularized by games like Minecraft.
Point clouds offer a direct and unstructured 3D representation, defined as a set of points in 3D space:

Math.text: formulae@(P = ((set@(p _ i)) _ (i = 1)) ^ N, p _ i = vector@(x _ i, y _ i, z _ i, a _ i) element-of R ^ 3 * R ^ C)

para.p:
Each point
p i
consists of its geometric coordinates
(
x i
,
y i
,
z i
)
and an optional
C
-dimensional attribute vector
a i
encoding properties such as color, intensity, or surface normals. They are the native output of active 3D scanning technologies like LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) and structured-light scanners [], as well as passive methods like photogrammetry [].

The primary strength of point clouds lies in their raw and unstructured nature; they represent geometry without imposing any explicit topological connectivity (unlike meshes) or spatial discretization (unlike voxels). This makes them a faithful and often highly precise representation of the captured data. However, this very lack of inherent structure poses significant challenges for downstream processing. The unordered and potentially sparse distribution of points makes tasks like feature extraction, segmentation, and reconstruction non-trivial, necessitating specialized algorithms and deep learning architectures (e.g., , PointNet [] and its successors []) that are designed to operate directly on irregular point sets.

A mesh is a canonical surface representation in computer graphics, defining an object’s boundary with a set of geometric and topological primitives. Formally, a triangle mesh is a tuple
= M
( V , F )
, where

Math.text: formulae@(V = ((set@(v _ i)) _ (i = 1)) ^ (absolute-value@(V)) subset-of R ^ 3, F subset-of V * V * V)

para.p:
Here,
V
is a set of vertices representing points in 3D space, and
F
is a set of faces (typically triangles) that define connectivity between vertices.

The key characteristic of a mesh is its explicit topological structure, which encodes the connectivity between these elements. This structure strikes an effective balance between descriptive power and computational efficiency. Its prevalence is due to several key advantages: meshes can represent complex, smooth surfaces with arbitrary fidelity through adaptive tessellation (i.e., , varying the polygon density); moreover, this representation is natively supported by modern Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), enabling highly efficient real-time rendering. The explicit connectivity also facilitates the straightforward computation of essential surface properties like normals and curvature, which are critical for realistic lighting and physical analysis. However, as a purely surface-based representation, standard meshes are ill-suited for modeling volumetric or internal structures, and representing objects with complex or changing topologies can be algorithmically challenging.
Implicit representations define 3D geometry not as a discrete set of primitives (e.g., , points or polygons), but as the level set of a continuous function:

Math.text: f colon R ^ 3 to R

para.p:
The surface
S
is implicitly defined as the set of points where the function evaluates to a specific value, typically zero:

Math.text: S = conditional-set@(x element-of R ^ 3, f * x = 0)

para.p:
A particularly powerful and popular form of this is the Signed Distance Function (SDF). An SDF maps any spatial coordinate
x
to the closest distance to the surface, where the sign indicates whether the point is inside (
<
⁢ f
( x )
0
) or outside (
>
⁢ f
( x )
0
) the object. This formulation inherently guarantees watertight, closed surfaces and provides a smooth, continuous description of the geometry, making it resolution-agnostic. A key advantage of implicit fields is their ability to elegantly handle complex and dynamic topologies; operations like merging, splitting, or creating holes do not require complex and error-prone re-meshing procedures. This makes them ideal for physical simulations, such as fluid dynamics and shape manipulation.

This paradigm has experienced a major resurgence with the rise of neural fields or neural implicit representations. Instead of storing the function in a grid, a neural network is trained to approximate it [] (e.g., , DeepSDF []). This approach is memory-efficient and can learn continuous, high-fidelity shape priors from data. Extensions such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) further generalize implicit fields to jointly model geometry and appearance, and are discussed in detail in Section . To visualize or use implicit surfaces in traditional rendering pipelines, an explicit mesh representation is often extracted via algorithms like Marching Cubes [].

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) represent a paradigm shift in novel view synthesis and implicit 3D scene representation []. The core innovation is to represent a static scene as a continuous function with a 5D input domain (3D location
+

To render an image from a novel viewpoint, rays are cast through the scene, and their colors are computed by integrating the predicted color and density values along each ray using principles of classical volume rendering and numerical quadrature. By optimizing the network’s weights to minimize the photometric reconstruction error between rendered and ground-truth images, NeRF can learn a highly detailed and coherent representation of the scene from only a sparse set of posed input images. The resulting state-of-the-art photorealism has established NeRF as a foundational technique, inspiring a vast body of follow-up research aimed at improving its speed, scalability, and applicability to dynamic scenes [].

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently emerged as a groundbreaking alternative to neural radiance fields, achieving state-of-the-art quality for novel view synthesis while enabling real-time rendering []. Unlike the implicit representation of NeRF, 3DGS represents a scene as a set of

The optimization process also includes an adaptive density control mechanism to dynamically add, split, or prune Gaussians to best represent the scene’s geometry. This combination of an explicit, flexible primitive with a fast, differentiable rasterizer has set a new standard for performance and quality in 3D scene reconstruction.

To harness the complementary strengths of different 3D representations, hybrid methods have emerged as a powerful paradigm. These approaches combine two or more representations, integrating the high-fidelity and continuous nature of implicit functions with the computational efficiency and explicit structure of primitives like meshes or voxels. This section reviews two influential hybrid techniques: Deep Marching Tetrahedra (DMTet) and Tri-plane.

Deep Marching Tetrahedra (DMTet) [] is an innovative hybrid technique that bridges learned implicit fields with explicit polygonal meshes. Its core concept involves using a neural network to predict an implicit representation of a shape, such as a Signed Distance Function (SDF) [] or an occupancy field. A differentiable version of the marching tetrahedra algorithm subsequently extracts a high-quality, explicit triangle mesh surface from this implicit representation.

The primary advantage of DMTet lies in its end-to-end differentiability. The entire pipeline, from the implicit field prediction to the final mesh generation, allows gradients to flow from a 2D-image-based loss function back to the 3D shape parameters. This enables direct optimization of the mesh geometry using 2D supervision, leading to highly detailed and accurate models. Furthermore, DMTet can learn to produce an adaptive mesh, allocating higher tetrahedral density to regions of fine detail, thus optimizing computational resources while maintaining high fidelity.

The Tri-plane representation [] offers an efficient, factorized approach to modeling 3D scenes and objects. Instead of encoding information in a dense 3D volume, it decomposes the 3D space into three orthogonal 2D feature planes (typically aligned with the XY, YZ, and XZ axes). This design significantly reduces the memory and computational complexity associated with 3D representations.

The working principle is to derive the feature for any 3D point by projecting it onto the three 2D planes, querying the features at the corresponding projected coordinates, and aggregating them (e.g., , through summation or concatenation). This aggregated feature vector is then fed into a small MLP to decode the final property of the point, such as its color, density, or SDF value. This “explicit-grid-plus-implicit-decoder” structure is the essence of its hybrid nature. It benefits from the efficiency of 2D grid-based feature storage, which can be processed by powerful 2D CNNs, while avoiding the prohibitive memory cost of a full 3D grid.

para.p: The 4D representations extend the 3D representations of Section into the temporal dimension, modeling not only the geometry and appearance of a scene at a single instant but also how both evolve over time. They are the substrate for tasks that involve dynamic content (moving objects, deformable bodies, fluid simulation, novel-view synthesis of casually captured videos), where a sequence of independent 3D reconstructions would either fail to maintain temporal coherence or be prohibitively expensive to recompute frame by frame.

We organize this section around five 4D representations (Figure ), each obtained by adding time to one of the 3D representations of Section : RGBD video, point clouds, meshes, neural radiance fields, and deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting. The voxel and implicit-field families of Section admit analogous time extensions but are less commonly used in the 4D literature, and we therefore omit them as standalone subsections here.
