The localization and detection panels emphasize different aspects of closely related tasks.

para.p: Figure organizes the methods by the three settings; each builds on the previous one’s representations.

Two-stream CNNs [] model appearance from RGB frames in one stream and motion from dense optical flow in another, fusing the two at the output. 3D CNNs [] convolve over space and time jointly, C3D [] and I3D [] being the standard examples, at the cost of a large parameter count that R(2+1)D [] and P3D [] reduce by factoring 3D convolution into 2D spatial and 1D temporal steps. TSN [] samples a few snippets sparsely across a long video and supervises at video level, which scales long-range temporal modeling cheaply, and Transformers [] model global spatio-temporal dependencies among sampled tokens beyond the local reach of convolution.

Early TAL ran a classifier over dense, fixed-size sliding windows, which was both slow and blind to the wide range of action durations. Structured segment networks [] instead model a proposal’s starting, ongoing, and ending stages and score its completeness, which refines boundary regression. Boundary-sensitive methods [] go further and predict start and end probabilities at every snippet, then pair high-confidence boundary points into proposals; this flexible boundary generation is the component on which later detection systems rest.

Because precise boundary annotation is expensive, weakly supervised TAL (WSTAL) [] learns from video-level labels alone. The task becomes multiple-instance learning: a video is positive if at least one segment contains the action, class activation sequences are derived from video features, and foreground segments are thresholded into proposals. Trained only with a classification loss, such models fire on the most discriminative moments rather than the whole action, so proposals are incomplete and high confidence does not imply accurate boundaries. Point-level supervision (P-TAL) [] adds one labeled frame per instance, which tends to fall near the temporally most salient, roughly central moment, and uses it to realign confidence and infer complete boundaries from that single anchor.

TAD methods differ in how they generate and score temporal proposals. Anchor-based detection [] transplants Faster R-CNN and SSD to the time axis: a dense set of multi-scale temporal anchors is classified and regressed, first in two stages (S-CNN []) and then in one (SSAD []); fixed anchors produce many redundant proposals and limit boundary precision, which anchor-free variants such as AFSD [] address by regressing boundaries from a temporal center representation. Boundary-based detection [] is bottom-up: start and end probabilities are predicted over the whole timeline and boundary matching scores every candidate pairing, which gives flexible, precise boundaries; TSA-Net [] adds multi-dilation temporal convolution for multi-scale context and BGCN [] graph convolution over co-occurring proposals. Query-based detection [] follows DETR: a small set of learned queries attends to global video features in a Transformer encoder–decoder and decodes the action set in parallel, removing anchors, NMS, and hand-designed matching at the cost of heavier computation. Across the three, anchors give dense parallel scoring but coarse boundaries, boundary methods give precise boundaries but complex matching, and query methods give the simplest end-to-end pipeline; all three keep moving toward longer-range context, continuous temporal representations, and less frame-level annotation.

Table lists the benchmarks by role. UCF101 [] and HMDB51 [] are trimmed-clip classification sets; AVA [] adds spatio-temporal boxes on movie footage. THUMOS’14 [], whose 20 classes carry dense temporal boundaries, and ActivityNet [], with 200 classes over 20K untrimmed videos, are the standard TAL and TAD benchmarks, extended in scale and granularity by HACS Segment [] and FineAction []. MultiTHUMOS [], Charades [], and TVSeries [] supply dense, multi-label, overlapping actions in sports, homes, and television; Breakfast [], 50Salads [], MPII Cooking 2 [], and COIN [] cover procedural cooking and instructional activity for segmentation and step detection; and MEVA [] (thousands of hours of surveillance) and MoVi [] (motion-captured actors) sit at the large-scale and controlled extremes.

para.p: Table shows how far the two settings have diverged. Trimmed-clip classification on UCF101 was effectively solved once Kinetics-pretrained 3D networks arrived, with I3D and R(2+1)D within a point of each other near 98%. Detection on THUMOS’14 tells a different story: mAP@0.5 moved from 19.0 (S-CNN) to 36.9 (BSN) over the anchor-to-boundary transition, jumped to 55.5 with anchor-free salient-boundary features (AFSD), and reached 70.4 with query-based decoding (DualDETR), while the best weakly supervised method (CoLA, 32.2) matches fully supervised accuracy of only a few years earlier, which quantifies what video-level labels still cost.

Fully supervised TAD depends on densely annotated boundaries, which scale poorly to long, loosely structured real-world video; weakly and semi-supervised methods relax this with video-level labels or sparse temporal cues [], at the accuracy cost the table above makes visible. Actions are also still detected in isolation. Coupling TAD with structured temporal representations such as scene graphs or event schemas [] would let a system infer boundaries, temporal relations, and higher-level activity structure jointly, which matters most in instructional video, driving, and human–robot interaction. Finally, benchmarks and detectors remain visual and closed-set, whereas real action understanding draws on audio, language, gaze, and context and must handle actions outside a fixed vocabulary []; multimodal temporal detection, where audio or language sharpens boundaries and disambiguates semantics, and open-vocabulary formulations that loosen the classification-centric setup are the directions large multimodal video corpora now make feasible.

Mapping builds a spatial representation of an unknown environment from streaming sensor observations, together with an estimate of the agent’s trajectory through it. Doing so from on-board sensors requires the agent to localize itself inside the partial map it is still building: the chicken-and-egg problem known as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). SLAM resolves it by estimating trajectory and map jointly from the same sensor stream, and observations of previously visited places supply the external references that bound the drift of purely proprioceptive odometry (IMU, wheel encoders). The result is a globally consistent spatial model that supports localization, path planning, obstacle avoidance, and exploration. Figure depicts the pipeline from sensors through front-end odometry and back-end optimization to the final map.

figure.toccaption: 6.19Example SLAM outputs: real-time visual SLAM (left), a keyframe trajectory over a sparse feature map with tracked image features in the inset, and LiDAR SLAM (right), a dense point-cloud map.

caption.text: Example SLAM outputs: real-time visual SLAM (left), a keyframe trajectory over a sparse feature map with tracked image features in the inset, and LiDAR SLAM (right), a dense point-cloud map.

para.p: The input is a stream of exteroceptive observations (camera images, RGB-D frames, LiDAR, or radar), optionally fused with proprioceptive readings (IMU, wheel odometry, velocity and steering commands) and priors such as a coarse map, an initial pose, or GPS. The output is a map plus the estimated trajectory. Maps lie on an abstraction–detail spectrum: a topological map is a graph of distinctive places and their traversable connections, with no metric layout; a sparse metric map stores registered keypoints or landmarks and the camera-pose graph that observes them, enough for accurate localization but not for geometry; and a dense metric map reconstructs a complete surface or volume (point cloud, mesh, TSDF, or occupancy grid) for obstacle avoidance and 3D reconstruction. Two dense representations have become prominent in the past three years: neural implicit maps that store geometry and appearance in network weights (an MLP in iMAP [], a voxel-grid encoder in NICE-SLAM []) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) maps that represent the scene as explicit, differentiable 3D Gaussians [].

SLAM systems are classified by the exteroceptive sensor and by the density of the map they build. LiDAR SLAM measures range directly with a stable error model; KISS-ICP [] and KISS-SLAM [] show that a minimal pipeline delivers robust real-time 3D LiDAR odometry and mapping at city scale. Visual SLAM uses monocular, stereo, or RGB-D cameras, exploiting texture for place recognition, with PTAM [] and the ORB-SLAM family [] as the foundational systems. Multi-sensor SLAM tightly fuses cameras, IMUs, and/or LiDAR (VINS-Mono, OKVIS, FAST-LIO2), and event-camera SLAM uses asynchronous per-pixel brightness changes for high-speed and high-dynamic-range operation []. By map density, sparse keypoint-and-pose-graph systems (ORB-SLAM) sit next to direct methods that minimize photometric error over semi-dense (LSD-SLAM []) or sparse (DSO []) image samples, dense geometric systems that fuse point clouds, meshes, or TSDFs (KinectFusion, ElasticFusion), neural implicit systems (iMAP [], NICE-SLAM [], Co-SLAM, NICER-SLAM), and 3DGS systems that render and optimize Gaussians jointly with poses (SplaTAM [], MonoGS [], SplatSLAM). Read historically, the field moved from feature-based geometry (PTAM, ORB-SLAM) to direct methods (LSD-SLAM, DSO), to tightly coupled multi-sensor systems (OKVIS, VINS-Mono, ORB-SLAM3), to learning-augmented pipelines (DROID-SLAM [], SuperPoint and SuperGlue matching []), to neural implicit and then 3DGS maps, and most recently to 3D geometry foundation models (DUSt3R [], MASt3R [], MASt3R-SLAM []).

figure.toccaption: 6.20SLAM module data flow. Sensor observations feed odometry and place recognition; odometry constraints and verified revisit constraints enter back-end optimization. Mapping registers raw observations using optimized poses and landmarks, producing a map and trajectory. The blue edge in the pose graph is a loop-closure constraint between previously visited poses, not an execution-loop arrow. Map representations are alternatives.

caption.text: SLAM module data flow. Sensor observations feed odometry and place recognition; odometry constraints and verified revisit constraints enter back-end optimization. Mapping registers raw observations using optimized poses and landmarks, producing a map and trajectory. The blue edge in the pose graph is a loop-closure constraint between previously visited poses, not an execution-loop arrow. Map representations are alternatives.

para.p: Whatever the sensor or map, a SLAM system runs the four modules of Figure in a loop. The front end is visual (or LiDAR) odometry, the incremental motion estimate between consecutive readings treated as a stand-alone task in §; because each pose is estimated relative to the last, its errors accumulate as drift. Back-end optimization corrects that drift globally. Modern back ends pose the problem as factor-graph optimization: robot poses and landmarks are nodes, and measurements between them (visual reprojection, IMU pre-integration, GPS, loop-closure relative poses) are factors; solving for all nodes at once yields a consistent trajectory and map, factor graphs absorb heterogeneous sensors naturally, and incremental solvers such as iSAM2 update the estimate in real time, with GTSAM, g2o, and OKVIS as representative libraries. Loop closing supplies the back end with its strongest constraints by recognizing that the agent has returned to a previously visited place, comparing current observations against the history and, on a match, adding a constraint between two temporally distant poses that pulls the accumulated drift of the intervening trajectory back into alignment. Mapping finally places the sensor data in the global frame using the optimized trajectory, in whatever representation the application needs; for neural implicit and 3DGS maps it also minimizes a rendering loss (photometric or perceptual such as LPIPS) between observed images and views rendered from the current map, optimizing geometry, appearance, and poses jointly [].

table.toccaption: 6.24Mapping and SLAM benchmarks. Scale counts sequences unless noted.

caption.text: Mapping and SLAM benchmarks. Scale counts sequences unless noted.

para.p: Table groups the benchmarks by what they stress. The classical trajectory sets are TUM RGB-D [] (handheld indoor RGB-D with motion-capture ground truth), KITTI [] (stereo and LiDAR driving), and the synthetic ICL-NUIM [] with exact ground truth, while COLD [] targets topological localization under changing conditions. Visual-inertial systems are tested on EuRoC [] (micro-aerial vehicle), TUM VI [], and OpenLORIS-Scene [], the last built for lifelong SLAM in changing indoor scenes, and Bonn RGB-D [] isolates dynamic objects. Large synthetic corpora (SceneNet [], InteriorNet [], Replica [], TartanAir []) supply photorealistic training and controlled evaluation, with Replica the standard testbed for neural implicit and 3DGS SLAM; ScanNet++ [] and ETH3D SLAM [] add laser-scanned geometry for dense reconstruction quality; and DSEC [] and CU-Multi [] extend evaluation to event cameras and multi-robot data association. AirSwarm [] is a multi-UAV research platform rather than a benchmark dataset.

Evaluation covers trajectory, map, rendering, and system cost. Trajectory accuracy uses the absolute trajectory error and relative pose error defined in §, after aligning the estimated trajectory to the ground truth by a rigid or, for monocular systems, similarity transform; RMSE is the usual summary, with mean, median, and standard deviation also reported. Dense maps are scored by accuracy (mean distance from reconstructed points to the nearest ground-truth point) and completeness (the reverse), summarized by an F-score at a distance threshold, with Chamfer distance common for neural and 3DGS maps. Neural implicit and 3DGS maps add novel-view-synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) on held-out views of the same trajectory. Memory footprint, tracking and mapping frame rates, and end-to-end latency decide embedded deployment []. Mature evaluation tools such as EVO 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://github.com/MichaelGrupp/evo and the RPG Trajectory Evaluation toolbox 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://github.com/uzh-rpg/rpg_trajectory_evaluation implement these protocols.

Deployment often violates common SLAM assumptions of static scenes, stable illumination, abundant texture, and ample computation. Dynamic objects induce correspondences that drift with their own motion; illumination change, reflective and transparent surfaces, and repetitive texture create perceptual aliasing that confuses data association and place recognition alike; and resource-constrained platforms must run ever heavier front and back ends. Current work answers each directly. Moving features are detected and excluded through semantic segmentation, motion-consistency checks, or learned masks; learned matchers (SuperPoint [], SuperGlue [], LoFTR []) replace hand-crafted descriptors and tolerate larger viewpoint and illumination changes; neural implicit and 3DGS maps are optimized jointly with poses and yield photorealistic reconstructions usable for inspection, telepresence, and policy learning; and the two-view geometry priors of DUSt3R [] and MASt3R [] remove the fragile hand-engineered front end, already enabling real-time dense monocular SLAM at the robustness of MASt3R-SLAM [].

Two broader shifts follow. Lifelong SLAM aims at months of continuous operation by combining relocalization, map update, and place re-identification against changing environments, and is now an evaluation track of its own; collaborative multi-agent SLAM fuses observations across robots for faster coverage and graceful degradation, increasingly together with event cameras and heterogeneous sensors for high-speed, low-light, and high-dynamic-range conditions. What remains open is concrete: 3DGS maps still do not scale to city-level memory and rendering budgets, learned components carry a sim-to-real gap, and incorrect loop closures under strong perceptual aliasing are still the failure that breaks every back end.

Most of what precedes has described a single instant. Spatio-temporal perception adds the missing axis, asking not only where entities are but how they move, when events happen, and which identities persist. Its three concerns rise from the pixel through the object to the event: scene flow recovers dense, per-point motion between frames; object tracking maintains the identity of an entity as it moves through space and time; and temporal localization fixes when an action or event occurs along a sequence. Together they give the largely static perception of the preceding sections a temporal thread, the continuity on which motion understanding and long-horizon perception depend.

Scene flow is the dense three-dimensional motion of every visible surface point between two instants: optical flow lifted out of the image plane and joined to the change in depth. The image-based pipelines surveyed here take stereo video, monocular video, or a multi-view sequence and produce per-pixel 3D motion; some refinement modules additionally consume estimated or measured depth. Dynamic scene reconstruction [], motion-aware rendering [], physical interaction modeling [], and egocentric world understanding [] all consume it.

The columns illustrate distinct mechanisms rather than successive stages of one pipeline.

para.p: Methods differ along two axes: what they observe (stereo, the classical and still dominant setting; monocular video, the self-supervised frontier; multi-view rigs) and what supervises them (synthetic ground truth, photometric and geometric consistency, or view synthesis). Figure groups them into five families along these axes.

RAFT [] introduced all-pairs correlation volumes with GRU-based iterative updates for 2D optical flow; RAFT-3D [] uses image and depth pairs to iteratively refine a per-pixel SE(3) field with rigid-motion embeddings. Depth can be obtained from stereo or RGB-D input; it is an input to the refinement rather than necessarily inferred jointly from appearance. Its scene-flow results are included in Table .

Mono-SF [] was the first monocular entry on KITTI Scene Flow, resolving scale with a learned single-view depth prior. Self-Mono-SF [] jointly predicts disparity and scene flow with a single decoder, using unlabeled stereo video during training and monocular image pairs at test time; stereo geometry provides the scale cue, while photometric and 3D consistency losses provide self-supervision. A separate test-time optimization approach for LiDAR point clouds (Neural Scene Flow Prior []) lies outside the image-based scope of this subsection.

A parallel line never targets scene flow as output but obtains a dense 4D motion field as a byproduct of dynamic view synthesis. Neural Scene Flow Fields [] trains a dynamic NeRF together with an explicit scene-flow MLP; D-NeRF [] represents motion as a deformation field into a canonical frame; Nerfies [] extends this to casually captured monocular video; and 4D Gaussian Splatting [] attaches time-parameterized motion to explicit Gaussian primitives. These methods are evaluated by rendering quality rather than by motion error, a split returned to under Challenges below.

Table lists the image-based benchmarks. Synthetic sets provide dense, exact ground truth at scale (FlyingThings3D as the standard pretraining corpus; Sintel and Spring for film-grade motion, with Spring at HD resolution and super-resolved ground truth; TartanAir for environment diversity), while KITTI Scene Flow 2015 [], built on the KITTI suite [], is the only real-world benchmark and carries sparse LiDAR-derived labels on 200 training and 200 test scenes. LiDAR-based scene-flow splits of nuScenes [], Waymo Open [], and Argoverse 2 [], and the event-camera flow of DSEC [], serve the point-cloud and event communities and are not image-based benchmarks in the sense used here.

para.p: The supervision landscape is lopsided. Every dense-ground-truth benchmark in Table is synthetic and stereo, so monocular methods are scored only against KITTI’s sparse labels, and models pretrained on FlyingThings3D or Sintel still lose accuracy on real driving footage after fine-tuning, most visibly on foreground motion where synthetic random-object trajectories differ from vehicle kinematics. All current benchmarks also emphasize rigid or random-object motion; dense ground truth for non-rigid humans, hands, and animals does not exist at scale, which leaves the family of implicit-field methods that handle such motion best without a quantitative yardstick.

That yardstick problem is the second challenge. Explicit-output methods [] are scored by KITTI’s outlier rates; implicit-field methods [] by PSNR and LPIPS of rendered views. No protocol evaluates both on the same input, so the two paradigms are compared only qualitatively, and whether a motion field is good depends on whether scene flow is the end (the KITTI leaderboard) or a means (reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, physical reasoning). The cost profiles diverge as well: RAFT-3D needs several GRU iterations per frame, variational methods minutes per frame, and implicit fields minutes to hours per scene.

Foundation priors are reshaping the monocular line. Depth Anything [] and DINOv2 [] supply the per-pixel depth and semantic features that Self-Mono-SF had to learn from scratch, and SAM 2 [] segmentation together with the object-pose estimators of Section makes an object-centric formulation (a per-object SE(3) trajectory plus residual non-rigid motion) practical, a bridge to the tracking problem of Section . As implicit-field scene flow merges into 4D reconstruction, with 4D Gaussian Splatting [] the early example, evaluation is likely to follow the downstream task rather than the KITTI leaderboard.

Tracking localizes entities in every frame and associates the detections across frames so that each entity keeps one identity through the sequence. Where detection and segmentation describe a single instant, tracking yields trajectories, the representation that autonomous driving [], surveillance [], AR/VR [], and robotics [] build on.

The variants, illustrated in Figure , differ in how the targets are specified and what state is tracked. Single object tracking (SOT) [] follows one target given its first-frame box; multiple object tracking (MOT) [] tracks every instance of given categories, typically pedestrians and vehicles, under identity constraints; MOTS [] and video object segmentation replace boxes with masks; 3D-MOT [] outputs world-coordinate 3D boxes from LiDAR, RGB-D, or multi-view input; pose tracking [] and landmark tracking [] follow skeletal joints or facial keypoints; and panoptic tracking combines pixel-level semantic classes for stuff with temporally consistent instance identities for things. Category-specific trackers for pedestrians [], vehicles [], or animals [] specialize any of these.

Figure organizes the methods into four families around image-plane box and mask tracking (SOT, MOT, MOTS, VOS). Pose, landmark, and panoptic tracking reuse the same propagate-or-associate machinery with a different state representation and are covered at the benchmark level in Table .

Because a target moves little between consecutive frames, its previous state is a strong prior for the current one, and the oldest tracking paradigm exploits this by predicting the next state from the current one and correcting it against the new frame. Correlation filters realize this in the frequency domain: MOSSE [] learns a minimum-output-sum-of-squared-error filter from a single frame and updates it online at hundreds of frames per second; KCF [] and MKCF [] add kernelization and multiple-kernel learning, respectively; ECO [] adds factorized convolution operators, a compact generative sample model, and conservative updates. These trackers are fast enough for embedded use but drift under large appearance change and clutter. MDNet [] answered with online discriminative learning, a shared CNN with per-sequence domain branches that separate target from background, at a high per-frame cost. Siamese trackers moved the representation learning offline: SiamFC [] correlates a template embedding with the search-region embedding in one forward pass, and SiamRPN [], ATOM [], and DiMP [] add region-proposal regression, IoU-prediction refinement, and a discriminatively learned prediction head. Transformer trackers then replaced correlation with attention: TransT [] fuses template and search features with self- and cross-attention, STARK [] predicts the box with an encoder–decoder that also carries temporal state, and OSTrack [] joins feature extraction and relation modeling in a single stream over concatenated template and search tokens, the current baseline design.

Mask propagation applies the same idea at the pixel level for video object segmentation [], with memory of past frames replacing a single template. XMem [] keeps multi-scale spatiotemporal memories that remain stable over videos of more than 10,000 frames; AOT [] and DeAOT [] encode object identities as tokens so that many objects propagate in one pass; and SAM 2 [] adds a streaming memory to the Segment Anything Model [], giving promptable tracking that transfers across VOS benchmarks.

figure.toccaption: 6.23Four method families for object tracking: (i) propagation-based, (ii) detect-then-associate, (iii) joint detection–association, and (iv) universal models with a shared backbone and task heads for SOT, MOT, VOS, and MOTS.

caption.text: Four method families for object tracking: (i) propagation-based, (ii) detect-then-associate, (iii) joint detection–association, and (iv) universal models with a shared backbone and task heads for SOT, MOT, VOS, and MOTS.

para.p: The MOT standard pipeline detects objects in every frame and then solves an assignment problem between detections and existing tracks. SORT [] predicts track positions with a Kalman filter [] and matches by IoU with the Hungarian algorithm []; DeepSORT [] adds an appearance embedding so that tracks survive occlusion. Track-RCNN [], JDE [], and FairMOT [] train the re-identification embedding jointly with the detector; association remains a separate step, which keeps them in this family. All of these discard low-confidence detections, and since occluded targets are exactly those with low scores, trajectories fragment where they are hardest to keep. ByteTrack [] associates nearly every detection and uses motion similarity to the existing tracks to reject the false positives among the low-score boxes, a change in association alone that raised MOT17 HOTA by several points (Table ). In 3D, the same pipeline reappears: AB3DMOT [] runs a 3D Kalman filter with Hungarian matching on LiDAR detections, and CenterPoint [] tracks 3D object centers through predicted velocities, with nuScenes [] using AMOTA/AMOTP and Waymo [] using MOTA/MOTP.

End-to-end trackers fold association into the detector. CenterTrack [] represents objects as center points and regresses their offset to the previous frame, so that association is a local lookup; TrackFormer [] introduces tracking-by-attention, in which track queries carried from the previous frame and new object queries are decoded jointly by a Transformer; MOTR [] extends DETR [] with track queries that persist across the whole sequence and are supervised with a sequence-level loss, which is what gives it its advantage on DanceTrack [], where appearance is uninformative and motion is non-linear. The price is training cost and data: these models need long annotated sequences and remain behind detect-then-associate trackers on MOT17 (Table ).

A single model for SOT, MOT, VOS, and MOTS is the most recent direction. UniTrack [] showed that one self-supervised appearance representation serves propagation and association tasks alike; Unicorn [] trains one network end to end for all four tasks; UTT [] unifies SOT and MOT in a Transformer; UniVS [] casts every video-segmentation task as prompt-driven segmentation; and OneTracker [] adapts a foundation tracker to RGB, depth, thermal, and event inputs with light adapters. In practice, SAM [] combined with a memory tracker (XMem, DeAOT) already provides promptable multi-object segmentation and tracking from points, boxes, scribbles, or text, and methods such as UASTrack [] and Un-Track [] extend unified tracking to RGB paired with depth, thermal, or event inputs. Language enters as a specification signal as well: LaSOT [] pairs every sequence with a sentence, TNL2K [] is built for text-initialized tracking, and LaMOT [] brings language-guided specification to the multi-object setting.

para.p: Table groups the benchmarks by what is tracked. The SOT line runs from short, category-agnostic clips (OTB100, TC128, the VOT challenges) to large, long-term, category-diverse training sets (TrackingNet, LaSOT, GOT-10k, whose test classes are disjoint from training) and to condition-specific tests for aerial footage (UAV123), high frame rate (NFS), and language initialization (TNL2K). MOT benchmarks are pedestrian-only in MOT16/17 and MOT20 and multi-class driving footage in BDD100K; the 3D-MOT counterparts are the nuScenes and Waymo tracking tasks. DAVIS and YouTube-VOS supply mask-level ground truth, the latter with categories unseen at training time; the RGB-D sets add depth and have grown from tens of sequences (PTB, STC) to over a thousand (RGBD1K); and pose tracking moved from single-person upper-body clips (VideoPose2.0, Poses in the Wild, ICDPose) to multi-person full-body sequences with person identities (PoseTrack18, CMU Panoptic).

para.p: Identity under occlusion remains the central failure. Motion models and appearance embeddings bridge short occlusions, but long occlusions and dense crowds still produce identity switches and fragmented tracks [], and memory-based propagation drifts or forgets over long videos even when each step is accurate []. HOTA and IDF1 measure the outcome but not robustness to occlusion length or the calibration of track confidence, so the metrics reward the easy part of the problem.

Trackers are also tuned to a few curated benchmarks and transfer poorly to UAV footage, thermal and event imagery, adverse weather, and multi-camera surveillance; foundation-model trackers such as OneTracker [] and the RGB-X methods UASTrack [] and Un-Track [] address this directly but inherit the biases of their pretrained backbones. Long streams add memory and compute limits on top of drift.

The accuracy of Transformer trackers comes at a cost that keeps them off embedded hardware, while the lightweight correlation-filter line gives up robustness; and the unified models that would amortize that cost across tasks meet negative transfer between objectives with different demands, mask precision against identity association in particular []. Language and segmentation priors widen what a tracker can be asked to do, at the price of prompt sensitivity that current benchmarks do not measure.

Temporal localization answers when something happens in a long, untrimmed video. The condition can be a category from a closed set, which gives temporal action localization (TAL) as treated in Section , or a free-form sentence, which gives temporal sentence grounding (TSG): return the segment that best matches “the person opens the microwave”. This subsection sets the two side by side, with the weight on the text-conditioned problem, which turns localization from exhaustive detection into retrieval and is what video search and interactive navigation [] rely on.

Both are studied under several settings, which Figure lays side by side. Offline methods see the whole video; online methods infer causally over the streamed prefix and are judged on low-latency detection of action starts []. Supervision ranges from frame-accurate boundaries to video-level labels only (weakly supervised TAL via multiple-instance learning, Section ; weakly supervised TSG by aligning the two modalities during training []), with self-supervised video pretraining [] and open-vocabulary or zero-shot variants [] reducing the labeled data needed. TSG additionally varies in scope, from a single video [] to corpus-level retrieval that first finds the video and then the moment (VCMR) [], and in output, with QVHighlights [] asking for a saliency ranking of highlight clips alongside the grounded moment.

para.p: Figure traces both tasks along the same path from hand-designed pipelines to end-to-end Transformers.

The TAL row is the detection lineage of Section : sliding windows over hand-crafted features such as improved dense trajectories [], then two-stage proposal-plus-classification systems (R-C3D [], SSN [], TAL-Net []) with dedicated boundary-sensitive proposal generators (BSN [], BMN [], G-TAD []), then anchor-free dense detectors and query-based set prediction. Three developments go beyond that treatment. Dense single-stage detectors were scaled by ActionFormer [], a multi-scale Transformer encoder over the feature pyramid, and TriDet [], which replaces self-attention with a convolutional scalable-granularity-perception module and a trident boundary head; both still regress boundaries at every position and rely on non-maximum suppression. DETR-style set prediction removes anchors and suppression: RTD-Net [] applies a relaxed Transformer decoder to proposal generation and TadTR [] decodes the full action set end to end []. And masked video pretraining [] now supplies the backbones that these heads are fine-tuned on.

TSG began with cross-modal matching. CTRL [] embeds the sentence and candidate clips in a shared space and ranks clips, with boundary regression on top; MCN [] does the same for DiDeMo with global video context. Later models reason over the candidates jointly: MAN [] refines moments iteratively through a graph over proposals, 2D-TAN [] scores every (start, end) pair on a two-dimensional temporal-adjacency map so that neighboring candidates inform each other, and VSLNet [] drops proposals altogether and predicts the start and end positions as span extraction, in analogy to reading comprehension. Moment-DETR [] brought set prediction to grounding, decoding moments and saliency scores directly from an encoder–decoder, while TVR [] extended grounding to corpus scale with a coarse-to-fine search over subtitles and frames.

Table lists the benchmarks; the TAL rows are those of Section , retained for comparison. The TSG benchmarks move from a closed domain (TACoS [], cooking) to open-domain sentences over indoor activity (Charades-STA []), Flickr videos with multiple references per query (DiDeMo []), and dense paragraph-level captions (ActivityNet Captions []); YouCook2 [] adds procedural structure, TVR [] multimodal (subtitle) context and corpus-level retrieval, and QVHighlights [] saliency labels for joint highlight detection.

para.p: Boundaries are soft. Actions span sub-second gestures to multi-minute activities, which no single temporal resolution serves, and annotators disagree about where an instance starts and ends; a sentence adds its own ambiguity about which part of an activity it describes. The tIoU-thresholded metrics treat these fuzzy boundaries as exact, so part of the measured error is irreducible [], and probabilistic boundary modeling with calibrated confidences is the natural response.

The two tasks are converging. A closed label set limits TAL, while TSG is bounded by the vocabulary of its query sets; text prompts in place of class labels [] and set prediction for moments [] point to a single architecture that grounds both categories and sentences. Doing this over minutes of video, across camera viewpoints (egocentric footage in particular), with audio, narration, or noisy subtitles as further evidence [], and causally for streaming use [] is where the current systems fall short: memory-efficient long-context encoders and corpus-scale coarse-to-fine retrieval are the two ingredients most actively developed.

The preceding sections perceive space largely through vision. Yet vision alone is often incomplete: it is blind past occluders, silent about what lies outside the frame, and mute on which entity a person actually means. Multimodal spatial perception closes these gaps by grounding spatial understanding in signals beyond the image. The section takes two complementary couplings: audio-visual spatial localization, which uses sound to place events that vision may miss, and vision-language grounding, which ties linguistic reference to the specific entity or region it denotes. Neither adds a new spatial primitive; each supplies a channel of evidence that makes perception more complete where a single modality falls short.

Humans localize a sound by combining auditory cues (interaural level and time differences, spectral shaping) with visual context (lip motion, object dynamics) []. Audio-visual spatial localization (AV-SL) asks a machine to do the same: find the pixel region, object, or 3D point that a sound comes from, under reverberation, noise, occlusion, and several simultaneous sources []. The two modalities are complementary. Binaural or array audio supplies directional cues, while distance requires additional geometric, near-field, or learned evidence; vision says which entities are plausible sounders and separates acoustically confusable ones (two similar instruments, only one playing). Spatial audio for AR/VR [], teleconferencing [], and audio-guided navigation [] are the main consumers.

The input is an audio stream
A
(mono, binaural, or multichannel, optionally ambisonic []) time-aligned with a video
V
(RGB, depth, or multi-view) of the same interval; the audio may contain zero, one, or several sources, and the video may show silent objects that look like sounders. The output localizes the sounding entity in a form that depends on the variant: a 2D heatmap or mask, a face or body box with a speaking state, an event class with its temporal extent and direction of arrival (DOA, azimuth and elevation) and optionally distance [], a 2D location with depth, or a 3D point or trajectory in camera or world coordinates. For visible-region localization, off-screen sources or audio with no visible source should yield a null prediction; 3D acoustic localization may still estimate an off-screen source.

Five variants are in common use. Visual sound source localization (VSSL) highlights the sounding region of a frame or clip as a class-agnostic heatmap, in single- and multi-source settings and increasingly with negative or off-screen audio as a robustness test. Active speaker detection (ASD) decides who is speaking and localizes the talker as a face track, often under streaming constraints []. Audio-visual sound event localization and detection (AV-SELD) couples what and when with where: event class, temporal extent, DOA, and in recent benchmarks distance []. The 2.5D variant adds depth or range to a 2D localization from monocular depth [], stereo, or echoes []; and 3D DOA estimation returns a spatial bearing, whereas source-position or trajectory estimation additionally uses range or triangulation constraints from calibrated cameras, arrays, or egocentric rigs [].
Figure maps the five variants onto four method families.

para.p:
VSSL is learned almost entirely without location labels, from the co-occurrence of sound and image. An audio encoder maps the clip to an embedding
a
, a visual encoder maps the frame to a feature map
⁢ v
( x )
, and the localization map is the per-position similarity

Math.text: S * x = (a ^ top * v * x) / (norm@(a) * norm@(v * x))

para.p: trained so that matching audio-image pairs score higher than mismatched ones []; Sound of Pixels [] instead mixes two clips and asks the network to separate them conditioned on pixel features, which forces the same alignment. Later work targets the failure modes of co-occurrence. LVS [] mines hard negatives inside the same image (regions that look like sounders but do not match the audio) and introduces the VGG-SS localization benchmark; deep multimodal clustering [] and coarse-to-fine mixture objectives [] handle several sources at once; and SLAVC [] shows that earlier methods depend on early stopping and adds momentum encoders and extreme visual dropout so that the alignment does not collapse onto background.

ASD runs a face detector and tracker and then decides, per track and per frame, whether the visible mouth produced the audio. The decision rests on audio-visual synchrony: a visual encoder over the lip region and an audio encoder over the spectrogram are compared across time [], and TalkNet [] adds long-term temporal modeling of both streams with cross-attention, which is what separates a brief pause from a non-speaker. Active Speakers in Context [] scores each candidate jointly with the other faces in the frame, and ASDNet [] makes the three stages explicit (per-frame audio-visual encoding, inter-speaker relation modeling, temporal modeling), with each stage trained for its role.

SELDnet [] set the template: a convolutional recurrent network over multichannel spectrogram features with two heads, one classifying active events per frame and one regressing their DOA. ACCDOA [] folds the two into one output, a vector per class whose direction is the DOA and whose length is the activity, which removes the need to balance two losses; the DCASE challenge tracks [] standardized the protocol, and STARSS23 [] added video and source distance.

Lifting a 2D localization to metric space uses geometry rather than learned correspondence alone. VisualEchoes [] shows that echoes of an emitted chirp carry depth: the time and spectrum of the return, fused with the image, improve monocular depth estimation and give the 2.5D variant its range. Audio-visual spatial alignment [] learns representations by predicting whether 360∘ video and ambisonic audio are spatially consistent, a pretext that encodes direction, and self-supervised spatial audio generation [] learns the inverse mapping from 360∘ video to ambisonics. Full 3D systems combine classical array processing (time differences of arrival from GCC-PHAT [], steered-response-power beamforming []) with calibrated cameras and triangulation, and in simulation (SoundSpaces []) with the agent’s own motion.
Table pairs each variant with its benchmarks and metrics; there is no shared benchmark across variants because their outputs differ.

caption.text: AV-SL task variants with representative datasets, outputs, and metrics. Newer VSSL test suites add negative or off-screen audio to measure robustness.

p.text: F-score, error rate, DOA error, distance error

para.p: VSSL is scored by thresholding the localization map and computing consensus intersection over union (cIoU) against the annotations; reported metrics include the fraction of test images with cIoU above 0.5 (localization accuracy) and the area under the IoU-threshold curve (AUC) []; the extended VGG-SS and Flickr protocols add clips whose audio has no visible source and report detection-style average precision requiring both visible-source presence and correct localization []. ASD uses detection-style mAP over face tracks with speaking labels []. SELD combines detection (F-score, error rate) with localization (DOA error, localization recall) [], while STARSS23 additionally provides source-distance annotations []; 2.5D inherits the depth metrics of Section , and 3D settings report angular and positional error.

Table collects the two variants with a stable leaderboard. On VSSL the negative-audio protocol changes the ranking: LVS leads the earlier methods on the standard Flickr test but drops to 9.8 AP when silent clips are mixed in, whereas SLAVC holds both. ASD on AVA-ActiveSpeaker has moved from 79.2 mAP for the dataset baseline to above 93 with explicit temporal and inter-speaker modeling, and the remaining differences among top systems are about latency and streaming rather than accuracy. AV-SELD has no such table: each DCASE edition changes the data and the metric, and distance-aware evaluation is not directly comparable to the DOA-only tracks that SELDnet and ACCDOA were evaluated on.

ASD: mAP (%) on AVA-ActiveSpeaker val, from the TalkNet [] and ASDNet [] papers.

caption.text: Visual sound source localization and active speaker detection. VSSL: cIoU (%) on the Flickr-SoundNet and VGG-SS test sets, and AP (%) on their extended versions with negative audio, all models trained on VGG-Sound 144k, as reported in the SLAVC comparison []. ASD: mAP (%) on AVA-ActiveSpeaker val, from the TalkNet [] and ASDNet [] papers.

para.p: Co-occurrence is not causation. A model that has learned which objects usually make which sounds will localize a guitar whether or not it is playing, and the negative-audio protocols [] exist because the standard tests rewarded exactly this; the open problem is grounding on the acoustic evidence itself, which matters most for off-screen and silent cases where the right answer is no localization.

Going from 2D saliency to metric 3D requires semantics and geometry together. Depth foundation models [] (Section ) and self-supervised visual features [] now supply priors that AV-SL pipelines previously learned from scratch, and STARSS23 [] provides joint event, time, DOA, and distance annotations, supporting distance-aware extensions; multi-object objectives for overlapping events are the current frontier there.

Multiple simultaneous sources, identity through occlusion, and on-screen/off-screen transitions over long videos [] are the AV-SL form of the identity problem of Section and the pose-continuity problem of Section . Streaming use adds causal encoders, low-latency fusion, calibration drift, and graceful fallback when one modality is missing [].

Vision-language grounding ties a linguistic reference to the element of a scene it denotes. Given “Put your hand on the small mug on the right side of the table behind the blue book”, a grounded system must resolve the noun phrase, its attributes, and its spatial relations to one particular mug in the image; this referential link is what instruction following, multimodal dialogue, and human-robot interaction build on.

Q

⁢ R

r

figure.toccaption: 6.27Vision-language grounding task variants: (i) REC / RES []; (ii) generalized REC / RES with zero, one, or multiple targets []; (iii) reasoning grounding []; (iv) video referring and reasoning grounding []; (v) 3D and embodied grounding [].

caption.text: Vision-language grounding task variants: (i) REC / RES []; (ii) generalized REC / RES with zero, one, or multiple targets []; (iii) reasoning grounding []; (iv) video referring and reasoning grounding []; (v) 3D and embodied grounding [].

para.p: Figure lays out the five variants, which differ in scene modality, output granularity, and query complexity.

Referring expression comprehension and segmentation (REC / RES). One image, one expression, one target, returned as a box (REC) or a mask (RES). RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ [] (short phrases, the latter without location words) and RefCOCOg [] (longer descriptions), all using MS COCO [] images, with expressions collected through ReferItGame [] or Mechanical Turk, have been the standard benchmarks for a decade; Flickr30k Entities [] grounds every entity mention of a caption at once.

Generalized REC / RES (GREC / GRES). An expression may match zero, one, or several objects (“the red carrots” versus “the unicorn”), which single-target methods cannot represent. gRefCOCO [], Ref-ZOM [], PhraseCut [], and OmniLabel [] evaluate this setting, and MaskGroups-HQ [] generalizes the prompt itself to arbitrary groups of masks specified by text and reference masks. The output is a set, so the metric must be as well (see Datasets and Metrics below).

Reasoning grounding. Some queries require inference beyond noun matching: “the loser” needs a judgment about the people shown, “turn on the TV” needs the remote. CLEVR-Ref+ [] diagnoses this on rendered scenes with ground-truth reasoning programs; ReasonSeg [] poses implicit, multi-step queries on real images with mask output, extended by MMR [] (194K implicit queries, multi-target and part-level), ReasonSeg-Inst [] (instance level), and MC-Bench [] (instances across image pairs). Ref-Adv [] keeps the classic REC format but makes expressions minimally sufficient, negation-heavy, and paired with same-category distractors.

Video referring and reasoning grounding. The referent must be found in every frame through motion, appearance change, and occlusion, and the query may name it by what it does (“the man waving his hand”). Refer-Youtube-VOS [], Refer-DAVIS17 [], A2D- and JHMDB-Sentences [], MeViS [], ReVOS [], and ReasonVOS [] add language to existing segmentation and actor-action datasets; Ref-VPS [] extends the referent from objects to processes such as smoke spreading or waves breaking, which have no object boundary at all. Tracking machinery is usually folded in to carry identity across frames [].

3D and embodied grounding. The scene is a point cloud or a set of views, and the query refers to an object in 3D (“the chair next to the window”). ScanRefer [] requires detecting the referent as a 3D box and Multi3DRefer [] allows zero to many targets; ReferIt3D [] provides the object instances and scores selection among them; Instruct3D [] and Multi3DRes [] ask for point-level masks from instruction-style queries. Embodied grounding makes the output an action: an agent told “go pick up the red cup on the right” must identify the cup and reach it [].

figure.toccaption: 6.28Vision-language grounding method families: (i) proposal ranking, (ii) compositional reasoning, (iii) end-to-end grounding, (iv) grounded pre-training, (v) foundation models, and (vi) tool-augmented agents. Panels (i)-(iv) correspond to families (A)-(D) in the text, (v) to (E)-(F), and (vi) to (G); family (H), generation for grounding, is not depicted.

caption.text: Vision-language grounding method families: (i) proposal ranking, (ii) compositional reasoning, (iii) end-to-end grounding, (iv) grounded pre-training, (v) foundation models, and (vi) tool-augmented agents. Panels (i)-(iv) correspond to families (A)-(D) in the text, (v) to (E)-(F), and (vi) to (G); family (H), generation for grounding, is not depicted.

para.p: The methods below fall into eight families, (A) to (H); Figure illustrates (A) through (G). They are trajectories rather than eras: the oldest paradigm has resurfaced at foundation-model scale.

The first grounding models instantiate the ranking form of Eq. (): detect region proposals, embed them and the query in a joint space, and pick the best-scoring region. Deep Fragment Embeddings [] aligned sentence fragments with detected regions, and scene-graph CRFs [] grounded structured queries to regions for retrieval. Proposal quality bounded these methods and context-dependent expressions defeated them. The same two-stage shape has returned with far stronger proposals: RAS [] has a segmentation foundation model propose candidate masks and a mask-centric multimodal LLM select the group that satisfies the prompt, and this non-autoregressive selection beats mask generation in both accuracy and latency.

Modular networks parse the expression and route its parts to dedicated modules. CMN [] decomposes an expression into a subject–relationship–object triplet handled by localization and relationship modules; MAttNet [] soft-parses phrases into appearance, location, and relationship attention modules; dynamic graph attention [] reasons over the linguistic structure on a scene graph. These models disambiguate compositional queries (“the man behind the woman in red”) but inherit every parsing error.

The regression form of Eq. () removes proposals: a single network fuses the sentence embedding with the image feature map and predicts the box. One-Stage Grounding [] did this with a detector head, TransVG [] with a pure Transformer in which a learnable token attends over visual and textual tokens and regresses coordinates. On the segmentation side, CRIS [] transfers CLIP’s image-text alignment to the pixel level with text-to-pixel contrastive learning and made end-to-end RES the standard formulation.

Phrase-region alignment learned at scale turned grounding into an open-vocabulary capability. MDETR [] trains a DETR-style set predictor on text-aligned detection corpora so that every box is tied to a span of the caption; GLIP [] reformulates detection as phrase grounding and scales to 27M region-caption pairs, giving zero-shot transfer; RegionCLIP [] adds region-level contrastive alignment, and Grounding DINO [] deep language fusion at every stage of a DINO detector, which made it the default open-vocabulary detector of later tool chains (family (G)). The residual weakness is the entity shortcut: models latch onto object names and ignore the description. DesCo [] counters it in the data, pre-training on LLM-generated rich descriptions with context-sensitive negative queries, which raises description-conditioned detection on LVIS and OmniLabel.

The first multimodal LLMs built for grounding gave the language backbone a region interface. Kosmos-2 [] emits location tokens that hyperlink phrases to boxes inside the generated text; Ferret [] and Ferret-v2 [] encode boxes, points, and free-form regions as inputs at any resolution. Mask output comes from attaching a decoder: LISA [] decodes a dedicated segmentation token’s embedding into a mask, which is what makes reasoning segmentation possible, and LISA++ [] extends it to instances within a dialogue; GLaMM [] unifies phrase grounding, referring segmentation, and free-form conversation under a grounded-conversation objective; Sa2VA [] couples a LLaVA-style backbone to SAM 2 [] and carries dense grounding from images to video referring segmentation. Moondream 3’s segmentation extension [] dispenses with the decoder and writes the mask autoregressively as a vector path, refined by a lightweight head and trained with reinforcement learning on mask overlap.

A parallel line keeps no grounding component at all: the model writes coordinates as plain text, and grounding is one capability among many. Florence-2 [] is the compact case, a sequence-to-sequence model trained on the 5.4B-annotation FLD-5B corpus that casts captioning, detection, grounding, and polygon-vertex segmentation into one text interface, with mask accuracy below the decoder-based models of family (E). The frontier generalists, Gemini [], Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL [], InternVL 2.5 and InternVL 3 [], and Seed1.5-VL [], now match or exceed the specialists on the RefCOCO family from prompting alone (Table ); Llama 3 [] folds phrase-to-box and phrase-to-mask annotations into its multimodal pre-training but reports no REC numbers.

A third line delegates localization to specialist models under an outer control loop, which has moved from fixed pipelines to generated programs to learned tool use. Grounded SAM [] chains Grounding DINO boxes into SAM [] masks without training; ViperGPT [] has a code LLM write a Python program that calls perception APIs, so that logic and arithmetic are symbolic and perception is delegated, with interpretable intermediate steps. SegAgent [] treats mask annotation as a sequential decision process, imitating the click sequences of human annotators on an interactive segmenter; DeepEyes [] internalizes the tool, using reinforcement learning to make the model emit coordinates that trigger zoom-in crops inside its own chain of thought. SAM 3 Agent [] wraps SAM 3, whose concept prompts return every instance matching a noun phrase, with an MLLM that proposes phrases, inspects the returned masks, and selects those satisfying the full expression, which gives zero-shot referring and reasoning segmentation without grounding-specific training.

The newest family treats a large text-to-image or text-to-video generator as a grounding model, on the premise that generative pre-training already induces a fine-grained map from language to spatial and temporal structure. VD-IT [] uses a frozen text-to-video diffusion model as the feature extractor for referring video segmentation and finds its features more temporally consistent and better aligned with language than discriminative video backbones; ReferEverything [] keeps the generator intact and fine-tunes it to predict mask latents decoded by the frozen VAE, which transfers zero-shot to rare objects, “stuff”, and the amorphous processes of Ref-VPS. Vision Banana [] instruction-tunes a state-of-the-art image generator to render the task output as an image, segmentation as painting the referred region a prescribed color, and matches specialist systems zero-shot while keeping its generative ability. Grounding quality in this family rises with the underlying generator.

Table lists the benchmarks by variant. Annotation cost rises steeply from a 2D box to a per-frame mask to a 3D box, so image-level REC/RES corpora dominate in size and maturity, video referring sets are an order of magnitude smaller, and 3D corpora smaller still. Within the image benchmarks a generational split has opened. RefCOCO/+/g now serve mainly as training corpora: specialists and generalist MLLMs report Acc@0.5 above 90% on them, an audit found label errors in 14%, 24%, and 5% of RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg [], and much of the score survives shuffling the word order of the expression []. The evaluation-oriented replacements are built to expose what saturation hides: Ref-L4 [] (cleaned labels, long expressions, a 365-category vocabulary), Ref-Adv [] (shortcut-suppressed, where the same models fall to roughly 60%), HC-RefLoCo [], GigaGrounding [], and GroundingME [], which scores discrimination, spatial reasoning, limited visibility, and the rejection of ungroundable queries, and on which the best model resolves 45% of samples while most score zero on rejection.

Table reports the two variants on which the families can be compared. On REC the step from proposal ranking and modular reasoning (MAttNet) to end-to-end regression (TransVG) and then to grounded pre-training (MDETR, Grounding DINO) is about 14 points of RefCOCO Acc@0.5, and the generalist MLLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL 2.5) sit at or above the best specialist without benchmark-specific training. On RES the grounding MLLMs with a mask decoder have passed the end-to-end specialists (CRIS to Sa2VA is eleven cIoU points on RefCOCO), and Sa2VA’s video columns show the same model carrying over to referring video segmentation; on ReasonSeg, LISA-7B reaches 52.9 gIoU after fine-tuning where open-vocabulary segmenters stay below 30 []. The tool-augmented and generative families are evaluated zero-shot on subsets of these benchmarks and are not directly comparable here. What the table cannot show is cross-variant breadth: methods strong on image REC routinely degrade on video, reasoning, and 3D grounding, and no single architecture leads all five variants.

para.p: Ambiguity and interaction. “The guy on the right” depends on the viewpoint, and “the red cup” presumes one salient red cup. People resolve this through shared context or a follow-up question; grounding models make an arbitrary choice or fall back on a dataset bias such as the largest instance. Recognizing that an expression matches several entities, abstaining under uncertainty, and asking for clarification are outside almost every current benchmark, which is one-shot (one query, one image), while real use is a dialogue with memory of what was grounded before.

Reasoning and commonsense. “The tool needed to open the box” cannot be resolved from the image alone, and adversarial evaluation shows that much of current REC accuracy rests on shortcut matching rather than reasoning []. LLM-based models carry the knowledge but may answer “a key” when none is visible, and vision-only models lack it entirely; reasoning-driven segmentation [] and agentic active perception [] are the two bridges. Video adds temporal and causal structure (“the man who picks up the phone and then leaves”, “the car that caused the accident”) that current video grounding, which attends mostly to appearance and simple motion, does not capture.

Open world and 3D. Open-vocabulary detectors and CLIP-based models have blind spots on rare objects, fine-grained distinctions (viola versus violin), proper nouns, and figurative references (“the blue crown” for a cap), and per-category analyses of large multimodal models show a strong bias toward common training categories []. Description-conditioned pre-training [] and generative pre-training [] are the routes to long-tail coverage that do not require labeling it. Functional references (“the driver’s seat”) also imply spatial context that only 3D understanding resolves, and the 3D-language work surveyed above [] will grow with augmented reality and robotics.

Efficiency and evaluation. The strongest systems are multi-model tool chains or LLMs with vision adapters and do not fit AR glasses or robots; compact models [] and non-autoregressive selection [] show that accuracy does not require scale, but the accuracy-efficiency frontier is unmapped. Evaluation has the saturation problem described under Datasets and Metrics above, and the new benchmarks, each with its own protocol, risk a cycle of leaderboard chasing; a single protocol spanning image, video, 3D, and dialogue, scoring rejection and clarification as well as localization, does not yet exist.

This chapter followed spatial perception from the elemental to the structured: recognizing the entities in a scene, fixing them in metric geometry, binding them into relations, layouts, and maps, carrying that structure through time, and supplementing vision with sound and language. Three observations recur across these tasks.

Priors fill gaps that observation leaves open. Monocular depth, surface normals, and camera motion are underdetermined by a single image: scale, reflectance, and the geometry behind an occluder are not fixed by the pixels (§, §). Learned models increasingly resolve this ambiguity with strong priors, which makes them confident on familiar scenes and fragile on transparent or reflective materials, moving objects, adverse conditions, and domains their training data under-represent. Distinguishing what a percept observes from what a prior supplies is a requirement the later chapters inherit, and Chapter returns to it as a question of observability.

Foundation models move the bottleneck rather than remove it. Open-vocabulary detectors and segmenters, zero-shot scene classifiers, and 3D geometry foundation models have widened what perception covers without task-specific training, yet the hardest cases persist at the long tail: small and rare objects, unseen instances in clutter, and metric judgments of distance, size, and angle, on which multimodal models remain weak even when their semantic predictions are strong (§). The accuracy–efficiency tension noted for detection recurs in every task of the chapter.

Evaluation rewards the easier part of each problem. Many benchmarks are synthetic, saturated, or confined to a few curated scenes; tracking metrics do not measure robustness to occlusion length (§), temporal-localization metrics treat fuzzy boundaries as exact, and grounding benchmarks pose a single query against a single image rather than an interaction (§).

What the chapter delivers is structured spatial evidence: entities with positions, relations, trajectories, and maps. Chapter takes that evidence as input and asks what can be inferred and planned from it, and Chapter runs the mapping in the opposite direction.

Spatial reasoning is the step that turns perceived structure into decisions: given detections, depths, poses, and a task, it works out the relations, the causes, and the actions that follow, the why and how of spatial interaction rather than merely the what and where. It is where perception becomes goal-directed, supporting inference, planning, and problem-solving in physical and virtual environments.

The chapter is organized along the spectrum by which spatial reasoning has actually developed, from explicit symbolic models to learned and foundation-model-driven ones. At one end, reasoning runs over hand-built representations of geometry, physics, and logic, whose structure is inspectable and whose conclusions can be certified. In the middle, it emerges from data, as neural models acquire spatial competence directly rather than being told the rules. More recently, large pre-trained models supply reasoning as a general capability to be elicited and steered. Hybrid approaches recombine these, pairing the semantic reach of foundation models with the precision and verifiability of symbolic and learned components; a closing survey of benchmarks then records how the field measures spatial reasoning as it shifts from passive observation toward active, situated interaction.

Rule-based symbolic spatial reasoning covers the methods that operate over explicit, model-based representations of space (geometric primitives, physical laws, graph connectivity, formal constraints, action rules, or causal mechanisms) rather than over learned latent representations alone. What sets this family apart is that reasoning happens inside a model that can be inspected: its state and transitions are legible, so claims about feasibility, optimality, or safety can be backed by certificates rather than empirical averages, and when a plan fails it fails legibly, as an infeasible inverse kinematics, a violated constraint, a missing precondition, or an inconsistent causal attribution, not as an opaque correlation.

The section surveys six kinds of explicit structure, ordered from the most concrete to the most abstract: geometric and algebraic models of position, orientation, motion, and feasibility; physical models of contact, friction, and stability; topological and graph abstractions of space that turn planning into search; formal constraint systems whose solvers return certified plans or proofs of infeasibility; rule-based and programmatic logic that sequences and supervises actions; and causal models that explain, predict counterfactually, and prescribe interventions.

These paradigms are not isolated alternatives. Modern robotic systems routinely compose them: geometric solvers serve as feasibility oracles inside constraint-based search; behavior trees wrap symbolic plans for fault tolerance; causal action languages compile to SAT; topological maps anchor both classical and learning-based navigation policies. The unifying thread is that each paradigm carries explicit structure (a state, an operator, a constraint, a rule, or a mechanism) that can be inspected, composed, and reasoned about.

Geometric and algebraic reasoning uses explicit mathematical models of position, orientation, shape, and motion to turn local measurements (image points, depths, joint angles, odometry) into quantities that can be analyzed and verified: where things are in a common frame, what a sensor can see, what a mechanism can reach, and whether a grasp will hold. The same models extend to time-varying settings, where relationships evolve under kinematic and differential constraints and the question becomes not only where entities can be but how they can move. Precision, interpretability, and domain independence have made this the common substrate of robotics [], AR/VR [], and autonomous systems [], and the source of the hard constraints that learned components are checked against. Figure gives the abstract formulation.

Geometric reasoning is evaluated against geometrically grounded ground truth: camera poses and intrinsics, depth maps and meshes, object models, grasp annotations. The pose, odometry, SLAM, and multi-view reconstruction benchmarks (TUM RGB-D [], EuRoC [], TUM-VI [], KITTI [], ETH3D [], Tanks and Temples [], DTU [], Middlebury [], HPatches []) and the long-term localization suites under seasonal and day-night change (Aachen, RobotCar Seasons, CMU Seasons [], InLoc [], 4Seasons []) are those of Section and Section , where their protocols and headline results are tabulated. Specific to the reasoning problems above are BAL [], which standardizes large bundle-adjustment problems for solver evaluation; the Active Vision Dataset [], ScanNet [], and HM3D [] for next-best-view, coverage, and exploration protocols; Cornell [], Jacquard [], and GraspNet-1Billion [] for grasp quality (rectangle labels, simulated grasp trials, and dense 6-DoF annotations with seen / unseen / novel splits respectively), with the YCB object set [] as the shared physical test set; and MoveIt [], whose reachability tooling is the de facto harness for inverse kinematics and motion-planning evaluation.

The formulations above assume exact geometry, and real sensing is noisy, incomplete, and subject to calibration drift []; bundle adjustment [] and reachability analysis scale poorly with problem size; many methods fail near singularities or degenerate feature configurations []; the frameworks are strongest for static rigid bodies and approximate deformable and human-centric geometry []; and evaluation is concentrated on a few canonical datasets and manipulators, which limits cross-domain comparison.

The response has been to keep the geometry and wrap it in probabilistic or learned machinery: factor-graph SLAM and robust bundle adjustment attach uncertainty to the symbolic model (Section ); learned correspondence priors are refined by RANSAC []; and the long-term benchmarks [] push the same pipelines toward continual adaptation under changing conditions.

Physically-aware spatial reasoning predicts how a spatial configuration evolves under physical law: rigid-body dynamics, contact and friction, and the conditions for static stability. Will a grasp hold? How will an object move when pushed? Will a stack of blocks stand or fall? Answering these from a model of mechanics, rather than from observed correlations, is what lets a robot anticipate the outcome of an interaction before committing to it; Figure shows the three canonical cases.

para.p: Model-based physical reasoning is carried out either numerically, in a physics engine that integrates the dynamics above, or analytically, with closed-form criteria for the quasi-static cases. Both rest on the same Newtonian foundation and differ in whether fidelity or interpretability is the priority.

MuJoCo [], Bullet [], ODE, and DART [] integrate rigid-body dynamics with contact by time stepping, and they resolve contact in one of two ways. Penalty methods treat a contact as a compliant spring-damper that resists interpenetration,

Math.text: f _ (list@(n, k)) = maximum@(0, k _ p * delta _ k + k _ d * (dot@(delta)) _ k)

para.p:
with penetration depth
δ k
, stiffness
k p
, and damping
k d
, and regularize friction similarly; they are cheap and simple, but stiff parameters destabilize the integration and soft ones introduce artificial compliance, which is acceptable in graphics and approximate planning but not in control. Constraint-based methods enforce Eq. () directly as complementarity constraints [], solved per step as a linear or nonlinear complementarity problem [], a convex quadratic program [], or a second-order cone program for exact friction cones [] (projected Gauss–Seidel and sequential-impulse schemes are the usual implementations). They give physically consistent, nearly penetration-free contact forces at higher cost and with harder scaling in the number of contacts, so engines in practice hybridize: hard constraints on normal forces, regularized tangential friction, warm starting, contact aggregation, and stabilization terms.
For the three settings of Figure , closed-form criteria replace simulation. At a point contact the admissible forces form the friction cone

Math.text: F _ k = conditional-set@(open-interval@(f _ (list@(n, k)), f _ (list@(t, k))), formulae@(f _ (list@(n, k)) >= 0, norm@(f _ (list@(t, k))) <= mu _ k * f _ (list@(n, k))))

which a polyhedral approximation turns into linear constraints. Mapping each contact’s cone through its moment arm into wrench space and taking the convex hull gives the grasp wrench space, and the grasp is force-closed when the origin lies strictly inside it, Eq. () []; form closure is the stronger, purely geometric condition in which contact geometry alone prevents motion, and the Ferrari–Canny
ϵ
-metric (the distance from the origin to the hull boundary) grades grasp quality. For planar pushing the limit surface relates the applied wrench to the resulting slip, and its ellipsoidal approximation yields a motion cone of object velocities reachable from a given push, the basis of stable pushing and closed-loop push planning. For stacking, stability under gravity requires that the gravitational wrench be balanced by the supporting contacts []: without friction, the center of mass must project into the support polygon; with friction, the contacts’ friction cones must generate a wrench cone containing the negative of the gravitational wrench.

PHYRE [] poses 2D physics puzzles in which an object must be placed so that simulated physics reaches a goal, scored by the log-weighted area under the success-rate curve as the attempt budget increases (AUCCESS) within and across puzzle templates; ShapeStacks [] labels 3D stacks as stable or unstable; PlasticineLab [] is a differentiable-physics suite for deformable manipulation; and the video suites IntPhys [], CLEVRER [], and Physion [] test prediction and counterfactual judgment of physical outcomes, with ComPhy [] asking for hidden properties such as mass to be inferred from motion. Grasp quality under quasi-static analysis is evaluated on the grasping benchmarks of § (Cornell, YCB, GraspNet-1Billion). Metrics are predictive: position or trajectory error against the simulated outcome, success rate (stable stack, successful push or grasp), binary stability accuracy, and physical-plausibility terms such as momentum conservation and constraint violation.

The parameters that matter most, mass, friction, elasticity, internal stability, are rarely observable. They must be inferred from interaction, from how far an object moves when pushed or how it responds to a collision; ComPhy [] tests exactly this, and most methods still either assume the parameters known, as classical simulation does, or approximate them in ways that fail outside the lab. Latent-dynamics learning [] and system identification [] are the two established routes.

The simulation-to-reality gap is the second limit. Small errors in restitution, micro-contact behavior, or unmodeled environmental factors compound once a policy leaves the engine, and fidelity trades against speed: high-fidelity simulation is too slow for large-scale training or real-time control, lightweight approximation too inaccurate. Hybrid physics-plus-learning models, domain adaptation between simulated and real dynamics, and uncertainty-aware transfer each address one side of this trade-off; none closes it.

Perception is the third. Geometry, material, and object state come from noisy, incomplete sensing, and a small error in shape, pose, or contact location propagates into a large error in predicted force or stability. Systems that couple vision to a physics engine, Galileo [] and PhyNet [] among them, show that physical priors improve perception and that physical consistency can constrain it in return, but end-to-end pipelines in which the two regularize each other remain the exception.

Topological and graph-based reasoning replaces continuous geometry with discrete connectivity, so that path planning, exploration, and coordination become combinatorial search over nodes and edges: places, corridors, and routes rather than metric trajectories. The abstraction is what makes large-scale, dynamic, or partially known environments tractable, where maintaining globally consistent geometry is hard but connectivity and reachability are stable. Figure gives the abstract formulation.

Connecting configurations that can see each other reduces shortest-path planning to graph search with interpretable waypoints. The visibility graph of Lozano-Pérez and Wesley [] links obstacle, start, and goal vertices and recovers exact Euclidean shortest paths in polygonal environments by Dijkstra or A*; the configuration-space construction via Minkowski sums [] extends it to robots of finite size by growing the obstacles instead of shrinking the robot; continuous-Dijkstra algorithms settle the complexity at

Grid planners bring line-of-sight into the search itself: Field D* interpolates across cell faces for smooth, replannable paths [], Theta* updates parents by visibility to produce near-Euclidean paths on the fly [], and Jump Point Search prunes symmetric grid paths by jumping to points where successor choices change [].
