para.p: Where safety matters more than length, free space is retracted to a skeleton that keeps connectivity and maximizes distance to obstacles. Voronoi diagrams and medial axes give maximal-clearance paths, with Fortune’s sweepline [] for efficient planar construction; the generalized and hierarchical Voronoi graphs [] let a robot follow ridges with its sensors and build the clearance roadmap incrementally while detecting junctions and loops; and distance-transform updates [] maintain the skeleton in dynamic environments for real-time replanning.

Discretizing space into cells trades geometric fidelity for simplicity and completeness. Occupancy grids [] are probabilistic cell maps updated from range data on which planning is grid search; exact decompositions serve coverage, with boustrophedon decomposition [] partitioning free space into monotone cells and ordering them through an adjacency graph for complete, low-redundancy sweeps; and the coverage literature is systematized in [].

In high-dimensional configuration spaces, the graph is discovered by sampling. Probabilistic roadmaps [] sample and connect configurations in a preprocessing phase amortized over many queries and are probabilistically complete; RRT and RRT-Connect [] grow trees toward unexplored regions for single-query planning under kinematic and kinodynamic constraints; PRM* and RRT* [] add connection-radius and rewiring rules that make them asymptotically optimal; and FMT* [] performs lazy dynamic programming over a batch of samples, while BIT* [] combines heuristic search with progressively denser sample batches for anytime improvement.

paragraph.title: Optimal, Any-Angle, and Incremental Graph Search.

para.p: On a given graph, Dijkstra’s algorithm and A* [] are the optimal single-source and heuristic searches; LPA* [] and D* Lite [] repair a shortest path incrementally as edge costs change; and the any-angle planners above (Field D*, Theta*) improve path quality, while JPS accelerates optimal search on its underlying grid.

With several agents on one graph, coordination is search over a time-expanded network. Conflict-Based Search [] splits the problem into a high-level search over conflict constraints and low-level single-agent planning and is complete and optimal; ICTS [] searches joint cost allocations backed by individual searches; ECBS and EECBS [] are bounded-suboptimal with focal heuristics and better conflict handling; and SAT or ILP compilations [] reach global optimality on moderate fleets at the cost of solver scalability. Hierarchical and multi-resolution planning [] and contraction hierarchies [] precompute abstraction layers that answer shortest-path queries on continental road networks in well under a millisecond, with standardized maps and instances [] for comparison.

The MovingAI suite [] supplies standardized 2D maps from games, cities, and synthetic generators for single-agent search (path cost, runtime, memory, node expansions) and the MAPF instances on which CBS, ICTS, ECBS, and compilation-based solvers are compared by makespan, sum of costs, and success under time and memory limits, with the ICAPS MAPF tracker [] as the community leaderboard. OMPL’s Planner Arena [] compares PRM, RRT, FMT, and BIT variants on success rate, planning time, path quality, and anytime behavior, and the DIMACS shortest-path challenge [] evaluates query latency, preprocessing cost, and optimality on continental road graphs. Topological mapping and pose-graph SLAM are stressed by place recognition under appearance change: RADISH [] provides classic multi-sensor logs, and Oxford RobotCar [], NCLT [], and Nordland [] span seasons and weather, with KITTI and EuRoC (Section ) for urban and indoor pose graphs.

Graph density sets the trade-off: sparse graphs lose connectivity or optimality, dense ones lose real-time response, and the problem sharpens in high-dimensional and lifelong settings []. Perceptual aliasing, drifting pose graphs, and dynamic obstacles complicate planning under partial information [], and on the topological SLAM benchmarks the binding difficulty is not search but appearance robustness, with cross-season and cross-weather queries far harder than same-condition retrieval. Multi-agent coordination strains conflict resolution and time-expanded representations as fleets grow, while fairness and deadlock avoidance must be kept [].

The directions are structured rather than end-to-end: hierarchical and multi-resolution planning that abstracts and refines [], risk-aware and formally verified planning under uncertainty [], bounded-suboptimal and distributed coordination for responsiveness [], and neuro-symbolic methods that enrich the graph with learned perception, heuristics, and semantics [].

Many robotics problems are not about finding a plan but one that must satisfy strict requirements: no collisions, no joint-limit violations, stable contacts, correct timing, sometimes guaranteed dynamics or safety margins. Constraint-based spatial solving states the problem as a collection of constraints, what must hold and what must not, and hands it to a solver that either returns a satisfying solution or proves that none exists. Compared with sampling- and heuristic-driven planning, this buys certificates of feasibility, an explanation of why a candidate fails, and, under an explicit model, optimality or bounded-suboptimality guarantees, which is what manipulation in clutter, multi-robot coordination in shared space, and assembly demand. Figure gives the abstract formulation.

The output types are alternatives; failure of a local solver alone is not an infeasibility proof.

The solver families differ in the variables and constraints they handle and the guarantees they return; practical systems are rarely pure, combining discrete reasoning over actions and modes with continuous optimization over motions and contacts, and calling fast geometric oracles (collision checking, inverse kinematics) inside the solver loop.

When the decisions are combinatorial (which object, which placement, which grasp) but each must pass a geometric test, constraint programming encodes the choices as variables under constraints and interleaves symbolic branching with propagation, pruning, and geometric checks. Lozano-Pérez and Kaelbling [] cast task-and-motion planning as constraint satisfaction over action skeletons, pruning symbolic branches as soon as a geometric feasibility test fails; Lagriffoul et al. [] propagate and filter continuous domains before any expensive collision or IK call, so that many failures become cheap inconsistencies; and Dantam et al. [] interleave discrete search with incremental feasibility queries that reuse information across related constraints.

Compiling planning and feasibility into Boolean formulas, or into formulas over richer theories such as real arithmetic, puts clause learning, incremental solving, and conflict-driven pruning to work. dReal [] decides nonlinear real arithmetic up to a numerical tolerance (
δ
-completeness), which gives certified answers where exact decidability is impossible; SMT-based planning for hybrid systems [] reasons first over an abstraction and adds constraints as counterexamples appear; SAT encodings of multi-agent pathfinding [] obtain optimal schedules on time-expanded graphs (the MAPF problem itself is treated in §); and SMT over linear real arithmetic extends the encodings to continuous time and to robustness against execution delays [].

When discrete mode choices (which region, which contact mode, which precondition) interact with continuous geometry and dynamics, binary variables encode the nonconvex choice and convex constraints capture feasibility within a mode. IRIS [] inflates large convex obstacle-free regions that serve as certified safe sets, turning collision avoidance into membership constraints with explicit margins; Graphs of Convex Sets [] compile motion planning through clutter into a shortest-path problem over convex nodes and edges that convex optimization, with mixed-integer selection where needed, solves with certificates; and later work constructs convex sets directly in configuration space and in space-time []. In each case a globally nonconvex feasibility problem is replaced by a sequence of convex ones without giving up the guarantee.

Even with the task fixed, an executable motion must satisfy kinematic limits, collision avoidance, smoothness, and often dynamics, which is a continuous, usually nonconvex, constrained optimization whose local optimum comes with optimality conditions and sensitivities. CHOMP [] deforms an initial path by functional gradient descent on a signed-distance field; STOMP [] replaces the gradient with stochastic perturbations to handle non-smooth costs and local minima; TrajOpt [] solves a sequence of convex programs with hinge-loss collision penalties; and GPMP2 [] writes planning as inference on a sparse factor graph with Gaussian-process priors, which gives scalability and incremental replanning. Increasingly these optimizers run inside the safe sets of IRIS and GCS, which supply initialization, constrain the search, or verify the result.

paragraph.title: Inverse Kinematics as a Constraint Subproblem.

para.p: “Is there a joint configuration that reaches this pose under limits and collisions?” is the most frequent feasibility query in any hybrid planner, so IK solvers are built as fast oracles. IKFast [] derives closed-form solutions and generates optimized code for repeated real-time queries; TRAC-IK [] combines complementary numerical strategies to raise the solve rate and avoid stalling the planner above it; and global IK by mixed-integer programming [] returns certifiable solutions for full chains when a feasibility proof is needed.

In long-horizon problems the discrete decision (what to do next) and the continuous one (how to do it) cannot be separated, and task-and-motion planners close the loop between them. Logic-Geometric Programming [] couples symbolic action sequences to bound-constrained nonlinear programs through a multi-bound tree search, so that continuous feasibility and cost decide which symbolic branches are worth expanding; PDDLStream [] integrates black-box geometric generators (grasps, placements, motions) into symbolic planning by optimistic refinement, requesting continuous witnesses only when needed while remaining complete under suitable stream assumptions; R-LGP [] biases the search with reachability guidance; and COAST [] uses constraints to communicate between task planner and stream generators, cutting wasted geometric proposals by an order of magnitude in planning time.

Evaluation asks whether a method returns solutions that satisfy strict feasibility conditions and, increasingly, whether it can show that it did (margins, certificates, optimality gaps) under a comparable oracle budget of collision checks and IK calls. OMPL’s benchmark suite and Planner Arena [] score planners on standardized problems with feasibility diagnostics and solution cost; the platform-independent TAMP benchmarks of Lagriffoul et al. [] specify symbolic operators together with IK and collision feasibility so that a jointly feasible task-motion plan is required; and the assembly benchmarks RAMP [] (real-world assemblies requiring geometric fit, stability under gravity, and grasp or fixture feasibility), ASAP [] (large-scale 3D assembly sequences validated by physics-based feasibility checks), and FurnitureBench [] (long-horizon real-world furniture assembly scored by success rate and completion time) stress feasibility across geometry, stability, and sequencing at once. Multi-robot coordination under space-time collision constraints uses the MAPF benchmarks of §.

The central difficulty is integrating a discrete task structure with continuous, highly nonconvex feasibility at scale and with certificates. Task-level choices (modes, grasps, placements, contact sets, schedules) interact combinatorially with geometric and dynamic constraints and fragment the feasible set; mixed-integer formulations grow expensive with the number of binary decisions [], trajectory optimizers return locally feasible motions that may violate a symbolic assumption such as the intended contact mode [], and symbolic planners propose sequences that are geometrically unrealizable. Information flows poorly in both directions: continuous solvers rarely return explanations (active sets, separating hyperplanes, unsatisfiable cores) that the symbolic layer could use to prune, and symbolic abstractions are often too coarse to keep the continuous subproblems tractable []. On the hybrid and assembly benchmarks this coupling, not raw search speed, is what separates planners: those that interleave symbolic branching with continuous oracles waste fewer feasibility checks and degrade more gracefully across domains.

Assurance under uncertainty is the second difficulty. Real systems need machine-checkable feasibility and fast infeasibility proofs, but nonlinear dynamics, contact, and hybrid interactions make strong certificates hard; convex surrogates and bounded-horizon relaxations buy speed at the price of completeness or tightness; execution requires real-time replanning with expensive oracles in the loop; and robustness to noise and model error calls for explicit risk and temporal-logic constraints []. Evaluations still under-report certificate quality, oracle counts, and failure explanations.

The trend is toward structure with certificates: graphs of convex or geodesically convex safe sets that reduce global nonconvex feasibility to sequences of convex subproblems with explicit proofs [], coupled to trajectory-optimization and MPC back-ends that return sensitivities and constraint activations for the search above them; chance constraints, temporal logic, and control barrier functions for persistent safety []; GPU acceleration for real-time replanning; and learning that guides branching, cutting, or warm starts without discarding the guarantee [].

Rule-based and programmatic reasoning is the explicit, human-auditable layer that decides when an action is allowed, in what order actions happen, and what to do next when conditions change, using symbolic operators, transition rules, or program-like control structures. In a robot it is the supervisory layer that sequences reusable skills (navigate, grasp, insert) and invokes geometric solvers or learned policies only when their preconditions hold, which is what makes a decision explainable (why the detour when the corridor was blocked), verifiable, and able to carry commonsense and safety constraints through a long task. Figure gives the abstract formulation.

The formalisms split by whether they plan (search for a correct sequence before acting) or react (choose a behavior continually at run time); deployed systems usually do both, with a planner proposing the sequence and an execution structure (FSM, behavior tree, rule engine) monitoring conditions and triggering recovery.

paragraph.title: Classical Symbolic Planning (STRIPS/PDDL and Heuristic Search).

para.p: STRIPS [] fixed the representation: planning as search over symbolic states with action schemas, so that a plan can be checked against the model and the continuous motion layer sits behind a clean abstraction boundary. PDDL [] standardized domain and problem specification so that planners could be compared across navigation, logistics, and assembly, with extensions (ADL, numeric fluents, temporal constructs) that capture robotic requirements without abandoning explicit semantics. Graphplan [] builds a planning graph whose mutual-exclusion constraints prune incompatible action combinations early, and FF [] made forward search fast with relaxed-plan heuristics that ignore delete effects, which capture ordering constraints such as unstacking before stacking in object-rich domains. Task-and-motion planning (§) extends these planners with geometric feasibility checks []; the common pattern is to keep the symbolic reasoning explicit, delegate feasibility to motion and IK solvers, and wrap the plan in an execution structure with monitors and recovery.

paragraph.title: Finite-State Machines and Reactive Mode Switching.

para.p: An FSM switches among a few well-defined behaviors (navigate, align, grasp) with explicit transition guards, which makes it transparent and fast but prone to state explosion as contingencies multiply. Statecharts [] add hierarchy and concurrency, so that complex controllers are nested reusable submachines with precise semantics; Brooks’ subsumption architecture [] layers behaviors so that higher ones override lower ones, a blueprint for composing navigation and avoidance without global planning, systematized as behavior-based robotics []; teleo-reactive programs [] evaluate conditions continuously and fire the highest-priority satisfied rule; and ROS tooling such as FlexBE [] provides hierarchical, event-driven state machines at deployment scale.

A behavior tree re-evaluates its conditions on every tick and chooses among structured alternatives (sequence, fallback, parallel), so that long-horizon execution survives disturbances without committing to one fixed sequence; subtrees encapsulate reusable routines, guards and fallbacks trigger immediate recovery, and the composition semantics fit perception and motion skills. BTs originated in game AI []; Marzinotto et al. [] formalized their semantics and their relation to other switching structures, and Colledanchise and Ögren [] showed which compositions preserve safety and robustness and consolidated the design principles. Compiling or wrapping a symbolic plan into a BT keeps the nominal task structure while exposing runtime guards and recovery branches []; ARIAC systems pair PDDL planning with BT execution monitors to handle failures, occlusions, and defective parts []; and event-driven BTs [] react to non-periodic stimuli rather than waiting for the next tick.

paragraph.title: Logic-based Execution and Production Rule Systems.

para.p: A production system keeps a working memory of facts and fires forward-chaining rules when their conditions hold, which suits event-condition-action policies, mode switching, and safety enforcement (no-go zones, mutual exclusions, priorities) and depends on fast incremental matching. OPS5 [] set the model; the Rete algorithm [] caches partial matches so that large rule sets update in milliseconds as facts change; CLIPS [] made the toolchain portable; and Soar [] integrated large rule bases with planning and execution in one architecture. In robotics, KnowRob [] and CRAM [] join symbolic knowledge to rule-driven execution for reasoning about actions, effects, and everyday manipulation, and LTLMoP [] compiles temporal-logic specifications into correct-by-construction reactive controllers whose safety and sequencing constraints are explicit at the program level.

The International Planning Competition supplies the canonical PDDL domains and problems across classical, temporal and numeric, probabilistic, and HTN tracks, compared by plan quality, makespan, and runtime [], with planning.domains [] mirroring and extending the sets for reproducible evaluation. Long-horizon embodied suites test execution under partial observability and variation: BEHAVIOR-100 in iGibson and BEHAVIOR-1K in OmniGibson [] specify household activities at the predicate level, ALFRED [] and TEACh [] score instruction-conditioned action sequences, and RoboTHOR [] and the Habitat challenge [] pair high-level decision logic with navigation policies under SPL. ARIAC [] injects faulty parts, occlusions, and failures into kitting and assembly, and FurnitureBench [] and RoboCup@Home [] stress recovery and explainability on real tasks; qualitative solvers over RCC-8 [] and Allen relations [] are tested on consistency problems, and composite pipelines reuse the TAMP and OMPL harnesses of §.

The results on these benchmarks divide along the closed-world boundary. On IPC-style domains with fully specified preconditions and effects, classical planners remain strong; on long-horizon embodied tasks the limit is perception noise and grounding ambiguity rather than search, and a logically applicable action may be geometrically unrealizable because of a collision, an IK failure, or a missing grasp. Hand-authored operators, rules, and recovery logic also grow combinatorially with object count and contingency. Integrated task-and-motion planning (§) answers the coupling problem by interleaving symbolic search with feasibility checks or compiling symbolic commitments into optimization back-ends [], and hierarchical abstraction and compositional skill models contain the search while keeping it auditable [].

Robustness to noise and nonstationarity is why the industrial and instruction-conditioned benchmarks reward compositions rather than single formalisms: a behavior tree around a symbolic plan makes disturbances and recoveries explicit through runtime guards, fallbacks, and safety-preserving composition [], and Rete-style engines [] supply fast event-condition-action policies over streaming facts, the pattern ARIAC entries converge on [].

Learned perception and language models increasingly propose the high-level procedure or heuristic while the symbolic structure stays as the safety shell that enforces preconditions, effects, and constraints: SayCan [] grounds language in robot skills by value-based scoring, and plan-to-BT compilation [] exposes parallelism, guards, and recovery at run time. Domain modeling, heuristic guidance, and recovery synthesis are being automated piece by piece while the programmatic structure is retained for auditing, debugging, and verification.

Causal reasoning moves from describing what happened to explaining why it happened and predicting what would have happened under a different action. For a robot the relevant outcomes are chains of spatial events (a collision, a delay, a deadlock, an unstable grasp, a near-miss in shared space), and making the causal assumptions explicit, rather than leaving them implicit in “actions cause state changes”, is what lets the system attribute a failure to its causes rather than its symptoms, evaluate counterfactual alternatives such as a different approach direction or timing, and, with several agents, separate primary causes from downstream effects when choosing an intervention. Figure gives the abstract formulation.

The method families serve different roles rather than forming a serial pipeline. Verification returns a satisfying witness or an unsatisfiability proof/core where supported; counterfactual scenes keep the objects fixed while changing the blue agent’s action.

The methods differ in where the causal structure comes from (assumed, learned from data, or written as domain knowledge) and in what they are asked (intervention effects, counterfactuals, responsibility, verification); in spatial domains they also differ in how they use locality, temporal precedence, and network connectivity as inductive bias.

An SCM makes mechanisms explicit (“clearance determines collision risk”, “traffic density sets delay”) and separates intervention from observation: the
⁢ d o
( ⋅ )
operator replaces a structural equation instead of conditioning on a value, which is what is needed when, say, congestion and delay are both driven by time of day. Spatial pipelines typically start from a graph fixed by temporal precedence and locality priors (edges among nearby regions, interacting agents, adjacent cells), estimate the mechanisms from data, and validate them against implied conditional independences and refutation tests []. Counterfactuals follow the abduction-action-prediction recipe: infer the exogenous noise consistent with the observed trace, apply the hypothetical intervention, predict the outcome []. DoWhy and DoWhy-GCM [] implement identification, estimation, and refutation for this workflow on real spatiotemporal data.

When the graph is unknown but observational data are plentiful, constraint-based methods read structure off conditional independences: the PC algorithm builds the skeleton by independence tests and orients what it can, returning a Markov equivalence class, and FCI [] handles latent confounding and selection bias by returning a partial ancestral graph. Score-based methods instead search graph space under an objective such as BIC: GES [] greedily adds and then removes edges over equivalence classes, and its forward-backward structure often recovers mesoscale organization such as bottlenecks that drive downstream congestion. Spatial data strain both. Large conditioning sets are expensive and statistically weak, so practice restricts conditioning to a radius or
k
-hop neighborhood, forbids edges that violate adjacency or reachability priors, and uses order-independent variants (PC-stable []) whose high-dimensional consistency is understood []; ambiguous orientations are then resolved by targeted interventions. causal-learn [] and the TETRAD / Py-Tetrad implementations of FGES [] provide these pipelines at facility and city scale.

In linear-Gaussian settings many edge directions are unidentifiable from independences alone. LiNGAM [] assumes a linear structural model with independent non-Gaussian noise, under which the causal ordering is identifiable, and DirectLiNGAM [] estimates it by regression rather than ICA. Spatiotemporal signals need care because autocorrelation violates i.i.d. sampling assumptions and aggregation may change the noise distribution; temporal blocking, prewhitening, and locality constraints are the usual remedies, and the recovered ordering then scaffolds an SCM for intervention analysis.

paragraph.title: Causal Action Languages and Plan-Space Causal Links.

para.p:
Much causal structure in robotics is designed knowledge rather than discovered: actions have direct and indirect effects, and the system must reason about change under incomplete information. The action language C+ [] writes causal theories of action with inertia and nonmonotonic semantics, compactly describing how fluents such as occupied(c) or visible(a,o) evolve; CCALC [] compiles them to SAT so that prediction, diagnosis, and plan synthesis use the same solvers; and multi-valued fluents and external geometric predicates (collision checks, IK) are being integrated without abandoning the formal semantics []. In plan space, partial-order causal-link planning [] represents a plan as partially ordered actions plus links
p →
A B
(action
A
establishes precondition
p
for
B
), which makes threats explicit and repairable by promotion, demotion, or binding constraints; UCPOP [] extended the representation to ADL and conditional effects and VHPOP [] added heuristics and reachability analysis. In spatial domains a causal link is often a physical dependency, “unblock door” enabling “move cart”, which bridges symbolic causality and spatial feasibility.

A causal plan must be realized in time and checked. Simple temporal networks [] enforce difference constraints between events with polynomial consistency and dispatchable forms [], and STNUs with dynamic-controllability analysis [] handle contingent durations, so that ordering and clearance constraints stay satisfiable under bounded disturbance. The SAT/SMT machinery of § enters here as an explanation device: when a schedule is unsatisfiable, the unsat core is a set of conflicting commitments, a concrete statement of which decisions caused the failure []; and for hybrid dynamics
δ
-complete SMT (dReal) [] and dReach [] verify safety and synthesize interventions with numerically sound proofs or counterexamples.

No single benchmark covers the causal pipeline, and the suites stress different links of it. CLEVRER [] pairs synthetic collision videos with descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual questions, and CLEVRER-Humans [] adds human-annotated causal event graphs against which model attributions can be compared; the video suites of § (PHYRE [], Physion and Physion++ []) score intervention selection and latent-property inference, and CRaFT [], ContPhy [], NExT-QA [], AGQA [], and SUTD-TrafficQA [] ask causal questions in natural language about synthetic and real-world videos, including traffic scenes. Embodied platforms with predicate-level state (BEHAVIOR-1K, ALFRED, iGibson 2.0 [], ManiSkill2 [], RLBench []; §) test whether inferred dependencies improve intervention selection and recovery; the MAPF suites and Flatland [] (§) test reasoning over space-time constraints in which one agent’s decision causes another’s delay; and ARCH-COMP [] with the dReal / dReach problem sets [] evaluate causal safety reasoning on hybrid dynamics by proof or counterexample and solve time. Discovery itself is evaluated on recovery of the Markov equivalence class under faithfulness, with scalability bounded by conditioning-set size.

Identification is brittle. Latent confounding, selection bias, and temporal aggregation can make a query non-identifiable from logs, and estimates become unstable when locality and precedence assumptions fail []; constraint- and score-based discovery is expensive on dense telemetry with strong short-range dependence and sensitive to test strength, ordering, and regularization []; and LiNGAM’s non-Gaussianity is exactly what smoothed trajectories and aggregated traffic signals lack []. The response is structure-aware discovery that constrains search by topology and locality and then resolves the remaining ambiguity by targeted robot interventions, connecting learning to actuation [].

Causal reasoning is only as good as its variables, and in embodied settings contact, occlusion, blockage, and object state must be grounded from noisy perception. The errors of that mapping propagate into SCM estimates and counterfactual conclusions []. Knowledge-enabled frameworks such as KnowRob and CRAM (§) show the shape of the interface, perception populating an explicit, interpretable model whose parameters are then estimated statistically, and the trend is toward such perception-to-symbol interfaces that tolerate sensor noise [].

Between a causal recommendation and a safe execution there is a verification-synthesis gap: the recommendation must become a temporally controllable schedule and a certified controller, and execution uncertainty invalidates a symbolic causal plan unless temporal networks and hybrid verification are integrated with it []. SCM toolchains are therefore being embedded in decision stacks so that counterfactual policies compile into action-language or plan-space structures and then into dispatchable networks [], with SAT/SMT certificates and unsat-core explanations supplying the accountability []; evaluation that scores explanation quality, interventional effectiveness, and certification cost on the same task is what the field still lacks.

Learning-based spatial reasoning refers to the class of methods that acquire and perform spatial reasoning from data, rather than from the hand-authored geometric, mechanical, or symbolic models surveyed in §. The six subsections that follow are ordered by the locus of the structural prior: it begins inside the learned representation (latent feature interaction, explicit programs, hard-coded symmetries, optimization layers in the forward pass), moves to the agent’s action-conditioned behavior (reinforcement learning with spatial inductive biases), and ends with joint decision-making across coordinated agents.

We define implicit neural spatial reasoning as the family of neural approaches in which spatial relations are encoded in learned feature representations, attention patterns, latent object interactions, or architectural inductive biases, rather than specified through hand-written rules, symbolic programs, or fully explicit relational graphs. Implicit does not mean that these models never use boxes, masks, object proposals, or task-level labels; it means that the reasoning procedure itself is never given as a symbolic program, so the model must learn spatial dependencies from end-to-end or weakly structured supervision. Several families below (latent scene graphs, capsule networks) expose partly inspectable structure, yet remain implicit in that their reasoning representations are learned rather than fixed by hand-written symbolic rules. Figure shows the representative tasks.

Graph neural networks and latent scene graphs generalize this from a complete graph to a learned, sparser topology, with proposals or feature regions as nodes and learned edges as spatial dependencies; iterative message passing for scene-graph generation [] alternates between refining node features and updating relation embeddings, learning the topology end-to-end. Such models are the clearest semi-explicit case in this subsection: the graph is inspectable and often trained with relation annotations (e.g., , from Visual Genome), yet the intermediate relational representation is learned rather than specified by a program, and its quality is bounded by the upstream proposal stage.

paragraph.title: Spatial Attention and Multi-Scale Feature Fusion.

para.p: A second family controls where and how strongly the model attends across the spatial layout, and fuses evidence across scales, rather than scoring all pairs. CNN spatial attention weights locations in a feature grid, from the hard and soft attention of [ ] for captioning and grounded VQA [] to SCA-CNN’s joint spatial and channel attention []; vision transformers make relating image parts intrinsic through self-attention over patches [], with locality-aware variants (Swin [], PVT [], Twins []) trading global receptive field for cost; and Feature Pyramid Networks [] add a top-down pathway so that a relation coupling a fine object with a coarse region (a car “on” a street) can be read from one map. These designs are representation backbones that preserve and aggregate spatial information for the reasoning built on top of them, not reasoning modules in themselves.

A third family conditions one representation on another rather than aggregating or attending. In FiLM (Feature-wise Linear Modulation) [], a conditioning vector (e.g., , an encoded query or global context) predicts affine parameters
( γ , β )
that are applied feature-wise to a target map, so the same backbone can be steered per task. For a query like “What is to the left of the green cube?”, a FiLM layer can learn to amplify features to the left of regions identified as the green cube, making reasoning adaptive and context-dependent.

A fourth family bakes geometric regularities into the architecture, trading data-driven flexibility for sample efficiency where the relevant geometry is known. Capsule Networks [] replace scalar activations with vector-valued capsules whose orientation encodes instantiation parameters (pose, deformation) and whose magnitude encodes presence; dynamic routing decides how lower-level capsules compose into higher-level ones by agreement in predicted pose, a stronger part-whole bias than translation-only convolution, though capsules have been hard to scale beyond small digit and shape datasets. Equivariant and steerable convolutions [], which commute with a chosen transformation group, are the subject of §; both share the cost that the symmetry must be chosen in advance.

CLEVR [] is the canonical benchmark, pairing rendered scenes with multi-step relational questions whose ground-truth program structure is known; Sort-of-CLEVR [] isolates a controlled relational vocabulary. The decisive stress tests are the systematic-generalization splits: CLEVR-CoGenT [] holds out attribute-composition combinations, and GQA [] scales compositional questions to real images. Open-domain VQA v2 [] and Visual7W [] probe whether implicit reasoning transfers beyond synthetic templates to natural images and free-form language. On CLEVR, RN reaches 95.5% and FiLM 97.7%; Table in § places these against the program-structured reasoners, which close the remaining gap only on in-distribution questions.

The interpretability challenge is intrinsic: because relations live in distributed activations rather than named symbols, it is hard to audit which relations a model actually exploits, and attention-map visualizations are only an indirect proxy. Compositional generalization is the most striking failure: even at 97–98% CLEVR accuracy, the same models drop sharply on CLEVR-CoGenT [] and GQA [], revealing dataset-specific shortcuts rather than transferable spatial concepts; the related shortcut-learning concern in open-domain VQA, where language priors and object co-occurrence dominate the signal, is the imbalance VQA v2’s balanced design targets []. Scalability divides the families: RN-style pairwise modeling is
⁢ O
(
n 2
)
in the number of objects, attention backbones trade receptive field against compute [], and GNNs inherit the brittleness of the proposal stage []. The more fundamental limit is the 2D-to-3D gap: these methods reason over 2D feature grids and image-plane relations, whereas much spatial reasoning depends on depth ordering, occlusion, viewpoint, and metric layout, and strong 2D backbones and vision–language models degrade sharply once relations hinge on 3D geometry [].

Two responses run through the rest of this section. The explicit-structured methods of § reintroduce programs and graphs over learned features, recovering inspectability while keeping the representational power of deep networks; the geometry-aware methods of § answer the 2D-to-3D gap directly by building the symmetry group into the architecture, where it is known. Whether web-scale pretraining alone closes the systematic-generalization gap, or explicit structure remains necessary, is the open question that § takes up.

Explicit structured neural reasoning decomposes a spatial problem into an inspectable intermediate structure, a program, a scene graph, a sequence of reasoning states, or executable code that calls vision tools, and obtains the answer by executing or traversing that structure over visual representations. Unlike the rule-based reasoning of §, the structure is learned or inferred from data rather than written by hand; unlike the implicit reasoners of §, it exposes spatial predicates directly, so that an inspectable edge or a named operation can represent containment, adjacency, support, or relative position, making them auditable and composable instead of entangled in a feature space. Figure previews the representative tasks.

The four families in Figure differ in how much structure they expose, enough to make reasoning inspectable and compositional, but not so rigid that a perception error, a parser error, or a missing primitive causes deterministic failure. Each exposes a different facet of space: recurrent architectures a temporal trace of attentional focus, scene-graph methods object-centric relations, program-based methods named operations such as filtering, relating, counting, and comparing, and LLM-generated programs tool-call traces that combine detection, segmentation, localization, and external knowledge.

This family imposes a step-wise reasoning structure in the architecture itself, so the model is fully differentiable and trained end-to-end from input–output pairs while still exposing a step-by-step trace. The Memory, Attention, and Composition (MAC) network [] chains
p
recurrent cells, each of which attends to the question to choose the operation for the current step (control unit), extracts the relevant visual information by spatial attention guided by that control signal (read unit), and integrates it into a reasoning state passed to the next cell (write unit); the attention maps of successive read units provide a transparent trace of where the model is looking, without a rigid symbolic program. MAC is thus a boundary case: explicit at the level of reasoning dynamics, implicit at the level of spatial representation, since the operations run over dense feature maps rather than named objects or relations. Because the spatial logic stays in the learned weights, it is prone to statistical shortcuts (if “red spheres” co-occur with “cubes” in training, the model may learn that correlation rather than “left of”), and soft attention maps are often diffuse, so “to the left” bleeds into irrelevant regions in cluttered scenes.

Four method families for explicit structured neural reasoning, ordered by the intermediate structure
S
each exposes: (A) the MAC recurrent reasoning cell []; (B) the Neural State Machine []; (C) program-based reasoning, a parse-to-execute pipeline whose executor ranges from neural modules (NMN [], IEP []) through the symbolic executor of NS-VQA [] to the quasi-symbolic executor of NS-CL []; and (D) LLM-as-program-generator pipelines that call vision tools (e.g., , ViperGPT [], VisProg [], Code-as-Policies []).

para.p:
A related line strengthens the structural prior on the reasoning substrate. Where MAC reasons over a soft grid of features, the Neural State Machine (NSM) [] reasons over a probabilistic semantic scene graph and performs differentiable state transitions over it: a concept-detection module (Mask R-CNN) identifies entities, each node
v i
is initialized with semantic properties over a learned concept vocabulary, each edge
e
⁢ i j
carries a distribution over spatial and semantic relation types (left of, behind, on top of, holding), and the query is answered by propagating a distribution over nodes through query-conditioned transitions. More broadly, scene graphs act as a generic structured substrate: a downstream reasoner can propagate probabilistic states over the graph (as in NSM), attend over it as a soft relational prior, or search it for graph-based question answering, in each case obtaining an inspectable cut-point between perception and reasoning. The price is that reasoning quality becomes tightly coupled to object detection, attribute grounding, and relation prediction, a dependency we return to in the challenges.

A third family translates the query itself into an executable program, and its members differ mainly in the nature of the executor. The Neural Module Network (NMN) [] is the canonical neural-executor instance: an external semantic parser converts a question such as “What color is the llama?” into a layout, e.g., , classify[color](attend[llama]), whose slots are instantiated by distinct learnable modules (attention, re-attention, classification, combination, measurement) trained jointly to maximize the likelihood of the gold answer. Because NMN relies on an off-the-shelf parser, IEP [] replaces it with a sequence-to-sequence program generator that emits the program as a sequence of functions, trained jointly with the execution modules via REINFORCE [] or by maximizing answer likelihood over a distribution of programs. Moving further toward symbols, Neuro-Symbolic VQA (NS-VQA) [] adopts a symbolic executor: a scene parser turns the image into a symbolic table, after which the program reduces to deterministic functional operators, yielding fully interpretable execution at the cost of a near-perfect-perception assumption. The Neuro-Symbolic Concept Learner (NS-CL) [] occupies the middle ground with a quasi-symbolic executor: a neural perception module produces object-centric representations and a semantic parser emits symbolic programs, but the executor relaxes discrete operations such as filtering and relating into differentiable ones, so concept learning and semantic parsing can be trained from question–answer pairs, while the object detector is pretrained using bounding-box annotations.

The most active recent extension lets a large language model emit the program directly, replacing the seq2seq parser of IEP or the hand-crafted parser of NMN with a tool-based executor. ViperGPT [] and VisProg [] pair a frozen LLM with a Python-style API of vision tools (detectors, captioners, attribute classifiers) that the generated code invokes, making the approach compositional and zero-shot without per-task training. Code-as-Policies [] pushes the same program-synthesis paradigm into embodied control, treating the LLM-emitted program as a closed-loop policy over perception and actuation primitives; it is included here as an embodied extension of the paradigm rather than as a VQA method. The interpretability gain is real, since the emitted code is human-readable, but these systems re-inherit the brittleness of the underlying LLM (hallucinated API calls, ungrounded tool routing) as a failure mode the earlier hand-coded DSLs were designed to avoid.

paragraph.title: Unifying View: Parser, Representation, Executor, and Supervision.

para.p: The four families are points in a shared design space with four axes. The parser that maps a query to structure may be hand-built (NMN), learned end-to-end (IEP, NS-CL), or a frozen LLM (ViperGPT, VisProg); the representation over which reasoning runs may be a dense feature map (MAC), an object-centric scene graph (NSM, and the scene-graph-generation literature [] supervised at scale by Visual Genome []), or a symbolic scene table (NS-VQA); the executor may be neural, symbolic, quasi-symbolic, or a code interpreter; and the supervision may be answer-only, program-supervised, or, in tool-based systems, augmented with execution traces and tool feedback. The inspectable structure between perception and answer is the common thread: it provides a natural cut-point at which symbolic and learned components can be swapped without retraining the rest of the stack, and the same four axes reappear in the foundation-model reasoners of §.

paragraph.title: Beyond VQA: 3D, Temporal, and Embodied Extensions.

para.p: The same design pattern extends beyond static images: referring-expression grounding has been lifted from 2D images to 3D scenes [], where object-centric and spatial-relation graphs supply the substrate for reasoning about support, containment, proximity, and navigability, and in video and embodied settings the intermediate structure becomes a temporal scene graph or a task plan that links perception to action (§, Part IV). These extensions also expose the central limitation of current explicit methods: most available program primitives and graph predicates are still designed for static 2D relations, whereas viewpoint change, object permanence, physical interaction, and multi-step navigation need 3D, temporal, and causal operators.

The CLEVR family [] of § is the canonical testbed here as well, with the added property that each question is generated alongside a ground-truth functional program, which gives both program-supervised and answer-only training signals; MAC, IEP, NS-CL, and NS-VQA all converge to the high-90s on it, making it attractive but saturated. GQA [] is the dominant open-domain benchmark: it pairs natural-image scenes with compositional questions whose ground-truth scene graphs (from Visual Genome []) make scene-graph-based reasoners directly applicable, and its out-of-distribution splits expose the systematic-generalization gap hidden by saturated CLEVR scores. VQA v2 [] is a general VQA benchmark, while the cited visual-program systems ViperGPT and VisProg report task-specific comparisons on GQA. Referring-expression grounding benchmarks (RefCOCO and RefCOCO+ [], RefCOCOg [], and the earlier ReferItGame []) are equally relevant, since they test whether a system can bind spatial language (“the object left of / behind / next to …”) to a localized region even when the output is a box or mask rather than an answer. Embodied program-as-policy systems such as Code-as-Policies are evaluated by task success in robotic or simulated manipulation environments and should not be compared against VQA accuracy. Table collects the headline numbers.

para.p: Exposing programs, graphs, state transitions, or tool calls buys interpretability but creates new failure modes, and the numbers above locate them. The first bottleneck is parsing: if a question is mapped to the wrong program or traversal path, even a correct executor produces the wrong answer. The second is symbol grounding and underspecification: spatial predicates such as Left, Behind, Near, or Between depend on viewpoint, scale, object extent, and task context, so many spatial queries do not determine a unique program, a single deterministic DSL operator is often too rigid, and new predicates demand manual re-engineering of the executor. The third is error propagation: mistakes by the detector, scene parser, relation classifier, or program generator are inherited by the executor and can cause deterministic failure, which is why NSM reaches 63% on GQA while the same family saturates CLEVR; on natural images the bottleneck has moved from reasoning execution to perception, scene-graph construction, language grounding, and long-tail relation coverage. A fourth, more structural tension is the differentiability–interpretability trade-off: the more symbolic the executor, the more auditable but the harder to train end-to-end; the more differentiable, the more robust but the less transparent. Because the value of explicit structure lies in the intermediate trace, evaluation should move beyond final-answer accuracy to whether the parsed program is faithful to the query, whether graph edges correspond to real relations, whether tool calls are necessary and grounded, and whether the execution trace actually supports the answer.

Most explicit systems also reason over static 2D layouts or object graphs rather than 3D geometry, temporal dynamics, or physical causality: they can answer whether
A
is left of
B
, but rarely simulate how a scene changes under motion, contact, containment, support, or occlusion, which is exactly the mental-simulation capacity human-level spatial reasoning requires. LLM-generated programs widen the scope by replacing fixed parsers with flexible code generation, trading a small accuracy gap on saturated benchmarks for zero-shot generality across VQA, grounding, and knowledge-grounded VQA, but they add hallucinated tool calls, invalid APIs, ungrounded intermediate variables, and the absence of a verifiable execution loop. The emerging direction is therefore not a return to purely symbolic reasoning but verifiable hybrid systems, in which learned perception produces object-centric representations, structured programs or graphs provide an inspectable scaffold, and neural or tool-based executors absorb the variability of real visual inputs, the direction of § and §.

Where the implicit and explicit methods above learn spatial relationships from data, geometry-aware approaches build the relevant symmetries into the network itself: an object rotated, translated, or re-indexed keeps its identity, and the architecture is constructed so that this holds by design rather than being learned from many transformed examples. The gain is sample efficiency and robustness under the chosen transformations; the cost is that the symmetry group has to be chosen in advance. Figure pairs three symmetry-driven task settings with the method families that supply the matching inductive bias.

para.p: Invariance is the right target when the output should not depend on orientation or position (classification), equivariance when pose and relative arrangement are the point (manipulation, keypoints, instance segmentation, molecular modeling); the layers below realize each.

The baseline strategies work without changing the architecture. Augmenting the training set with rotated, flipped, or scaled copies pushes a standard CNN toward assigning the same label to all variants, but buys only an approximate invariance and requires examples of every transformation to be tolerated; global average pooling [] at the end of a feature extractor discards the “where” of each feature and keeps only its presence, which is the main reason classification CNNs are robust to translation. Neither guarantees invariance to anything beyond translation.

paragraph.title: Active Alignment with Spatial Transformer Networks.

para.p: Rather than ignoring transformations, a Spatial Transformer Network (STN) [] learns to undo them: a small localization network regresses the parameters of an affine transformation that it predicts will bring the object into a canonical pose, a grid generator turns these parameters into a sampling grid, and a differentiable sampler produces the rectified feature map, so the localization network is trained by backpropagation from the task loss alone. The module can be inserted at any point in a network and acts as learned attentional alignment, normalizing a region of interest for the layers downstream; the invariance it provides is learned, not guaranteed.

A separate symmetry arises when the input is an unordered set rather than a grid: the model must be invariant to the ordering of its elements. DeepSets [] shows that any permutation-invariant function over a set can be written as

, encode each element independently, sum, then decode, which turns set-level invariance from an ad-hoc choice into a constructive recipe and makes explicit which aggregators preserve invariance and which silently break it; the same framework yields permutation-equivariant layers for per-element outputs (per-point labels, per-atom properties). PointNet [] is the canonical instance on raw point clouds, a shared multilayer perceptron per point followed by symmetric max pooling, and PointNet++ [] adds locality by repeatedly grouping points within a metric ball and applying the same shared-MLP-plus-pool pattern at multiple scales. Permutation invariance comes for free in this family; rigid-motion invariance does not, which is the gap the equivariant methods below address.

A standard convolution is translation-equivariant (shifting the image shifts the feature map) but not rotation-equivariant: rotating the input changes the feature map unpredictably. Group equivariant convolutions (G-CNNs) [] generalize the operation to a larger discrete group such as the four planar rotations: a single filter is rotated into a set of transformed copies, all are correlated with the input, and the feature map gains an orientation dimension, so a feature that reads “edge at
45 ∘
” becomes “edge at
135 ∘
” at the corresponding location when the input rotates by
90 ∘
. Equivariance is therefore not learned but imposed, layer by layer.

paragraph.title: Steerable Filters and Equivariance in Every Layer.

para.p: Steerable CNNs [] replace the group-indexed filter copies by filters expressed in a steerable basis, so that the response at a transformed orientation follows by linear combination of basis responses rather than by explicit rotation; the general E(2) framework [] extends this to continuous rotations and reflections with circular-harmonic bases under one configurable interface, and library efforts such as e3nn [] do the same for E(3) / SE(3). Full equivariance also requires that pooling, nonlinearities, and normalization respect the group: a standard ReLU applied to the components of a geometric vector breaks it (activations are therefore applied to invariant quantities such as the vector norm), and channel-wise batch normalization breaks the coupling between channels, which motivates equivariant normalization []. The guarantee is only as strong as its weakest layer; one non-equivariant operation anywhere in the stack silently undoes the symmetry the rest preserve.

paragraph.title: Equivariant Attention and Continuous SE(3) Symmetries.

para.p: Benchmarks in this area are constructed to expose behavior under symmetry transformations. MNIST-rot is the standard 2D testbed, separating methods that learn rotation robustness through augmentation from those that build it in; ModelNet40 [] evaluates point-cloud classification under three protocols, aligned training and test (z/z), training with azimuthal rotations and testing under arbitrary SO(3) rotations (z/SO(3)), and arbitrary rotations in both (SO(3)/SO(3)), which is where augmentation, STN-style alignment, and PointNet’s permutation-invariant pooling are separated from genuine rotation handling; ScanObjectNN [] adds real scan noise and occlusion. For equivariance as a hard constraint, QM9 [] (small-molecule property prediction) and interatomic-potential tasks are the reference, where the SE(3)-equivariant models NequIP [] and MACE [] set the current points for data efficiency and accuracy. Table reports the two ladders on which the method families can be compared directly.

The most fundamental difficulty is choosing the symmetry group: invariance to a group that is too large (SO(3) when only SO(2) is task-relevant) destroys discriminative information, invariance to one too small leaves the model brittle to the symmetries the task actually exhibits, and the trade-off has no purely data-driven solution []. Cost scales with the group: classical equivariant architectures index filters by group elements, so parameters and memory grow with the size of the chosen group, limiting how freely reflections, multi-scale rotations, or higher-order tensor representations can be included []. The assumption of exact symmetry is also brittle: point clouds with self-occlusion, partial-view RGB, and noisy LiDAR scans do not realize an SO(3)-orbit, so an architecture that is mathematically equivariant can still fail when the input violates the assumed structure. Table shows where the two targets diverge: on 2D classification both hand-coded invariance and learned equivariance saturate, so data efficiency rather than accuracy becomes the discriminating axis, while on ModelNet40 the invariance-only PointNet family collapses under unseen rotations and the equivariant family holds its accuracy, because the task requires geometric information to be preserved, not discarded. Finally, hard equivariance sits uneasily with the attention-based representations that dominate the rest of the stack (§, §, vision–language pretraining): self-attention is permutation-equivariant but not rotation-equivariant, and bolting an equivariant layer onto an attention pipeline often degrades the inductive bias that motivated the choice.

Equivariant attention is the main compromise on offer, and frame averaging [] moves in the opposite direction, turning any off-the-shelf backbone into an invariant or equivariant one by symmetrizing its outputs over a small input-dependent set of group frames, which decouples the choice of symmetry from the choice of architecture and sidesteps the parameter cost of group-indexed filters. These threads are pulling geometry-aware reasoning back toward the rest of the chapter: vision–language and vision–language–action models attach equivariant heads where 3D pose and geometric consistency matter, as in grasp policies and pose-conditioned generation, and primitives first devised for object classification are finding second lives in world models, embodied control, and 3D generation.

Where the three preceding subsections put structure into the learned representation, differentiable optimization layers put it into the computation: selected feed-forward operations are replaced by the solution of a constrained optimization problem, so that hard logical, geometric, or physical constraints are enforced inside the forward pass while the whole system stays end-to-end differentiable []. In spatial reasoning this is how a network enforces distances, collision avoidance, or alignment, or solves a sub-problem such as pose estimation, within a learnable pipeline. OptNet learned to solve Sudoku from data where conventional architectures could not, which showed that implicit layers can handle discrete or constrained reasoning problems.
[ ] generalized the idea to any disciplined convex program: CVXPY Layers [] canonicalize the problem into conic form, solve it, and differentiate through the cone program’s optimality conditions, so a constrained least-squares, a constrained logistic regression, or a robot-motion-limit constraint can be inserted as a layer without deriving gradients by hand.

All of these layers share one mechanism. Rather than unrolling an iterative solver, one differentiates the closed-form optimality (KKT) conditions, which for a convex program comprise primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementarity, and stationarity []; differentiating this system and solving one linear system yields
∂
z ⋆
∂ θ
exactly, without back-propagating through solver iterations. Where OptNet hand-codes this backward pass, Deep Declarative Networks [] apply automatic differentiation to the KKT system itself. The same principle extends to root-finding, fixed-point, and equilibrium layers via the implicit function theorem; deep equilibrium models [] treat an entire weight-tied network as a single fixed-point layer differentiated this way, and differentiable physics engines and planners propagate gradients through the equilibrium or optimum conditions of a physical system.

Differentiable optimization layers have been validated across symbolic, geometric, and control settings. Sudoku [] and its visual variant [] test whether a layer models constraint satisfaction and propagates gradients through discrete reasoning; Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPM / I-RAVEN) [] test whether differentiable logic captures relational structure in visual analogy puzzles; cart-pole, inverted-pendulum, and reaching tasks in MuJoCo and OpenAI Gym [] test whether differentiable MPC [] or convex layers improve control while enforcing physical feasibility; and maze navigation and obstacle avoidance test QP-based collision-avoidance layers by whether the agent reaches its target without violating safety constraints. Evaluation combines task metrics with criteria specific to the embedded solver: geometric accuracy (translation / rotation error in pose estimation, trajectory or map error for a bundle-adjustment layer), task success rate (puzzles solved, feasible plans produced) together with the count or magnitude of violated constraints and, for physics-informed layers, residual energy or momentum drift, and solver cost and gradient stability (forward / backward runtime, iterations to converge, and sensitivity of training to approximate versus exact implicit gradients). Table lists the representative layers by solver type.

para.p: Solving an optimization problem inside a layer is more expensive than a convolution or a matrix product, and the forward pass becomes the bottleneck as problem size grows, which is exactly the regime of SLAM, bundle adjustment, and motion planning. OptNet’s batched GPU solver shows how problem structure buys tractability for many small problems, but global route planning or large-scale 3D reconstruction still overwhelms existing solvers, forcing approximate solves, warm starts, or hierarchical decomposition to keep each optimization manageable.

Gradient stability is the second difficulty. If the solution is non-unique or depends discontinuously on the input, as at boundary optima, at active-set changes in a linear program, or in the presence of discrete variables, the implicit gradient is unstable or undefined; strict convexity guarantees a well-defined Jacobian, and real problems frequently violate it. Entropy smoothing, small regularizers, and perturbation methods restore usable gradients in many cases, and in others the backward pass has to be designed by hand.

The third is physical consistency. An optimization layer enforces only the constraints it is given: if the formulation omits a friction constraint in a contact model, the network exploits the gap and converges to implausible solutions, and because the layer sits inside a trainable system, the surrounding network can learn to feed it inputs that satisfy the constraints superficially while violating their intended meaning. The benefits of interpretability and correctness therefore depend on the optimization model reflecting the real dynamics, which in practice means careful constraint modeling, additional penalties, or iterative refinement of the solver design; current work refines solvers, numerical stability, and integration with deep-learning frameworks toward layers that are both theoretically grounded and deployable in spatial systems.

Where the previous four subsections constrain the learned representation, reinforcement learning shifts the locus of structure to the action-conditioned setting, in which an agent must reason about spatial relationships as a consequence of its own behavior over a long horizon. Many spatial tasks, such as navigation, exploration, manipulation, and embodied interaction, cannot be reduced to static perception or single-step prediction; they require reasoning about how actions transform the agent’s position, orientation, and relations to surrounding objects over time, under geometric constraints, partial observability, and delayed reward. Generic RL policies built on unstructured function approximators struggle to generalize across unseen layouts, so a growing body of work introduces spatial inductive biases, explicit planning iterations, map-like latent representations, differentiable search operators, or relational state abstractions, that constrain the hypothesis space of policies or value functions to reflect the compositional and geometric structure of spatial decision-making.

para.p: Figure shows the loop every method below shares: the agent observes, acts, receives a reward and a new state, and updates its policy to maximize long-term return. Learning a good policy requires balancing exploration of untried actions against exploitation of the actions currently believed best, the exploration–exploitation trade-off that underlies all of RL. The subsections that follow walk through the optimization backbones in the order the field developed them, value-based, policy-based, actor–critic, PPO, and the recent preference-based and group-relative objectives, and note at each step where spatial structure enters.

Deep Q-networks (DQN) [] made this scale to high-dimensional observations with experience replay and a slowly updated target network; their convergence is analyzed theoretically by [ ] , and Figure shows the resulting workflow. Beyond control, value-based RL drives active visual perception: [ ] cast object localization as a sequential decision process in which a Q-network iteratively transforms an attention window until it tightly bounds the target, turning detection into a learned spatial search policy, a formulation since applied to active detection, visual search, and region selection for fine-grained recognition, where the agent learns where to look rather than scanning exhaustively. In spatial domains the limitation of vanilla DQN is that any planning behavior must be learned implicitly from data, which generalizes poorly to novel layouts, so several works embed planning structure in the value estimate itself. Value Iteration Networks (VIN) [] unroll Bellman updates as convolutions over a spatial grid, a differentiable approximation of value iteration; Gated Path Planning Networks (GPPN) [] replace the recurrence with gated units to improve optimization stability and long-range dependencies; and under partial observability QMDP-Net [] integrates belief updates and approximate POMDP planning (QMDP) [] into one differentiable network. In each case the learned value function is constrained to follow spatially structured dynamic programming rather than arbitrary function approximation.

The separation between actor and critic matches the structure of spatial tasks, with the actor responsible for geometry-aware decisions and the critic supplying global, long-horizon value signals, which is why actor–critic methods dominate navigation benchmarks that require memory, planning, and partial observability [].

para.p: Eliminating the value network reduces memory and stabilizes training. Although explored first for language models, the formulation transfers to spatial decision-making wherever several candidate plans or trajectories can be scored against one another, and it has become the standard recipe for reinforcement fine-tuning of spatial vision–language models on visual reasoning, navigation, multi-step assembly, and video spatial reasoning [].

The backbones above are domain-agnostic; what makes a policy spatial is the prior
S
in its architecture, and three families recur across the examples already met. Map-based representations give the agent an explicit allocentric memory: cognitive maps [] and Neural Map [] write observations into a spatially indexed latent grid, while Neural SLAM [] and Active Neural SLAM [] couple differentiable mapping with a hierarchical exploration policy. Differentiable planning modules embed dynamic programming in the network, as in the VIN / GPPN / QMDP-Net line discussed under value-based RL, or learn a value-equivalent model and plan by lookahead search, as in MuZero []. Relational abstractions replace flat feature maps with object- or graph-structured state, letting attention or message passing capture relations that transfer across layouts []. In each case the RL objective is unchanged; the spatial competence comes from the prior, which is why these architectures generalize across geometries where unstructured policies overfit.

Two complementary benchmark families shape the empirical landscape. Embodied navigation and exploration benchmarks stress long-horizon planning under partial observability in photorealistic 3D scenes: Habitat [] is the dominant platform, paired with real-world scans from Matterport3D [] and Gibson [] for large, scene-diverse PointGoal and ObjectGoal navigation that exercises geometry-aware exploration and cross-scene generalization; SoundSpaces [] adds audio-visual cues as a multimodal test of spatial state estimation; and SOON [] extends vision-and-language navigation to scenario-oriented object goals in unseen environments. Symbolic and relational benchmarks test whether structured priors yield combinatorial and compositional generalization: PDDLGym 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://github.com/tomsilver/pddlgym builds Gym environments from PDDL domains with relational observations and actions, and lightweight gridworld suites such as MiniGrid 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://github.com/Farama-Foundation/Minigrid support controlled evaluation of planning, memory, and compositional generalization; the differentiable planners (VIN, GPPN, QMDP-Net) are evaluated on procedurally generated gridworld mazes and POMDPs of increasing size, where the question is whether the architectural prior generalizes to unseen layouts rather than memorizing training mazes. Across both families the choice of RL algorithm matters less than the choice of prior: PPO has converged as the standard optimizer for embodied navigation, and differences between agents mostly reflect the map, planning module, or relational encoder on the policy, while on gridworld benchmarks the methods that embed planning structure consistently dominate unstructured DQN, with the largest gains where the task is most planning-shaped.

Sample inefficiency comes first. Spatial tasks involve long horizons, sparse rewards, and combinatorial state spaces, so naïve exploration is prohibitively expensive; architectural priors such as learned maps, planning modules, and relational representations improve efficiency [], but current RL systems still need orders of magnitude more interaction than humans or classical planners to acquire robust spatial competence.

Generalization and transfer come second. Many agents perform well in their training environments and degrade sharply in unseen layouts, novel geometries, or altered dynamics, which suggests that much of the learned behavior rests on superficial correlations rather than abstract spatial structure; structured state representations, world models, and modular policy design [] help, but how to enforce spatial invariances and compositional generalization in RL in a principled way remains open.

Reward specification is the third. Spatial tasks often lack dense, well-defined rewards, especially when success depends on long-term plan quality, safety, or efficiency rather than immediate outcomes. Preference-based methods such as DPO [] and group-relative objectives such as GRPO [] learn from comparative feedback instead, at the price of reward-model bias, preference inconsistency, and the difficulty of aligning learned preferences with the true task objective in complex spatial domains.

The directions that follow from these three are hybrid methods that integrate learning with explicit planning or search [], structure-aware representations (object-centric, relational, graph-based) that scale spatial reasoning beyond grid-based and navigation-centric benchmarks [], and evaluation protocols that weight out-of-distribution generalization, robustness to environmental variation, and reasoning quality over performance on fixed benchmarks.

Where the previous five subsections study a single learning agent, multi-agent spatial reasoning (MASR) moves to the joint regime: multiple embodied or abstract agents perceive, communicate, and act within a shared environment to accomplish cooperative or competitive goals, and the structural prior now governs decentralized decisions over a shared spatial state. MASR links low-level sensorimotor streams (proprioception, occupancy grids, trajectories) to relational decision processes (joint planning, role assignment, coalition formation); its core problem is credit assignment and coordination under spatial constraints, that is, how agents with partial, decentralized observations reason over nearby entities, infer latent intent, and synthesize actions that produce coherent team-level behavior. Deep learning has moved the field from rule-driven coordination to end-to-end policies that integrate perception, communication, and control under partial observability and non-stationarity [], with autonomous driving and interactive motion forecasting over road geometry (WOMD [], nuScenes []), multi-robot exploration, formation control, and patrol under attrition [], and real-time strategy and team-sports simulation [] as its representative domains. We stress at the outset that the canonical algorithms surveyed below (VDN, QMIX, COMA, MADDPG) are themselves spatially agnostic: they solve a generic cooperative Dec-POMDP and see geometry only through the environment and the reward. Explicit spatial structure enters chiefly through the benchmarks and through the graph-based family, where the interaction graph
G t
makes neighborhood relations a first-class part of the policy.

para.p: In predictive variants, auxiliary heads output multi-agent forecasts or spatial fields with confidences for planning or losses; these are not environment actions. Settings differ along two further axes: online methods act in streaming settings under tight latency, whereas offline methods learn from logged interaction data (e.g., , driving datasets) with batch updates and conservative behavior constraints; and centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) exploits global state to train joint value functions or critics while enforcing decentralized policies at test time [], whereas fully decentralized learning never accesses global state, trading sample efficiency for deployability.
Figure summarizes the tasks above and the method families discussed below.

Before learning, coordination relied on potential fields, formation keeping via graph Laplacians, and optimal multi-agent pathfinding with conflict-based search [], treated in §; these methods offer strong guarantees but struggle with perception noise, combinatorial scaling, and model mismatch in open worlds.

Two lines made CTDE work. Centralized critics resolve credit assignment and non-stationarity while keeping execution decentralized: COMA uses a counterfactual baseline computed by a centralized critic for decentralized actors [], and MADDPG extends deterministic policy gradients with agent-specific centralized critics []. Value factorization instead decomposes the joint value: VDN sums per-agent utilities to approximate
Q tot
for cooperative tasks [], and QMIX generalizes the sum to a monotonic mixing network that preserves individual-global argmax consistency with more representational capacity []. These approaches made MARL scalable on SMAC [], where the value-decomposition line dominated the early cooperative leaderboard while the centralized-critic methods anchored other regimes (MADDPG on the particle environments, COMA on StarCraft micromanagement); the monotonic constraint and homogeneous-role assumptions limit expressivity, as the challenges below detail.

Graph-based MARL encodes agents as nodes and interactions as edges, and message passing or attention over the neighborhood learns role-specialized coordination []; this family improves sample efficiency and robustness under topology changes and communication limits, and MAGEC [] shows resilience to agent attrition and communication disturbance in multi-robot patrol by combining GNN encoders with PPO-style multi-agent optimization. Graph MARL targets a different axis from the leaderboard methods, robustness to topology disturbances rather than headline return, which exposes a gap between coordination-quality benchmarks (SMAC, MPE) and deployment-quality ones (multi-robot patrol, driving forecasting on WOMD and nuScenes) that standardized suites still under-represent.

Casting MARL as sequence modeling applies attention over multi-entity, multi-horizon contexts: the Multi-Agent Transformer [] maps the sequence of agents’ observations to a sequence of actions with an encoder–decoder, using the multi-agent advantage decomposition to turn joint policy search into sequential decisions with linear complexity in the number of agents. Transformer controllers, often hybridized with graph layers, address long-range temporal and relational dependencies, unify perception and control, and support offline RL through trajectory modeling; learned memory alleviates partial observability, while quadratic attention and credit assignment over long horizons remain open.

Benchmarks span two regimes: simulation suites that stress cooperation, partial observability, and communication learning under controlled physics and reward shaping, and real-world multi-agent trajectory datasets that test interactive prediction and motion forecasting at deployment scale. Multi-agent spatial reasoning faces structural difficulties that distinguish it from the single-agent settings of §–§, organized here along four axes within the classical multi-agent paradigm.

paragraph.title: Credit Assignment under Partial Observability and Long Horizons.

Under sparse reward shaping, policies trained against these signals tend to chase short-term spatial cues (“move toward the closest enemy”, “follow the nearest teammate”) rather than team-level objectives.

Sparse, learned interaction graphs are the natural mitigation, but they introduce their own credit-assignment difficulty: the edges
E t
