caption.text: Illustration of the agentic hybrid orchestration pattern: a foundation-model controller dynamically selects perception, world-modeling, symbolic-reasoning, memory, and action tools within a closed-loop perceive–reason–act–reflect cycle.

para.p:
The fifth pattern makes the orchestration function itself the object of design: a foundation model acts as a deliberative controller that decides, at each step, which of the perception, world-model, symbolic, memory, and action modules to invoke, within a closed perceive–reason–act–reflect loop (Figure ). It differs from the agentic reasoning of § in what is being scheduled: there, tools and memory; here, additionally symbolic engines and physics simulators, with the scheduler
π
of Eq. () itself a candidate for learning. VADAR [] (§) is the program-synthesis version of such a controller, generating the API it then calls. “See it. Say it. Sorted” [] is a training-free version for sketch-to-diagram generation: a critic VLM proposes a few qualitative relational edits, several LLMs synthesize candidate SVG programs, and a judge VLM selects among them, which keeps global constraints such as alignment and connectivity intact where numerical estimation would drift.
[ ] arrive at the same module inventory from neuroscience, arguing that such a controller should sit over multimodal sensing, multisensory integration, egocentric–allocentric conversion, a cognitive map, spatial memory, and spatial reasoning. The gain is compositionality and long-horizon consistency that no static architecture provides; the cost is the latency and attribution problems discussed below.

Hybrid systems are evaluated end to end on the benchmark of their target task rather than module by module, and the benchmark is often one the paper introduces. Among the systems above, Embodied-R reports on UrbanVideo-Bench and VSI-Bench, MindJourney on SAT, NS3D on ReferIt3D, MSNav on R2R and REVERIE, and PhysVLM on RoboVQA and OpenEQA alongside its own EQA-phys; LLMPhy ships TraySim, CLEVRER-LLMPhy, and Real-TraySim, MindExplore ships SandGo-1k and SandThink-21k, and DrawingBench [] is built specifically for agentic hybrids, scoring an LLM’s sequence of low-level mouse actions against eight rule-based criteria for the spatial configuration it was asked to draw. Physics-side components are still checked against PHYRE and ShapeStacks (§) and symbolic components against the constraint- and rule-based suites of §–§, but no current benchmark attributes an end-to-end score to the modules that produced it; that gap is taken up under Challenges and Trends below and in the cross-paradigm survey of § (Table , whose 15-row agentic subset is Table of §).

Hybrid spatial reasoning has produced architectures that combine complementary inductive biases in principled ways, but several recurring limitations originate in the module-composition framework itself rather than in any individual module.

Frame, Scale, and Geometric Consistency. Unlike generic modular systems, spatial hybrids must reconcile heterogeneous spatial representations across modules: perception emits camera or egocentric frames, map and memory modules operate in world or allocentric coordinates, symbolic reasoners abstract to topological relations, and physics engines expect metric units. Misaligned reference frames, scales, or conventions silently corrupt downstream reasoning, and because each module reports confidence in its own terms, small upstream pose, depth, or scale errors propagate and compound across the pipeline without a coherent notion of uncertainty. Maintaining frame, scale, and geometric consistency is thus a first-order obstacle with no analogue in non-spatial hybrid systems.

Interfaces, Latency, and Attribution. The strength of a hybrid system is bounded by its worst module interface. Symbolic-to-neural translation is particularly brittle when the symbolic side uses closed-vocabulary predicates while the neural side proposes open-vocabulary ones, and the interface design becomes a hidden first-class hyperparameter that current literature seldom isolates. Each module invocation also adds wall-clock latency that compounds across a perceive–reason–act–reflect loop, so high-frequency manipulation and navigation may not be reachable through orchestration alone. And when a hybrid fails, attributing the failure to a specific module is non-trivial; this complicates iteration and is often cited as a practical reason why end-to-end models can outperform hybrid stacks on aggregate benchmarks despite offering weaker per-module guarantees.

The orchestration function
π
is migrating from hand-coded rules to learnable orchestration policies trained with reinforcement or imitation learning, which blurs the boundary with §. Differentiable hybrid stacks, built from differentiable physics simulators, differentiable optimization layers (§), and differentiable retrieval, make end-to-end training of a hybrid viable and remove the historical interface penalty, offering a path through the precision–grounding asymmetry that motivates this section. Evaluation is changing too, toward the holistic and diagnostic: in response to the attribution problem, emerging practice pairs aggregate task metrics with per-module diagnostic probes and counterfactual module-swap ablations that isolate where a hybrid system succeeds or fails, a direction consolidated in the cross-paradigm benchmark survey of §.
z

Early spatial-reasoning benchmarks positioned the model as a detached observer. CLEVR [] and VSR [] ask for relative geometric relations from a static third-person viewpoint, and their 2D inputs leave depth ambiguous, a weakness that 3DSRBench [], MMSI-Bench [], DSI-Bench [], and STI-Bench [] now probe directly. SQA3D [], OpenEQA [], and EmbSpatial-Bench [] instead place the model inside the scene, so that it must self-localize before it can answer, and ScanQA [], ScanRefer [], and Multi3DRefer [] ground queries in point clouds and RGB-D data, where the answer is a coordinate rather than a relation. The reasoning demanded has deepened in parallel: IntPhys [] and Physion [] test whether a model expects gravity, collision, and friction to hold over time, and OpenEQA and RealWorldQA [] ask functional questions (“Can I navigate through this gap?”, “Where would I find a cloth to clean a spill?”) in which geometry matters only through what it affords.

Data provenance splits the field. Simulators, the sources behind SpatialVLM [], AI2-THOR [], and Habitat [], yield unlimited, perfectly annotated data; real-world collections such as ScanNet [] and OpenEQA supply the clutter, occlusion, and sensor noise that simulation does not reproduce. The resulting practice is sim-to-real: pre-train on large synthetic corpora for general spatial logic, then fine-tune on the scarcer real data. Annotated 3D data remain scarce and fine-grained metric estimation remains hard for large models; both limits recur throughout the table below.

Table compiles 61 spatial-reasoning benchmarks across four categories (physical-focused, rooted in §; vision-based, overlapping with §; 3D-focused, rooted in § and §; and robot-environment, rooted in § and §). A narrower 15-row subset focused specifically on agentic spatial reasoning is provided in Table of §; this subset filters Table to image-and-video benchmarks that exercise agentic deployments.

para.p: A modality migration runs from the top of the table to the bottom: the physical-focused benchmarks rely on synthetic 3D renderings, the vision-based block is image- and video-heavy with growing 3D extensions, the 3D-focused block is built on point clouds and RGB-D scans, and the robot block has moved largely to 3D environments. The Perspective axis is imbalanced: a large fraction of vision-based benchmarks carry Undeclared ego/exo annotations, the physical-focused benchmarks lean exo (a third-person observer judging physical plausibility), and the robot block is entirely ego; the field is migrating from spectator-style observation to situated cognition faster than benchmark annotations record it. The Data-Source spectrum is bifurcated between predominantly synthetic or simulated (top block and robot block) and predominantly real (middle blocks), with the Real/Sim benchmarks (SpaRE, 3DSRBench, RoboSpatial, SpatialVLM, SITE) as the bridge that the sim-to-real training practice of the opening relies on.

No single benchmark in Table exercises a model along all of perception fidelity, symbolic precision, memory persistence, and long-horizon action conditioning simultaneously. A unified benchmark covering all four § paradigms (§ rule-based, § learning-based, § foundation-model-driven, § hybrid) would close the evaluation-attribution challenge flagged under Challenges and Trends in §.

The current axes (Modality, View, Perspective, Data Source, Task Type) under-specify the cross-modal demand of contemporary spatial reasoning. Future benchmarks should explicitly probe modality-to-modality transfer (e.g., , 2D-trained models evaluated on 3D queries; text-conditioned policies evaluated on video-grounded tasks), so that the modality-mismatch challenge flagged in § (text-vs.-image-vs.-3D retrieval) becomes a first-class evaluation axis rather than a per-paper case study.

The Robot block in Table covers navigation thoroughly but under-represents long-horizon manipulation and multi-room interactive tasks. The § 15-row subset (Table ) further restricts attention to image-and-video benchmarks; the embodied long-horizon suites ALFWorld and VirtualHome (§) and cross-embodiment evaluation on Open X-Embodiment (§) are the nearest existing coverage, and standardizing on them would close the long-horizon-spatiotemporal-coherence challenge flagged under Challenges and Trends in §.

paragraph.title: From Descriptive to Interactive Spatial Reasoning.

para.p: The Task Type column of Table is dominated by visual question answering: the overwhelming majority of benchmarks ask a model to describe static spatial relations (“where is the object”), and only the small Robot block evaluates reasoning that is conditioned on the agent’s own actions. Yet the trajectory traced in this chapter, from passive observation to situated interaction, calls for benchmarks that test interactive spatial reasoning: predicting how an action changes the spatial state, judging affordances and reachability (“can I fit, reach, or grasp this”), and reasoning counterfactually about manipulation outcomes. Such evaluation couples the action-conditioned reasoning of § with the embodied hybrid pipelines of §, extending the descriptive benchmarks surveyed here toward the manipulation- and affordance-grounded settings that embodied deployment ultimately demands.

This chapter followed spatial reasoning along the spectrum on which it developed: inference over explicit geometric, physical, topological, logical, and causal models (§); reasoning acquired from data (§); reasoning elicited from large pre-trained models (§); hybrids that combine these components (§); and the benchmarks that measure them (§).

Precision and grounding sit at opposite ends of the spectrum. Rule-based methods are inspectable and can certify feasibility or safety, but they assume exact, fully specified inputs and a closed vocabulary of predicates, and they break down where perception is noisy or a task falls outside the authored rules. Learning-based methods acquire spatial competence from data, yet often reach high benchmark accuracy through dataset-specific shortcuts that do not survive novel compositions (§), and they need far more interaction than classical planners. Foundation models bring broad semantic competence, but their visual encoders retain only coarse geometry, textual reasoning mistracks coordinates over multi-step chains (§), and vision-language-action models often interpret an instruction correctly and execute it incorrectly (§). Hybrid systems aim to pair the semantic reach of the last family with the metric precision and verifiability of the first two.

The failures concentrate at interfaces. Across tool-augmented, memory-augmented, and hybrid reasoning, the recurring limitations arise less within any single component than where components meet: in forming a query that a memory or tool can answer, in translating between closed and open vocabularies, and in keeping coordinate frames and scales consistent across modules (§).

Evaluation lags the shift toward situated reasoning. The field is moving from questions posed to a detached observer toward agents that must localize themselves, gather evidence, and act, yet no current benchmark exercises perception fidelity, symbolic precision, memory persistence, and long-horizon action together, and few attribute an end-to-end score to the components that produced it (§).

Reasoning in this chapter takes the evidence of Chapter as given. Chapter turns to the inverse problem of producing spatial content, and its world models (§) supply the simulators that world-model-based reasoning (§) consults.

Spatial reconstruction and generation is the productive counterpart to spatial perception and reasoning: rather than analyzing a scene that is given, it synthesizes spatial content, recovering or creating the geometry, appearance, and dynamics of objects, scenes, and worlds from conditions such as text, images, partial observations, or explicit constraints. Where perception (Chapter ) maps observations into structured spatial representations and reasoning (Chapter ) draws inferences over them, generation closes the loop by mapping intent back into concrete spatial artifacts, a capability central to embodied agents, content creation, simulation, and world modeling.

The chapter is organized along an axis of increasing output structure and dimensionality, from flat images to volumetric objects and scenes, to video, embodied motion, and full four-dimensional space-time content, and finally to world models and to programmatic generation that emits interpretable, executable structure. What holds this range together is a single recurring backbone: an encoder maps conditions into a latent, a generator samples structure, and a decoder or renderer produces the final artifact, specialized to each output domain. Read this way, the subfields are less seven separate problems than one conditional-generation abstraction instantiated against progressively richer codomains.

The 2D spatial generation encompasses a broad spectrum of tasks that require synthesizing or editing images under explicit spatial constraints. These constraints may be user-specified (bounding boxes, masks, sketches, keypoints, depth maps) or derived from scene understanding (layout graphs, semantic maps, relational structures), and the overarching goal is to produce images that are not only visually realistic but also faithful to the specified spatial configuration: objects appearing in the correct locations, at the correct scales and orientations, while remaining globally coherent in lighting, perspective, and style. 2D generation is where the most mature semantic-to-pixel prior in contemporary AI is taught to honor spatial structure: it is the proving ground on which large pre-trained visual priors are forced to localize objects, follow geometric scaffolds, respect occlusion ordering, and obey region- or instruction-level edits, all without falling out of the implicit grammar of natural images.

The section follows the 2D pipeline in three steps that share one latent-generator framework. § reviews foundational text-to-image generation, the semantic-to-pixel prior on which everything else here is built, and the three paradigms (adversarial, autoregressive, and diffusion with its flow-matching generalization) that parameterize it. § adds a structural condition (layouts, masks, edges, depth, pose, scene graphs, region phrases) and asks how it is injected into a frozen or co-trained generator. § replaces the empty canvas with an existing image and a mask, so that the generator must change what lies inside the mask while preserving what lies outside it.

Text-to-image (T2I) generation synthesizes an image from a natural-language description. For the rest of this chapter its importance lies less in the images themselves than in the prior it provides: a high-capacity mapping from compositional language to the visual space of objects, surfaces, layouts, and viewpoints, learned once at web scale and then reused. The spatial controllers of § and the editors of § impose constraints on this prior rather than replacing it, and the text-to-3D pipelines of § distill it through score distillation or multi-view consistency objectives; whatever relational competence the prior has, or lacks, therefore propagates downstream. The field has passed through three architectural paradigms, from adversarial training to autoregressive token modeling to iterative denoising, with diffusion and its flow-matching generalization now setting the standard for quality and prompt fidelity [].

The remaining weakness is sampling cost, dozens of sequential network evaluations per image; higher-order ODE samplers and the distillation methods below address it. The formulation was introduced concurrently by [ ] (Flow Matching) and [ ] (Rectified Flow); [ ] gave the unifying stochastic-interpolant view in which diffusion is the special case of a noisier interpolation schedule. Three consequences matter in practice. Straight-line interpolations yield nearly straight ODE trajectories, so matched quality is reached in noticeably fewer steps (genuine one-step generation still needs a reflow or distillation stage); the objective is a single regression with no noise-schedule design and no per-schedule guidance recalibration; and the loss scales smoothly with model size and resolution. Stable Diffusion 3 [] scaled the recipe to T2I on a DiT-style transformer backbone and reported the best GenEval scores among open models together with favorable human preference on Parti-prompts; the Flux family followed the same recipe. Flow matching composes with every refinement below as readily as a noise-predictor core does and has become the default continuous-time formulation in 2024-onwards systems.

paragraph.title: Backbone Evolution: From U-Net to Diffusion Transformers.

para.p:
Early diffusion models used the U-Net for its multiscale feature fusion and locality bias. The Diffusion Transformer (DiT) of [ ] replaced it with a stack of transformer layers over latent patch tokens, giving every denoising step a global receptive field, and showed that FID improves monotonically with depth, width, and token count along predictable scaling laws, reaching FID 2.27 on class-conditional ImageNet at
256 2
. Attention cost grows quadratically with resolution, so hybrid CNN-transformer designs and efficient attention remain active; the DiT lineage nonetheless underlies SD3 and most 2024-onwards systems, and it points toward a single transformer that generates several modalities, differing only in tokenization and training data.

Fifty or more denoising steps rule out interactive use and low-power deployment.
[ ] distilled a
T
-step teacher into a
/ T 2
-step student and iterated the halving to reach
1
–
4
steps. Consistency Models [] train a network to map a noisy latent at any timestep directly to the clean image, either from scratch with a consistency loss or by distilling a pretrained diffusion model, and Latent Consistency Models [] applied the idea to Stable Diffusion’s latent space, matching
50
-step quality in
2
–
4
steps. All of these are post-training procedures that leave the architecture untouched, so any strong backbone can be made fast after the fact.

Leading systems have migrated to proprietary, industrially scaled stacks of three kinds. Native multimodal models such as OpenAI’s GPT Image 1.5 [] and Google’s Gemini 3 Pro Image (Nano Banana Pro) run a unified transformer over interleaved text and image tokens and emphasize semantic reasoning and multi-turn editing; latent-diffusion iterations such as Imagen 4 scale the LDM recipe with stronger text encoders and curated data; preference-tuned systems such as Midjourney v7 [] and FLUX.2 [max] [] fine-tune strong priors on human-preference data (FLUX.2 on the rectified-flow recipe of §; Midjourney’s architecture is undisclosed). Each reduces to one of the three paradigms plus some of the refinements just listed; because architectural and training detail is withheld, public benchmarking and reproduction still rest on the open SD / DiT stack.

Three independent things are usually conflated under “benchmark”: the training corpora on which models are fit, the evaluation suites of prompts that probe particular capabilities, and the metrics that score the resulting images. A model trained on LAION-5B can be evaluated on GenEval prompts and scored by FID, CLIPScore, or an LLM judge, and disagreement between those scores is itself informative.

Corpus scale has driven much of T2I progress. Early work fit fine-grained sets with ten captions per image, CUB-200-2011 (11,788 bird images) [] and Oxford-102 Flowers (8,189 images) []; MS-COCO Captions [] (123,287 images, five captions each) became the standard general-scene corpus and, for years, the evaluation set as well, a conflation that the suites below were designed to end. Current models train on web-scale image-text pairs: LAION-5B [] releases 5.85 billion CLIP-filtered pairs, and proprietary corpora of similar scale, less documented, underlie DALL-E 2 and Parti. Scale brought duplication, demographic bias, unsafe content, and licensing disputes with it, and filtered subsets such as LAION-Aesthetics and curation pipelines are now part of every training recipe.

An evaluation suite is a curated prompt set plus a verification protocol: prompts are adversarial or capability-stratified, reference images are usually absent, and scoring is automatic (an object detector, a VQA model, or an LLM/MLLM judge) rather than reconstruction-based. Table lists the main suites since 2022. The earliest, DrawBench [] and PartiPrompts [], are human-pairwise prompt sets released with Imagen and Parti; HRS-Bench [] and HEIM [] are holistic, scoring 13 and 12 axes respectively; TIFA [], GenEval [], and T2I-CompBench [] introduced automatic verification by VQA, object detection, and BLIP-VQA plus UniDet, and the latter two are now reported alongside FID and CLIPScore in most papers. For spatial intelligence the salient suite is VISOR [], which isolates two-object relations (left/right, above/below) over
25 , 280
prompts and finds that otherwise strong models frequently render the wrong configuration. DPG-Bench [] targets dense, long compositional prompts, GenAI-Bench [] pairs compositional prompts with VQAScore judging, and WISE [] asks whether generated images agree with real-world facts (flag colors, landmarks, anatomy), a knowledge axis orthogonal to compositional binding.

Several suites combine multiple scoring channels.

inline-block.p: Object-centric: single/two-obj., counting, color, position, attribute
Compositional: attribute binding, object relationships, complex prompts

para.p:
Metrics fall into four tiers. Distributional metrics compare the generated and real image populations and say nothing about any individual prompt: the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [] is the Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussian fits of Inception-V3 features of generated and real images, the Inception Score rewards images that are individually confidently classified yet collectively diverse, and generative precision/recall [] separate quality from coverage through neighborhood tests in feature space. Alignment metrics score one image against its prompt; CLIPScore [], the cosine similarity between the CLIP embeddings of
^ y
and
x
, is cheap and reference-free but inherits CLIP’s insensitivity to attribute binding, counting, and spatial relations. Learned preference models, HPSv2 [], ImageReward [] (fit to
137
K human comparisons), and PickScore [] (fit to the
∼
500
K real-user comparisons of Pick-a-Pic), regress a scalar that correlates with average user preference, bundling realism, alignment, and aesthetics; they have become the default automatic ranking while inheriting their raters’ biases and degrading out of distribution.

The newest tier uses a vision-language model as judge. TIFA [] has a language model write verification questions from the prompt and a VQA model answer them against the image, the score being the fraction answered correctly; VQAScore [] collapses this to a single yes/no probability under a fine-tuned CLIP-FlanT5 model and reports the best human correlation on compositional suites; VIEScore [] and LLMScore [] prompt a multimodal LLM with a structured rubric and return per-axis scores with brief rationales, and direct prompting of frontier VLMs with custom rubrics has become routine for ad-hoc capability probes. Judge metrics track human preference on compositional and spatial prompts far better than CLIPScore, at the cost of a frontier-model call per image, sensitivity to rubric wording, and drift across judge-model versions that makes numbers from different papers hard to compare. No single tier suffices, and current papers report a tuple (FID or IS, CLIPScore, one or two preference scores, one judge score) on several suites plus a small human study; cross-metric disagreement is read as a warning rather than averaged away.

The weakness that matters most for this handbook is spatial-relation faithfulness, a sub-problem of compositionality. Models frequently misplace objects relative to one another: a prompt that puts a cup to the left of a laptop is often rendered with the two swapped or stacked, and VISOR [] shows that language-specified relations are frequently ignored outright. Data-centric remedies help; SPRIGHT [] re-captions training images with explicit spatial descriptions and measurably improves consistency, but reliable control over where objects appear remains open. Because layout-conditioned generation (§) and text-to-3D (§) inherit whatever relational competence this prior provides, the limitation is foundational rather than cosmetic. Fine structure is a second gap: legible text, hands, and faces still fail in otherwise strong models and appear to need architectural or data-specific fixes rather than scale alone.

Evaluation reliability is the third. Automatic scores correlate imperfectly with human judgment precisely on the compositional, counting, and spatial-relation prompts that matter here; judge-based metrics close part of the gap but add rubric sensitivity and judge-version drift, so headline numbers across papers are not directly comparable. As GenEval and T2I-CompBench become standard, their prompts risk leaking into web-scraped training corpora, in which case high scores increasingly measure memorization rather than capability; periodic refresh of held-out prompts, blinded judges, and explicit train/test decontamination are the obvious countermeasures and are not yet routine.

Societal concerns follow the data. Models inherit demographic bias from their corpora and will produce unsafe content on request; prompt classifiers, safety filters, and fine-tuning on curated subsets reduce but do not remove the problem, and photorealistic synthesis raises misinformation and intellectual-property questions that watermarking and data curation address only in part. The extension of these priors along the time axis, where identity and motion must stay consistent across frames, is the subject of §; the next two subsections stay in the image plane and ask how the prior can be made to obey spatial constraints and local edits.

2D spatial-aware image generation synthesizes images that are faithful not only to a text prompt but to explicit spatial constraints in the image plane: where objects appear, how large they are, what shape they take, and how they relate to one another (left of, on, behind). The constraint may be a set of boxes or a scene layout, an instance or semantic mask, an edge or sketch map, a depth or normal map, 2D keypoints, a scene graph, or a phrase bound to a region, and the pipelines that honor it are almost all diffusion models augmented with a conditioning pathway or a guidance term. The tension that organizes the subfield is three-way: adherence to hard constraints against perceptual realism and diversity, and both against compositionality when many small or occluding objects carry discrete relations. Depth and normal maps enter here as structural guides for occlusion ordering and surface orientation, not as metric measurements; recovering true distance belongs to reconstruction (§).

Interactive constraints supplied by dragging handles during generation belong to the editing regime of §.

Two axes organize the methods: the conditioning modality (what kind of structural input
c
is consumed) and the injection mechanism (how
⁢ κ
( c )

G θ
). They are nearly independent. One mechanism, a ControlNet-style side branch, serves canny edges, pose skeletons, depth, and segmentation alike, and one modality, bounding boxes, is served by side branches, grounded cross-attention, or inference-time attention shaping, so the design space is a matrix of (modality
×
mechanism) cells rather than a list of monolithic methods. Figure draws the five mechanisms on one backbone silhouette.

Dense pixel-level scaffolds supply a value at every location, which makes them the easiest channels to follow and the most restrictive on creativity. Instance and semantic masks drive region-conditioned synthesis, with MultiDiffusion [] offering a training-free protocol that samples jointly over overlapping mask windows; edges, sketches, and line art, popularized by the canny and soft-edge variants of ControlNet [] and the edge head of T2I-Adapter [], fix only the location of intensity discontinuities and leave texture and appearance to the prompt; depth and normal maps, served by ControlNet’s depth variant, impose coarse occlusion ordering and surface orientation without requiring a metric reconstruction. Coordinate-level scaffolds drop to per-region or per-point supervision. Boxes with labels are the most studied channel, a set of
( box , label )
tuples fixing location and rough scale, with LayoutDiffusion [], LayoutLLM [], and the open-set GLIGEN [] as representatives; 2D keypoints (typically human pose) are sparser still, a handful of joint coordinates, injected through ControlNet or handled by GLIGEN as a special case of grounding. Discrete symbolic structure carries no pixel- or coordinate-level information at all, and the model must map it onto the image plane itself. Scene graphs reach back to the sg2im line of [ ] and re-emerged in the diffusion era through LLM-emitted layouts, as in LayoutLLM, where the graph is first decoded into a coordinate-level layout; region phrases and referring expressions bind a text span to a box, mask, or free-form polygon and are served by GLIGEN’s grounded cross-attention and by phrase-grounding heads attached to SD and SDXL [].

Five mechanism families cover the literature; production pipelines routinely stack a side branch for dense geometric channels, an adapter for style or a reference image, and inference-time guidance to sharpen adherence on adversarial prompts.

Side-branch controllers. The backbone weights stay frozen and an auxiliary branch mirroring the encoder half of the base U-Net is trained, connected through zero-convolution layers whose weights are initialized to zero so that the augmented model reproduces the base model exactly at the start of training and degrades gracefully if the branch is poorly tuned. ControlNet [] is the prototype and the first widely adopted retrofit pathway for non-text structural control: the condition (a canny edge map, an OpenPose skeleton, a depth or normal map, a segmentation mask, or a scribble) is encoded by the side branch in parallel with the noisy latent and injected into the base U-Net through additive residual connections at each scale. One branch is trained per modality on labeled image–condition pairs, which produced a library of plug-in controllers for SD 1.5 and SDXL [] that compose with prompt conditioning at inference time without retraining the backbone; most later designs either shrink this recipe or fold it into a unified adapter library.

Lightweight adapters. Where the side branch spends capacity (half a U-Net per modality), T2I-Adapter [], developed concurrently with the same goal of plug-in control over a frozen backbone, spends as little as possible: a few residual blocks per modality whose multi-scale features are added directly into the corresponding encoder stages. Several adapters can be combined at inference, an image conditioned simultaneously on an OpenPose skeleton, a depth map, and a color palette with a scalar weight on each, so the adapter is preferred for multi-channel fusion and fast iteration, and the side branch where maximum single-channel fidelity matters.

Grounded cross-attention. Side branches and adapters run an external pathway alongside the backbone; the next two families intervene inside its attention stack. GLIGEN [] inserts a new gated self-attention layer between the existing self-attention and cross-attention of each U-Net transformer block; the layer attends jointly over the visual tokens and a set of grounding tokens that encode each
( phrase , box )
pair, a learned scalar gate controls how strongly the grounding signal enters the residual stream, and only the new layer is trained, so the network falls back to ungrounded behavior when no constraint is supplied. The problem it solves is complementary to the side branch: not how to inject a dense pixel-level scaffold, but how to introduce open-set symbolic grounding (any category named in text, localized by a box, keypoints, or a reference image) into a frozen T2I backbone, with several grounding channels interleaved within one mechanism.

Layout-aware cross-attention. LayoutDiffusion [] is the dense-supervised cousin of grounded attention: rather than gating a new layer onto a frozen backbone, it co-trains a layout-aware cross-attention block end to end for layout-to-image (L2I) generation specifically. A structured layout, a set of
( box , class label )
tuples, becomes a sequence of region tokens fused with the noisy latent at every denoising step, and an explicit object–scene factorization models global scene context separately from per-object features so that object identity, scale, and pairwise relations survive in cluttered scenes. It reports stronger layout IoU and relation satisfaction than ControlNet or T2I-Adapter on multi-object COCO benchmarks, at the cost of being specialized to box-and-label input rather than the broader modality library.

Inference-time guidance. The fifth family adds no parameters and modifies only sampling. BoxDiff [] is the canonical training-free spatial controller: it shapes the cross-attention maps so that activations of box-localized prompt tokens concentrate inside their boxes while the backbone stays untouched. MultiDiffusion [] fuses overlapping mask windows at sampling time, and composing scores from several conditional models or tuning the classifier-free guidance scale per region are related strategies. Because nothing is retrained, these methods suit rapid prototyping, backbones whose weights are unavailable for fine-tuning, and per-prompt sharpening on top of the trained mechanisms above.

para.p:
Two things change relative to §. The ground truth is a structural annotation (a layout, a mask, a keypoint set) rather than a reference image, so reconstruction-style metrics give way to adherence metrics that score how closely the generated image honors
c
; and every channel admits its own adherence metric, so a meaningful report combines a channel-specific score with the realism and alignment scores inherited from the previous subsection.

Spatial-aware models are typically trained on corpora that pair images with rich structural annotations: COCO Captions [] for layouts and captions; ADE20K [] (
20
K images,
150
classes) for semantic and instance masks; Visual Genome [] for object boxes, attributes, and pairwise relations supporting scene-graph conditioning; RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg [] for phrase grounding; and PhraseCut [] for region-prompt mask supervision. Additional structure (canny edges, depth, normals, OpenPose skeletons) is typically derived on the fly from these base corpora by running pretrained predictors over each image, producing the paired image–condition data on which ControlNet-style and adapter-style pipelines are trained.

Most of the suites surveyed in § (Table ) include axes that probe spatial-aware generation directly and serve as its primary out-of-the-box benchmarks. GenEval [] exposes a position subset that scores whether two objects appear in a specified relation (left of, above); T2I-CompBench [] provides explicit spatial and non-spatial relationship categories with BLIP-VQA and UniDet scoring; HRS-Bench [] includes a spatial skill among its thirteen; GenAI-Bench [] offers compositional prompts on which spatial relations are a frequent failure of CLIP-based scoring; and WISE [] measures knowledge-grounded location accuracy. Beyond these, the L2I literature reports task-specific evaluations on COCO layouts: detection-based AP for box-localized objects alongside FID and CLIPScore.

Layout adherence is box IoU between the conditioning layout and the boxes recovered by a frozen detector on
^ y
, often with per-object center distance; mask adherence uses mask IoU and boundary
F
-score against the conditioning mask; edge and sketch adherence report recall (sometimes precision) of edges re-extracted from
^ y
; geometry adherence reports depth RMSE and normal angular error where ground-truth geometry exists; pose adherence reports keypoint reprojection error or PCK; and relational adherence reports relation-satisfaction accuracy and per-entity object AP for scene-graph and phrase-grounded settings. These numbers do not aggregate: averaging layout IoU with mask IoU has no operational meaning, since the two live on different scales and reward different shape regimes, and most papers report a different subset of them, which is the main obstacle to cross-paper comparison in this subfield.
Spatial-aware T2I inherits the compositionality and evaluation problems of § and sharpens them.

Faithful multi-object composition. Crowded scenes with many small or partially occluded objects and hard relations (support, containment, depth ordering) fail in three recognizable ways: attention dilution, in which a prompt token’s cross-attention spreads across the canvas and no object is well localized; attribute leakage, in which color, material, or count attaches to the wrong object (the canonical “red cube on a blue sphere” confusion); and object dropping, in which small or rare entities in a multi-object layout are simply omitted. On GenEval the position and counting subsets remain the weakest axes across SD 1.5, SDXL, and SD 3 []. Remedies work at three levels: Attend-and-Excite [] reweights cross-attention at inference so that every subject token is strongly activated somewhere in the canvas; StructureDiffusion [] uses prompt syntax to constrain attention structure without training; and LLM-emitted layouts, LayoutGPT [] and the multimodal-LLM-driven RPG of [ ] , plan a structured layout from the free-form prompt and hand it to an L2I renderer. Whether the gap closes through a stronger compositional prior in the backbone or through planning as a separate stage is unresolved, and the two are not exclusive.

Constraint satisfaction against creativity and diversity. Turning guidance up tightens adherence until, past a model-dependent threshold, edges oversharpen, textures flatten, and variation across seeds collapses; the same curve appears for the ControlNet conditioning weight, GLIGEN’s gating strength, and the classifier-free guidance scale, leaving practitioners to tune two or three knobs at once. Annealing the control weight along the denoising trajectory, per-region or per-token guidance scales, and down-weighting guidance where the base model is already confident are the current responses; how to expose such schedules to end users without overwhelming the interface is open. Chaining spatial-aware generation with repeated local edits adds a drift problem of its own, treated in §.

Geometry-aware realism in 2D. Depth and normal conditioning fix coarse occlusion but introduce their own artifacts: boundary banding where a sharp depth discontinuity meets a smooth gradient in the generated image, scale ambiguity because a monocular depth map carries no absolute scale and two objects at the same depth value can be rendered at incompatible physical sizes, and lighting incoherence because the map fixes geometry but not the light field, so shadows disagree with the implied surface orientations. Better estimators are the first lever, with the diffusion-prior Marigold [] producing sharper and more globally consistent depth than CNN baselines and Depth Anything [] staying robust on out-of-distribution conditioning images; differentiable geometry proxies that translate depth into shading constraints are the second, explored at the boundary with full 3D synthesis (§) but not yet integrated into general T2I backbones. Region grounding also changes the safety picture, since a harmful edit can be confined to a footprint that whole-image forensics miss; that concern belongs to editing and is taken up in §.

2D spatial inpainting & editing modifies an image inside a specified region while leaving the rest intact: filling holes and occlusions, removing or inserting objects, changing attributes (color, material, texture, text), adjusting layout, or harmonizing pasted content with its new background. The intent arrives as a mask, a structural hint (edges, sketches), a geometry proxy (depth, normals), or a natural-language instruction, and the tensions are between local editability and global consistency of lighting, perspective, and shadow, between constraint adherence and realism, and between semantic plausibility and identity preservation for person- or product-centric edits. Editing holds the model to its strongest geometric account: the unedited region of
I
supplies ground-truth pixels that any plausible edit must respect, exposing failure modes that pure synthesis can hide, among them color drift, lighting reflow, identity loss, and attribute leakage across the mask boundary.

Object-level edits treat the region as an object whose identity or embedding in the scene is the unit of change: insertion with harmonization of color, grain, lighting, shadows, and reflections; attribute and appearance editing that changes material or style while preserving identity (garments, products, logos); and exemplar-guided transfer that drives content or style from a reference patch. Interactive workflows replace declarative constraints with actions taken at edit time: point- or handle-based reshaping, and multi-round, multi-region sessions in which stability across rounds is itself the requirement. The metrics appropriate to each are collected in Benchmarks below.

para.p:
Masked latent denoising. The most direct realization of Eq. () runs the diffusion sampler only inside
M
while clamping the latent outside
M
to a noise-perturbed copy of
z in
at every step. RePaint [] does this with a pretrained, unconditional DDPM and no retraining, replacing the known-region pixels with a forward-noised sample of the input at each reverse step and adding a resampling schedule that re-injects noise periodically so the in-fill can re-harmonize with its context over several rounds. Blended Diffusion [] made the same scheme text-driven by interleaving a CLIP-guided gradient step that steers the content inside
M
toward a target prompt with the context-clamping step outside it, the first widely cited text-guided local editor. LaMa [] predates the diffusion line and is instead a feed-forward inpainter whose fast Fourier convolutions give every layer an image-wide receptive field, a Fourier-domain inductive bias that stays robust on the very large holes that defeat purely local CNN backbones. Region-aware noise schedules and classifier-free guidance are standard add-ons, and ControlNet-inpaint and the inpainting variants of T2I-Adapter (§) compose with masked denoising by supplying the inside-
M
condition.

Inversion + rewrite. A complementary strategy first recovers the noise trajectory that the model would have used to generate
I
(inversion) and then re-runs the reverse process under an edited prompt while reusing or swapping the attention maps of the original (rewrite). Prompt-to-Prompt [] reuses or reweights source cross-attention maps during generation under the edited prompt, which preserves spatial structure while changing selected semantic content; for a real image an inversion step first supplies a suitable noise trajectory. Imagic [] jointly optimizes the text embedding and lightly fine-tunes the model to reconstruct
I
, then interpolates the embedding toward the target prompt, preserving identity-level features (faces, garments) under non-rigid edits. Null-Text Inversion [] fixes the practical failure that plain DDIM inversion drifts away from
I
under classifier-free guidance, by optimizing the null-text embeddings used in the inverse pass so that exact reconstruction holds at ordinary guidance scales. The family needs no full backbone fine-tune for Prompt-to-Prompt or Null-Text and dominates attribute, style, and structure-preserving real-image edits.

Instruction-tuned editing. A third family avoids inversion entirely by retraining a diffusion editor on paired (before, instruction, after) triplets, mapping
I
directly to
^ I
from a natural-language instruction with no explicit mask. InstructPix2Pix [] built its corpus by pairing GPT-3-generated edit instructions with Prompt-to-Prompt edits of Stable Diffusion samples and fine-tuned Stable Diffusion on the triplets, so that at inference the user supplies only
( I , instruction )
and the editor localizes the change itself. MagicBrush [] replaced the synthetic data with about 10K manually annotated real-image edits across multi-turn sessions, yielding both a stronger supervised editor and the standard instruction-editing test set. Emu Edit [] trained a single model on a heterogeneous mixture of recognition (segmentation, detection) and generation (insertion, removal, style change) tasks with learned task embeddings that route each input, and leads its own benchmark on precision and instruction following. Instruction editors are the most user-friendly mechanism, no mask and no inversion, at the cost of large supervised retraining.

Exemplar / reference-guided editing. A visual exemplar, an example image or patch encoding the desired content or style, replaces the textual instruction and enters through an auxiliary cross-attention pathway beside the standard text conditioning. Paint-by-Example [] fine-tunes Stable Diffusion to fill
M
with the content of an exemplar whose identity is encoded by a CLIP image encoder, with strong exemplar augmentation (cropping, color jitter) at training time to prevent copy-paste behavior and force semantic rather than pixel-level transfer. IP-Adapter [] generalizes this into a plug-in reference channel: a lightweight decoupled cross-attention head consumes a CLIP image embedding of the exemplar and is inserted into a frozen SD or SDXL backbone, so that any number of reference images can be combined with text prompts and with structural adapters such as ControlNet at inference time. It is the standard route for subject personalization and style transfer when the desired content is hard to describe in words.

Drag-based latent optimization. The most interactive family takes user-supplied (source point, target point) pairs and iteratively optimizes the latent so that the features at each source point migrate to the corresponding target while a locality regularizer pins the latent outside the user-marked region. DragGAN [] introduced the recipe on a StyleGAN backbone: a motion-supervision loss tracks the source feature and pulls it toward the target by gradient descent in the
W +
latent space, and a point-tracking step re-localizes the moved feature at each iteration to prevent drift. DragDiffusion [] ported the recipe to the LDM latent space, running a per-timestep latent-update loop together with an identity-preserving LoRA fine-tune of the U-Net so that both the dragged subject and the unmarked context survive. Both are inference-time optimizers with latency proportional to the number of drag iterations, and no other family yet offers the same directness of spatial control.

Read across the five families, the mechanisms track the generative substrate: feed-forward inpainters such as LaMa gave way to inversion-based diffusion editors (Prompt-to-Prompt, Imagic), which in turn yielded to supervised instruction-tuned editors (InstructPix2Pix, Emu Edit) as paired data became available at scale. Orthogonal to that migration, the structural conditioning interfaces of § compose with every mechanism here, so a production pipeline pairs a mechanism with a structural channel rather than choosing one: Blended Diffusion with ControlNet-depth for geometry-aware text-guided edits, or IP-Adapter with DragDiffusion for exemplar-driven drag edits.

Editing is evaluated in two regimes: reference-based, where a held-out ground-truth region exists (holes synthesized over real images), and reference-free, where only constraint satisfaction and human preference are available (instruction editing). No single suite covers both, so the field keeps a small library of task-specific benchmarks next to the holistic T2I suites of §.

Inpainting draws on Places2 [] and Paris StreetView for scene-level masks, DIV2K for high-resolution patches, and the COCO / ADE20K mask supervision of § []. Constraint-driven local synthesis reuses the structural channels of the previous subsection, RefCOCO / RefCOCO+ / RefCOCOg [] and PhraseCut [] for referring-expression masks, SA-1B masks [], and COCO edge and depth predictions, with the convention that the mask is supplied or derived from the expression; geometry-guided editing adds depth and normal supervision from NYUv2 [], Replica [], and synthetic corpora, and insertion with harmonization uses composite datasets such as iHarmony4. Instruction editing has its own data ecology: the synthetic InstructPix2Pix corpus of Prompt-to-Prompt-generated triplets, the manually annotated MagicBrush triplets [], and the multi-task Emu Edit training mixture [].

The holistic suites of § (Table ) carry over in part: T2I-CompBench [] and GenAI-Bench [] score the attribute and compositional fidelity that edited images must also satisfy, and HEIM [] includes alignment and quality axes that apply to edits. The dedicated suites are EditBench [], released with Imagen Editor, a curated set of text-guided inpainting prompts over object, attribute, and scene categories that serves as the standard evaluation for text-driven mask inpainting; the MagicBrush test set [],
1 , 053
manually annotated single- and multi-turn triplets, which is the standard for instruction-tuned editors; and the Emu Edit benchmark [], which extends instruction editing to per-task subsets (insertion, removal, style change, color change, global change). Drag-based methods evaluate on small custom test sets curated by [ ] and [ ] ; a community-wide drag-editing benchmark has not yet emerged.

Reconstruction quality (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS against ground truth, with FID / KID for diverse-completion settings) is defined only where held-out content exists. Region adherence uses mask-restricted CLIPScore or region-level VQAScore to ask whether the edit honors the prompt inside
M
; edit locality measures
ℓ 1
or LPIPS outside
M
against
I
, lower being better; harmonization is scored by color-statistic divergence, shadow-direction consistency, and the rate at which an off-the-shelf forgery detector flags the composite; identity preservation uses feature-cosine similarity over face or landmark regions for people and CLIP-image similarity for products and characters; and instruction following is paired accuracy, whether
^ I
honors the instruction better than
I
, judged by human raters or by a VLM over a structured rubric, as is now standard on MagicBrush and Emu Edit. Change inside
M
and preservation outside it are reported together; a method that wins on one and loses on the other has not solved the task.
Several problems are specific to editing an existing image.

Structure-faithful hallucination in large holes. Large irregular holes and rare structures remain the hardest case: inpainters tile a salient local texture across the hole instead of synthesizing appropriate content, straight lines, perspective cues, and silhouettes break at the mask seam, and in-fills that are locally plausible contradict the global scene (a patch of grass inside a room). Quality degrades sharply with hole size. LaMa’s image-wide Fourier convolutions and RePaint’s resampling schedule (§) are the established responses; retrieval-augmented priors, which search a paired corpus for candidate completions and use them as soft conditioning, are an emerging one at the intersection of editing and retrieval.

Edit locality against drift across rounds. A single well-calibrated edit does not guarantee a stable session. Across rounds the unedited background shifts in white balance or saturation (color drift), shadows and highlights migrate as if the edit had changed the global illumination (lighting reflow), and salient textures from the edited region reappear in nearby unedited regions through attention leakage (texture replication); the errors compound even when each round individually meets its locality budget. Hard attention masking that confines non-edit tokens to
M
, mask-aware noise schedules that anneal noise inside
M
only, and edit-history-aware sampling that conditions on the trajectory of prior edits are the active mitigations. Inversion-based editors (Null-Text Inversion [], Imagic []) carry a variant of the problem: any residual reconstruction error in the inverted trajectory leaks into the edit and accumulates.

Harmonization under complex illumination. Inserted content betrays itself when the host scene has structured light: its shadow disagrees with the dominant light direction recoverable from the scene, there is no interreflection between the object and adjacent surfaces, and its albedo is tone-mapped inconsistently with the host, producing the cut-and-paste look that off-the-shelf forgery detectors flag. Differentiable rendering proxies that turn depth and normals into shading constraints and back-propagate harmonization losses into the editor, illumination maps as an additional conditioning channel, and explicit shadow-synthesis modules are being explored; integration with the 3D-aware methods of § is the natural next step and remains nascent.

Language grounding and safety. Region-level instructions must be grounded reliably: an edit aimed at one object spills onto neighbors with similar attributes, spatial referring expressions are misparsed (“the left cup” lands on the right one), and mildly perturbed instructions produce large deviations in the edit trajectory. Borrowing GLIGEN’s gated grounding [] (§) to confine edit attention, and using LLM-emitted layouts to harden the grounding before the edit is applied, are the current responses. The same precision cuts the other way for safety. A harmful edit (an identity swap inside one bounding box, watermark removal inside one mask) can be confined to a footprint that whole-image forensic detectors miss; large generative models reproduce individual training images under targeted prompting [], which becomes acute when the training set contains copyrighted artwork or identifiable faces and motivates artist-side defenses such as Glaze [], which perturbs source artworks so that downstream fine-tunes mimic a different style; and most pipelines still lack robust per-image watermarking, so a photograph with a small synthesized region cannot be told from a wholly synthetic one. Watermarking, region-aware safety filters, and licensing frameworks for the underlying corpora are all needed, and none is settled.

Evaluation under plausibility ambiguity. Ground-truth pixels are often not the only plausible completion: a removed pedestrian leaves a hole that could contain road, curb, or shadow, and any reconstruction metric that compares against one ground truth over-penalizes good alternatives, while PSNR and SSIM rate sharp but contextually wrong in-fills highly. The field is converging on paired evaluation, asking whether
^ I
honors the instruction better than
I
under a held-out judge, now standard on MagicBrush [] and Emu Edit []; the judge-prompt sensitivity and benchmark-contamination caveats of § apply here as well.

Scalability and interactive latency. Inversion-based methods store cross-attention activations at every timestep, multi-step sampling at
4
K and above scales with image area for standard U-Net backbones, and drag editors run an inner optimization loop per operation, so interactive editing lags behind the user’s hand by hundreds of milliseconds. Consistency-style distillation [] (§) compresses the reverse trajectory to a handful of steps, memory-efficient adaptive patching runs the denoiser only in a window around
M
, and progressive-refinement schedules return a coarse preview within a perceptual-latency budget and refine in the background. Closing the gap to the responsiveness of a photo editor is increasingly a systems problem shared with production T2I inference stacks.

The 3D spatial reconstruction and generation encompasses the tasks that turn images, video, sensor readings, or high-level prompts into an explicit 3D representation (a textured mesh, a signed-distance or occupancy field, a neural radiance field, or a 3D Gaussian field) of an object, a scene, or a complete navigable environment. Whereas § taught a 2D semantic-to-pixel before honor spatial structure on the image plane, this section lifts that prior off the plane and into the volumetric substrate on which embodied perception, simulation, and interaction ultimately operate. This is where appearance and geometry are forced into a single, view-consistent representation: a model must not only produce plausible pixels but place matter correctly in
R 3
so that the result can be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints, physically simulated, navigated, and edited. It is the bridge between the flat generative priors of § and the embodied world models, simulators, and digital twins that consume 3D structure downstream.

The five subsections are organized by the direction and source of the map into a shared 3D-representation space
R
. § starts with a single asset: 3D object synthesis turns the 2D prior of § into a volumetric generator through 3D-native training, score distillation, multi-view lifting, or feed-forward reconstruction. § scales that generator to a structured scene of placed objects and a room envelope. § reverses the direction: reconstruction recovers a representation faithful to sensor observations, and meets synthesis exactly where the observations run out. § routes through a 360-degree panorama as a structured 2D intermediate that is then lifted to 3D, and § closes the loop by editing an existing representation under user control.

3D object synthesis generates a complete, usable 3D asset (geometry and, optionally, appearance) from text, a single image, or a sparse set of views. Where reconstruction recovers an object consistent with given observations, synthesis additionally asks for plausible completion of what was never observed, for generative diversity, and for usability in downstream graphics and embodied pipelines (e.g., , game engines, simulators, manipulation); the output is a textured mesh, a radiance field, or a set of 3D Gaussians depending on which of fidelity, editability, rendering speed, and toolchain compatibility matters most. It is also the point at which the semantic-to-pixel prior of § (the conditional latent sampler
G θ
of Eq. ()) becomes a semantic-to-3D prior
G θ
3D

The unlocking factor was the arrival of Objaverse and Objaverse-XL []. LRM [] and its follow-ups [] show that large transformers trained purely with rendering losses capture object geometry and texture in detail and generalize to unseen images, and a parallel line introduces compact 3D-native latent codes [] whose distribution a latent diffusion model can learn; TRELLIS [], CLAY [], HiGS-RGBN [], and Hunyuan3D [] build on this to bring generated assets close to production grade while keeping the open-vocabulary reach that the SDS family pioneered.

Two design choices cut across the four paradigms. The representation
R
(mesh, SDF, voxel, triplane, NeRF, 3DGS, or structured latent) is largely independent of the paradigm: SDS has been run on NeRFs and on 3DGS, feed-forward reconstructors output triplanes, meshes, or Gaussians, and latent-diffusion stacks decode to almost any explicit representation through a learned VAE. So is the conditioning modality: the same backbone takes text, a single image, or sparse views by changing only the encoder
κ
and the camera-pose embedding, and production systems chain them (image-to-3D conditioned on a text-to-image preview). The succession of paradigms itself tracks the accumulation of supervision at each level, from 3D-native corpora to 2D image–text pairs to Zero-1-to-3-style multi-view priors to Objaverse-XL-scale 3D, with the most recent industrial systems sitting in the fourth paradigm while inheriting the multi-view-consistency tricks of the third.
Evaluation draws on object-scale training corpora, on dedicated benchmark suites that curate prompts and human ratings, and on metrics that probe alignment, geometry, and appearance separately.

para.p: Object-scale 3D corpora drive the feed-forward and latent-diffusion paradigms; Table lists the ones most commonly used, and Figure shows representative Objaverse-XL assets. They span the classical CAD repository ShapeNet [], category-bounded real-world scans with accurate geometry and PBR textures (Google Scanned Objects [], OmniObject3D [] with dense multi-view imagery), the open-vocabulary web-scraped Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [] that unlocked the fourth paradigm, and G-Objaverse [], which adds text-driven synthesized assets between the two.

para.p: Recent benchmarks have moved to multi-dimensional assessment beyond plain text–image alignment. GT23D-Bench [] curates a high-fidelity dataset and a suite of 3D-aware metrics spanning alignment and visual quality; MATE-3D [] provides designed prompt categories with large-scale human annotations across several perceptual dimensions and introduces HyperScore as a learned evaluator; T23D-QA [] adopts a question-answer protocol that scores geometry, texture, and alignment independently; and Gen3DEval [] fine-tunes a vision-language model for 3D quality assessment, scoring text fidelity, appearance, and surface quality from rendered surface normals. Together with the 3D-relevant subsets of the 2D suites collected in § (Table ), they form the de facto evaluation protocol for 3D object synthesis.

Because an asset is judged from many viewpoints and under different downstream uses, evaluation reports complementary metrics along three axes. Text-3D alignment renders multi-view images from the asset and measures text–image similarity with CLIP-like encoders, aggregated across views (mean, worst-case, or view-consistency variants); pure CLIP alignment can be misled by texture “shortcuts” and does not guarantee geometric correctness, which motivates the 3D-aware alignment scores of GT23D-Bench [] and learned evaluators such as HyperScore []. Geometry quality is measured against ground-truth shapes, where they exist, by Chamfer Distance (CD) [], F-score at varying thresholds, normal consistency, and volumetric IoU for watertight meshes; for text-to-3D without ground truth it falls back on multi-view depth and normal consistency, silhouette consistency, and learned 3D-quality predictors. Appearance and multi-view consistency are measured by perceptual distances (LPIPS) between rendered views and references where available, by view-consistency measures (variance across views under fixed lighting and camera trajectories), and by human studies, which recent benchmarks collect as multi-dimensional ratings to calibrate the automatic metrics [].

The paradigm succession of § shows up in two measurable quantities. Generation time has fallen by about three orders of magnitude: DreamFusion [] needs roughly 1.5 hours per asset and Magic3D [] about 40 minutes, whereas LRM [] reconstructs a shape in about 5 seconds and InstantMesh [] completes image-to-3D in around 10 seconds. Image-to-3D geometry is now routinely scored on Google Scanned Objects [] with Chamfer Distance (lower is better) and F-score at
= τ 0.2
(higher is better), where InstantMesh [] reaches CD
≈
0.18
and FS
≈
0.88

Coarse text-to-3D alignment, by contrast, is saturated: CLIP-style scores no longer separate the strongest systems, so Hunyuan3D 2.0 [] reports ULIP- and Uni3D-based image- and text-to-shape similarity backed by a study in which 50 participants rated 300 unselected results, and learned evaluators (HyperScore on MATE-3D [], T23D-QA []) score geometry and texture on separate axes. The reconstruction metrics carry their own caveat: CD and F-score saturate on coarse geometry and can reward visually plausible but physically thin assets, so reported gains are credible mainly where geometric, perceptual, and human ratings agree. Commercial text- and image-to-3D services now ship these capabilities with PBR export to game engines, alongside research systems such as Meta 3D Gen [] and the open-vocabulary 3D-native-latent systems CLAY [], TRELLIS [], and Hunyuan3D [].

Four problems remain open, and they depend on one another: the multi-view consistency of the asset, the representation it lands in, whether progress on either can be measured reliably, and the data that ultimately drives all three.

paragraph.title: Multi-View and 3D Consistency under Open-Vocabulary Prompts.

para.p: Enforcing consistent geometry and texture across viewpoints while preserving fine detail remains difficult in all four paradigms, and the failures have names. The Janus artifact renders both the front and the back of an object as a frontal face, most acutely in SDS pipelines, where the 2D prior cannot disambiguate camera direction; view drift makes adjacent views of a multi-view stack disagree on geometry, a residual concern in Zero-1-to-3-style cascades that SyncDreamer’s cross-view attention and Zero123++’s tiled six-view trick only partly remove; and texture seams appear where neighboring views’ color and lighting cannot be merged into a globally coherent UV map, a persistent weakness of feed-forward reconstructors. These failures motivate 3D-native backbones with structured latents [] that share parameters across views by construction, and benchmarks that score multi-view consistency rather than a single rendered view [].

paragraph.title: Representation Trade-offs between Fidelity, Editability, and Deployability.

para.p:
Even a consistent asset must land somewhere a downstream tool can consume, and the choice of representation is not neutral. Meshes with UV/PBR textures are what game engines and simulators want but lose detail to discretization; radiance fields and Gaussians give high visual fidelity and fast rendering but require conversion, which introduces its own failures: topology breakage during marching-cubes-style meshing, baked illumination that fuses lighting into albedo when converting from a NeRF or 3DGS, and texture bleeding across UV seams. The response is unified latent representations that decode to several formats [], so that a single generator serves diverse downstream requirements and the choice of
R
is deferred to inference.

paragraph.title: Scalable, Reliable Evaluation and Human-Aligned Metrics.

para.p: These representation choices complicate evaluation, because the metric panel a paper reports tends to depend on which format its generator targets, and the automatic metrics remain imperfect for geometry plausibility and asset usability. CLIP-style alignment is fooled by texture shortcuts that ignore the underlying shape; Chamfer Distance saturates on coarse geometry while penalizing semantically irrelevant fine detail; and LPIPS on rendered views cannot distinguish a physically plausible asset from a visually plausible cardboard cut-out. Multi-dimensional evaluators trained on large human-annotation sets (e.g., , HyperScore on MATE-3D []) and diagnostic benchmarks (e.g., , GT23D-Bench [], T23D-QA []) that score alignment, geometry, and texture on independent axes are the current answer, so that progress on one axis is no longer masked by averaging.

Underlying consistency, representation, and evaluation alike is the supply of training data and the industrial scale at which it can be exploited. Large-scale corpora such as Objaverse-XL [] and industrial-scale systems such as Hunyuan3D [] and Meta 3D Gen [] point toward high-resolution, engine-ready assets with controllable materials, relightable textures, and post-processing for watertightness and topology. The question has shifted from whether a paradigm can be trained at scale, which the fourth paradigm has settled, to which slice of the 3D-asset distribution the available corpora still under-represent: articulated objects, semi-transparent or refractive materials, and topologically non-trivial assemblies are visibly thinner in current open corpora than in production pipelines, and closing this gap is the explicit target of recent industrial releases.

Scene-level synthesis extends 3D generation from a single asset
∈ r R
to an entire environment: a clutter of objects whose positions, orientations, and pairwise relations together compose a navigable room or open-world scene. Where § models the conditional distribution of one object given a prompt, scene synthesis must jointly model (i) a variable number of objects, (ii) their global
⁢ SE
( 3 )
placements, (iii) their pairwise spatial and functional relations, and (iv) the envelope geometry (floor, walls, ceiling) that closes the scene; the output is a structured set rather than a vector in
R

The result must be navigable, not only renderable, which makes the problem harder than object synthesis along three axes at once: geometric coherence across the clutter, semantic consistency between related objects, and view generalization along an
⁢ SE
( 3 )

Four families answer it: layout- and scene-graph-conditioned generators that produce the structured set from a symbolic prior; view-to-3D synthesizers that regress or sample a continuous radiance or Gaussian field from sparse calibrated views; view-to-view synthesizers that skip the explicit 3D representation and learn a conditional map from observed to novel views; and video-model-based synthesizers that treat a pretrained video diffusion model as an implicit 3D prior with the camera trajectory as an additional conditioning channel.

para.p:
A major line of research generates 3D environments from high-level structural priors such as layouts
L

SceneFormer [] explored autoregressive modeling of room layouts and furniture placement, and DiffuScene [] introduced diffusion over object arrangements, improving realism and diversity. Recent work adds language and visual reasoning for compositional control: LayoutGPT [] plans the layout with an LLM before neural scene construction, and LayoutVLM [] optimizes layout consistency under multimodal alignment. Scene-graph approaches (GraphDreamer [], CommonScenes [], EchoScene []) use relational reasoning to keep placements plausible, and InstructScene [] adds natural-language conditions for controllable scene creation. Beyond indoor settings, CityCraft [] scales layout synthesis to the city level, and GALA3D [] couples layout-guided diffusion with Gaussian-based rendering for photorealistic multi-object environments.

The second paradigm trades the explicit structured set for a continuous 3D representation, recovering the scene as a radiance field or 3D Gaussian collection from sparse calibrated views; the scene tuple collapses into a single field,

This scales the multi-view-and-lift recipe of § from one asset to a full scene by replacing the per-object reconstructor with a scene-scale one. Deterministic regressors such as PixelNeRF [], PixelSplat [], DepthSplat [], and MVSplat [] / MVSplat360 [] stay strictly faithful to the input views and are reconstruction methods, treated in §. The generative variant samples the field instead: DreamScene [] introduces a diffusion prior over Gaussian fields for text-conditioned scene creation, and Generative 3DGS [] generates 3D Gaussians for scenes with video priors.
The third paradigm skips the explicit 3D representation altogether and formulates novel view synthesis as a direct conditional 2D-to-2D map from observed to target views,

Math.text: (hat@(I)) _ (pi ^ *) similar-to p _ theta * conditional@(I _ (pi ^ *), list@(((set@(open-interval@(I _ v, pi _ v))) _ (v = 1)) ^ V, pi ^ *))

Regression-based approaches learn a deterministic map: SRT [] encodes the scene into latent tokens that support interpolation and extrapolation across viewpoints, and LVSM [] predicts novel views with a large feed-forward transformer and minimal 3D inductive bias. Generative approaches model the conditional distribution over unseen views, which permits stochastic synthesis under ambiguity and large viewpoint changes: Photoconsistent-NVS [] and SEVA [] use diffusion to improve diversity and robustness along extended camera trajectories, and CausNVS [] generates views autoregressively and causally, modeling inter-view dependencies explicitly to stay coherent across complex viewpoint transitions.

The fourth paradigm adds temporal coherence to the viewpoint variety of the view-to-view family by exploiting large video generation models as spatiotemporal priors; the scene tuple is materialized as a frame sequence,
