para.p: The four paradigms draw on different training corpora and report on different metric panels, each inherited from a precursor task.

Table lists the corpora in use. Layout-conditioned methods rely overwhelmingly on 3D-FRONT [], usually combined with its companion 3D-FUTURE [] furniture library for instance-level geometry. View-based methods (P2 / P3) draw on real-world scans of residential interiors (ScanNet [], Matterport3D []), on photorealistic synthetic corpora with ground-truth depth and normals (Hypersim []), and on Replica [] for compact high-fidelity indoor benchmarks. Video-model-based methods (P4) inherit the web-scale supervision of their underlying video prior, far larger than any 3D corpus but without explicit 3D supervision, supplemented by camera-pose-annotated subsets distilled from ScanNet, RealEstate10K [], or hand-labeled trajectories.

table.toccaption: 8.3Representative training corpora for 3D scene synthesis.

caption.text: Representative training corpora for 3D scene synthesis.

para.p: Layout-conditioned methods report the metrics introduced with ATISS on 3D-FRONT (object-category frequency, pairwise-relation accuracy, and FID on rendered top-down or perspective views). View-to-3D and view-to-view methods adopt the NeRF-era panel of PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on held-out views of ScanNet, RealEstate10K [], or DL3DV-10K []. Video-model-based methods add FVD and a camera-trajectory-adherence metric, the mean translation and rotation error between requested and recovered camera poses.

Four axes mirror the scene tuple of Eq. (): layout adherence (object-count agreement, pairwise-relation accuracy on
G
, and bounding-box IoU between requested and synthesized placements); geometric fidelity where ground truth exists (Chamfer Distance, F-score, and depth and normal consistency against held-out views); photometric quality (PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS against ground-truth views, FID / KID against held-out scene distributions, and FVD for video outputs); and camera-pose adherence, most relevant for P4 (translation and rotation error of poses recovered by structure-from-motion or a learned pose regressor). A paper reports the subset of axes its paradigm can be scored on, which is why comparison across paradigms remains difficult.
Scene synthesis meets the problems of object synthesis on a structured set: more conditioning variables, more output components, and longer trajectories enter the cost at once.

The four paradigms solve subtly different problems, and each leaves a gap when used alone: a layout-conditioned generator can satisfy the symbolic prior
G in
yet produce a non-traversable static scene, and a view-to-3D generator can produce a navigable Gaussian field that ignores the requested object semantics. The gaps surface as layout-adherence drift, where the generated NeRF or 3DGS no longer satisfies the input layout once the user roams outside the trained view envelope; object drop, where small or thin objects from
L
are silently omitted during continuous-field synthesis; and geometry flattening, where a multi-object composition collapses into a single textured slab when the 2D or video prior dominates. Hybrids such as GALA3D [] and ViewCrafter [] chain a layout or geometry prior with a Gaussian or video renderer to keep both halves honest, and future systems will more likely compose the four paradigms than choose among them.

Almost all paradigms remain anchored to furnished indoor rooms because that is where the training corpora live: 3D-FRONT [] alone supplies the layout supervision for the dominant P1 methods, and ScanNet, Matterport3D, and Hypersim dominate P2 / P3. The result is an outdoor and urban scale gap that CityCraft [] is among the few systems to address, a category imbalance with many furniture classes but few terrain, vegetation, or industrial ones, and an open-world domain shift under which methods trained on residential interiors fail on industrial sites, excavations, or invented environments. Web-scraped open-vocabulary scene corpora and hybrid synthetic-real pipelines that blend procedurally generated environments with captured scans are the active responses, both for breadth and to control the long tail of the scene-class distribution.

The video paradigm (§) excels at short camera moves but degrades on long, unbounded trajectories that require persistent world memory. Long trajectories expose temporal blur, where textures shimmer or drift between frames; scene amnesia, where objects reappear with different geometry when the camera revisits a location; and pose-conditioning collapse, where the model learns to ignore the camera signal in favor of the marginal video distribution. ViewCrafter []’s unprojection and reprojection scaffold, Gen3C []’s 3D cache, and CAT4D []’s joint multi-view and video training all inject an explicit 3D inductive bias back into the video prior, but the trade-off between the video prior’s perceptual quality and the geometric prior’s rigidity remains an open design tension.

A P1 layout-adherence score and a P3 PSNR cannot be ranked against each other, no single dataset evaluates layout faithfulness, geometric fidelity, photometric quality, and pose adherence jointly, and no human-aligned evaluator analogous to HyperScore [] has been validated on scene outputs.

Scene synthesis targets static geometry conditioned on camera poses, but the same formulation is being extended toward 4D synthesis and action-conditioned world modeling: Dreamer [], GameNGen [], Diamond [], RTFM [], and Genie3 [] move from static view or video synthesis toward open-ended environment generation in which spatial structure, temporal evolution, and interaction are modeled together. From the standpoint of this subsection, scalable, temporally coherent video generation with explicit viewpoint control is the foundation those systems build on; they are treated as world models in §.

3D reconstruction recovers a digital 3D representation of a scene or object from sensor observations such as RGB images, video, depth maps, or point clouds, and has long been a foundational problem in computer vision, graphics, and immersive systems such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and digital twins. Its difference from the synthesis tasks of § and § is one of intent: synthesis is open-ended generation in which plausibility and diversity dominate, whereas reconstruction must explain the input views faithfully before any inference about unobserved regions is attempted. Reconstruction is where perception becomes geometry: it turns raw sensor streams into an explicit, metric 3D substrate that simulators, AR / VR systems, digital twins, and embodied agents can reason over, manipulate, and render, and it supplies the ground-truth geometry against which the generative tasks of § are ultimately measured. Three families follow: iterative reconstruction, which solves a per-scene optimization against the input views; feed-forward reconstruction, which amortizes that cost into a learned map from observations to a 3D representation; and complete reconstruction, which generatively fills the occluded regions and so makes the boundary with synthesis explicit. Figure previews representative reconstruction tasks.

para.p: Classical image-based reconstruction is rooted in Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [], which estimates camera poses from unposed images, followed by Multi-View Stereo (MVS) [], which recovers dense geometry. Decades of refinement have made SfM + MVS a mature and widely used pipeline (see [] for a comprehensive treatment), yet it still struggles with textureless surfaces, reflective objects, and large illumination changes.

A more recent line represents the scene as a continuous function parameterized by a neural network: signed distance functions [], occupancy fields [], and neural radiance fields []. The original formulations were expensive to train and render and limited in quality; PlenOctrees [], Plenoxels [], Instant-NGP [], RefNeRF [], TensoRF [], and ZipNeRF [] are among the many follow-ups that improved efficiency and fidelity, but all of them still require a large number of input images per scene. Sparse-view variants add auxiliary information such as regularization [], depth priors [], point clouds [], and surface priors [], or distill a 2D diffusion prior into the per-scene representation, the SDS recipe of § applied to reconstruction from one or a few images []. 3D Gaussian Splatting [] then made per-scene optimization fast, training within minutes and rendering in real time, with subsequent work adding depth regularization, anti-aliasing, mesh extraction, and surface alignment []. All of these systems, however, work well only over nearby views or a small scene and must be re-optimized from scratch for every new input, which motivates the amortized paradigm.

The feed-forward paradigm amortizes the per-scene optimization of Eq. () across a learned prior: a network
G θ
rec
is trained once on a large multi-view corpus, then deployed in a single forward pass on unseen inputs, minimizing

Math.text: L _ [FF] * theta = E _ (open-interval@(O, r _ [gt]) similar-to p _ [data]) * delimited-[]@(D * open-interval@((G _ theta) ^ [rec] * O, r _ [gt]))

para.p:
where
D
is a representation-specific distance (Chamfer Distance for point maps, a rendering loss for radiance fields) and
( O ,
r gt
)
are observation–asset pairs drawn from a 3D corpus. This is the reconstruction-side analogue of the view-to-3D paradigm of §: sparse calibrated views are mapped feed-forward to a continuous scene representation, but the supervision is a reconstruction loss against ground-truth 3D rather than a rendering loss against held-out views alone.

Early feed-forward work applied 2D networks to individual 3D representations, for depth estimation [], voxel reconstruction [], point-cloud reconstruction [], and mesh deformation [], but remained limited to single objects or small datasets. Learned components then replaced individual stages of the SfM + MVS pipeline, keypoint detection and description [], image matching [], pose estimation [], and depth prediction [], proving more robust and accurate than their hand-designed counterparts and being integrated into the classical pipeline []. DUSt3R [] and MASt3R [] then reconstructed large scenes from unposed images end to end: similar in spirit to MVS but without explicit keypoint detection, matching, and pose estimation, the model predicts point maps in the reference view directly and recovers camera poses in post-processing, and follow-ups [] have improved quality and efficiency at scale.

Beyond geometry alone, a parallel line recovers geometry and appearance together through differentiable rendering. Scene Representation Networks [] and Light Field Networks [] introduced ray-based querying for novel-view synthesis and were followed by epipolar attention [], large transformers [], and integration with pretrained generative models []; PixelNeRF [] pioneered pixel-aligned features for NeRF-based reconstruction and inspired 3D volume representations [], feature-matching fusion [], and large transformers []. 3D Gaussian Splatting [] has since become the representation of choice for feed-forward reconstruction, in PixelSplat [], Splatter Image [], MVSplat [], Flash3D [], LatentSplat [], Splatt3R [], GS-LRM [], NoPoSplat [], and DepthSplat []. These methods synthesize novel views with high appearance fidelity, but the views remain confined to small camera changes within the observed envelope, which motivates the generative paradigm below.

A harder regime is to reconstruct a complete scene from an observation
O
that covers only part of it, which requires inferring both visible and occluded regions; the operator shifts from a deterministic map to a generative posterior over the unobserved regions,

which shares the formal structure of the synthesis sampler of Eq. () with the conditioning replaced by a strong observation constraint
O
.

Complete reconstruction has been studied extensively for single objects [] but remains under-explored for large scenes. Classical scene-scale methods fuse depth maps from multiple views into a volumetric representation [], but they are sensitive to depth errors and produce noisy, incomplete reconstructions. A newer line fine-tunes large pretrained diffusion models [] for the task, conditioning on controlled camera trajectories [] or on auxiliary signals []; these methods synthesize observation-consistent views but leave the underlying geometry implicit. A small but growing body of work addresses geometry directly: WVD [] and Bolt3D [] generate a hybrid RGB + point-map output that recovers geometry and appearance rather than novel views alone, and LaRI [] reconstructs a complete scene from a single image, still limited to small indoor scenes.

Two design choices cut across the three paradigms. The density of the observation decides which paradigm applies: a dense calibrated multi-view set calls for per-scene optimization, a sparse uncalibrated capture for a feed-forward map, and a single image for a generative posterior, since progressively more of the scene must be inferred rather than observed. The output representation
R rec
, by contrast, is largely independent of the paradigm and driven by the downstream consumer: a point map (DUSt3R), a mesh (classical MVS post-processing), a NeRF (per-scene optimization, PixelNeRF), a 3DGS field (3DGS, PixelSplat), or a hybrid RGB + point map (Bolt3D, WVD).

Datasets span object-centric collections, indoor scenes, and outdoor environments, and partition further by acquisition (synthetic or real-world) and dynamics (static or dynamic); Table summarizes those most commonly used.

Synthetic corpora such as Objaverse [] supply large and diverse 3D assets, and MegaSynth [] and Zeroverse [] explore procedurally generated data for scalable supervision. Real-world static corpora include ARKitScenes [] and ScanNet++ [] for indoor capture, dynamic corpora such as KITTI-360 [] capture outdoor scenes with temporal variation, and TartanAir [] contains both static and dynamic scenes, which permits evaluation across both settings.

caption.text: Representative training corpora for 3D scene reconstruction. “Type” indicates synthetic / real-world acquisition; “Dynamics” indicates whether the corpus contains temporal variation.

para.p: Iterative methods (P1) are evaluated on DTU [] and Tanks-and-Temples [] for geometric fidelity and on the NeRF-era benchmarks LLFF [], MipNeRF360 [], and RealEstate10K [] for novel-view quality. Feed-forward methods (P2) adopt the same panel together with ScanNet [] subsets that supply ground-truth point maps for direct geometry supervision. Complete-reconstruction methods (P3) have no standardized suite and typically report on the precursor benchmark of their underlying 2D or video prior.

Four axes mirror the rendering-versus-geometry decomposition of Eq. (). Photometric quality is measured by PSNR, SSIM [], and LPIPS [], covering pixel-level fidelity, structural similarity, and perceptual consistency of novel views. Camera-pose adherence uses Relative Translation Accuracy (RTA), Relative Rotation Accuracy (RRA), and the Area Under the Curve (AUC) that summarizes pose accuracy across angular thresholds. Geometric fidelity of point maps and point clouds is measured by Accuracy (precision), Completeness (recall), and Chamfer Distance, where Accuracy reflects geometric precision, Completeness measures surface coverage, and Chamfer Distance aggregates both. Depth quality for monocular estimation uses the absolute relative error
/
|
- y
^ y
|
y
and the inlier ratio
< δ T
(the fraction of predictions within a multiplicative threshold of the ground truth), with median scaling or least-squares fitting applied beforehand because monocular depth is scale-ambiguous; multi-view depth reports Accuracy, Completeness, and Overall, the mean of the first two and equivalent to Chamfer Distance.

The paradigm succession of § is visible in two quantities. Per-scene optimization has moved from NeRF [], which trains for hours and renders at a few frames per second, to 3D Gaussian Splatting [], which trains a scene in minutes and renders in real time (
≥
30
fps at 1080p); the feed-forward paradigm removes per-scene optimization altogether, with DUSt3R / MASt3R [] and VGGT [] recovering point maps, depth, and camera poses in a single sub-second forward pass and Fast3R [] processing over a thousand images at once. On pose, learned reconstructors now rival classical pipelines: VGGT [] reports a camera-pose AUC@30 of 85.3 on RealEstate10K in pure feed-forward mode and 93.5 with bundle-adjustment refinement. Two caveats apply. There is no cross-paradigm leaderboard, since P1 is scored on novel-view PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS, P2 adds geometric Accuracy / Completeness / Chamfer Distance and pose AUC, and P3 inherits whichever protocol its 2D or video prior used; and on raw depth-map accuracy feed-forward models still trail tuned MVS pipelines, with quality degrading under free-viewpoint extrapolation (§), so the strongest numbers hold inside the observed view envelope. Phone-based NeRF and Gaussian-Splatting capture apps and the open-source Nerfstudio stack have brought per-scene reconstruction to commodity devices, while classical photogrammetry suites remain the production baseline for metric accuracy.

Four problems span the pipeline end to end: the data the model trains on, the accuracy it can deliver, the quality of the views it renders, and the compute envelope that constrains all three at long input lengths; reconstruction shares the first and third with its synthesis counterparts but sharpens the other two because it commits to recovering ground truth from raw sensor data.

Most reconstruction and view-synthesis datasets cover a narrow band of modalities. Widely used benchmarks such as RealEstate10K [] and MipNeRF360 [] are RGB-only, without depth, LiDAR, or semantic annotation, and even Objaverse-XL [], with 10.2M objects, is primarily synthetic mesh data without real-world sensor modalities. Merging datasets of different modalities is the usual workaround, at the cost of domain shift and annotation inconsistency, and the gap is widest for dynamic scenes: datasets with synchronized RGB, depth, optical flow, and 3D motion remain far fewer than static ones, and most dynamic datasets record either camera motion or object motion rather than both with a full sensor suite. The open problem is a scalable, modality-rich corpus that combines the diversity of Objaverse [] with the multi-sensor completeness of ScanNet++ [], collected under one protocol so that aligned RGB, depth, and semantic signals supervise the same model.

Feed-forward models still trail traditional MVS pipelines [] on raw depth-map accuracy, because MVS exploits known camera parameters and a hypothesized depth set to build cost volumes from which depth is predicted. Whether feed-forward reconstructors [] learn an approximation of such cost volumes implicitly in their attention layers is an open question; injecting explicit camera parameters or other priors into the backbone, for instance through Diffusion Transformers [], is one route to closing the gap.

The accuracy gap is most visible at free-viewpoint rendering, where the model must produce novel views far from the input camera distribution. Disocclusions, geometric uncertainty, and limited generalization conspire: regions never observed come out blurred, ghosted, or geometrically wrong, because current methods rely on local consistency and cannot infer plausible content for occluded areas, and view-dependent effects and complex light transport demand reasoning beyond interpolation. Hallucinating missing detail while keeping novel views consistent is exactly the generative regime of §.

Reconstruction from many views meets a hard computational ceiling: methods for geometry reasoning and novel-view synthesis rely on full attention, whose compute grows quadratically with the number of tokens; exact-attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2 [] remove the quadratic memory of the attention matrix but not the quadratic compute. VGGT [], for example, needs about 21 GB of GPU memory for 100 input frames and about 41 GB for 200, so inference over long sequences and training on many views quickly exceed a single GPU. Recurrent alternatives such as CUT3R [] integrate new views incrementally while maintaining a memory state, which keeps inference memory near constant, but they forget earlier views and degrade as the number of inputs grows. Reasoning efficiently over hundreds or thousands of views while keeping memory and compute manageable remains open, with recurrent and sparse-attention architectures the main candidates.

3D panorama synthesis occupies a distinctive position in spatial generation: rather than producing a 3D representation directly, it generates a complete 360-degree omnidirectional image as a structured intermediate from which a full 3D environment can then be lifted. The panorama gives embodied agents, AR / VR pipelines, and world models a holistic spatial context with minimal occlusion anchored at one observation point, and it bridges the mature 2D generative prior of § with the 3D substrate on which the rest of § operates. Four method families trace the path from a single omnidirectional snapshot to an explorable world: panoramic image synthesis, panoramic video generation, panoramic 3D reconstruction, and panorama-based 3D scene generation.

Panorama synthesis generates a complete 360-degree environment conditioned on text, a reference panorama or NFoV image, a spatial layout, or a specified viewpoint; unlike object-centric or narrow-field-of-view (NFoV) generation, it covers the whole environment around the observer at once rather than a fragment of it. The projection
Π
fixes how the sphere is laid out for a 2D network and which distortions the generator must absorb. Equirectangular projection (ERP) maps the sphere onto a rectangle in latitude–longitude coordinates; it stretches content near the poles but is continuous and directly compatible with standard 2D pipelines and convolutional networks, which has made it the dominant format for learning-based synthesis. Cubemap projection represents the sphere as six perspective faces (front, back, left, right, top, bottom), removing polar distortion at the cost of discontinuities along face boundaries, and is the native format of real-time rendering and VR / AR systems, where each face is processed as an ordinary perspective image. Tangent images and perspective patches decompose the panorama into overlapping tangent-plane projections so that models trained on ordinary perspective images can be reused. Fisheye and dual-fisheye projections capture 180–220 degrees per lens with radial distortion; most consumer 360-degree cameras capture two hemispheres this way and stitch them, so dual-fisheye is the native acquisition format even when methods operate on ERP.

para.p: Two task formulations differ in their conditioning: text-to-panorama generation, which leans on the prior of a pretrained generator and is judged on semantic alignment and diversity, and image-conditioned panorama generation, which expands an NFoV image or an incomplete panorama by inpainting or outpainting and must preserve the content, style, and panoramic distortion of its input. Formally, this family is the base case of Eq. () with the lifting operator disabled: it samples a single static omnidirectional image and stops,

Early approaches [] relied on GANs [] and were constrained by limited training data and mode collapse; diffusion models [] brought diversity and fidelity, and current methods divide by projection format and architecture. ▶
Equirectangular projection (ERP) methods. The direct-ERP case generates on the latitude–longitude grid and must handle polar distortion and the wrap-around seam architecturally. For text-to-panorama generation, DiffPano [] fine-tunes a diffusion model with LoRA on ERP, SMGD [] guides the diffusion process with spherical manifold convolutions that respect geometry across the sphere, and PAR [] replaces diffusion with autoregressive modeling to avoid the mismatch between ERP and the noise assumptions of standard diffusion. The seam is treated at the denoising or decoding stage: PanoDiff [] uses geometric augmentation when completing a panorama from unregistered NFoV images, PanoDiffusion [] generates depth jointly and rotates the latent circularly to enforce left–right continuity, StitchDiffusion [] re-denoises the wrap-around region at every step together with global cropping, and PanFusion [] pairs an ERP branch with a multi-view perspective branch to draw on both representations. For image-conditioned generation, OmniDreamer [] introduced mask-based outpainting from NFoV images with GANs, AOG [] and ODIS [] explore alternative conditioning for inpainting and outpainting, and PanoDecouple [] separates distortion guidance from content completion to counter the “visual cheating” in which a model buys image quality at the cost of geometric accuracy.

▶
Cubemap-based methods. The second case of Eq. () generates six perspective faces, which removes polar distortion but moves the problem to the face boundaries. CubeDiff [] introduced the cubemap representation for text-to-panorama generation, and DreamCube [] synchronizes the six planes to suppress discontinuous seams and inconsistent color tone; overlapping the fields of view of adjacent faces reduces seams further but duplicates generation in the overlap and lowers the effective resolution. JoPano [] models the faces jointly with a DiT and a Joint-Face Adapter, applies Poisson blending along the boundaries, and introduces the seam metrics (Seam-SSIM, Seam-Sobel) used in §.

▶
Perspective image-based methods. The third case leaves a perspective text-to-image model untouched and pushes the consistency burden into the stitch operator
S
, with or without panorama-specific training. Training-free methods apply a pretrained perspective model directly: MultiDiffusion [] denoises overlapping patches independently and blends them, PanoGen [] outpaints recursively from an initial view until the sphere is covered, DiffCollage [] casts the panorama as a factor graph whose factor nodes are portions and whose variable nodes are their overlaps so that portions are generated in parallel rather than autoregressively, PanoFree [] iterates warping and inpainting over multi-view images, and SphereDiff [] moves MultiDiffusion onto a spherical latent with dynamic spherical sampling and distortion-aware weighted averaging so that quality holds up to the poles. These methods ride on advances in perspective generation but struggle with global consistency across the full sphere. Training-based methods fine-tune on panoramic data: MVDiffusion [] generates eight perspective views with consistent geometry and reprojects them into a closed-loop panorama, and TanDiT [] decomposes the panorama into a structured grid of tangent-plane images that a Diffusion Transformer generates jointly in one denoising pass under spatial attention.

Extending synthesis over time adds temporal coherence to omnidirectional consistency. Formally, this family extends the static generator of Eq. () over time, sampling a sequence under a joint spatial-and-temporal coherence constraint,

▶
Text-to-panoramic video generation. 360DVD [] adapts a pretrained text-to-video model to the ERP domain through adapter modules, keeping wrap-around consistency across frames but struggling to balance text alignment against spherical geometry and to vary style under several control conditions. TiP4GEN [] adopts a dual-branch panoramic-and-perspective architecture in the spirit of PanFusion and lifts the generated video into a geometry-aligned 4D Gaussian scene. PanoWan [] and PanoDiT [] fine-tune large video diffusion transformers on panoramic video data and gain motion quality from scale, and PanoLora [] treats the task as a projection adaptation from perspective views that LoRA can learn with little data. Training-free alternatives carry the static-panorama machinery into time: SphereDiff [] extends its spherical latent to video, and DynamicScaler [] denoises through a seamless rotating window with an offset-shifting scheme and Global Motion Guidance, which yields arbitrary output resolution at constant memory. Text alone, however, offers little control over layout and motion, which motivates the richer conditioning below.

▶
Image-to-panoramic video generation. Animating a static panorama anchors the video spatially and asks for plausible omnidirectional motion that respects the input geometry. 4K4DGen [] animates user-selected regions with an image-to-video model under overlapping windows, at the cost of fixed-window artifacts and limited motion. ViewPoint [] introduces a panorama representation that keeps global spatial continuity while Pano-Perspective attention transfers a perspective video prior, and HoloTime [] reconstructs the result as 4D Gaussian Splatting so that the animated scene can be explored under viewpoint changes. GenEx [] generates a 3D-consistent imaginative environment from a single image as a panoramic video stream with loop consistency over long trajectories, which makes it usable for embodied exploration. For explicit control, PanFlow [] conditions on synthetic optical flow as a scene-agnostic motion signal and warps noise spherically so that camera and object motion can be controlled separately while the seam stays consistent; OmniDrag [] adds drag-style interaction at scene and object level through a spherical motion estimator; and PanoWorld-X [] reprojects ERP features onto the sphere inside a Sphere-Aware Diffusion Transformer to follow diverse camera trajectories.

▶
Perspective-to-panoramic video generation. Expanding an NFoV video to a full 360-degree video requires coherent hallucination in space and time at once, under visibility masks that change with camera motion. VidPanos [] frames the task as space-time outpainting and uses a generative video model to fill the regions a panning camera never observed; Imagine360 [] combines a global panoramic branch with local perspective priors and an elevation-aware design for the moving masks; and Beyond the Frame [] adds geometry-aware modules and motion-aware conditioning to improve realism and motion consistency in the outpainted regions.

para.p: re-solved from scratch for each scene, these methods fit a radiance field or an explicit representation to multi-view panoramas, the panoramic analogue of §. NeRF-based work includes 360Roam [] for geometry-aware indoor reconstruction, 360FusionNeRF [] for novel views from a single panorama under geometric and semantic supervision, EgoNeRF [] with spherical grids for egocentric capture, and OmniNeRF [], which processes raw dual-fisheye input and its lens distortion. Gaussian-splatting alternatives are faster: 360GS [] projects Gaussians onto spherical tangent planes, ODGS [] rasterizes on tangent planes with elevation-aware densification, OP43DGS [] corrects the projection bias of the local affine approximation across camera models, OmniGS [] exploits omnidirectional optical properties, and Seam360GS [] calibrates dual-fisheye input by jointly optimizing translation vectors and learnable angular-distortion embeddings. Scene4U [] reconstructs from a single panorama in depth layers: an open-vocabulary segmenter and an LLM decompose it semantically, diffusion inpainting restores occluded regions, and 3D Gaussians are fitted per layer.

▶

PanoGRF [] pioneered feed-forward reconstruction of wide-baseline panoramas with depth guidance; PanoSplatt3R [] extends DUSt3R [] to unposed wide-baseline panoramas through RoPE rolling, a rotary positional embedding rolled across attention heads so that ERP periodicity and correspondences across the seam are modeled; and PanSplat [] builds spherical 3D Gaussian pyramids on a Fibonacci lattice to reach 4K novel views with feed-forward inference and cubemap rendering for memory efficiency.

▶
Panorama-based 3D generation and world modeling. This family realizes the full composition of Eq. (): it first generates the panorama and then lifts it,

Math.text: formulae@((hat@(r)) ^ [rec] = Lambda * hat@(P), hat@(P) similar-to (p _ theta) ^ [pano] * conditional@(P, kappa * c))

so that the synthesized omnidirectional image of Eq. () becomes the structured intermediate fed to the reconstruction operator of Eq. (); Figure (d) depicts this generate-then-lift pathway. Text
→
panorama
→
3D pipelines generate the omnidirectional image with a diffusion model [] before reconstructing a NeRF, Gaussian, or mesh scene. LayerPano3D [] parses the panorama into hierarchical depth layers and reconstructs each with 3D Gaussian Splatting, DreamScene360 [] fits panoramic Gaussians for free-roaming text-conditioned scenes, Matrix-3D [] couples trajectory-guided panoramic video generation with a dual-pathway reconstruction that conditions on scene-mesh renders, and HunyuanWorld [] treats the panorama as a 360-degree world proxy for text- and image-conditioned explorable scenes with mesh export and disentangled object representations. The panoramic video generators GenEx [] and PanoWorld-X [] (above) turn the same intermediate into an action- or trajectory-conditioned observation space, which is where panorama synthesis meets the world models of §.

Panoramic datasets must supply geometric consistency over the full sphere, a declared projection format, and, for reconstruction, camera poses and depth; Table lists the corpora in use, grouped by modality.

For static synthesis, Structured3D [] (synthetic indoor scenes with controlled geometry) and SUN360 [] (real-world indoor and outdoor panoramas) are the standard benchmarks for distortion handling and seam artifacts, in the splits adopted by JoPano, PanoDecouple, and DreamCube []; Matterport3D [], with RGB-D panoramas, camera poses, and mesh geometry across 90 buildings, is the most widely used corpus for both generation and reconstruction [], and Upright360 [] filters Matterport3D, web, and Blockade Labs panoramas with GeoCalib [] to near-zero pitch and roll for realistic indoor synthesis. Panoramic video with geometric annotation has been the bottleneck. 360+x [] and WEB360 [] are small real-world collections (the latter captioned for text conditioning), 360-1M [] scales to over a million videos for world-model pretraining, PanFlow [] adds optical flow and camera poses on motion-rich sequences, PANOVID [] aggregates these with Imagine360 [] and public VR videos but lacks poses and depth, and Matrix-Pano [] fills that gap with Unreal Engine 5 renders carrying depth maps and camera trajectories; embodied work renders action-conditioned observations in Unreal Engine directly []. For reconstruction, Replica [] and Residential [] serve as synthetic indoor benchmarks at baselines of about 1.0 m and 0.3 m respectively [], 360Loc [] supplies posed panorama sequences used for 4K fine-tuning [], and the scarcity of posed real panoramic video led PanSplat [] to capture its own dual-fisheye footage with poses from visual SLAM.

para.p: Panorama evaluation combines general image and video quality metrics with panorama-specific measures of distortion, seam consistency, and spherical topology.

▶
Image fidelity and semantic alignment. FID measures distributional similarity between generated and real panoramas []; PanFusion [] shows that FAED (Fréchet Auto-Encoder Distance), computed in the latent space of an auto-encoder trained on the target data, tracks panorama quality more closely than Inception features do. Text-to-panorama generation reports CLIP-Score between prompt and output [], image-conditioned tasks report CLIP-I between input and output [], and no-reference quality is scored with BRISQUE and NIQE [], complemented by aesthetic scorers and human preference studies, for instance the Average User Ranking protocol of LayerPano3D []. Layout-conditioned synthesis measures adherence by 3D and 2D IoU against layouts recovered with HorizonNet [], following PanFusion [].

▶
Panorama-specific consistency. Projection-induced distortion and boundary discontinuities call for metrics of their own. JoPano [] scores cubemap seams with Seam-SSIM (SSIM between adjacent edge pixels of neighboring faces) and Seam-Sobel (gradient discontinuity along the seam); PanoDecouple [] introduces Distort-CLIP, a CLIP variant trained to detect panoramic distortion, so that the “visual cheating” of models that improve image quality while degrading geometry becomes measurable; and loop consistency across the 360-degree wrap-around is assessed by PSNR in overlapping regions [] or across the left–right boundary [].

▶
Reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. Because pixel density on the sphere is non-uniform, WS-PSNR (Weighted Spherical PSNR) weights pixels by latitude and replaces plain PSNR for equirectangular outputs [], complemented by SSIM and LPIPS [].

▶
Video quality and spatiotemporal dynamics. Panoramic videos are often projected to several perspective views (e.g., , four views at azimuths
{
0 ∘
,
90 ∘
,
180 ∘
,
270 ∘
}
with a
90 ∘
field of view) so that human raters and perspective-domain tools can be used []. Q-Align [], a large multimodal model trained to score visual quality on discrete text-defined levels, is increasingly used for images and videos alike []; FVD [], computed in the feature space of an inflated 3D ConvNet, is the standard distributional metric for video []; VBench [] adds imaging quality, aesthetic quality, motion smoothness, and subject consistency over projected views; and trajectory-conditioned generation is scored by frame-to-frame consistency and by the range of camera motion it sustains []. Two limits remain. Ground truth is scarce for dynamic panoramic video with depth and camera annotation, so evaluation falls back on projected perspective views or user studies; and world-level properties such as loop consistency over long trajectories and action-conditioned spatial coherence have no dedicated benchmark yet.

Modeling a complete omnidirectional environment imposes constraints that NFoV synthesis never meets. The first is distortion-aware learning: ERP stretches content near the poles, so visual information is non-uniformly distributed over the image and convolutional kernels designed for translation invariance on the plane struggle with the varying distortion, which motivates spherical manifold convolutions and latitude-aware architectures []. The second is seamless boundary consistency: wrap-around coherence across the longitudinal boundary must be preserved to avoid visible seams, typically through circular padding or latent rotation during denoising []. The third is scaling structured generation to 4K and beyond while keeping global geometric and semantic consistency over the whole sphere, which pushes toward memory-efficient attention and hierarchical spherical representations [].

The clearest trend is the move from static spherical snapshots toward interactive 3D world modeling, in which the panorama is the interface through which an embodied agent reasons about a complete environment rather than a fragment of one. The systems that lift a generated panorama into an explorable world (HunyuanWorld [], Matrix-3D []) and World Labs’ Marble [] show what panoramic priors make possible, and temporal panoramic modeling supplies the 4D half: generating temporally coherent panoramic video requires motion dynamics that respect spherical topology and occlusion boundaries []. Integrated with interactive systems, such panoramic world simulations become a basis for embodied interaction, long-range spatial reasoning, and environment simulation in robotics and immersive media.

Efficiency and fidelity both hinge on the omnidirectional representation. Efficient omnidirectional representations such as the Fibonacci-lattice Gaussian pyramids of PanSplat [] render at high fidelity without the redundancy of uniform grids, and multi-modal panoramic fusion, which binds 360-degree RGB to depth, semantic labels, and geometric proxies such as surface normals [], makes the synthesized environment both more realistic and more editable, closing part of the gap between 2D generative priors and full 3D scene intelligence.

The preceding subsections build 3D content; 3D scene editing takes an existing asset and modifies it under user control while preserving everything the edit should leave untouched. Such incremental control is exactly what spatial intelligence asks of a 3D world model: an agent that must correct a mistake, personalize an environment, or keep a scene consistent as its task unfolds cannot afford to regenerate the world from scratch every time it changes. Technically, 3D editing lifts the 2D inpainting-and-editing machinery of § from the image plane to a multi-view-consistent 3D representation, adding a cross-view coherence requirement that has no analogue in the 2D case; the five method families below are distinguished by how the edit signal is injected into that representation.

para.p: 3D scene (and object) editing modifies an existing 3D asset or reconstructed scene according to a user intent (typically language or reference images, as in Figure ) while preserving 3D consistency for novel-view rendering. Unlike text-to-3D generation, editing operates on a given representation (e.g., , NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, or meshes) and requires (i) locality and identity preservation for unedited regions, (ii) multi-view (and potentially temporal) coherence, and (iii) controllability over the edited attributes, whether geometry, appearance, material, or semantics.

Formally, 3D editing is the 3D-lifted counterpart of the 2D inpainting-and-editing operator of § (Eq. ()). Given an input 3D representation

Recent 3D object and scene editing methods can be categorized by how the edit signal of Eq. () is injected into the 3D representation, from lifting 2D edits view by view, through enforcing cross-view consistency, to operating directly on 3D primitives, reasoning with language models, and amortizing the edit into a single feed-forward pass. Figure schematizes the five families and how each realizes the operator

para.p:
A dominant paradigm inherits from instruction-based NeRF editing []: the method iterates between rendering views from the current scene, applying a 2D diffusion-based editor to them, and updating the 3D representation to match the edited guidance under geometric regularization. Formally, this family instantiates

E 2D

Instruct-NeRF2NeRF [], EditNeRF [], Free-Editor [], and CTRL-D [] lift instruction-driven 2D edits into the radiance field this way, and with the rise of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [] the same principle moved to Gaussian primitives: Instruct-GS2GS [] iteratively edits the training images with InstructPix2Pix [] and re-optimizes the 3DGS to reflect the instruction while preserving 3D structure []. The recipe is simple and borrows the full strength of 2D editors, but it is slow, prone to view-dependent artifacts, and only as good as the stability of the 2D editor and the coverage of the rendered guidance views.

Because independently edited views can disagree (inconsistent textures, hallucinated geometry), recent work [] enforces multi-view consistency at the guidance level rather than relying on the 3D update to reconcile conflicting edits. Formally, rather than editing each view independently as in Eq. (), this family makes the guidance images mutually consistent before the lift,

GaussCtrl [] edits several rendered views in a coupled fashion rather than sequentially, improving multi-view consistency for text-driven 3DGS editing [], and VcEdit [] integrates the 3DGS into the image-editing process itself with consistency modules that counter cross-view disagreement and mode collapse. A complementary line transfers a single-view edit to other views via geometry: [ ] extracts diffusion attention features from a reference edit, warps them across views using depth from the Gaussian splats, and injects the warped features to propagate a coherent edit. These methods preserve 3D coherence more robustly but still struggle with large non-rigid shape changes or severe occlusion, where reliable correspondence and geometry are hard to come by.

To reduce reliance on unstable 2D guidance and enable interactive use, 3D-native approaches operate directly on explicit scene primitives. Formally, this family bypasses the rendering loop of Eq. () entirely: a grounding or segmentation operator
G

T

Math.text: formulae@(hat@(r) = T * list@(r ^ [in], G * open-interval@(r ^ [in], c)), T element-of set@([add], [delete], [move], [recolor], [replace]))

para.p: acting on explicit Gaussians or mesh facets so that the unedited primitives are preserved by construction: the identity-preservation term of Eq. () is satisfied structurally rather than by a penalty; Figure (c) shows this pathway. 3DSceneEditor [] runs a fully 3D pipeline, combining instance segmentation and zero-shot grounding to localize the target and then performing Gaussian-level addition, deletion, relocation, recoloring, and replacement with strong controllability in real time, and InterGSEdit [] adds user-in-the-loop key-view selection and a geometry-consistent attention prior for iterative, preference-guided 3DGS editing with control over the edit degree. More broadly, GaussianEditor and 3DSceneEditor [] impose higher-level structure on the Gaussians, grouping them by object identity or semantic coherence (typically through zero-shot grounding or segmentation [] followed by anchoring) so that an edit can be formulated at the level of an instance rather than of individual primitives, which localizes the target more precisely and protects the background.

Large language models have been integrated into 3D editing pipelines not merely as text encoders but as high-level reasoning and control modules. Formally, the LLM decomposes the instruction into an ordered program of geometry-aware operators applied to the asset,

Math.text: formulae@(hat@(r) = (o _ K compose cdots compose o _ 1) * r ^ [in], vector@(o _ 1, dots, o _ K) = LLM * open-interval@(c, r ^ [in]))

para.p:
so that high-level reasoning (attribute inference, edit planning, dependency resolution) is separated from the low-level operators
o k
, often the primitive transforms of Eq. (), that it dispatches; Figure (d) depicts this plan-then-execute pathway. ShapeLLM-Omni [] casts 3D editing as language-grounded reasoning in which the LLM performs shape understanding, attribute inference, and edit planning before invoking geometry-aware operators, and LL3M [] extends this to multimodal 3D manipulation requiring compositional understanding of geometry, appearance, and spatial relations. A complementary line [] uses the LLM to guide or parameterize image-to-3D or text-to-3D backbones in a feed-forward setting rather than a per-scene optimization, and LLMs also serve as coordination agents for global consistency []: [ ] shows that reasoning over object identities, relations, and edit dependencies reduces the conflicts that arise in purely diffusion- or optimization-based pipelines when several objects and attributes must be edited at once.

A final trend reduces test-time cost through feed-forward reconstruction or reuse of pretrained models []. These strategies are distinct: a training-free editing pipeline can still involve iterative diffusion inference. The amortized feed-forward case evaluates the editing operator of Eq. () directly,

Math.text: hat@(r) = list@(E _ theta * open-interval@(r ^ [in], kappa * c), [(amortized, no per-scene optimization)])

eliminating the per-scene
arg min
of Eq. () by amortizing inference into a trained network. Training-free alternatives instead reuse pretrained components, potentially through single-view guidance, mesh proxies, or iterative native-3D latent editing; Figure (e) distinguishes these routes from the per-scene optimization loop in panel (a). Free-Editor [] edits a NeRF zero-shot from text without scene-specific retraining, countering multi-view style inconsistency with a “single-view editing” scheme and an Edit Transformer; on the scene-operation side (insert, replace, delete), FreeEdit [] uses a mesh proxy to perform training-free edits guided by foundation models at near real-time rates in complex indoor scenes. These methods improve usability but typically trade away edit fidelity and coverage, especially for fine-grained geometry, and depend strongly on robust grounding and localization in 3D.

Several benchmarks have recently been introduced for systematic evaluation. 3D-Alpaca-Editing [] focuses on instruction-following 3D editing, assessing whether a model interprets natural-language commands correctly while preserving unedited content. CMD [] emphasizes compositional and multi-step instructions, where reasoning and planning matter. Edit3D-Bench [] is a general-purpose suite covering geometry, appearance, and object-level operations, with 3D edit regions annotated on 100 source models (300 edits), which allows fair comparison across editing paradigms. 3DEditVerse [] is a large-scale paired benchmark built for robustness and generalization across varied objects, scenes, and intents. Together they standardize evaluation in terms of instruction compliance, edit locality, and scalability; Table summarizes their scale and the evaluation axes each one annotates.

para.p: Edit cost is the clearest axis separating the five families. Instruct-NeRF2NeRF [] takes on the order of 30–90 minutes per edit; GaussianEditor [] brings this under 20 minutes by operating on explicit Gaussians; PrEditor3D [] edits a shape in a few minutes, and VoxHammer [] performs precise local edits training-free in a native 3D latent space. On quality the field reports DINO-I and CLIP-T on Edit3D-Bench [], directional CLIP [], and GPT-4V judgment []; the 3D-native and feed-forward families lead on locality and speed, while 2D-lifted methods keep an edge on open-vocabulary appearance edits where a strong 2D editor does the work. The speed of feed-forward editing comes at a cost in fine-grained geometry control and a dependence on robust 3D grounding, taken up below.
Several problems remain genuinely open and define the current frontier of 3D editing.

Most current methods edit color and texture well but treat geometry as fixed: precise, instruction-driven changes to shape, including thin, transparent, or high-frequency structures, remain unreliable, and edits that should alter the underlying surface often only repaint it. Closing this gap requires editors that operate on geometry and appearance jointly rather than deferring geometry to a frozen reconstruction.

Adding, removing, or substantially deforming structure while preserving the identity of the rest of the asset is still difficult: drag-driven, as-rigid-as-possible Gaussian editors [] handle moderate deformation, but large non-rigid motion and topology changes frequently lose original detail. Robust structural and compositional editing, including relation-aware multi-object edits, remains an active frontier.

Because most representations bake illumination into appearance, an edit that changes an object’s material or color is not guaranteed to stay consistent when the scene is relit. Relightable representations that decompose geometry, BRDF, and incident light [] are a prerequisite for edits that survive relighting and for inserting edited content into new lighting, yet stable material–light decomposition under editing is not solved.

paragraph.title: The consistency bottleneck has moved to 3D grounding.

para.p: Now that native-3D editing handles appearance coherence, the limiting factor is localization: methods such as VoxHammer [] are highly sensitive to 3D mask accuracy and degrade rapidly when the target region is imprecisely grounded. Robust open-vocabulary 3D grounding and segmentation [], ideally without user-provided masks [], is therefore the new gate on edit quality, and it is most acute in dynamic scenes, where the edited region must be tracked with temporal identity preserved across frames [].

Two pressures cut across all four. Evaluation remains immature: the benchmarks of § are small (Edit3D-Bench annotates 100 source models and 300 edits) and no metric panel is yet standard, so progress on the harder edits above is difficult to measure reliably. And the strongest forward trend is unification, bringing generation, segmentation, grounding, and editing into a single structured pipeline [] with interfaces that go beyond text to reference images [], masks [], sketches [], and object-level operations, so that an agent can specify and verify a geometry-, material-, and relighting-consistent edit rather than only a repaint.

Video spatial generation is the task of synthesizing a temporally coherent image sequence (a video clip) from a high-level prompt together with optional spatial, temporal, and other conditioning signals. It has advanced substantially in recent years, evolving from early generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches [] through autoregressive token models to the diffusion- and diffusion-transformer-based systems that now dominate the field []. This rapid progress has stimulated a wide range of downstream tasks, extending beyond basic text-to-video generation to encompass fine-grained control mechanisms (spatial, e.g., , image, pose, depth, landmark, sketch, and bounding box; temporal, e.g., , optical flow, trajectory, camera, and motion; and other conditional controls, e.g., , style, audio, bird’s-eye view) as well as sophisticated video editing capabilities.

Within the arc of §, video spatial generation is the temporal extension of the priors built in the preceding two sections. Whereas § learned a 2D semantic-to-pixel prior on a single image plane and § lifted that prior into a static volumetric representation, this section adds the time axis: the model must place matter and appearance correctly and make them evolve plausibly as the camera or the scene itself moves through time. Appearance, geometry, and dynamics must now be jointly consistent: a generated clip is judged not only frame by frame but on object permanence, motion plausibility, and multi-view coherence under camera motion, which makes video the natural substrate for the dynamic world models and simulators that consume spatial structure downstream.

The subsections are organized by the axis of control each introduces into Eq. (). Text-to-video generation (§) is the base case without auxiliary control; spatial control (§) adds a per-frame scaffold such as a pose or depth sequence; temporal control (§) adds a motion or camera signal that governs dynamics rather than appearance; § covers the remaining modalities and the frameworks that fuse several at once; and video editing (§) modifies an existing clip, lifting the 2D editing of § into time. § compares the five and discusses the challenges they share.

Text-to-video (T2V) generation [] synthesizes photorealistic, temporally coherent video from a natural-language description. It extends text-to-image (T2I) synthesis along time, so the model must produce plausible motion and state transitions as well as high-fidelity frames, and it does so with no explicit spatial scaffold: object permanence, motion plausibility, and view coherence under camera motion cannot be supplied from outside but must emerge from the generator itself. That is why the unconditional T2V model is the substrate on which the explicit control axes of §–§ are built. Its architecture has followed the image case, from generative adversarial networks (GANs) through autoregressive models to the diffusion models that dominate today, with progress driven as much by data as by architecture [].

para.p: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The first T2V systems extended the image GANs of § to clips. TGAN [] and TGAN-v2 [] used a temporal generator to produce latent motion vectors from which an image generator rendered frames; MoCoGAN [] and MoCoGAN-HD [] disentangled content from motion, generating the motion code recurrently; DVD-GAN [] instantiated Eq. () directly with separate spatial and temporal discriminators; and DIGAN [] used implicit neural representations for longer sequences. Even with architectures such as StyleGAN-V [], GANs suffered from flicker, training instability, and mode collapse, which limited the diversity of their motion and pushed the field toward other paradigms.

Autoregressive Models. Autoregressive (AR) models recast T2V as the sequential prediction of §, tokenizing a clip with a 3D Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (3D VQ-VAE) and predicting each token from its predecessors with a large transformer. The video-specific change is the order of the factorization: where the image model of Eq. () runs over the spatial tokens of a single frame, the video model factorizes over space and time,

VideoGPT [] demonstrated the approach for unconditional generation, NÜWA [] and CogVideo [] adapted it to text-to-video synthesis, and TATS [] addressed quality degradation in long sequences. The paradigm has since resurged in large multimodal backbones: Emu3 [] generates video inside a language-model backbone by treating frames as discrete visual tokens, and CausVid [] and MAGI-1 [] scale to long-form generation with autoregressive diffusion transformers. Sequential decoding nevertheless remains expensive and prone to the error accumulation that Eq. () makes explicit.

One widely used design factorizes attention into spatial attention within each frame and temporal attention across frames, as illustrated in Figure (c); other architectures use joint spacetime attention. VDM [] applied the idea in pixel space with a 3D U-Net; the breakthrough was moving diffusion into the compressed latent space of a video-specific autoencoder, as in VideoLDM [], LVDM [], and the open-source Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [], which cut training and inference cost enough to make high-resolution generation practical.

A second recipe adapts pretrained T2I models. Imagen Video [] and Make-A-Video [] freeze a T2I model and insert trainable temporal modules (e.g., , temporal attention layers or 1D convolutions) between its spatial layers, which are then trained on video to learn motion while the image prior is inherited intact. VideoCrafter [] and LaVie [] built high-quality generators on this recipe, Tune-A-Video [] adapted it to one-shot tuning on a single clip, and AnimateDiff [] turned the temporal modules into plug-and-play motion modules that animate personalized T2I models without further fine-tuning.

Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have since replaced the U-Net backbone, operating on “spacetime patches” (unified tokens representing blocks of video) and scaling well. Sora [] demonstrated long-duration (up to one minute), high-resolution clips and presented the approach as a step toward world simulation, and a wave of DiT models followed, including Open-Sora [], LATTE [], CogVideoX [], StepVideo [], Movie Gen [], Wan [], and Veo []. Large open DiT foundation models have substantially narrowed the gap to proprietary systems. HunyuanVideo [], at
13
B parameters the largest open T2V model at release, couples a “dual-stream-to-single-stream” full-attention DiT (text and video tokens processed in separate streams before fusion) with a multimodal-LLM text encoder and a 3D causal VAE, and reports human-evaluated quality competitive with leading closed systems. Mochi 1 [] introduces an asymmetric DiT (AsymmDiT) that allocates most capacity to the visual stream, and LTX-Video [] uses a high-compression video VAE to run latent video diffusion in near real time. NVIDIA’s Cosmos [] reframes the video generator as a world-foundation model for “Physical AI”, trained so that embodied and robotics systems can use it as a learned simulator, which ties video generation to the world models of §. Across these shifts the T2V trajectory has trailed the T2I trajectory of § by roughly a year, each image paradigm being inflated along the time axis once it matured.

Video adds a requirement at every level of evaluation: corpora must pair clips with captions at scale, suites must stratify by temporal phenomena (motion, object permanence, dynamic degree), and metrics must measure cross-frame coherence as well as per-frame quality.

Caption–clip scale has been the principal driver of T2V quality, and high-quality paired video–text data is far scarcer than image–text data. Early work repurposed action-recognition corpora such as UCF-101 [] and Kinetics [], which supply short, class-labeled clips but no captions. WebVid-10M [], the first web-scale captioned corpus, underpinned most 2022–2023 systems despite noisy alt-text captions and watermarks; later corpora raised caption density and clip length, with Panda-70M [] captioned automatically by cross-modality teachers, MiraData [] targeting long clips with dense structured captions, and Koala-36M [] explicitly optimizing the consistency between caption and content, the property that most directly limits a generator’s controllability. Table gives their scale.

Action-recognition sets (top) supply class labels rather than captions; web-scale captioned corpora (bottom) supply the clip–text pairs on which modern generators are fit. para.p: Classical T2V evaluation reported zero-shot distributional scores on the held-out splits of UCF-101 and MSR-VTT [], which probe frame quality and coarse text relevance but say nothing about temporal or compositional faithfulness. Recent suites are purpose-built: VBench [] decomposes quality into fine-grained dimensions (subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, temporal flicker, per-frame aesthetic and imaging quality), each with an automatic protocol validated against human preference; EvalCrafter [] aggregates objective metrics over prompts derived from real-world usage; and T2V-CompBench [] targets compositional faithfulness over time (attribute binding, spatial relations, motion binding, interactions), the temporal analogue of the T2I-CompBench probe of §. Table lists them.

para.p: The metric that defines video evaluation is the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [], the spatio-temporal analogue of FID: it compares distributions of features extracted from generated and real clips by a pretrained video backbone (I3D), and is therefore sensitive to motion realism in a way that per-frame FID [] and Inception Score are not. Text–clip alignment is measured by CLIPSIM, the per-frame CLIPScore [] averaged over the clip, which captures topical relevance but is blind to whether the described motion actually occurs. Because none of these scalars captures coherence or dynamics, papers report several VBench dimensions alongside them, which exposes a trade-off a single number hides: dynamic degree (how much genuine motion a clip contains) against temporal consistency (how stable it stays), since a near-static clip trivially maximizes consistency while failing the prompt. Headline claims are corroborated with human preference.

Three problems belong to the unconditional base case. Long-horizon coherence from text alone is the first: with no scaffold, object permanence and motion plausibility must emerge implicitly, and all three paradigms degrade as clips lengthen (GANs flicker, autoregressive roll-outs accumulate the error of Eq. (), diffusion models lose consistency beyond their trained window), so coherence beyond a few seconds remains the binding constraint. Motion realism without a control signal is the second: prompts under-specify dynamics, so the generator must sample from a highly multi-modal motion posterior, and the easy optimum is near-static or physically implausible motion that still scores well on per-frame metrics. The video–text data bottleneck is the third: paired data is scarce relative to images, web captions are short and weakly aligned, and this caps both controllability and the reliability of the automatic captioning used to scale corpora, which is what the dense-caption efforts (Panda-70M, MiraData, Koala-36M) address. The explicit control interfaces of the following subsections relieve the first two by moving structure and dynamics from the prompt into the input.

While textual descriptions provide high-level semantic guidance, they often lack the granularity required for precise control over object placement, scene geometry, or character appearance. Spatial-controlled video generation addresses this limitation by augmenting the generation process with explicit spatial conditioning signals, affording users more direct and deterministic influence over the synthesized visual output. The geometry, articulation, and layout that the text-to-video base case of § had to hallucinate from the prompt alone are here externalized into a per-frame scaffold: the spatial structure becomes an input the model must honor rather than an emergent property it must invent, which is precisely what makes the output controllable and verifiable.

a trainable control branch (dependence on the noisy latent, diffusion step, and other conditioning is omitted, and the backbone may be frozen while the adapter trains); latent concatenation and attention-based conditioning are the other common implementations. Figure shows the six channels alongside this adapter pathway: a reference image acts as a static appearance anchor, the other five are usually frame-indexed sequences, and compatible channels can be combined.

caption.text: Six spatial-control channels for video generation, (a)–(f), which can be selected or combined, and an example injection route (right) in which a trainable adapter adds residual features to a frozen video backbone (Eq. ()). Frames and control maps are illustrative.

para.p: Image Control. A reference image (Figure a) specifies the style, content, or initial state of a video, which is the basis of animating a still and of keeping a subject’s appearance consistent. I2VGen-XL [], Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [], VideoCrafter1 [], and Lumiere [] use the reference image as an initial condition, often by concatenating its latent with the initial noise, and ConsistI2V [] refines this for consistency. The model then generates a plausible motion sequence that evolves from the image, typically under a text prompt, as in DynamiCrafter [].

Pose Control. Pose-guided generation (Figure b) animates articulated subjects, predominantly humans, along a predefined sequence of skeletal poses, the video counterpart of pose-guided image generation [] and the core of avatar animation and character generation. The pose keypoints (e.g., , from MMPose []) are encoded and injected at each denoising step, frequently through a ControlNet-style adapter []. MagicAnimate [], Animate Anyone [], Follow-Your-Pose [], and DreamPose [] pair a reference image for appearance with a pose sequence for motion, DisPose [] disentangles the pose guidance, and Champ [] and MagicPose [] target high-fidelity motion, so that the output keeps the subject’s identity while following the target poses.

Depth Control. A sequence of depth maps (Figure c), estimated from an existing video or rendered from a 3D model, specifies dense 3D structure and so enforces consistent object layout and realistic occlusion. ControlVideo [], Make-Your-Video [], Control-A-Video [], and ControlNeXt [] adapt the ControlNet framework to video, processing each frame’s depth map with a trainable adapter that guides the denoiser; DreamDance [] and SparseCtrl [] also use depth for dynamic scene generation.

Landmark Control. Facial landmarks (Figure d) give fine-grained control over expression and are the standard interface for talking-head animation. EchoMimic [], HunyuanPortrait [], and LivePortrait [] animate a static portrait from landmarks, often themselves driven by audio, so that lip movements, blinks, and subtle expressions stay synchronized; TASTE-Rob [], Takin-ADA [], and Follow-Your-Emoji [] extend landmarks to more expressive control.

Sketch Control. Sketches (Figure e) let users define compositional layout and motion with simple line drawings, an intuitive interface for animation. ToonCrafter [], VidSketch [], AniDoc [], and SketchBetween [] take a sequence of sketches to guide interpolation or generation, encoding the line art and injecting it as a condition; LayerAnimate [] animates hand-drawn characters and scenes layer by layer, and MagicStick [] uses sketch-like structural cues for editing.

Bounding Box (BBox) Control. Bounding-box tracks (Figure f) specify where objects are and how they move over time, and dominate autonomous-driving simulation: MagicDrive [], DriveDreamer [], DriveScape [], and DreamForge [] use 3D boxes to control the position and motion of vehicles and pedestrians. The box information enters either through cross-attention, as in DiVE [], or as a spatial feature map, and Boximator [] and Ctrl-V [] generate and control object motion from box sequences.

Nearly every structural channel (pose, depth, sketch, box) is paired with an appearance reference image, since structure alone cannot fix identity or texture, and the channels cluster by application: image and landmark control in portrait and talking-head synthesis, pose and sketch control in character animation, depth and box control in geometry-faithful and driving-simulation settings.

Unlike the text-to-video base case of §, spatial control has no single canonical corpus or suite: each channel is trained and evaluated on data specialized to its application. Models are typically built on the general web-scale corpora of § (WebVid-10M [] and successors) for appearance priors, then specialized on task data: human-animation channels on dance- and fashion-video collections paired with extracted pose keypoints (e.g., , via OpenPose [] or MMPose []), talking-head landmark control on portrait-video sets, and bounding-box driving simulation on annotated driving datasets such as nuScenes [], whose 3D box and trajectory labels supply the control signal directly.

Spatial control is judged on two axes simultaneously: the generic video-quality metrics of § (FVD [], CLIPSIM, and VBench [] dimensions) and channel-specific adherence metrics that measure how faithfully the output respects
c s
. The latter are necessarily per-channel: pose and landmark control report keypoint accuracy (re-detected-keypoint distance to the target skeleton or face mesh); depth control reports depth consistency between the re-estimated and the conditioning maps; image control reports identity and appearance preservation (face-/subject-similarity to the reference); and bounding-box control reports detection mAP and trajectory IoU of the generated objects against the conditioning boxes. Neither axis suffices alone, so methods report a quality-plus-adherence tuple: a model can maximize adherence by ignoring the prompt (rigid, texture-collapsed output) or maximize quality by ignoring the control. The same holds for every controlled axis that follows.

Single-channel spatial control has three problems of its own; those that arise once several conditions are fused are discussed in §. Because the structural scaffold and the appearance reference pass through the same denoiser, strong control leaks structure into texture: pose and depth conditioning induce identity drift or bake the scaffold’s silhouette into the surface, and disentangling what moves from what it looks like (as DisPose [] attempts for pose) remains open. Dense scaffolds (image, depth) over-constrain and suppress plausible motion, whereas sparse ones (boxes, coarse sketches) leave appearance and fine geometry ambiguous, so no channel is uniformly preferable and the right granularity depends on the task. And adapters trained on, say, frontal human dance transfer poorly to unusual viewpoints or non-human subjects, which is the data cost of per-channel specialization and one motivation for the multi-condition frameworks of §.

Temporal control regulates how motion and timing evolve across frames, the lever behind cinematic camera work, narrative pacing, and believable physical interaction. It is the complement of the spatial scaffold of §: where spatial control fixes where things are in each frame, temporal control fixes how they move between frames, externalizing the dynamics (object motion, camera path, timing) that the text-to-video base case of § otherwise had to sample blindly from a highly multi-modal motion posterior.

The four channels specify inter-frame dynamics through different signals, and no single injection architecture serves them all. One implementation uses a trainable temporal-control branch
