More broadly, two routes recur: explicit transformations that use the motion to warp noise, latents, or attention features, and encoded conditioning that steers generation through adapters, attention, or learned motion features. They are not tied to particular channels (flow and trajectories can drive learned conditioning, and camera control can use geometry-aware warping), and Figure keeps the four input channels separate from the two routes.

figure.toccaption: 8.15Four temporal-control channels for video generation, (a)–(d), and two alternative ways of applying them (right): warping noise or latents, and encoding the signal as conditioning features. Frames are illustrative.

caption.text: Four temporal-control channels for video generation, (a)–(d), and two alternative ways of applying them (right): warping noise or latents, and encoding the signal as conditioning features. Frames are illustrative.

para.p: Flow Control. The most explicit motion signal (Figure a) is an optical-flow field, which records the per-pixel displacement between consecutive frames and so specifies dynamics at the finest granularity; conditioning on a sequence of such fields yields specific, coherent motion at the cost of authoring or estimating a dense signal. Motion-I2V [] integrates a motion-field predictor into its diffusion framework so that generation follows the supplied flow, I2VControl [] disentangles flow for unified control, and MOFA-Video [] animates a still image from user-painted motion fields. Go-with-the-Flow [] dispenses with the adapter altogether, warping the diffusion noise prior along the target flow so that the motion constraint lives in the sampling process rather than in an added branch.

Trajectory Control. Sparsifying the dense field into a few object paths (Figure b) trades pixel-level precision for an interface a user can actually author: a sequence of 2D or 3D coordinates, or a path drawn interactively, directs character movement or object kinematics, entering the denoiser either by modifying the latents or by steering cross-attention maps. MotionCanvas [], MagicMotion [], and Tora [] consume a predefined curve, FreeTraj [] relaxes this to free-form trajectories, Peekaboo [] also schedules when objects appear and disappear along the path, and DragNUWA [] and DragAnything [] let the user drag regions through the frame interactively. MotionCtrl [] handles object trajectory and camera motion in one controller, treating an object path and a camera path as two facets of the same inter-frame displacement.

Camera Control. Moving that displacement from objects to the observer (Figure c), camera-guided generation manipulates the virtual camera’s extrinsics (translation, rotation) and intrinsics (e.g., , focal length) to produce pans, tilts, zooms, and dolly moves. CameraCtrl [] and CameraCtrl II [] encode the camera trajectory as a conditioning feature; Direct-a-Video [], ViewCrafter [], and Cavia [] couple it with novel-view synthesis; and 3DTrajMaster [], MotionFlow [], and CineMaster [] control camera and objects jointly in 3D. Two directions now lead. ReCamMaster [] and TrajectoryCrafter [] re-render an existing monocular clip under a new camera path rather than generating from scratch, and Diffusion-as-Shader [] and GS-DiT [] route the camera signal through a 3D proxy (a rendered shader pass or a pseudo-4D Gaussian field), which sharpens control by making it geometry-aware.

Motion Control. At the abstract end (Figure d), the signal is no longer a geometric displacement but a behavioral concept (walking, dancing, jumping) transferred from a reference video as a pose sequence or a learned motion embedding. Unlike the pose control of §, it captures the dynamic style and cadence of a behavior rather than a frame-exact skeleton, so the central technical problem is disentanglement: extracting the motion while discarding the reference’s appearance. MotionDirector [], MotionClone [], and VMC [] learn this motion–appearance separation; Motion Prompting [], MotionAgent [], and MotionMatcher [] refine its granularity through trajectory- or feature-level motion descriptors; and DreamMotion [] and Customize-A-Video [] apply a reference clip’s dynamics to a new subject or scene fixed by the text prompt.

The channels trade precision against ease of specification: dense flow gives pixel-accurate control but is laborious to author, a motion embedding is effortless to supply but steers the result only loosely, and the most usable systems therefore pair an abstract signal (a drawn path, a reference clip) with a learned predictor that densifies it into the flow- or latent-level displacement the backbone actually consumes.

As with spatial control (§), temporal control has no single canonical suite: each channel is evaluated against data specialized to its signal. Models build on the general corpora of § for appearance and motion priors, then evaluate on task-specific resources: camera control on the posed-video collection RealEstate10K [], whose per-frame camera poses supply both the conditioning signal and the evaluation ground truth, increasingly supplemented by the larger and more scene-diverse DL3DV-10K [] to test generalization beyond real-estate walkthroughs; flow control against the MPI-Sintel optical-flow benchmark [] or flow re-estimated from generated clips with RAFT []; and motion- and trajectory-control quality through the motion-smoothness and dynamic-degree dimensions of VBench [].

Alongside the generic video-quality metrics of §, each channel measures adherence by re-extracting the control signal from the generated clip and comparing it with the conditioning input; the estimator and the error differ per channel.

Flow adherence. The optical flow of the generated clip is re-estimated with RAFT [] and compared to the conditioning flow by the end-point error (EPE), the per-pixel
L 2
displacement difference averaged over pixels and frames. A complementary flow-warping error warps each generated frame onto the next with the target flow and reports the photometric residual, which tests whether the rendered motion realizes the commanded displacement rather than merely correlating with it.

Trajectory adherence. The controlled object is re-localized in the output with a dense point tracker such as CoTracker [] or a detector, and its tracked center is compared to the target path by the mean
L 2
distance, normalized by frame size and averaged over time and instances; this is the object motion-control error reported by Tora [] and DragNUWA [], and it penalizes both spatial deviation and mistimed arrival.

Camera adherence. The camera trajectory of the generated clip is recovered by structure-from-motion (COLMAP []) and aligned to the target up to a similarity transform, since pose is recoverable only up to scale. Following CameraCtrl [], a rotation error (the geodesic angle between estimated and target rotations, summed over frames) and a translation error (the
L 2
distance between scale-normalized camera centers) are reported; failure to reconstruct a stable trajectory at all is itself diagnostic of an incoherent output.

Motion-transfer fidelity. With no ground-truth video, fidelity is measured from two sides: a motion-similarity term compares the dynamics of output and reference (the correlation of tracked point trajectories or temporal feature statistics), and an appearance-divergence term (CLIP similarity to the new prompt together with low feature similarity to the reference’s appearance) confirms that the subject was re-synthesized rather than copied.
As for spatial control, these adherence errors are reported together with generic quality, since a near-static clip trivially minimizes EPE and pose error while ignoring the prompt.

Three problems are specific to temporal control; fusing it with other conditions is discussed in §. Because the motion signal passes through the same backbone that renders appearance, a transferred motion often drags the source clip’s identity or texture with it, the leakage that MotionDirector [] and VMC [] try to disentangle and that remains unsolved for large appearance gaps between reference and target. Dense flow over-constrains and suppresses generative freedom, whereas a single trajectory or a short reference clip under-specifies the global dynamics, which is why methods increasingly interpose a learned predictor that densifies an abstract signal into a flow- or latent-level field. And a commanded camera path or object trajectory can demand views or dynamics inconsistent with the scene geometry, producing parallax errors and object distortion; 3D-aware camera control (ViewCrafter [], CineMaster []) routes the control through an explicit geometric proxy for exactly this reason, which links temporal control back to the volumetric representations of §.

Beyond the spatial scaffolds of § and the motion signals of §, a video can be steered by further, application-specific conditions: an artistic style reference, a handful of draggable points, a bird’s-eye-view road layout, a target text string to render, or a synchronizing audio track. Each externalizes an attribute that text specifies only loosely, extending controllable generation to creative, interactive, and domain-specific settings; together they raise the question the single-axis interfaces leave open, how to honor several conditions at once, which the universal frameworks at the end of this subsection try to answer.

para.p: Style Control. Style-guided generation transfers the artistic style of a reference image or video to a target video. Per-frame style transfer flickers; diffusion-based approaches such as Rerender A Video [], StyleCrafter [], FRESCO [], and StyleMaster [] instead integrate the style into generation, often by guiding it with the CLIP embedding of the style reference so that the style holds across frames, and UniVST [] generalizes this into a universal framework. FrameGuidance [] and OmniVDiff [] add training-free frame-level guidance and omni-controllable diffusion, respectively.

Point Control. Point control fixes motion through a sparse, interactive interface: the user drags a few points on an object from an initial frame to a new position in a later frame, and the model infers a plausible motion for the whole object. Drag-A-Video [] introduced the approach by optimizing latent codes to satisfy the point constraints, Track4Gen [] focuses on tracking the user-specified points robustly, and the 3D-aware camera controllers of § [] also accept sparse point input for non-rigid manipulation.

Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) Control. BEV-guided generation serves autonomous-driving simulation: a sequence of top-down semantic maps dictates the road layout, the positions of other vehicles, and the movements of pedestrians. DriveDreamer-2 [], MagicDrive-V2 [], DiVE [], DreamForge [], and Panacea [] take these maps as input and generate first-person driving video consistent with the specified layout and dynamics.

Text Rendering. Many generators cannot render coherent, legible text inside a scene, so a dedicated channel treats the target string itself as the control signal. Text-Animator [] adds text-embedding injection and refinement modules that improve the structure and temporal stability of rendered text, and Wan [] reports being the first video foundation model able to render legible Chinese and English text.

Audio Control. Audio-controlled generation synthesizes video synchronized with an input audio signal, in two sub-domains. Voice-guided generation produces talking heads: EMO [], VASA-1 [], DreamTalk [], and AniPortrait [] take a reference image and a speech clip, extract audio features with a pretrained encoder, and drive facial motion with accurate lip-sync and expression; Say Anything [], MuseTalk [], and CAFE-TALK [] focus on high-fidelity lip synchronization, and V-Express [] and MegActor [] balance audio against other control signals. Sound-guided generation follows more general audio such as music or ambient sound, using its rhythm, pitch, and emotional tone to drive visual elements, motion, and scene transitions: TA2V [], MotionCraft [], AV-Link [], and ASVA [] generate music visualizations or scenes that follow the energy and structure of a track, and MagicInfinite [] and Sound2Sight [] explore more open-ended audio-driven generation.

Universal and Multi-Task Control. The single-modality channels each add one encoder; universal frameworks realize the fusion of Eq. () in a single model, along two lines. Autoregressive models built on multimodal large language models generate video from discrete visual tokens, as in VideoPoet [] and Emu3 []. Diffusion models are being adapted to many conditions at once: VideoComposer [] integrates depth, pose, motion, and other conditions by channel concatenation, OmniHuman [] generates human video under multiple controls by mixing cross-attention and concatenation, and FullDiT [] processes all conditions with unified attention, the third realization of
F ψ
.

Being heterogeneous, the “other” modalities share no single suite: each is evaluated against data and metrics specialized to its signal, with the general corpora of § supplying the appearance and motion priors. BEV control is evaluated on driving collections such as nuScenes [], whose paired BEV layouts and front-camera footage furnish both the conditioning signal and the ground truth. Voice-guided talking-head generation is evaluated on portrait-video collections (HDTF [] and VFHQ [] are standard) and sound-guided generation on audio–video corpora with aligned music or ambient tracks. Style and point control, having no canonical benchmark, are assessed on the general corpora plus qualitative and user studies.

Beyond the generic video-quality metrics of § (FVD [], CLIPSIM, and VBench [] dimensions), each modality adds an adherence metric tailored to its signal, reported together with generic quality as in §. Style adherence combines a CLIP style-similarity to the reference with a temporal-consistency term that penalizes flicker. Point adherence re-localizes the dragged keypoints in the output and reports their
L 2
deviation from the target path, as in the trajectory metric of §. BEV adherence renders or detects objects in the generated clip and reports detection-mAP and layout-IoU against the input map. Text adherence runs OCR on the rendered frames and reports recognition accuracy and legibility. Audio adherence measures lip-sync quality with SyncNet-style confidence and landmark error for voice, and audio–visual synchrony for sound.

The central difficulty here, fusing conditions of incommensurate dimensionality and strength without one washing out or dominating the others, is shared with the spatial and temporal axes and discussed in §. Two problems are specific to these modalities. Text rendering must keep glyphs legible and stable at once, and per-frame legibility and temporal coherence pull against each other as the camera or the text moves. BEV control covers a narrow domain: models trained on a handful of driving datasets inherit their sensor rigs, cities, and traffic statistics, and generalize poorly beyond them.

Video editing takes an existing clip and modifies it under user instruction, rather than generating one from scratch (§) or steering that generation with controls (§–§). It is the temporal lift of the image editing of §, and its defining demand is selective preservation: the operator must change only the targeted content while holding the source’s geometry, layout, and motion fixed across every frame, so the central technical problem is to balance editability against spatio-temporal consistency without artifacts or unintended drift.

The five paradigms are overlapping choices of training strategy and preservation mechanism: training-free editing keeps the weights fixed, one-shot tuning updates selected parameters on the source clip, trained instruction editors learn across editing data, attention-based editing reuses or modifies source attention, and structural guidance conditions the edit on source-derived depth, edges, or poses. Many of them share a diffusion recipe that inverts the source clip and re-denoises it under the instruction; writing

figure.toccaption: 8.17Five overlapping video-editing paradigms, (a)–(e), applied to one task (top): restyling a driving clip while preserving its layout and motion. The dashed link in (c) marks a paired training example; scene sequences are illustrative.

caption.text: Five overlapping video-editing paradigms, (a)–(e), applied to one task (top): restyling a driving clip while preserving its layout and motion. The dashed link in (c) marks a paired training example; scene sequences are illustrative.

para.p: Training-Free (Zero-Shot) Methods. The lightest realization of Eq. () (Figure a) edits a video without any fine-tuning, analogous to zero-shot image editing []: DDIM inversion encodes the source into latent codes and noise maps, and the denoising process is rerun on them under the edited prompt. Text2Video-Zero [] and Pix2Video [] established the category, and vid2vid-zero [], I2VEdit [], RAVE [], and FastVideoEdit [] add latent-code warping and feature injection to improve temporal consistency without fine-tuning.

One-Shot Tuning Methods. Trading a little training for sharper fidelity (Figure b), Tune-A-Video [] fine-tunes a limited subset of a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model’s parameters on the frames of a single source video, so that the model learns its content and motion and can regenerate it under a new prompt. Dreamix [] builds on one-shot fine-tuning to improve both editability and fidelity to the original motion.

Training-Based Methods. The limited control and quality of inference-time editing have motivated editors that learn a reusable operator from editing data (Figure c), particularly for instruction-based editing. InsV2V [] extends the InstructPix2Pix [] framework directly to video; GenProp [] propagates an edit from a user-modified first frame to the rest of the sequence; and VideoPainter [] uses a video inpainting model as an intermediary. UNIC [] handles many editing tasks in one model by concatenating the conditions into a sequence with task-aware positional embeddings, and EditVerse [] unifies video generation and editing by representing text, image, and video as one token sequence processed with self-attention, which permits in-context learning and flexible inputs.

Attention-Based Editing. To protect preservation within the inference-time recipe (Figure d), many techniques manipulate the cross-attention maps directly: following Prompt-to-Prompt in images, they blend the attention maps of the original and edited prompts so that the inverted source structure of Eq. () survives the re-denoising. FateZero [] and Video-P2P [] were early examples, and Edit-A-Video [], TokenFlow [], UniEdit [], and AnyV2V [] improve temporal consistency at the token or feature level, enabling localized edits such as changing an object’s material or color while the scene structure is kept.

Editing with Structural Guidance. At the explicitly guided end (Figure e), editing is conditioned on spatial signals extracted from the source video, the conditioning machinery of § repurposed for preservation rather than generation. Rerender A Video [] feeds the source’s depth or edge maps to a ControlNet-like module during editing so that geometry and layout stay intact, and MagicEdit [] accepts a variety of spatial inputs (e.g., , pose, sketches, segmentation maps) for high structural fidelity, which suits style transfer and object replacement, where preserving structure is what prevents distortion and keeps motion coherent.

The paradigms trade cost against control: training-free editing avoids per-clip weight updates but may still need iterative inference, whereas a trained instruction editor is expensive to build but generalizes across edits.

Video editing has no single canonical suite, and evaluation has moved from shared source-video collections toward purpose-built, fine-grained editing benchmarks. Early evaluations report on DAVIS [], the de facto source set for object-centric edits, and on the LOVEU text-guided video-editing (TGVE) benchmark [], which supplies prompt–clip pairs with human ratings; VPBench, released with VideoPainter [], adds masked clips with dense captions for inpainting-style edits. The most recent suites target instruction-guided editing and pair richer data with model-based scoring. FiVE [] contributes
74
real clips (drawn from DAVIS) and
26
generated clips across six fine-grained editing types, with
420
object-level prompt pairs and masks, evaluated under a
15
-metric protocol spanning background preservation, text–video similarity, temporal consistency, video quality, and runtime. IVEBench [] scales this to
600
source videos spanning seven semantic dimensions and clip lengths from
32
to
1 , 024
frames, across eight task categories (
35
subcategories) whose prompts are generated by LLMs and refined by experts, and adopts a three-dimensional protocol (video quality, instruction compliance, and video fidelity) that fuses traditional metrics with multimodal-LLM-based assessment.

Editing is judged on three axes that mirror the editability–preservation tension of Eq. (). The classic metrics are, for edit adherence, the CLIP similarity between each edited frame and the target prompt; for temporal consistency, frame-to-frame CLIP similarity together with a warping error that flow-aligns adjacent frames and reports the photometric residual; and for structure and background preservation, PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS on the unedited regions against the source, atop the generic FVD [] quality score. These scalars correlate only loosely with human judgment on fine-grained edits (an object recolored but mislocalized can still score well), so the latest benchmarks add vision-language judges: FiVE-Acc [] uses a VLM to test whether the intended fine-grained edit succeeded, and IVEBench [] scores instruction compliance and fidelity with multimodal LLMs alongside the traditional metrics. Results are reported as an edit-versus-preservation pair, since ignoring the instruction trivially maximizes preservation.

Three problems are specific to editing. Pushing the edit harder erodes the unedited regions and the source motion, while protecting them too strongly suppresses the requested change; this editability–preservation trade-off of Eq. () is what every paradigm above negotiates differently. The invert-and-re-denoise recipe of Eq. () is imperfect, and its reconstruction error compounds over long clips, so edits that are clean over a few seconds degrade over minute-scale video. And training-based editors follow only the edit types seen in their training pairs, so a flexible instruction editor that handles arbitrary edits remains open; the unified generate-and-edit models UNIC [] and EditVerse [], which treat the source clip as one stream among many in shared attention, are the current attempt.

subsection.title: 8.3.6Summary and Critical Challenges and Future Directions

para.p: Table places the five control axes side by side: the control signal each introduces, the operator it instantiates over the shared sampler of Eq. (), the paradigms it surveys, the methods anchoring each, and the benchmarks on which it reports.

para.p:
The axes partition not by output domain, since all five decode a clip from the same
Z vid
, but by the control fed to one shared sampler: text-to-video is the
= κ ∅
limit, spatial, temporal, and other control progressively enrich
κ
, and editing alone reverses the direction of the map, taking an existing clip in place of pure noise. The injection mechanism converges across axes: the spatial residual branch (Eq. ()), the temporal branch (Eq. ()), and the multi-condition interface (Eq. ()) are one idea, a trainable control pathway added to a pretrained backbone, generalized from one condition to many, and the most recent systems (VideoComposer, FullDiT, UNIC, EditVerse) go further by folding every axis, editing included, into a single token sequence processed by shared attention. Evaluation has not converged: no suite spans the five axes, each reports generic quality together with a channel-specific adherence score, and the newest editing benchmarks (FiVE, IVEBench) add vision-language and multimodal-LLM judges to improve human alignment.

Video generation inherits every difficulty of the 2D and 3D priors of § and § and adds the time axis, which turns several already-hard problems into open ones; the four below cut across all five axes.

Temporal coherence and long-horizon drift. The defining difficulty of video over image generation is keeping content stable across frames. The signature artifact is flicker, the high-frequency appearance instability between adjacent frames that plagues per-frame and early GAN-based methods (§); over longer spans it gives way to identity drift, the gradual mutation of a subject’s appearance, color, or fine texture across a clip; and in autoregressive roll-outs to error accumulation, the compounding of small per-step mistakes that caps usable clip length. Latent video autoencoders with temporal compression [] and dedicated spatio-temporal attention suppress flicker, while autoregressive–diffusion hybrids such as CausVid [] and MAGI-1 [] combine sequential consistency with diffusion fidelity to push toward minute-scale generation; coherence over arbitrarily long horizons remains unsolved and is the binding constraint on the world-model applications that motivate the section.

Controllability versus fidelity under multi-condition fusion. As §–§ stack heterogeneous conditions (spatial scaffolds, camera paths, audio, style) onto Eq. (), the conditions begin to conflict. Over-strong conditioning yields rigidity and texture collapse; weak conditioning ignores the control; and naive fusion produces control-signal dilution (summed adapters wash one another out), condition leakage across frames, and collapse to the dominant condition when one modality (e.g., , audio in talking-head generation) overwhelms the rest. Compositional and universal frameworks (VideoComposer [], OmniHuman [], and the unified-attention design of FullDiT []) replace per-axis injection with joint token fusion and task-aware positional embeddings, but a principled account of how to weight and arbitrate competing conditions is still missing.

Physical and 3D plausibility. Even a temporally coherent, well-controlled clip may depict an impossible world, which is the bridge back to §. Generated motion frequently violates object permanence (objects teleport, morph, or vanish), contact and rigid-body dynamics (rigid objects warp non-rigidly; feet slide; occlusions resolve implausibly), and multi-view consistency under camera motion, where the same scene is rendered inconsistently from successive viewpoints. Systems presented as steps toward “world simulators”, Sora [] among them, still exhibit these failures on closer inspection. Camera-control methods [] and explicitly 3D-aware video diffusion (Diffusion-as-Shader [] and GS-DiT []) narrow the gap by conditioning generation on geometry, which suggests that the more promising route to physical plausibility runs through the volumetric representations of § rather than through scale alone.

Compute, latency, and evaluation. Underlying all three is cost: a spatio-temporal latent is an order of magnitude larger than an image latent, so long, high-resolution clips strain memory and make iterative sampling slow, which in turn limits the context length available for coherence and the conditioning budget available for control. Consistency distillation and few-step samplers, together with sparse and causal attention, are the active responses. Evaluation compounds the problem: distributional scores such as FVD and per-frame FID are blind to temporal and control adherence, and automatic metrics correlate weakly with human judgment, so reported progress is hard to compare across methods; benchmarks and human-aligned protocols that jointly score fidelity, temporal coherence, and per-axis control adherence are a central near-term need.

Coherence and physical plausibility both demand longer temporal context, which inflates compute, and every added condition enlarges the evaluation surface, so progress on any one of the four is bounded by the others. Together they mark the last step of the progression traced across §, from the static 2D prior of § through the static volumetric prior of § to dynamic, navigable models that consume spatial structure over time.

Motion generation is the temporal, embodied output channel of spatial generation: where §–§ synthesize static images, volumetric assets, and controllable video, motion generation produces the articulated dynamics that an avatar, character, or robot can actually enact. A generated motion is a time series of body poses that must be believable in its dynamics, physically plausible (balance, ground contact, non-penetration), and faithful to its driving signal, whether a text description, audio, a scene, or a key frame. The conditional-sampler template that turns a prompt into pixels (Eq. ()) is here instantiated over a sequence of poses in a structured kinematic space, so geometric priors meet physical constraints: the output must respect the biomechanics of an articulated body as well as the semantics of the condition.

The subsections are indexed by the moving agent and then by one cross-cutting operation: human motion (§), animal motion with its cross-species morphology (§), vehicle motion planning, where the body is rigid and the difficulty moves into the multi-agent traffic scene (§), and motion editing (§).

Human motion generation produces natural, varied sequences of human body poses from intentions, environmental stimuli, or explicit conditions, and supports animation, virtual characters in film and games, AR/VR, and human–robot interaction.

para.p: The body is modeled as a collection of keypoints, each a distinct anatomical landmark (joints or salient surface locations) given by its 2D or 3D coordinates in a chosen frame (pixel space or world space), and motion is encoded as a temporal series of such configurations. Keypoint representations are directly available from many motion-capture systems and are highly interpretable, but many downstream uses (character animation, robotic control) require converting keypoints to joint rotations through the IK problem. Some works instead augment or replace sparse skeletal keypoints with dense body markers distributed across the body surface [], which carry richer information about body shape, limb twisting, and fine geometric detail.

A pose is represented by joint angles, the rotations of body segments relative to their parent in a hierarchical kinematic tree. Most studies model these in three dimensions, treating each non-root joint as an element of
⁢ SO
( 3 )
, parameterized as Euler angles, axis–angle vectors, or unit quaternions.

Beyond pure joint rotation, statistical mesh models jointly capture pose and body shape, including non-rigid deformations associated with articulation. The Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) model [] defines a template mesh with fixed topology (6,890 vertices, 23 joint rotations plus a root) and uses linear blend skinning augmented by learned blend shapes: identity (shape) blend shapes for inter-subject variation and pose blend shapes for rotation-dependent deformations such as muscle bulging and twisting.

Methods for human motion generation are organized along two axes. The first is the learning paradigm: regression-based techniques learn a deterministic mapping from conditions to a single target motion, whereas generative approaches model the full conditional distribution of motion using GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows, or diffusion models (the generative paradigms themselves are detailed in §). para.p: Given a discrete action label (e.g., , “walk”, “throw”), these methods generate a corresponding sequence. Early work used GANs with graph convolution and self-attention (SA-GAN [], Kinetic-GAN []) for realism and diversity, while VAE/CVAE frameworks (Action2Motion [], ACTOR []) produced probabilistic, controllable motions. More recent models adopt contrastive latent learning (ODMO []), discrete autoregressive sequences (PoseGPT []), and diffusion (MDM [], the latent-diffusion hybrid MLD []). As most methods excel only at single actions, MultiAct [] recurrently composes multiple action motions into long sequences via a canonicalization scheme.

Conditioning on free-form language exploits richer semantic cues than fixed labels allow. Early methods used GANs (Text2Action []) or joint text–motion embeddings (JL2P [], two-stream encoder–decoders []); later ones added variational modeling and attention (TEMOS [], TEACH []). For zero-shot generalization, MotionCLIP [] and AvatarCLIP [] align the motion latent space with CLIP. The current frontier combines VQ-VAE tokenization [], autoregressive transformers (T2M-GPT []), and diffusion (FLAME []), with multimodal conditioning extensions such as MoFusion [] fusing text and audio. More recent masked-generative models (MoMask []) push quality and inference speed further by predicting quantized motion tokens with a bidirectional, iteratively-refined masking schedule rather than left-to-right.

The goal is coherent, expressive dance aligned to a music track. Early approaches framed this as supervised sequence-to-sequence translation via LSTM autoencoders [], transformers (AI Choreographer []), and multi-person frameworks (GroupDancer [], GDancer []). Because music–dance is inherently one-to-many, generative models model the diverse distribution: MNET [] with style conditioning, Transflower [], Bailando [] (VQ-VAE + GPT), and EDGE [] (diffusion). Graph-based methods (ChoreoMaster [], PC-Dance [], ChoreoGraph []) use motion graphs and shared music–motion embeddings for rhythmic coherence, while curriculum learning, dynamics-prior denoising, and hierarchical pose/motif/choreography modeling target long-term, genre-consistent full-song dances [].

Co-speech gesture synthesis generates upper-body or full gesture sequences from speech (audio, sometimes text). Early adversarial methods modeled person-specific gesture patterns []; subsequent work disentangled shared versus motion-specific variation [] and decomposed body, hands, and face []. Recent methods employ diffusion [], VQ-VAE quantization [], and style or speaker embeddings [] to handle diversity, identity, rhythm, and expression more robustly.

Human motion datasets group naturally by conditioning modality; Table gives their representation, scale, and condition. Text- and action-conditioned corpora dominate, led by the language-annotated KIT Motion-Language [] and HumanML3D [], BABEL []’s sequence- and frame-level labels over the AMASS [] aggregate, and the action taxonomies of UESTC [], NTU-RGB+D 120 [], and HumanAct12 []. Audio-conditioned resources split into music-to-dance sets (AIST++ [], AIOZ-GDANCE [], and several genre-specific collections) and co-speech gesture sets (Trinity [], BEAT [], PATS []), many built by fitting parametric body models to in-the-wild video. Scene-conditioned datasets (PROX [], GRAB [], HUMANISE [], CIRCLE []) capture human–scene and human–object interaction with synchronized geometry, from Vicon and IMU rigs to synthetic engines such as GTA-IM []. Across all three groups, the cost of high-quality capture forces a trade-off between scale and annotation fidelity.

para.p: Evaluating synthesized motion is hard because the condition–motion map is one-to-many, judgments are partly subjective, and quality depends on high-level conditional cues, so the literature reports an ensemble of metrics along three axes. Fidelity captures naturalness, smoothness, and plausibility: distance-based measures such as NPSS [] and NDMS [], keypoint accuracy (PCK []), motion-space statistics (AVE, Hellinger distance over speed histograms [], Fréchet Distance over pose rotations [], PSKL []), feature-space distributional distances led by FID (with IS [], MMD [], and related scores), and physical-plausibility proxies for foot sliding and foot–ground contact (FCS [], non-collision ratios [], contact accuracy []), the last still lacking a standardized definition. Diversity guards against the long-sequence “freezing” failure via intra-motion variation and freezing rate [], inter-motion manifold coverage, and multimodality metrics (n-APD, ADE/FDE and their multimodal variants []) computed by sampling many motions per condition. Condition consistency measures alignment to the driving signal: recognition accuracy and R-Precision for text/action, feature-level text–motion distance (Multimodal Distance [], mCLIP and MID []), audio–motion beat metrics (beat coverage, hit rate [], beat alignment [], SRGR [], Semantic Score []), and, for scene conditioning, non-collision and human–scene contact scores []. No single metric is decisive, so methods are compared on a task-appropriate composition of the three.

Data scarcity is the most basic constraint: high-quality motion capture is expensive and slow, so dataset scale trades against annotation fidelity, and heterogeneous pose representations and conditioning signals fragment the data that exist; fusing heterogeneous sources through weak supervision and multimodal foundation models is the main response. Semantic alignment is the second. Motion encodes culture, communication, and context, not only mechanics, and a model that fits joint trajectories while missing their relation to language, music, or environment produces motion that is kinematically clean but perceptually empty; semantic priors from language and foundation models help, but how to measure the result is unresolved. That is the evaluation problem: every objective metric above has blind spots, none replaces a user study, and the field still needs metrics that are both interpretable and better correlated with human perception. Controllability matters for practical use as much as in image generation, and joint masking, attribute prompts, and style conditioning are moving toward editing tools with textual, spatial, and temporal handles (§). Interactivity remains underexplored: most methods animate one person in a static scene, and socially coupled groups (conversation, group dance) and motion grounded in dynamic, actionable scenes need both new corpora and new models.

Most motion-generation work targets the human body and ignores the diversity of animal behavior, although synthesizing animal motion matters for wildlife conservation, ecology, and biomechanics. Relative to §, animal motion is harder on two fronts that the human setting never confronts: species vary widely in skeletal topology and morphology, so a single fixed-skeleton representation no longer suffices, and the same textual description (“walk stealthily”) maps to radically different gaits across species. These two pressures, i.e., , data scarcity and morphological heterogeneity, shape every method below, which is why animal motion generation borrows the architectures, datasets, and training recipes of human motion generation while adding species-conditioning machinery on top.

OmniMotionGPT [] tackles limited animal data by jointly training motion autoencoders on human and animal corpora and aligning their latent encodings to text via CLIP embeddings; it relies most directly on transfer, and at inference it still depends on human-motion priors, which prevents truly text-only animal generation. Motion Avatar [] uses SinMDM [] for data augmentation in its ZooGen pipeline (the route by which the Zoo-300K dataset is built) and extends the masked-motion modeling of MoMask [] to animals, adding an LLM planner that orchestrates joint motion and 3D-avatar mesh generation; it makes little use of species-specific structure, which is what Eq. () addresses. AniMo [] makes that remedy central, injecting species-aware modulation into a joint-aware spatiotemporal tokenizer and learning, through masked modeling, a mapping from text plus species attributes to motion tokens; its AniMo4D dataset (78,149 sequences over 114 species) yields markedly better morphological and behavioral fidelity than transfer-only baselines. X-MoGen [] pushes toward a single model spanning humans and animals: it embeds motion into a shared space with graph-based VAEs and latent autoencoders, generates via masked modeling, and adds a morphological-consistency module that enforces skeletal plausibility across species, supported by the UniMo4D corpus (
∼
115

∼

K sequences). OmniMotionGPT and Motion Avatar still lean on human priors, whereas AniMo and X-MoGen promote species morphology to a first-class, explicitly regularized conditioning variable, so the four together trace a progression from transfer toward native cross-species modeling.

para.p: Animal motion resources fall into two groups (Table ). Capture and pose-estimation corpora supply ground-truth articulated motion but no language: RGBD-Dog [] and 3DDogs-Wild [] pair RGB-D or RGB video with marker-based mocap for canine pose, and DeformingThings4D [] provides synthetic 4D sequences with dense mesh-deformation annotations across humanoid and animal categories. Text-to-motion corpora drive recent progress: AnimalML3D [] is the first text–animal-motion dataset, and the field then scales sharply through Zoo-300K [] (built by the ZooGen pipeline with SinMDM and LLM annotators), AniMo4D [] (normalized to a 30-joint cross-species skeleton), and UniMo4D [], which merges AniMo4D with HumanML3D and KIT-ML. Even the largest text-conditioned sets remain smaller and more morphologically fragmented than their human counterparts of §, which is what forces the transfer-and-modulate methodology above.

caption.text: Benchmarks for animal motion generation. “Subjects / species” counts individual animals for the canine capture sets and species or categories elsewhere; “Texts / frames” gives text descriptions for text-conditioned corpora and frames for capture corpora.

para.p: Animal motion evaluation reuses the three-axis human protocol of §, adapted for species-specific biomechanics. Fidelity is measured by FID against real movement distributions and by MPJPE against ground-truth poses, augmented with physical-plausibility checks for gait-cycle regularity, ground contact, and the absence of foot sliding or limb penetration. Condition alignment carries over R-Precision and Multimodal Distance to score text-/action-to-motion correspondence, and diversity / multimodality metrics quantify behavioral variety within and across species. The animal-specific addition is perceptual and biomechanical judgment of naturalness, balance, and anatomical consistency, which matters more for quadrupeds and multi-limbed morphologies than for the single human skeleton.

Physical realism is the most basic gap: most methods do not simulate ground-contact forces, quadruped balance, or the fluid dynamics of swimming and flight, so artifacts the human setting has largely learned to suppress reappear, and differently for every body plan. Behavioral diversity is harder than for humans because one instruction such as “walk stealthily” realizes into different gaits, postures, and speeds across species, so the conditional distribution to be captured is far wider while the data to capture it are scarcer. Unseen species and radical morphologies remain out of reach: species-aware modulation (Eq. ()) and morphological-consistency constraints generalize across the skeletons seen in training, but insects and winged or aquatic creatures violate the shared-skeleton, fixed-topology assumptions on which current methods rest. AniMo and X-MoGen already move toward treating morphology as a variable rather than a template, and topology-flexible representations are the direction this points.

Where § and § generate the motion of an articulated body, vehicle motion planning generates the trajectory of a (near-)rigid agent moving through a traffic scene. The body is far simpler, since a vehicle has essentially no internal articulation, but the difficulty moves outward into the environment: a planned trajectory must obey vehicle dynamics, stay on the drivable surface dictated by an HD map, and remain socially compatible with the future motion of many surrounding agents whose intentions are unobserved. This is the setting where motion generation becomes inseparable from multi-agent spatial reasoning and physical feasibility: trajectory forecasting (predicting how others will move) and planning (deciding how the ego vehicle should move) are two readings of the same generative object.

Prediction methods vary along two axes: how the scene context is encoded and how the multimodal future is decoded. Early encoders rasterize the scene into a bird’s-eye-view image, but the field has converged on vectorized encoders that represent lanes and agent tracks as polylines: VectorNet [] and LaneGCN [] build graph representations of the HD map, and transformer encoders such as Wayformer [] and the Motion Transformer (MTR) [] attend jointly over map and agents; graph-attention predictors [] model spatial and temporal interaction in the same spirit. On the decoding side, the defining property is multimodality, since a single context admits many plausible futures, so models predict a set of
K
modes with probabilities,

Math.text: p _ theta * conditional@(tau, kappa * c) = ((sum _ (k = 1)) ^ K)@(pi _ k * N * list@(tau, mu _ k * kappa * c, Sigma _ k))

para.p: rather than the single point estimate of Eq. (), which here would average distinct maneuvers (turning vs. going straight) into an infeasible mean. The earliest learned predictors modeled social interaction directly in agent-coordinate space, Social-LSTM [] through pooled recurrent states and Social-GAN [] through adversarial sampling, and Trajectron++ [] added dynamic feasibility to a graph-structured latent-variable model. Goal-based decoders make the modes explicit: DenseTNT [] samples dense candidate endpoints on the map and scores trajectories conditioned on them, exposing the maneuver structure that Eq. () captures only implicitly. Generative decoders replace the fixed mixture with a learned sampler: MotionDiffuser [] denoises whole multi-agent trajectory sets jointly.

Planning turns the same machinery on the ego vehicle. ChauffeurNet [] learns the ego policy by imitating expert driving and augments the demonstrations with synthesized perturbations and worst cases, so that the policy stays robust when it drifts off the data manifold. Figure situates these families along the encode/decode axes.

para.p:
Progress is measured on large real-world driving logs that pair agent tracks with HD maps: nuScenes [], Argoverse and Argoverse 2 [], and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset [], the last two offering the scale and interaction density that current transformer models require. Evaluation centers on the multimodal-aware displacement metrics that match Eq. (): minimum average and final displacement error over the
K
predicted modes (minADEK, minFDEK), miss rate (the fraction of scenes where no mode lands within a tolerance of the ground truth), and the soft mean-average-precision of the Waymo protocol, which jointly scores accuracy and the calibration of mode probabilities
π k
. Off-road and collision rates further test the feasibility constraint
f dyn
that purely displacement-based scores ignore.

The subsections above synthesize motion from scratch; motion editing instead modifies an existing motion so that it satisfies a new constraint while leaving the rest intact. It is the temporal, articulated analogue of the image editing of § and the video editing of §, and its demand is again selective preservation: change a targeted aspect (a trajectory, a joint, a style, a semantic action) while holding the body’s identity, timing, and untouched portions fixed, which makes editing the controllability layer that closes the generate-and-refine loop for motion.

A second family handles spatial controls that masking alone cannot express (a target root path, or a specific joint at specific times) through classifier-style guidance: GMD [] and OmniControl [] steer the denoiser toward arbitrary spatial constraints at any joint and time. Finally, semantic editors take a natural-language instruction in place of a geometric mask: MotionFix [] learns text-driven edits from paired source–target motions, and LLM-driven approaches [] decompose an instruction into a program of primitive edits applied iteratively. Rendered people illustrate edits rather than measured model outputs.

para.p: Motion editing inherits the corpora of § (HumanML3D [] and BABEL [] over AMASS), used in editing protocols where keyframes, joints, or trajectories are held out as the constraint, together with the dedicated MotionFix [] benchmark of paired source–edit–instruction triples that supplies the ground truth most editing tasks lack. Evaluation must report the editability–preservation pair jointly: editability through control adherence (instruction-conditioned R-Precision, target-joint or trajectory error) and overall realism (FID, foot-skating), and preservation through the deviation from the source outside the edit region. As in video editing, single scalars correlate weakly with perceived edit quality, so reporting a tuple, and increasingly a learned or VLM-style judge of instruction compliance, is becoming standard.

The central tension is the editability–preservation trade-off of Eq. (): pushing harder on a control propagates unwanted change through the kinematic chain (editing one arm disturbs balance and foot contact), so a good editor must respect the body’s global coordination, not just the masked entries. This is compounded by sparse-control ambiguity: a single keyframe or a root path under-determines the full-body motion, and the model must fill the gap plausibly, which the guidance and noise-optimization families address with differing robustness. Underlying both is an evaluation gap sharper than in synthesis: because the “correct” edit is rarely unique, ground-truth-based metrics under-reward valid alternatives, motivating the paired-triplet and judge-based protocols above. The trend mirrors the rest of § and §: from per-mechanism, training-free editors toward unified models that generate, control, and edit motion within a single conditional sampler, increasingly driven by natural-language instructions rather than geometric masks.

Generative modeling has moved outward from static images [] to video [], multi-view imagery [], and static 3D assets [], yet each stops short of a scene that is at once three-dimensional and alive. A 3D asset holds geometry but not motion; a video holds motion, but no view-consistent geometry one can navigate or simulate. 4D generation is where the two meet: the synthesis of dynamic 3D content whose geometry stays view-consistent as it moves and deforms over time []. This is the representation an embodied system needs to rehearse how a scene will unfold, and it underwrites photorealistic digital humans [], interactive AR/VR [], and high-fidelity simulation for autonomous driving and embodied AI [].

Two advances make this tractable. Temporal 3D representations, deformation-aware fields over NeRFs [], point clouds, and Gaussian splatting [], supply a geometry that can bend and move without losing view consistency, while the extension of generative diffusion into this domain supplies the realism and controllability to drive it. Together they open dynamic scene synthesis, 4D editing, and interactive agent simulation, at the cost of the difficulty this section returns to throughout: holding long-range temporal coherence while still granting flexible, user-driven control.

Formally, we cast 4D generation as the latent-generator framework of § unrolled along time over a shared 3D representation. Let

The subsections are organized by the conditioning input (text, image, video, a static 3D asset, or several at once). Figure previews this organization together with two methodological strategies that recur across all five, per-scene score distillation and explicit “generate-then-reconstruct” supervision; feed-forward generators and rig-based animation of meshes appear alongside them in the subsections where they apply.

para.p: Text-to-4D generation synthesizes dynamic content directly from natural language, supporting text-driven asset creation and character animation []. Its progress has been propelled by large language models for semantic understanding and by video foundation models that supply motion priors.

Text-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. () to a textual condition

Two strategies recur throughout this section, implicit distillation and explicit supervision, implemented across various 4D representations (Figure ). The more common implicit strategy leverages Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) to indirectly optimize the geometry and motion of a 4D representation, using pre-trained diffusion models as frozen priors []. Formally, it applies a score-distillation update to per-scene parameters

The update differentiates through the renderer while treating the prior noise residual as the supplied gradient signal; this lifts the static score-distillation objective of § to a temporal sequence. In contrast, explicitly supervised methods initialize the 4D generation from text-to-3D or text-to-video outputs and use these generated assets as direct supervisory signals []. This “generate-then-reconstruct” strategy first synthesizes target frames
^ y

G 2D

Math.text: formulae@(hat@(y) = G _ [2D] * c, (hat@(r)) ^ (1 colon T) = argument@(minimum _ (r ^ (1 colon T))) * (sum _ (list@(pi, t)))@((norm@(Render * open-interval@(r ^ t, pi) - ((hat@(y)) ^ t) _ pi)) ^ 2))

para.p: replacing score-distillation guidance with explicit pixel targets; reconstruction may itself require per-scene optimization, so a speed advantage depends on the implementation. The two strategies are realized across mesh, NeRF, and 3DGS representations.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes offer explicit geometric control, which suits precise text-driven shape manipulation and animation. CT4D [] implements a three-stage “Generate-Refine-Animate” pipeline in which a mesh is generated from text, its texture refined, and its vertices animated; TextMesh4D [] deforms a generated mesh through a per-face Jacobian deformation field under video-diffusion priors; and AvatarCLIP [] generates a static avatar zero-shot and animates it by registering motion to an SMPL skeleton.

NeRF-based Methods. NeRFs represent continuous geometry and complex temporal variation well. MAV3D [] introduced multi-stage SDS optimization that refines texture, geometry, and motion with priors from both T2I and T2V diffusion models; 4D-fy [] blends 3D-aware, image, and video score signals in a hybrid SDS; and Dream-in-4D [] first generates a static asset with a multiview diffusion model and then adds dynamics with a video diffusion model.

Gaussian Splatting-based Methods. 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) [] renders efficiently and differentiably, which speeds up text-driven dynamic scene synthesis. Early methods followed the two-stage implicit pipeline of Eq. (): AYG [] generates a static 3D Gaussian model from text via SDS and adds dynamics under a T2V prior, and Comp4D [] uses an LLM to parse a complex prompt into several dynamic objects and their trajectories for a compositional scene. Later works moved to explicit supervision (Eq. ()): PLA4D [] aligns the 4D Gaussians pixel by pixel with generated video targets, and 4Real [] uses generated multiview video frames as the reference for photorealistic scene-level generation. For digital humans, AvatarGO [] generates 4D human–object interactions zero-shot by animating a text-to-3D human with the SMPL-X skinning function.

Text-to-4D, like the other subfields of this section, has no standardized benchmark, because large-scale dynamic 3D data with text descriptions is hard to capture and annotate. Training and evaluation instead adapt static 3D repositories (Table ): Diffusion4D [] filtered Objaverse and Objaverse-XL [] down to 54K high-quality animated assets, and SV4D [] built ObjaverseDy by adaptive sampling and viewpoint adjustment. These are synthetic renderings and lack the multimodal annotations, text in particular, needed to train and evaluate text-conditioned models robustly.

para.p: Evaluation across 4D generation combines user studies with metrics borrowed from image and video generation, and the subsections that follow use this same set. Semantic alignment with a prompt is measured by CLIP Score [] between rendered views and the text; fidelity by PSNR [], SSIM [], and LPIPS [] where a reference view exists; temporal quality and motion by the Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) []; and overall plausibility and aesthetics by user studies. None of these scores the two properties that make content 4D, cross-view consistency and long-range spatio-temporal coherence.

The challenge specific to text-to-4D is semantic-to-motion ambiguity: a prompt such as “a dancing dog” admits endlessly many movements, styles, and trajectories, and methods that lean on generic T2V priors struggle to produce diverse, fine-grained motion that matches a nuanced description. One response uses LLMs for motion planning, as Comp4D [] does when it decomposes a prompt into a structured spatio-temporal plan for several interacting objects; another targets human–object interaction [], moving toward story-driven dynamic scenes.

Image-to-4D generation synthesizes dynamic content from a single static image, combining the spatial information in the image with temporal priors learned by video models []. No large image–4D paired dataset exists, which has ruled out direct end-to-end training and pushed the field toward optimization and toward generated supervision.

Image-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. () to a single-image condition
= c I
,

Math.text: (hat@(r)) ^ (1 colon T) similar-to p _ theta * conditional@(r ^ (1 colon T), kappa * I)

para.p:
where the source view at
= t 0
is fixed by
I
while every unseen viewpoint and time step must be inferred. Both the unseen 3D geometry and the entirely absent temporal dynamics have to be inferred from one 2D view, which requires combining the spatial cues of the input with temporal priors from large video models [].
Both strategies of § apply, and most methods use 4D Gaussian Splatting as the representation [].

Implicit Optimization with Diffusion Priors. These methods instantiate Eq. (), typically combining a multiview diffusion model for geometric consistency with a video diffusion model for temporal coherence. Animate124 [] first generates a static NeRF from the image and then refines its dynamics with a video-diffusion SDS loss, and Diffusion2 [] reconciles the scores of heterogeneous priors (multiview and video) through Variance-Reducing Sampling, improving both multiview and temporal consistency of the resulting 4D Gaussians.

Explicit Supervision with Generated Data. The slow, iterative nature of SDS motivates the two-stage pipeline of Eq. (), in which an image-to-video model first generates an intermediate video that then supervises the 4D reconstruction directly. DreamGaussian4D (DG4D) [] generates a static 3D Gaussian model and learns a deformation field to animate it, using the generated video for texture refinement and dynamic supervision, and EG4D [] avoids SDS entirely by chaining image-to-video and image-to-multiview models into coherent image sequences that guide a fast reconstruction.

Unified and Tuning-free Generation. GenXD [] trains one model on both 3D and 4D data, using multiview-temporal modules that separate camera motion from object motion, and Free4D [] builds a 4D scene from a single image without fine-tuning any model, distilling pretrained image-to-video and multiview priors into a consistent 4D representation.

Specialized Methods for Human Generation. Dynamic human avatars form a sub-domain in which strong body priors raise fidelity. Human4DiT [] uses a hierarchical 4D transformer that integrates human-specific features, camera parameters, and temporal signals to generate 360-degree human animations from a single image, and Disco4D [] models the body with SMPL-X while representing clothing separately with Gaussian splats, allowing detailed animation of clothed humans.

With no image–4D pairs, methods are evaluated on images from Objaverse [] or on in-the-wild photographs chosen by the authors, which makes comparison across papers unreliable. The metric set is that of §, applied to the source view and to pseudo-ground-truth novel views where available.

Inferring a complete shape and a plausible motion from one viewpoint is extremely ill-posed, which shows up as geometric inconsistency in unseen views (e.g., , the “Janus problem”) and as unnatural or repetitive motion, since every dynamic detail must be hallucinated. Domain-specific priors are the main remedy: Human4DiT [] and Disco4D [] regularize geometry and motion with parametric body models and reach much higher fidelity, at the cost of generality.

Video-to-4D generation lifts a single-view video into a dynamic 4D representation that can be viewed from new angles with consistent geometry and motion, turning ordinary video into interactive 4D content. Annotated video-to-4D datasets are hard to curate, so current methods build on pretrained video diffusion priors, either as multi-view supervision or through score distillation.

Video-to-4D generation specializes the 4D sampler of Eq. () to a monocular video condition
= c
v
: 1 T
,

Math.text: (hat@(r)) ^ (1 colon T) similar-to p _ theta * conditional@(r ^ (1 colon T), kappa * v ^ (1 colon T))

para.p:
so that re-rendering
^ r
: 1 T
from the input viewpoint reproduces
v
: 1 T
while novel views remain geometrically consistent. Unlike image-to-4D (Eq. ()), the temporal dynamics are now observed and the residual ambiguity is purely geometric: the unseen off-axis structure.
Most methods densify the monocular input into multi-view supervision and reconstruct against it (Eq. ()), some add score distillation (Eq. ()), and the newest predict the 4D asset feed-forward.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes are interpretable and efficient to animate. DreamMesh4D [] obtains a coarse mesh and drives it with a sparse deformation graph and linear blend skinning (LBS), reaching strong spatio-temporal consistency more cheaply than implicit volumetric methods, and V2M4 [] reconstructs an animated, textured mesh asset directly from a monocular video.

NeRF-based Methods. NeRF-based methods model the continuous volumetric content of a video well, and they overcome the single view by generating data. Consistent4D [] densifies the monocular input through temporal and multiview interpolation before optimizing a NeRF with SDS, 4Diffusion [] fine-tunes a video diffusion model with a learnable motion module on synthetic multiview data so that it produces consistent multiview video to guide generation, and SV4D [] completes missing views and frames with a diffusion model and uses the resulting multiview video to supervise the reconstruction.

Gaussian Splatting-based Methods. 4DGen [] grounds 4D Gaussian generation in the input video with spatial-temporal pseudo labels; Efficient4D [] converts the video into a multiview image matrix with a multiview-consistent generator (SyncDreamer) for rapid reconstruction; SC4D [] first fits sparse control Gaussians for coarse shape and motion and then drives dense Gaussians through LBS; and L4GM [] predicts the 4D Gaussians of a whole clip in a single feed-forward pass, trained on rendered animated objects.

Video-to-4D has the one dedicated evaluation set in this section, released with Consistent4D []: synthetic and real monocular videos with training and test splits. The metrics are those of §, with reconstruction fidelity measured at the input view and novel-view quality measured where synthetic ground-truth multiview video exists.

The video constrains motion but not the unseen 3D structure, which leads to geometric distortion, depth ambiguity, and a “painted-on” look in novel views. Explicit geometric structure is the main remedy: DreamMesh4D [] and SC4D [] constrain the reconstruction with meshes or sparse control points under LBS, which improves both coherence and efficiency, and combining such structure with the appearance modeling of neural representations is the obvious next step.

3D-to-4D generation animates a static 3D model, so that the geometry is given and only motion and deformation must be synthesized, which makes the large stock of existing 3D assets usable for simulation, virtual reality, and character animation. Unconditional generators of dynamic neural fields, such as HyperDiffusion [], which runs diffusion directly on the weights of neural fields, sample 4D content without a given asset; 3D-to-4D instead starts from one, either through explicit mesh deformation and rigging or through neural and physics-based deformation models.

Here the condition is itself a 3D representation
c =
r 0
∈ R
, so only its temporal evolution must be generated. We therefore specialize Eq. () to a deformation operator that takes the static asset and an optional auxiliary driving signal
c aux
(text, audio, or a motion sketch) to a sequence,

Math.text: formulae@((hat@(r)) ^ (1 colon T) = D _ theta * open-interval@(r _ 0, kappa * c _ [aux]), (hat@(r)) ^ 0 = r _ 0)

para.p: with the first frame pinned to the input asset. This places 3D-to-4D in the same family as the editing operators of § and §: it transforms an existing representation rather than synthesizing one from scratch.

Methods realize the deformation operator
D θ
of Eq. () either with explicit mesh structure, increasingly through learned rigging, or with neural and physics-informed deformation fields.

Mesh-based Methods. Meshes give explicit structure and precise control over deformation. Motion3DGAN [] generates 3D facial animation from a static face mesh by first predicting the displacement of facial landmarks for a target expression and then deforming the full mesh, with a GAN keeping the sequence temporally coherent. A recent line makes arbitrary meshes animatable by predicting the rig itself: MagicArticulate [] and RigAnything [] predict skeletons and skinning weights feed-forward, Puppeteer [] rigs a mesh and then animates it by fitting the rig to videos generated from renderings of the mesh, and AnimateAnyMesh [] generates text-driven mesh animation in a single forward pass with a rectified-flow model over a dynamic-mesh latent.

NeRF-based Methods. ElastoGen [] generates physically grounded elastodynamic behavior: it rasterizes a static 3D model and then predicts and refines deformation fields iteratively with recurrent and 3D convolutional modules, so that the motion obeys physical principles.

No benchmark with ground-truth dynamic sequences exists; methods are evaluated on a few individual assets, often faces or generic objects, mostly by user study and with the metrics of § where a reference animation is available. Physical plausibility, specific to this subfield, can be measured for physics-informed methods such as ElastoGen [] as deviation from a high-fidelity simulator or as violation of conserved quantities such as energy and momentum.

Even with the geometry given, the space of plausible animations of a static model is unbounded, so without guidance the task is unconstrained, and current methods specialize to narrow categories such as faces. Physical priors constrain it (ElastoGen [] grounds motion in elastodynamics), learned rigging makes arbitrary assets animatable, and pairing the asset with text, audio, or motion sketches turns open-ended generation into controllable animation.

Multi-conditional 4D generation steers dynamic scene synthesis with several signals at once: semantic conditions (text), appearance conditions (images, video), structural conditions (skeletal poses, explicit trajectories), and rule-based priors (differentiable physics). The central design problem is to fuse them so that each is respected without one overpowering the others.

We generalize the single-condition cases of Eqs. ()–() to a set of
K
conditions, each mapped by its own encoder
κ k
and fused into the shared embedding:

Math.text: (hat@(r)) ^ (1 colon T) similar-to p _ theta * conditional@(r ^ (1 colon T), list@(kappa _ 1 * c _ 1, dots, kappa _ K * c _ K))

para.p:
which recovers a single-modality sampler when
= K 1
. Users can then specify not only what is generated (semantics) but how it behaves (motion path, physical behavior, artistic style), which complex applications such as character animation and driving simulation require.

Methods fuse the encoders
κ k
of Eq. (), usually combining score distillation (Eq. ()) with explicit supervision (Eq. ()) tailored to each condition.

Motion and Trajectory Control. TC4D [] lets users define a spline trajectory that guides both the global rigid transformation and the local deformation of an object, with text supplying the semantics. For human animation, skeletons are the natural condition: Beyond Skeletons [] integrates text and image conditions with the skeleton to refine motion, and STAR [] uses skeleton-aware SDS and motion retargeting so that avatar movement is both visually coherent and anatomically accurate.

Physics-Informed Control. Sync4D [] and Phy124 [] integrate differentiable Material Point Method (MPM) simulation, so that the generated content follows realistic dynamics such as elasticity and collisions under video or text guidance.

User-Centric and Artistic Control. Generative Rendering [] uses a pre-existing dynamic mesh to guide a pretrained text-to-image model, giving precise control over the style and detail of the rendered output, and sketch-based interfaces [] let users draw the dynamics they want.

Complex, Application-Specific Control. MagicDrive3D [] generates dynamic driving scenes from 2D bounding boxes, Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) maps, agent trajectories, and text together, producing tightly controlled traffic scenarios.

No benchmark exists; building one would require 4D assets annotated with several aligned conditions (e.g., , a clip with a description, a skeletal motion sequence, and a trajectory map). Text adherence is scored with the CLIP Score of §, while adherence to sketches or trajectories relies on task-specific errors (e.g., , distance from the specified trajectory) or on user studies, which remain the only holistic judge of how well a combination of inputs was followed.

Semantic guidance from text, geometric constraints from skeletons, and rule-based priors from physics can contradict one another, and keeping each respected without one overpowering the rest while preserving fidelity is the open problem. Domain-specific stacks such as MagicDrive3D [] sidestep it by fixing the set of inputs for one application, and interactive interfaces such as sketches [] point toward iterative creation in which several control channels are adjusted in turn.

Table compares the five subfields as specializations of the 4D sampler of Eq. (): image- and video-to-4D progressively replace hallucinated structure with observed pixels, 3D-to-4D is given the geometry and generates only motion, and multi-conditional generation fuses several signals at once.

para.p: Large, annotated 4D datasets are the field’s main missing ingredient: real dynamic 3D data with multi-view consistency and multimodal annotation (text, motion capture) is expensive and technically hard to collect, which has largely ruled out end-to-end training. The field has therefore converged on distilling pretrained text-to-image, text-to-video, and text-to-3D models, the de facto way to guide 4D synthesis.

paragraph.title: From Score Distillation to Explicit Supervision.

para.p: Score distillation [] converges slowly, is costly and unstable, and produces multi-faced geometry and flickering textures. The generate-then-reconstruct pipeline of DreamGaussian4D [] and EG4D [], which first generates target videos and then reconstructs against them, is replacing per-prompt SDS, and feed-forward predictors such as L4GM [] and AnimateAnyMesh [] take the next step by removing per-scene optimization altogether.

paragraph.title: 4D Gaussian Splatting as the Default Representation.

para.p: NeRF-based works rendered well but trained and rendered slowly. 3D Gaussian Splatting [] and its temporal extension offer real-time, high-fidelity rendering with efficient gradient-based optimization, and their explicit, point-based form is easier to edit and to couple with physical simulation, so 4DGS has become the representation of choice for current methods [].

Keeping geometry, appearance, and motion coherent across all viewpoints and over long horizons remains the central difficulty, and control is moving beyond single prompts toward fine-grained manipulation of motion, appearance, and interaction. Physical plausibility is the newest goal: integrating differentiable simulators, as PhysSplat [] and Phy124 [] do, makes generated dynamics more realistic and predictable. Progress on all three is hard to measure while evaluation relies on small, author-curated test sets and on image and video metrics that ignore cross-view and long-range consistency; 4D-aware benchmarks and metrics are a prerequisite for the rest.

Despite its growing popularity across AI research, the notion of a “world model” does not yet enjoy a unified or universally agreed-upon definition. Its conceptual roots trace back to the psychologist Kenneth Craik, who argued in his 1943 monograph The Nature of Explanation that the mind “carries a ‘small-scale model’ of external reality and of its own possible actions within its head”. In its original form, a world model referred to an individual’s internal representation of external reality; contemporary AI has generalized the concept far beyond mental representations to structured models of physical and spatial environments.

Fei-Fei Li has framed the gap between current AI systems and physical understanding in these terms []: modern LLMs resemble “wordsmiths in the dark”, fluent in symbols but divorced from the physical world that gives them meaning, and capable AI must instead understand, act within, and reason about three-dimensional space. On this view world models are new-generation generative models that simulate, predict, and imagine the world’s dynamics rather than only describe it, which ties world modeling directly to spatial intelligence.

Complementing Li’s generative perspective, another influential formulation comes from Yann LeCun []. He describes a world model as a system capable of predicting how the world will evolve given its current state and an action. Formally, it consumes the current state
⁢ S
( t )
and an action
⁢ A
( t )

What exactly constitutes a “state” remains open: some work defines it as a compact latent representation in which the world model operates at an abstract semantic level, much as human cognition forecasts events without simulating every physical detail.

Although no single definition of world modeling has been universally accepted, a survey of the literature [] reveals three recurring paradigms, three realizations of Eq. () that differ in what they predict. Representation world models learn abstract latent spaces that capture the state and dynamics of the environment. Generative world models explicitly simulate or generate future states of the world through data-driven or hybrid mechanisms. Mental world models aim to infer and represent the mental states of humans or agents, enabling social reasoning and Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities. Figure contrasts them side by side.

para.p: A representation world model learns an internal latent description of the environment by compressing multimodal observations into structured, predictive embeddings, prioritizing the extraction of physical and semantic regularities over the generation of photorealistic pixels. Much as LLMs learn abstract linguistic representations through self-supervised pretraining, representation world models are trained on “world data” to infer the principles that govern physical and semantic dynamics; the objective is to predict how the world evolves at an abstract level, not to reconstruct pixels. The latent state is meant to encode objects and their properties (shape, size, appearance, material), their spatial relations (topology, distance, configuration), the dynamics that govern how the scene evolves, and the causal dependence of outcomes on actions. With such a state, an agent can predict over long horizons, reason, and plan without operating in high-dimensional sensory space.

A world model draws on several sensory streams, whose encoding is the subject of Chapter . Vision dominates: images and especially video carry objects, geometry, interaction, and temporal dynamics, and modern systems rely on high-capacity encoders trained with contrastive vision–language objectives for semantic and geometric priors. Audio adds direct evidence about events and the physical state of the surroundings, which language conveys only symbolically. Touch is indispensable where vision is unreliable, occluded, or unavailable (grasping inside a bag, fine manipulation, tool use), yet it remains underexplored because tactile sensors are limited and tactile data are hard to collect at scale.

A major line of representation world modeling builds latent spaces from visual observations: video frames are encoded into a compact latent space by self-supervised learning, and a transition model predicts future latent states from past latents and actions, which captures the dynamics of the visual world more efficiently than pixel-space prediction. Concretely, an encoder
E ϕ
maps observations to latent states and a predictor
P θ
is trained to minimize a prediction loss defined entirely in latent space,

Math.text: L _ [rep] * open-interval@(theta, phi) = E * delimited-[]@((delimited-∥∥@(P _ theta * open-interval@(E _ phi * O _ (absent <= t), A * t) - sg@(E _ (bar@(phi)) * O _ (t + 1)))) ^ 2)

where

⁢
