taken to be an abstract embedding rather than raw pixels (Figure (a)), which is precisely what allows representation world models to capture dynamics efficiently while discarding perceptually salient yet predictively irrelevant detail.

The World Models architecture [] decomposes the problem into a VAE-based vision model, an RNN-based memory model, and a lightweight controller; the vision and memory components learn latent dynamics from raw pixels without supervision, and the controller then learns its behavior inside the “dreamed” environment, which greatly simplifies policy learning. The Dreamer agents carry this idea into reinforcement learning at scale: Dreamer [] learns a latent dynamics model from pixels and trains an actor and critic entirely on imagined latent trajectories, and DreamerV3 [] applies a single configuration across a wide range of domains. MuZero [] learns a model that predicts only the quantities planning needs (reward, value, and policy) and plans with it by tree search, mastering Atari, Go, chess, and shogi without being given the rules.

Yann LeCun’s autonomous intelligence framework proposes the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) [] as the core mechanism for constructing world models. JEPA learns latent representations and predictions through self-supervised objectives rather than pixel-level reconstruction, and Eq. () is its generic form. I-JEPA [] first instantiated it on images, predicting the embeddings of masked target regions from a visible context block, and V-JEPA [] carried the same feature-prediction objective to video, predicting masked spatio-temporal embeddings in latent space with no pixel reconstruction, text, or negative examples, and so avoiding the cost and ambiguity of pixel prediction. V-JEPA 2 [] turns this encoder into a world model. Pretrained on more than a million hours of internet video, it is extended with an action-conditioned predictor, V-JEPA 2-AC, post-trained on less than 62 hours of unlabeled robot video; deployed zero-shot on Franka arms, it picks and places objects by planning actions whose predicted embeddings reach a goal image.

The stop-gradient and slowly updated target encoder in Eq. () exist only to keep the representation from collapsing, and the most recent JEPA work removes them. LeJEPA [] shows that an isotropic Gaussian is the optimal embedding distribution for downstream prediction and enforces it with a single sketched regularizer (SIGReg), leaving one trade-off hyperparameter and no teacher–student machinery. LeWorldModel [] uses the same regularizer to train an action-conditioned JEPA world model end to end from raw pixels with only two loss terms; at about 15M parameters it trains on a single GPU, plans up to 48 times faster than world models built on foundation-model encoders, and its latents encode physical quantities well enough to flag physically implausible events. The principle has also reached language: VL-JEPA [] predicts continuous embeddings of the target text instead of generating tokens, and LLM-JEPA [] adds an embedding-prediction objective to the next-token training of language models.

DINO-World [] instead freezes DINOv2 as a universal visual encoder, whose features are already semantic, geometric, and object-centric, learns a latent-space predictor from large-scale unlabeled video, and adds action-conditioned prediction to model how interventions change future visual states.

Another important direction expands representation learning beyond vision by incorporating additional modalities such as LiDAR, camera trajectories, or multi-view geometric signals. These hybrid models aim to overcome the limitations of purely visual latent spaces by injecting explicit spatial structure, depth cues, and geometric consistency constraints. For instance, MUVO [] is a multimodal generative world model that learns jointly from synchronized camera and LiDAR streams. By integrating LiDAR-derived depth priors into the latent world representation, MUVO achieves more reliable 3D scene prediction, improved object motion modeling, and long-horizon forecasting in autonomous driving environments. UniWorld [] introduces a unified pretrained architecture that merges 3D object detection, motion prediction, and scene representation learning. Through joint training of BEV features, temporal dynamics, and multisensor context, UniWorld produces a structured latent state that simultaneously supports perception and trajectory forecasting. Aether [] proposes a geometry-aware unified world model where camera trajectories are treated as explicit action signals. This allows the model to learn action-conditioned scene transitions and perform predictive visual planning. By binding egomotion with geometric consistency constraints, Aether generates spatially coherent future predictions and supports counterfactual simulation within a 3D-aware latent space.

A final category examines language as a central medium for latent world representation. This raises an important question: can LLMs themselves be viewed as world models? From a formal perspective, LLMs indeed share structural similarities with classical world models. They maintain internal states, treat textual context as observations, accept prompts as actions that alter these states, and generate predictions that correspond to inferred future states. Models such as Dynalang [] demonstrate that natural language can serve as a universal intermediate representation for encoding environment states, predicting transitions, and expressing causal relations. LLMs also exhibit emergent knowledge of commonsense physics, intuitive causality, and human behavior derived from massive text corpora. However, their limitations remain clear: they are trained on symbolic descriptions rather than direct interaction with the physical world; their internal dynamics reflect linguistic statistics more than physical laws; and their world representations tend to be sparse, fragmented, and disconnected from geometric or temporal continuity. Thus, while LLMs can be interpreted as language-driven world models, their predictive capacity is primarily symbolic and semantic, rather than grounded in spatial or physical understanding.

In contrast to representation-based foundation models, generative world models focus on explicitly predicting future states or synthesizing the evolution of the environment over time. Rather than only learning compact latent encodings, these models aim to simulate how the world might change under different conditions, capturing temporal dynamics and causal structure. Whereas the representation paradigm of Eq. () predicts in an abstract latent space, generative world models learn an explicit conditional distribution over future observations and can be unrolled autoregressively over a horizon
H
,

Math.tex: p_{\theta}\big{(}O_{t+1:t+H}\mid O_{\leq t},\,A_{t:t+H-1}\big{)}=\prod_{k=0}^{% H-1}p_{\theta}\big{(}O_{t+k+1}\mid O_{\leq t+k},\,A(t+k)\big{)},
Math.text: p _ theta * conditional@(O _ (t + 1 colon t + H), list@(O _ (absent <= t), A _ (t colon (t + H) - 1))) = ((product _ (k = 0)) ^ (H - 1))@(p _ theta * conditional@(O _ (t + k + 1), list@(O _ (absent <= t + k), A * (t + k))))

para.p: so that sampling from Eq. () realizes the transition of Eq. () directly in observation space (Figure (b)). This explicit synthesis is what allows generative world models to be rendered, inspected, and acted within, at the cost of having to model a high-dimensional output distribution. Broadly, generative world models can be grouped into two main families: physics-driven simulation, which relies on hand-crafted rules and equations, and learning-driven world generation, which learns world dynamics directly from data. The former can be viewed as the deterministic limit of the latter: it fixes the transition of Eq. () to a hand-specified rule set instead of a learned distribution, trading sample diversity and coverage for exact reproducibility and verifiability. A third route, growing quickly since 2024, sits between the two: a learned model writes the rules as code and a simulator executes them (Section ).

Physics-driven simulation builds interactive virtual worlds from human-designed physical, geometric, and logical rules rather than from learned latent spaces. The environment is governed by predefined physical laws, rendering rules, collision logic, and behavioral scripts, specified top-down as explicit mathematical formulations, so the same initial conditions always produce the same outcome; this determinism, together with interpretability and verifiability, is what makes such systems suitable for safety-critical engineering.

Game engines are the canonical example. Physics engines such as Bullet, Havok, PhysX, and Box2D implement Newtonian, rigid-body, soft-body, cloth, particle, and volumetric dynamics, and the engines around them add acceleration structures (e.g., , BVH trees), real-time ray tracing, and navigation meshes for path planning, which gives them a natural foothold in spatial-intelligence tasks. Film production relies on the same principle at higher fidelity: pipelines built on Pixar USD, Maya, or Houdini simulate cloth, hair, smoke, fire, and fluids with differential-equation and fluid solvers (e.g., , FLIP/MantaFlow) and physically based path tracing. Engineering, architecture, and scientific visualization extend rule-based simulation to structural mechanics, electromagnetics, illumination, and material response through finite element methods, computational fluid dynamics, and photonic simulation.

For embodied AI, physics-driven simulators such as CARLA [], AirSim, and Isaac Sim [] remain the standard platforms for testing and training in autonomous driving, navigation, and manipulation, because they model lighting, collisions, dynamics, and sensor noise closely enough to yield data distributions near those of the real world. The same engines underpin digital twins built on platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse, Unity, and Unreal Engine, which are discussed in Part IV, Section .

In contrast to simulation frameworks based on explicit physical rules, learning-driven world generation seeks to acquire world structure, dynamics, and causal regularities directly from large-scale data, in a bottom-up fashion. These models do not encode Newtonian equations, lighting models, or geometric constraints by hand; instead, world behavior emerges as statistical patterns during training. For example, a model may never be given the analytic form of the gravity equation, yet by observing countless videos of falling objects, it can still infer the regularity that objects tend to accelerate downward. The resulting world models are probabilistic and can exhibit complex, emergent behaviors without explicit programming.

Current learning-driven world generation follows two technical directions: (1) video-centric generative models that learn dynamic world evolution in pixel or latent space, and (2) 3D/4D asset generation methods that directly model spatially structured worlds in three or four dimensions.

Recent advances in video generation have renewed interest in the idea of a “world simulator”. Video models are intrinsically suited to encoding spatiotemporal structure, and when they produce sequences that are not only visually coherent but also consistent with basic physical intuition, they begin to resemble implicit world models. This became especially prominent with the release of OpenAI Sora [], whose generated videos demonstrate strong temporal consistency, long-horizon stability, and apparent physical plausibility, prompting the community to reconsider whether deep video generation might be converging towards a form of physical world modeling. Subsequently, Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 [] extended video generation from passive “watchable” content to interactive experiences: the model updates the generated world in response to user actions, enabling agent-in-the-loop, closed-loop world simulation, complementing the action-conditioned scene generators surveyed in §. World Labs’ RTFM [] further highlights real-time performance, achieving high frame-rate and low-latency prediction. Systems such as Wan [], Emu3.5 [], OpenAI Sora 2 [], and Veo 3 [] continue this trajectory, gradually pushing video generation from mere visual fidelity towards world coherence, physical consistency, and interactivity. Action-conditioned diffusion has also turned games into testbeds: GameNGen [] simulates the game DOOM interactively in real time, and DIAMOND [] trains reinforcement-learning agents entirely inside a diffusion world model of Atari games, while NVIDIA’s Cosmos [] offers pretrained video world foundation models intended to be post-trained as simulators for robotics and driving.

Video world models are particularly promising in autonomous driving. GAIA-1 [] proposes a generative world model tailored for driving scenarios, built around a spatiotemporal Transformer that generates future multi-view scenes based on past observations. By implicitly capturing traffic patterns, pedestrian behavior, scene geometry, and multi-agent motion, GAIA-1 can support closed-loop evaluation, behavior prediction, and synthetic data generation, thereby reducing the cost and risk of traditional real-world testing.

A complementary avenue is to build world models that operate directly on structured three- or four-dimensional representations, such as 3D geometry, occupancy fields, or 4D spatiotemporal volumes. Unlike video-based approaches that primarily model dynamics in pixel space, these methods explicitly parameterize geometry and temporal evolution, making it easier to represent interactive, spatially consistent worlds.

Genesis [] exemplifies this direction. It is not only a generative 3D/4D physics simulation platform, but also integrates a vision-language model-driven “world-building agent” that uses a tool API to create dynamic 4D environments (geometry plus dynamics). These generated worlds can be rendered into multiple modalities (RGB, depth, semantics, contact events, etc.), providing rich supervision for training embodied AI systems. Genesis thus combines a unified physics engine with generative agents for large-scale world construction.

Autonomous driving again serves as a natural application domain for 3D world models. DriveArena [] builds a closed-loop generative simulation platform, allowing planning modules to iteratively probe and learn within synthesized 3D driving environments. Its diffusion-model-based multi-agent scene generation can rapidly produce long, interactive driving episodes. OccWorld [] and OccSora [] adopt 4D occupancy grids as the core representation, predicting future 3D occupancy over time from continuous video and sensor streams, thereby providing a unified motion-and-structure world model. Copilot4D [] tokenizes LiDAR scans and forecasts future LiDAR point clouds with discrete diffusion, learning a world model from unlabeled sensor data alone.

Generating interactive 3D worlds brings generative world models closest to their conceptual ideal. Marble [] from World Labs combines action-conditioned generation, geometric consistency constraints, and multimodal inputs, so that users can act within the generated world and observe the consequences. Its next-generation model, Atlas [], is an omni world model pretrained from scratch on text, images, video, and 3D: an autoregressive diffusion transformer that conditions every generated image and depth map on an explicit camera pose and grounds them all in a shared 3D context, so that the same model generates camera-controlled video of up to a minute, reconstructs scenes from a handful of images, and exports its output as point clouds or 3D Gaussian splats. World Labs reports that it outperforms specialized open-source reconstruction models, and that it will power future versions of Marble.

Between hand-written simulation and learned generation sits a route that has grown quickly since 2024: a language model writes the world model as executable code, and a simulator or engine runs it. The learned component is the author of the rules, not the rules themselves,

Math.text: formulae@(P similar-to p _ theta * conditional@(P, c), hat@(S) * (t + 1) = Sim * vector@(S * t, A * t, P))

para.p:
where
c
is the conditioning context (a description, observations, or a history of interactions),
P
the generated program, and
Sim
the interpreter or engine that executes it: plain Python, a physics engine such as MuJoCo or PyChrono, or Blender. Compared with Eq. (), the learned
W θ
is replaced by a program that can be read, tested, and repaired, so the resulting world keeps the determinism and verifiability of physics-driven simulation while gaining the open-endedness of a generative model. The scene programs of Section rest on the same idea; the difference here is that
P
encodes how the world changes under actions, not only how it is laid out.

In one line of work, code is an agent’s transition model. Code World Models [] synthesize Python implementations of reinforcement-learning environments with a generate, improve, and fix search over programs (GIF-MCTS), evaluated on a benchmark of 18 environments, and plan with them faster and more sample-efficiently than with learned dynamics; WorldCoder [] builds its world model as a program from its own interactions and transfers knowledge to a new environment by editing that program.

In the other, code builds a simulated 3D world. SceneCraft [] turns a description into Blender Python, planning with a scene graph, converting spatial relations into numerical layout constraints, and checking renders with a vision-language model. GenSim [] and RoboGen [] have language models write robotic simulation tasks, scenes, and rewards, making the simulator an open-ended source of training data, and the world-building agent of Genesis [] follows the same pattern. Recent systems close the loop with the simulator itself. Code2Worlds [] generates 4D worlds as Blender code refined by a vision-language motion critic; Code2Worlds-2 [] compiles such worlds into physically valid MuJoCo scenes and revises them from penetration, contact, and stability signals; and ChronoAgentic [] has cooperating agents write and repair PyChrono simulations, meeting the joint semantic and physical correctness criterion on 82.5% of PhyWorldBench demos against 52.5% for the best of ten text-to-video models.

The price is coverage. A program can express only what its simulator supports, so photorealistic appearance, deformable and fluid materials, and open-ended visual variety still favor learned generators, while code-and-simulator models win where physical correctness has to be checked.

Physical world models enable agents to understand and predict how the external environment evolves. However, intelligent behavior in real-world settings also requires an internal model of other minds. Humans naturally construct such models, i.e., , often referred to as mental models, to reason about others’ beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions, and social context. This ability, commonly associated with Theory of Mind (ToM) [], underlies human social interaction, collaboration, communication, and decision-making.

Craik’s “small-scale models” of reality are the origin of this notion too [], and Johnson-Laird later argued that human reasoning, problem solving, and causal inference rely on abstract internal representations of situations rather than on replaying detailed physical dynamics. These representations selectively capture the most relevant structure, i.e., , objects, relations, causal dependencies, and possible outcomes, while abstracting away low-level perceptual details. For example, when cycling, a human does not mentally simulate every joint torque or physical trajectory; instead, one imagines “whether I would fall or not” when encountering an obstacle. This high-level, conceptual simulation is a defining property of mental world modeling.

subsubsection.title: 8.6.3.1From Physical to Cognitive Mental World Models

para.p: Human mental simulation operates by combining current observations with stored knowledge to predict plausible futures. Perception provides the immediate sensory input, which is then transformed into an internal symbolic and probabilistic representation of the world. Within this representation, the brain runs rapid, approximate simulations that evaluate different hypothetical actions. These simulations are not physically precise but are cognitively meaningful: they help determine risks, anticipate others’ responses, or evaluate alternative courses of action. In this sense, mental models serve as a compact, abstract, and counterfactual “world engine” for decision making.

In artificial systems, the distinction between physical and mental world models mirrors that in human cognition. Physical world models predict state transitions in the environment (e.g., , dynamics, geometry, object motion), whereas mental world models encode the latent mental states of human users or other agents. These models allow an AI system to reason about what humans know, believe, want, or intend to do, capabilities that embodied agents, collaborative robots, intelligent tutors, and multi-agent planners all need.

Inspired by the Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) [] framework, a mental world model for AI typically includes a small set of structured variables. Beliefs. These are representations of what the human knows, perceives, or believes about the world. Desires. These capture user goals, preferences, motivations, and values. Intentions. These are planned or ongoing actions that the agent expects the human (or another agent) to follow. Such decomposition enables an AI system to explicitly reason about human rationality, goal pursuit, and action planning. Formally, a mental world model can be cast as the inference of a latent mental state
⁢ M
( t )
, comprising the beliefs, desires, and intentions above, from observed behavior, followed by a prediction of the other agent’s next action,

Math.text: formulae@(hat@(M) * t = (argmax _ M)@(p) * conditional@(M, O _ (absent <= t)), (hat@(A)) ^ [other] * (t + 1) = pi * hat@(M) * t)

para.p: This formulation mirrors the transition of Eq. () but replaces the physical state with the inferred mental state of another agent (Figure (c)), so that the predicted quantity is no longer how the environment will evolve but how a human or peer agent is likely to act.

Machine Theory of Mind is now measured directly. ToMi [] tests false-belief reasoning in short stories with controls against shortcut solutions, BigToM [] generates controlled social scenarios with language models to probe whether models infer beliefs from percepts and actions, and MMToM-QA [] poses belief and goal questions about a person acting in a household from video and text together. Large language and multimodal models remain unreliable on these tests, whereas MMToM-QA’s BIP-ALM, which performs Bayesian inverse planning over a symbolic state with a language model scoring the likelihoods, does better; it is an explicit instance of the inference in Eq. ().

Beyond the belief-desire-intention core, a mental world model for embodied agents must span several further layers of internal state and social context. It has to read affect, recognizing emotional cues and how they shift a person’s risk tolerance and willingness to cooperate. It has to represent social dynamics: the relationships, roles, group structures, and cultural norms that shape behavior. And it has to interpret communication, both the verbal channel and the non-verbal one carried by tone, gesture, posture, and facial expression. These layers are what turn a bare goal estimate into a socially situated account of why a person acts as they do.

Human spatial reasoning is social as well as geometric, which ties mental modeling to spatial intelligence. To assist or collaborate with humans in homes, factories, classrooms, or vehicles, an agent must infer the intention behind a spatial action (e.g., , where a person intends to move next), anticipate trajectories from goals or habits, adapt navigation or manipulation to user preferences, and interpret spatial configurations that reflect what a person believes or misunderstands.

The benchmarks above still treat the mental state as something inferred next to a world model, not as part of it: Eq. () estimates another agent’s mind, but the environment it acts in is predicted separately. Mental World Modeling (MWM) [] makes the mental state part of the state that the world model of Eq. paragraph.title: Representation-based World Models as an Alternative Foundation Model Paradigm.

para.p: Representation world models may emerge as a parallel paradigm to current LLMs, functioning as large-scale foundational models trained through massive self-supervised representation learning to capture physical regularities, causal dynamics, and environmental constraints. Unlike LLMs, which learn the world indirectly through linguistic abstraction, representation world models aim to model the physical world directly from multimodal observations. Such models could serve video generation, action prediction in VLA systems, 3D and 4D understanding and generation, and decision-making in autonomous driving.

paragraph.title: The Necessity of Multi-source Intelligence Integration.

para.p: World models will likely require the integration of heterogeneous informational sources. On the one hand, LLMs embody language-driven intelligence, while world models emphasize physically grounded intelligence; rather than being mutually exclusive, a truly capable world model must incorporate both forms of reasoning. On the other hand, accurate world understanding requires far more than visual perception alone: audio, speech, tactile signals, force feedback, and even proprioception provide essential supplementary cues about the dynamics and structure of the physical environment. Yet the current research community focuses overwhelmingly on visual-only modeling. Building world models that holistically integrate multimodal sensory information remains a major challenge.

paragraph.title: Unifying Physical Modeling and Mental Modeling.

para.p: Another promising direction is the integration of physical and mental modeling within a unified world-modeling framework. Embodied agents operating in real environments must simultaneously reason about the physical evolution of the environment and the mental or behavioral responses of humans (or other agents). Recent work in multi-agent systems, social navigation, pedagogical reasoning, human-robot collaboration, and interactive LLM agents emphasizes the growing need for AI systems to build internal hypotheses about both external dynamics and human mental states. Mental World Modeling [] is an early formulation of such a joint state (Section ). Ultimately, scalable general-purpose world models must simulate not only what will happen but also what others believe, intend, desire, or misunderstand.

paragraph.title: Balance between Generative Fidelity and Physical Correctness.

para.p: A central challenge for learning-driven world models is reconciling generative expressiveness with physical accuracy. High-capacity video generators often produce visually stunning but physically implausible outcomes, while models optimized for strict physical consistency may underperform in realism or diversity. Achieving stable long-horizon predictions without temporal drift or compounding errors remains unsolved. Designing architectures, training objectives, and constraints that jointly enforce physical laws, spatial coherence, and generative flexibility is a key open problem for the next generation of world simulators.

paragraph.title: Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Verifiability of World Models.

para.p: Unlike language models, which can be evaluated through perplexity, benchmarks, or task accuracy, world models lack standardized, reliable, and comprehensive evaluation protocols. Physical correctness, causal consistency, interactive fidelity, multimodal coherence, and long-horizon stability are difficult to quantify in a unified manner. Furthermore, world models that aim to simulate open-ended environments raise issues of verifiability, reproducibility, and safety: how can we assess whether a world model reliably generalizes to unseen real-world scenarios, or whether its internal dynamics exhibit hidden biases or unsafe behaviors? Establishing principled evaluation methodologies and shared benchmarks for both representation-based and generative world models is an urgent research direction.

Programmatic and symbolic spatial generation synthesizes 2D and 3D scene structure through explicit rules, executable programs, and symbolic geometric abstractions. It generates the structural backbone of a scene (spatial layout, hierarchical organization, geometric constraints, executable logic) rather than its raw appearance, which gives it controllability, compositional generalization, global spatial consistency, and interpretability.

Where the largely neural samplers of §–§ map a condition directly to pixels, voxels, or a neural latent, programmatic methods emit an intermediate program that a deterministic renderer executes into the final scene. This intermediate layer is what makes the structure auditable, editable, and compositionally reusable, properties that flat neural outputs lack. Three paradigm families mark the historical and technical progression of the field: rule- and grammar-based procedural generation, symbolic graphics programs and domain-specific languages, and neuro-symbolic language-to-program synthesis driven by large language models.

para.p:
The earliest line of work, procedural content generation (PCG) [] in computer graphics and game development, synthesizes scenes such as dungeon maps, terrains, architectural plans, or UI layouts from hand-crafted rules or parameterized procedural programs. Classical formalisms instantiate
G θ
as a fixed production system rather than a learned model. The Lindenmayer system (L-system) [], originally developed to model biological growth, employs parallel rewriting rules to simulate natural growth processes and fractal patterns, making it ideal for self-similar structures such as vegetation and complex terrain. Formally, the program evolves by repeated parallel application of a production set
Π
to an axiom
ω
,

Math.text: formulae@(rho _ 0 = omega, formulae@(rho _ (t + 1) = Pi * rho _ t, hat@(s) = R * rho _ T))

para.p:
where the generated symbolic string is not the geometry itself but a sequence of Turtle Graphics commands that the interpreter
R
parses to draw the final shape in 2D or 3D space. Shape grammars, introduced by [ ] , provide another influential symbolic mechanism by defining geometric primitives and rewrite rules for composing architectural or engineered shapes. These early paradigms demonstrated a fundamental insight: spatial structures can be synthesized by executing symbolic generative rules, rather than by directly predicting raw geometry.

paragraph.title: Symbolic Graphics Programs and Domain-Specific Languages.

para.p: Symbolic graphics programs (SGPs) encode spatial layouts and geometric configurations as formal programs that execute deterministically into images, vector graphics, UI designs, or 3D shapes, bridging abstract scene intent and concrete visual realization. Common languages such as SVG [], TikZ/LaTeX [], and HTML/CSS [] already carry rich symbolic layout specifications in real-world use. In parallel, researchers have developed domain-specific languages (DSLs) tailored for fine-grained spatial and visual synthesis. Examples include hierarchical GUI-code generators [] that translate visual structures into programmatic UI specifications, and ShapeAssembly [], a 3D assembly language in which objects are represented as executable programs describing part composition, symmetry, and connectivity. Such DSLs make the advantages of explicit symbolic control concrete: precise geometry, modular design, verifiable constraints, and systematic compositionality.

A more recent direction couples symbolic programs with learned models, so that
G θ
becomes a trained synthesizer rather than a fixed rule set. The Scene Language [] unifies neural and symbolic components: a program specifying relational and hierarchical layout structure, natural-language labels summarizing entity semantics, and learned embeddings capturing visual identity. Executable structure, rather than raw geometry, thus becomes a primary representational layer for scenes. Large language models [] have accelerated the move toward language-to-program spatial generation: instead of predicting images or layouts directly, LLM-based systems act as symbolic planners that synthesize the program by approximately maximizing its conditional likelihood,

Math.text: rho ^ star = (argmax _ (rho element-of L))@(p _ theta) * conditional@(rho, kappa * c)

para.p: mapping natural-language descriptions to executable layout programs []. These programs then guide downstream renderers to produce UI designs, graphic layouts, architectural plans, or 3D scenes with precise structural fidelity, and users can edit or refine the underlying program with fine-grained control.

The three families differ along two cross-cutting axes. The first is the representation of
ρ
: a parallel string-rewriting system (grammar-based generation), an executable program in a general-purpose or domain-specific graphics language (SGPs and DSLs), or a hybrid structure that interleaves code, language, and learned embeddings (neuro-symbolic synthesis). The second is the inference procedure that produces
ρ
: hand-authored production rules, human-written or template-instantiated programs, or learned program synthesis and LLM-based planning. Across all three, the target modality (2D raster, vector graphics, UI, or 3D) is determined solely by the renderer
R
, which keeps the symbolic and rendering concerns cleanly separated.

Evaluation in this area differs from the distributional metrics of § because the immediate output is a program, not an image, so quality is assessed along several complementary axes. Program validity measures whether the emitted
ρ
parses and executes without error in its target language, a prerequisite that purely neural generators do not face. Rendered-output fidelity then compares the executed scene
⁢ R
( ρ )
against a reference, using pixel- or perceptual-level similarity for raster and vector targets and geometric agreement for 3D shapes. Constraint satisfaction checks whether explicitly specified spatial relations, counts, alignments, or symmetries hold in the rendered result, a property that symbolic methods are designed to guarantee. Controllability and editability assess how reliably localized edits to
ρ
produce the intended localized changes in the scene without unintended global drift. Concretely, these axes are exercised across vector-graphics and SVG synthesis [], UI and GUI code generation [], 3D program induction over part-structured shapes [], evaluated against part-hierarchy benchmarks such as PartNet [], and full scene-program synthesis [], where the executable program serves simultaneously as the prediction and as the verifiable ground for measurement.

The field has moved from entirely hand-authored rules toward neuro-symbolic integration with large models, driven by the demand for generators that are more controllable and interpretable than end-to-end neural methods.

Generalization. Automatically synthesized programs still struggle with novel constraints and complex semantic specifications []. Program synthesis has to infer the structural logic of a scene rather than memorize surface patterns if the generator is to extrapolate to compositions and constraint combinations absent from training.

Efficiency and differentiability. Neuro-symbolic programs that are both efficient and fully differentiable [] would let a rendering-level loss propagate back through the program, so that the whole pipeline, from symbolic planning to neural rendering, could be trained and fine-tuned end to end.

Embodied interaction. Procedurally synthesized interactive environments already supply large-scale embodied worlds [], and the next step is for agents to generate or validate symbolic scene structure through active exploration rather than from static datasets alone, yielding symbolic representations of physical spaces that can be checked against what the agent observes.

This chapter has surveyed spatial reconstruction and generation across seven subfields that, taken together, span an axis of increasing output structure and dimensionality: 2D images (§), 3D objects and scenes (§), video (§), embodied motion (§), 4D space-time content (§), world models (§), and interpretable symbolic programs (§). Despite their different output domains, the subfields are unified by a single conditional-generation backbone, established in §: an encoder
κ
maps a condition
c
into a latent code, a generator
G θ
samples structure from that code, and a decoder or renderer turns the sampled structure into a concrete artifact (Eq. (), Eq. ()). What distinguishes the subfields is not this backbone but the output space and the decoder that closes it: a pixel decoder for images, a volumetric or splatting renderer for 3D, a spatio-temporal decoder for video, a kinematic sampler for motion, a time-indexed 3D representation for 4D, a state-transition predictor for world models, and an exact, non-learned program executor for symbolic generation. Table consolidates this view.

para.p: A shared backbone, specialized by output space. The progression from § to § is best read not as seven disjoint problems but as one generative abstraction instantiated against progressively richer codomains, and each section casts its own subtasks as conditional specializations of that common sampler. The symbolic case (§) is the limiting instance in which the decoder degenerates to an exact program executor, trading the expressiveness of a learned renderer for interpretability and verifiable control.

The 2D prior as a reusable engine. The image generators of § recur throughout the chapter not as terminal systems but as priors to be distilled or lifted: 3D synthesis distills frozen 2D diffusion through score distillation and multi-view consistency (§), video models inflate text-to-image backbones along the temporal axis (§), and 4D pipelines compose both (§). A single advance in the 2D substrate therefore propagates outward across every higher-dimensional subfield, which concentrates research leverage but also propagates the substrate’s failure modes.

Physical plausibility and fragmented evaluation. Across subfields, the recurring failure mode is not low visual fidelity but violated physics and geometry, manifest as multi-view inconsistency in 3D, temporal drift and flicker in video, foot-skating and interpenetration in motion, and dynamic implausibility in 4D. Evaluation remains correspondingly fragmented: each subfield has evolved its own metric tuples, and all are migrating toward learned and vision-language-model judges as scalar similarity scores prove insufficient for spatially structured output. A unified, physically grounded evaluation protocol that spans these subfields remains an open goal.

Outlook. These observations point toward convergence rather than further fragmentation. World modeling (§) already acts as a conceptual capstone that absorbs reconstruction, generation, and dynamics into a single predictive substrate, while programmatic and symbolic generation (§) supplies the controllability and interpretability that purely neural pipelines lack; their integration, neural generators steered and verified by symbolic structure, is a natural trajectory for the field. The capabilities surveyed here also form the generative substrate for the applications of Part , where embodied agents, digital twins, and interactive environments consume generated spatial content rather than producing it for its own sake.

figure.toccaption: 8.26Part IV at a glance. (1) Leave the lab: deployment tests spatial intelligence under latency, safety, sensor failure, and the cost of error. (2) Domain by domain: embodied agents, extended reality, geo-spatial and scientific settings, assistants, and further fields, each stressing a different axis. (3) A horizontal foundation: one shared layer beneath science, industry, and daily life, with gaps found in the field feeding back into it.

caption.text: Part IV at a glance. (1) Leave the lab: deployment tests spatial intelligence under latency, safety, sensor failure, and the cost of error. (2) Domain by domain: embodied agents, extended reality, geo-spatial and scientific settings, assistants, and further fields, each stressing a different axis. (3) A horizontal foundation: one shared layer beneath science, industry, and daily life, with gaps found in the field feeding back into it.

para.p: The preceding parts built spatial intelligence as a set of capabilities; this part asks what those capabilities are worth once they leave the laboratory. Applications are not a victory lap over Parts II and III but a stress test: a method that reconstructs a scene cleanly on a benchmark must, in the field, do so under a latency budget, a safety constraint, a sensor that fails, or a cost of error measured in more than accuracy. What a domain demands of spatial intelligence, and what it reveals about the gaps that remain, is visible only at deployment.

This part is therefore organized by domain rather than by capability, because the interesting content lives in the delta each domain adds over a general treatment. The tour runs from embodied agents that must act in the physical world, through the extended-reality systems that render it back to a user in real time, to the geo-spatial and scientific settings that model it at the scale of planets and of cells, to the assistants that inhabit a person’s own environment, and out into a long tail of further fields. Each stresses spatial intelligence along a different axis: real-time action, on-device perception, metric fidelity, human-centered interaction. Read together, they make the case that spatial intelligence is not one more application but a horizontal foundation on which applications across science, industry, and daily life are increasingly built.

Embodied systems are the arena in which spatial intelligence stops being a matter of analysis and becomes a matter of consequence. An embodied agent does not merely describe a scene; it occupies one, and every perception it forms and every inference it draws is ultimately answerable to an action it must take in the physical world, under real time budgets, sensor noise, and the cost of being wrong. This chapter turns from the capabilities of the previous part to their deployment, examining how perception, reasoning, and generation are brought to bear inside agents that move, manipulate, and assist.

What makes this more than a restatement is that embodiment changes the problem. The same spatial competence looks different in a manipulator closing a grasp, a car threading traffic, a wearable inferring its user’s intent, a drone holding position in wind, or a fleet of robots coordinating on a warehouse floor: each fixes its own sensors, latencies, safety margins, and notion of success. The chapter is organized by these domains rather than by capability, because the interesting content lives in the domain-specific delta, what each setting demands of spatial intelligence that a general treatment does not reveal.

Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly, driven by strides in perception, learning, and control. Yet a significant gap remains between competent laboratory systems and robust, general-purpose robots capable of operating in unstructured settings. A central bottleneck is that manipulation is fundamentally spatial: every decision (where to reach, how to establish contact, how to route a trajectory through clutter, or how to use a tool) hinges on perceiving, representing, and reasoning about three-dimensional structure under uncertainty. Manipulation is thus a direct test of the spatial intelligence developed throughout Parts I–III: it demands that systems go beyond semantic recognition to build actionable 3D world models, ground tasks in geometric constraints, predict contact outcomes, and plan behaviors that respect the physical laws of the environment. The perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities that such systems presuppose are surveyed in Chapter , Chapter , and Chapter ; this section focuses not on re-deriving those capabilities but on how they are composed, grounded, and constrained for physical manipulation.

subsection.title: 9.1.3Pivotal Task-1: Grounding Action in Spatial Anchors

para.p: This pivot reframes visuomotor learning from operating over raw pixels to reasoning through explicit spatial anchors (sparse semantic keypoints, dense correspondences, point tracks, or affordance-based contact points) that compress high-dimensional observations into spatial tokens tied to object- or task-centric reference frames and designed to remain comparatively stable across viewpoint, instance, and clutter. As Figure indicates, the approach follows a three-step logic: large-scale vision priors first produce the anchors, policies are then conditioned on them, and the payoff is read off as a generalization gap between seen and unseen instances.

figure.toccaption:
9.2Grounding action in spatial anchors: (1) anchors
P t
produced or transferred from vision priors across views, (2) an anchor-conditioned policy, and (3) generalization measured as the seen–unseen success gap
Δ gen
. Scenes, correspondences, and score bars are schematic, not measured results.

caption.text:
Grounding action in spatial anchors: (1) anchors
P t
produced or transferred from vision priors across views, (2) an anchor-conditioned policy, and (3) generalization measured as the seen–unseen success gap
Δ gen
. Scenes, correspondences, and score bars are schematic, not measured results.

para.p: The dominant methodology leverages large-scale vision priors to generate, propagate, or retrieve these anchors, then trains standard visuomotor learners on the resulting structured inputs. A common strategy prescribes anchor points in a few reference frames and propagates them across large datasets via off-the-shelf correspondence models: P3-PO [] propagates manually specified keypoints using dense features from DINO [], DINOv2 [], or diffusion-based representations [] (these visual representations are surveyed in Chapter ). Relatedly, Robo-ABC [] retrieves affordance contact points from an external memory and transfers them to novel scenes via dense semantic correspondence, while Track2Act [] learns long-term point tracks from Internet-scale video and uses them to infer object-centric transformations that serve as open-loop manipulation plans. Once anchors are obtained, policy learning conditions action prediction directly on them, through keypoint-conditioned behavior cloning (KALM []), diffusion policies in object-relative frames (AffordDP []), and shared human–robot 3D keypoint spaces (Point Policy []). Across these variants, anchoring actions to spatial structure reduces perceptual ambiguity and improves robustness under distribution shift.

Because the central claim is out-of-distribution generalization, evaluation pairs high-fidelity simulation with real-robot deployment rather than relying on either alone. In simulation, affordance-centric methods such as AffordDP [] run on IsaacGym [] over articulated objects from GAPartnet [] whose functional parts (handles, knobs, levers) vary widely in geometry, while imitation suites such as Robomimic [] and RoboTwin [] isolate trajectory tracking and dual-arm coordination, with P3-PO [] using them for controlled spatial-anchoring ablations. Real-world suites then stress in-the-wild generalization on articulated (drawers, microwaves), deformable (towel folding), and tool-use (sweeping) tasks, as in Point Policy [] and Track2Act [], and a zero-shot cross-category protocol (train on one knife, test on spatulas or novel knives) is formalized by Robo-ABC [] to measure how well retrieved anchors transfer without extra supervision. Performance is reported as Task Success Rate and, to isolate the contribution of anchoring, a Generalization Gap between seen and unseen instances. Spatially grounded policies outperform pixel baselines under shift in these studies: P3-PO reports large gains on cluttered, novel-object scenes [], and Robo-ABC improves both affordance-retrieval accuracy and real-robot success without heavy robot-data collection, binding demonstrations to reusable spatial structure more effectively than classic one-shot imitation [].

This pivot shifts from general object recognition to extracting object affordances, i.e., , the specific action possibilities implied by an object’s functional properties, and uses them as the intermediate representation that bridges raw perception and contact-rich execution. Whereas Pivotal Task-1 treats contact points as viewpoint-stable anchors for conditioning a policy, affordances here are studied as functional possibilities that specify what action an object supports. As Figure shows, the thread runs from how affordances are represented, through the actions they drive (grasping, placement, tool use), to outcome-oriented benchmarks that score achieved function rather than imitated trajectory.

figure.toccaption: 9.3Affordances as functional action possibilities: a task- and context-conditioned affordance representation (left) supports three parallel task examples (6-DoF grasp, stable placement, hook-and-pull tool use), each judged by its functional outcome. Green checks mark intended outcomes in these illustrations, not measured results.

caption.text: Affordances as functional action possibilities: a task- and context-conditioned affordance representation (left) supports three parallel task examples (6-DoF grasp, stable placement, hook-and-pull tool use), each judged by its functional outcome. Green checks mark intended outcomes in these illustrations, not measured results.

para.p: To capture functional properties beyond whole-object categorization, prior work builds object-centric representations (part-level segmentation [], dense visual descriptors [], and keypoint-based encodings []) that directly support action synthesis, and more recent vision–language models predict spatial affordance points directly from open-vocabulary prompts (RoboPoint [], MOKA []). These representations drive learning-based 6-DoF grasping [] and stable object placement [] by grounding generation in functional structure rather than raw geometry, and a specialized strand further models tool–behavior relationships, either learning tool–action–effect pairs [] or predicting specific affordances such as pulling [], so as to infer end-effector poses that achieve the intended functional outcome.

Benchmarks for affordance methods emphasize understanding object functionality over geometric matching: the property under test is functional generalization, not trajectory imitation. For grasping, YCB-based real-world evaluations [], GraspNet-1Billion [], and simulation suites such as Dex-Net [] score 6-DoF stability and contact validity across novel instances and viewpoints; placement benchmarks such as RLBench [] and ManiSkill [] test stable stacking and insertion in cluttered, articulated scenes, and M2T2 [] explicitly evaluates valid placement poses conditioned on object geometry and scene context. For articulated objects and tools, Where2Act [] and PartNet-Mobility [] score the prediction of actionable parts and interaction parameters for pulling, pushing, and rotating, while tool-use tasks judge whether the inferred end-effector pose produces the intended causal effect (drawing, hooking, pulling) rather than reproducing a specific trajectory. Evaluation therefore centers on outcome-oriented success: stable grasps that lift and hold unseen objects under pose, scale, and appearance variation; placement success, pose accuracy, and post-release stability under clutter and occlusion; and, for articulated and tool interactions, whether the predicted parameters yield the desired functional result.

subsection.title: 9.1.5Pivotal Task-3: Encoding Spatial Reasoning in Generalist Models

para.p: This pivot moves from specialized, single-task policies toward generalist robotic foundation models. Existing Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models such as RT-2 [] and OpenVLA [] show strong semantic understanding but often lack the spatial common sense needed for precise manipulation or robust generalization to novel viewpoints, so the central challenge is to strengthen spatial grounding during pre-training, enabling explicit reasoning about 3D geometry and generalization across environments and embodiments []. The general foundation-model and spatial-reasoning machinery these policies inherit is treated in Chapter ; here we examine only its manipulation-specific adaptation, which Figure groups into three families: explicit 3D representations, view-invariant representations, and grounded reasoning traces.

figure.toccaption: 9.4Spatial grounding mechanisms for generalist robot policies: (1) explicit 3D features fused with task tokens (3D-LLM, 3D-VLA), (2) view canonicalization (OG-VLA) and spatial action discretization (SpatialVLA), two separate methods rather than stages of one, and (3) grounded reasoning traces that condition action prediction. The bottom row shows evaluation of viewpoint robustness and cross-robot transfer; all maps and overlays are schematic.

caption.text: Spatial grounding mechanisms for generalist robot policies: (1) explicit 3D features fused with task tokens (3D-LLM, 3D-VLA), (2) view canonicalization (OG-VLA) and spatial action discretization (SpatialVLA), two separate methods rather than stages of one, and (3) grounded reasoning traces that condition action prediction. The bottom row shows evaluation of viewpoint robustness and cross-robot transfer; all maps and overlays are schematic.

para.p: The first family builds explicit 3D representations: models such as 3D-LLM [] and 3D-VLA [] bridge point clouds and large language models, with 3D-VLA adding a 3D generative pre-training objective that lets the model reason about action outcomes in a consistent geometric space, effectively “imagining” future states. The second groups view canonicalization and spatial action encoding as distinct mechanisms: OG-VLA [] projects multi-view observations into a point cloud and re-renders canonical orthographic views to reduce sensitivity to camera placement, while SpatialVLA [] uses Ego3D position encoding for observations and Adaptive Action Grids to discretize spatial movement actions; adapting to new setups can involve re-discretizing the grids. The third injects spatial reasoning through grounded reasoning traces: “thinking” models such as Emma-X [], MolmoAct series [], closely related to TraceVLA [], replace direct pixel-to-action regression with intermediate, grounded outputs (2D motion trajectories or relative depth maps) that explicitly condition the final action prediction.

These approaches are evaluated under method-specific zero-shot and adaptation protocols across embodiments, viewpoints, and environments, with key metrics including multimodal goal-generation quality, robustness to extrinsic camera perturbations, and skill transfer across robot morphologies such as from a fixed-base Franka arm to a mobile manipulator []. The reported gains point the same way: canonical orthographic views keep grounding consistent under viewpoint change (OG-VLA), spatially aligned action grids share 3D structure across setups through discretized movement (SpatialVLA), and intermediate visual or depth-aware reasoning traces act as a regularizer on action prediction (Emma-X, MolmoAct).

subsection.title: 9.1.6Pivotal Task-4: Satisfying Geometric and Logical Constraints

para.p: This pivot moves planning from heuristic trajectory generation toward formal constrained optimization that enforces geometric feasibility, fundamental physical laws (non-penetration, friction cones, force limits), and high-level logical task structure. By casting manipulation as multi-objective optimization, these methods seek to satisfy modeled hard constraints while optimizing soft task objectives, spanning both high-frequency control and long-horizon decision-making. Figure organizes the thread along three fronts (symbolic–geometric planning, contact and trajectory optimization, and constraint-aware generative planning) before synthesizing the roles constraints play in learning-based systems.

figure.toccaption:
9.5Geometric and logical constraints in manipulation: (1) symbolic–geometric planning with revision after infeasibility, (2) contact and trajectory optimization (inset: normal force
f n
into the object, tangential force
f t
along its surface), and (3) constraint-aware generative planning. The bottom row shows three roles constraints play for learned policies.

para.p: Methodological progress has moved from purely symbolic planners toward neuro-symbolic, learning-augmented optimization frameworks that unify discrete logic with continuous physics. Classical Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and Logic-Geometric Programming (LGP) [] provide the foundation by jointly reasoning over symbolic task structure and geometric feasibility, and recent systems augment them with Large Language Models and Vision-Language Models for scalability in open-ended domains; for example, VIZ-COAST [] uses the spatial reasoning of VLMs to predict refinement failures before expensive geometric optimization, substantially reducing search complexity on long-horizon problems. At the level of physical interaction, contact-implicit optimization discovers contact schedules without explicit mode enumeration but is traditionally too slow for real-time control; GPU-parallelized systems such as SPaSM [] compile constraint evaluation and gradient computation into CUDA kernels, accelerating joint optimization of object placements and robot trajectories. Beyond deterministic constraints, learning-based and generative models capture uncertainty and complex structure: differentiable physics engines [] let gradients flow through physical interactions, stochastic implicit neural signed distance functions [] model geometric uncertainty directly within the planning manifold, and diffusion-based planners such as JM2D [] couple model-free diffusion with model-based constraint optimization during sampling, rather than relying only on a sequential plan-then-filter interface.

Such systems are benchmarked on multi-stage re-grasping under uncertainty, forceful tool use, and tight-tolerance sequential interaction, since what they promise is reliability over long, contact-rich horizons; suites such as the Functional Manipulation Benchmark (FMB) [] scoring not only task completion but constraint satisfaction under partial observability, external disturbance, and compounding execution error. In these systems constrained optimization plays three roles: it acts as a teacher, generating physically valid trajectories that supervise imitation and offline reinforcement learning; as a safety shield, where model-based projections map unconstrained neural or diffusion policy outputs onto constraint-satisfying sets at execution time []; and as a structural prior that prunes physically infeasible regions of the action space and curbs compounding error in long-horizon tasks. Together these roles keep learned and generative planners grounded in geometric and physical reality, reducing physically implausible outputs and supporting interpretable, feasible plans under the modeled assumptions; real-world execution still depends on state estimation, model accuracy, solver convergence, and disturbance handling.

para.p: Progress in spatially grounded manipulation has been inseparable from a maturing ecosystem of simulators, open software stacks, shared datasets, and, increasingly, commercial robot platforms that serve as common development and deployment substrates.

Simulation and physics engines. GPU-parallel engines such as NVIDIA IsaacGym and the newer Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab 1 footnote 1 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim [], articulated-object simulators such as SAPIEN [] (with its PartNet-Mobility assets), and general-purpose physics engines including MuJoCo [], PyBullet 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://pybullet.org, and the recent Genesis 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://github.com/Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis provide high-throughput, contact-rich environments, while ManiSkill [], RLBench [], Robomimic [], and RoboTwin [] package standardized task suites, demonstrations, and evaluation protocols that have become de facto testbeds for imitation and policy learning.

Open software stacks and datasets. On the software side, the Robot Operating System (ROS 2) with the MoveIt motion-planning framework 4 footnote 4 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 4 footnote 4 https://moveit.ai remains the de facto middleware for real-robot integration, and Hugging Face’s LeRobot 5 footnote 5 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 5 footnote 5 https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot packages datasets, pretrained policies, and training pipelines for low-cost reproduction. Large cross-embodiment efforts such as Open X-Embodiment 6 footnote 6 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 6 footnote 6 https://robotics-transformer-x.github.io, which aggregates demonstrations and the RT-X policies across dozens of robot platforms, together with open generalist checkpoints such as Octo [] and OpenVLA [] and NVIDIA’s GR00T humanoid foundation models 7 footnote 7 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 7 footnote 7 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/gr00t, expose pretrained weights and fine-tuning interfaces that lower the barrier to transferring foundation-model policies onto new morphologies.

Commercial and humanoid platforms. On the deployment side, a rapidly growing set of companies is moving spatially grounded manipulation out of the laboratory. Boston Dynamics 8 footnote 8 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 8 footnote 8 https://bostondynamics.com (the electric Atlas and the Stretch warehouse robot), Tesla Optimus 9 footnote 9 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 9 footnote 9 https://www.tesla.com/we-robot, Figure AI 10 footnote 10 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 10 footnote 10 https://www.figure.ai, 1X Technologies 11 footnote 11 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 11 footnote 11 https://www.1x.tech, Agility Robotics 12 footnote 12 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 12 footnote 12 https://agilityrobotics.com (the Digit humanoid, piloted in logistics), Physical Intelligence 13 footnote 13 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 13 footnote 13 https://www.physicalintelligence.company (the
π 0
generalist policy), and Sanctuary AI 14 footnote 14 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 14 footnote 14 https://sanctuary.ai each pair learned manipulation with humanoid or mobile-manipulator hardware, while firms such as Covariant 15 footnote 15 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 15 footnote 15 https://covariant.ai target warehouse pick-and-place at commercial scale. These platforms are the clearest evidence that the spatial-intelligence capabilities surveyed above are crossing from benchmark tasks into economically deployed systems.

Together these tools convert the representation and reasoning machinery of Chapter into reproducible, physically grounded manipulation pipelines; their principal limitation remains the fidelity gap between simulated and real contact dynamics, which the following discussion revisits.

Despite rapid progress across all four pivots, bringing spatial intelligence to robust, general-purpose manipulation remains bounded by a set of intertwined difficulties that cut across perception, policy, and planning. They cluster into four threads: keeping a persistent and calibrated internal model of the scene; closing the loop between contact physics and active sensing; transferring skills across embodiments while sourcing the data to do so; and meeting the reliability budget of a deployed system.

Persistent, calibrated world models. The first requirement is a persistent 3D belief: an actionable, temporally consistent world model that survives heavy occlusion, articulation, deformation, and sensor drift, and that is maintained at control rates rather than reconstructed from scratch each frame. Persistence alone is not enough if the model cannot say how much it trusts itself. Calibrated uncertainty asks that distributional beliefs over geometry, contact state, friction, and articulation propagate through perception, policy, and planner, so that a decision reflects confidence rather than a bare point prediction and a low-confidence grasp can trigger caution instead of failure.

Contact modeling, sensing, and active perception. Manipulation is ultimately about contact, yet most spatial models still reason about collision-free geometry rather than the physics of touch. Progress on contact modeling and sensing hinges on tightly integrating vision with force and tactile feedback to reason about stick–slip, compliance, and incipient failure. Because contact is often unobservable until it happens, this couples naturally to information-seeking control: interleaving manipulation with active perception and probing (touch-to-disambiguate, look-while-acting) inside tractable belief-space planners. And because contact is precisely where simulators diverge from reality, sim-to-real for contact stays open, demanding better material, friction, and compliance models together with fast system identification for on-robot adaptation.

Cross-embodiment transfer and data at scale. Skills learned on one platform rarely move cleanly to another. Cross-embodiment and cross-scene transfer requires aligning action spaces and spatial tokens across grippers, cameras, and environments without hand-tuned frames or retraining. Sustaining that transfer is a data problem as much as an algorithmic one: data and evaluation at scale calls for “long-tail” data engines that cover rare geometries, materials, and tools with counterfactual and safety labels, and for benchmarks that measure calibration, persistence, recovery, and long-horizon competence rather than success rate alone.

Systems reliability. Finally, a deployed manipulator must hold together as a system: meeting latency budgets, absorbing calibration drift, detecting out-of-distribution geometry, and enabling safe fallback and continual learning without catastrophic forgetting. Closing these gaps will require tighter couplings among 3D world models, affordance predictors, language-grounded objectives, and constraint-aware planners, so that spatial representations are not only expressive but actionable, calibrated, and safe in unstructured settings.

Autonomous driving sits at the intersection of spatial intelligence, transportation engineering, and human–machine interaction, and it is one of the most demanding real-world testbeds for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part . A self-driving vehicle must continuously close a perceive–localize–decide–act loop: it has to recognize and track the surrounding traffic scene, estimate its own pose within a metric map, reason about how nearby agents will move, and commit to safe control actions, all under tight latency and safety budgets. Advances in deep learning, multi-sensor fusion, and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication have steadily pushed the boundaries of what vehicles can perceive, predict, and decide, while fundamental questions around robustness, trust, ethics, and regulation remain open. Perception and reasoning themselves are treated in Chapter and Chapter ; what is specific to driving is that each capability must hold up at speed, in all weather, and with lives at stake.

Figure summarizes the SAE J3016 automation levels that frame this domain. The SAE J3016 standard 16 footnote 16 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 16 footnote 16 https://www.sae.org/news/2019/01/sae-updates-j3016-automated-driving-graphic provides a widely adopted framework for defining automation levels, with most current production systems still operating at Level 2. Progress toward higher levels, especially full Level 5 autonomy, faces major technical [], ethical [], and financial [] challenges.

Deep learning has driven most of this progress, from Transformers [] and graph networks [] that model multi-agent interaction to lifelong learning for open-world adaptation [], but its opacity raises safety concerns compounded by sensor noise and the limited reach of vehicle-to-vehicle communication, and reaching Levels 4 and 5 depends as much on redundant hardware, large-scale data pipelines, and verifiable safety assurance as on model architecture.

Levels 0–2 retain a human driver; Level 3 requires a human to resume driving when necessary, whereas Levels 4–5 do not rely on human fallback within their operating scope. The stair heights indicate ordered categories, not measured safety, model complexity, or technology readiness.

para.p: Modern self-driving stacks realize the perceive–localize–decide–act loop as a modular pipeline, sketched in Figure . A front-end perception module converts raw, multi-modal sensor streams (camera, LiDAR, radar) into a structured model of the scene: what objects are present, where the drivable surface and lane geometry lie, and which agents are most safety-critical. A localization and mapping module places the ego-vehicle within a metric, typically HD-map-anchored, representation of that scene, so that perception outputs can be expressed in a stable world frame. A decision and control module then predicts how the scene will evolve and selects the steering, acceleration, and braking commands that are sent to the actuators and fed back into the environment, closing the loop. Each of the three stages is a distinct spatial-intelligence problem with its own representations, benchmarks, and failure modes, and they are the pivotal tasks below, in pipeline order.

figure.toccaption: 9.7Closed-loop spatial intelligence for autonomous driving: complementary sensor streams feed perception and localization and mapping, whose scene and ego/map state drive decision, planning, and trajectory tracking; vehicle–environment interaction returns new observations. The controller also receives ego state; the curved wire crossing is not a junction. Dashed execution logs feed evaluation separately from control. Scenes, maps, and evaluation plots are illustrative, not measured results.

caption.text: Closed-loop spatial intelligence for autonomous driving: complementary sensor streams feed perception and localization and mapping, whose scene and ego/map state drive decision, planning, and trajectory tracking; vehicle–environment interaction returns new observations. The controller also receives ego state; the curved wire crossing is not a junction. Dashed execution logs feed evaluation separately from control. Scenes, maps, and evaluation plots are illustrative, not measured results.

para.p: Perception is the front-end of the pipeline: it turns raw camera, LiDAR, and radar streams into a structured, layered model of the scene that every downstream module consumes, reusing the detection, segmentation, and 3D scene-understanding machinery of Chapter but specializing it to the driving Operational Design Domain (ODD). It is best read as a set of complementary structured representations, sketched in Figure : object detection localizes traffic participants, semantic and occupancy prediction labels the surrounding space, lane detection recovers the road geometry that constrains motion, and pedestrian recognition isolates the most safety-critical agents.

figure.toccaption: 9.8Four complementary driving perception tasks feeding a shared scene model: (1) object detection, (2) semantics and 3D occupancy, (3) lane geometry, and (4) pedestrian/VRU tracking and motion prediction. Annotations and the dashed pedestrian path are illustrative, not measured predictions.

caption.text: Four complementary driving perception tasks feeding a shared scene model: (1) object detection, (2) semantics and 3D occupancy, (3) lane geometry, and (4) pedestrian/VRU tracking and motion prediction. Annotations and the dashed pedestrian path are illustrative, not measured predictions.

para.p: The base layer is object detection, which identifies and localizes obstacles and is the most direct determinant of collision safety []. Its central practical constraint is the ODD: environmental factors such as poor weather degrade sensor visibility and model accuracy [], so recent work formalizes and iteratively validates the ODD through quantifiable environmental models and scenario catalogues, trusting a detector only within conditions it has demonstrably handled, though the absence of a standardized ODD specification still makes cross-system safety claims hard to compare. Robustness to adverse weather is therefore a first-class concern []: rain, snow, fog, and glare corrupt LiDAR, radar, and camera signals alike, and because driving datasets under-represent these conditions, models trained on fair-weather data generalize poorly. Responses range from dedicated robust pipelines, such as multi-stage visibility enhancement coupled with deep CNN tracking [], to new sensing hardware, e.g., , frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) LiDAR and high-dynamic-range cameras that recover usable signal in glare at higher cost. Moving from the image plane into metric space, 3D object detection localizes and tracks objects in the vehicle’s surroundings [], where the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation has become dominant because it yields a unified top-down map well suited to planning. BEVFormer [] fuses multi-camera and temporal cues with spatiotemporal transformers to approach LiDAR-level accuracy on nuScenes, while Fast-BEV [] and SparseBEV [] trade marginal accuracy for the lightweight, sparse, query-based computation needed for real-time on-vehicle deployment, together tracing the field’s balancing of accuracy, latency, and deployability.

Detections tell the planner where objects are but not which space is free; that dense layer is supplied by semantic segmentation and its 3D extension, occupancy prediction []. The progression runs from 2D pixel labeling with FCN [] and DeepLab [] to volumetric reasoning: the Tri-Perspective View [] lifts RGB into a 3D representation rivalling LiDAR, SurroundOcc [] uses multi-camera 2D–3D attention to capture arbitrary shapes, and occupancy world models such as OccWorld [] extend this to forecasting how the 3D scene evolves, moving beyond the limits of bounding boxes. Because these dense predictors are data-hungry and domain-sensitive, robustness techniques such as the SePiCo pixel-contrast framework [] and GAN-based synthetic data [] are used to survive scene variability, occlusion, and weather shift. On top of the free-space layer, lane detection recovers the road geometry that defines the lateral reference for lane-keeping and planning; early CNN- and YOLO-style detectors trace markings well in clear conditions but are brittle on curved, worn, or occluded lanes, motivating successors that lift lanes into 3D and use attention over global context to infer occluded segments. Finally, pedestrian recognition focuses on vulnerable road users whose behavior can be difficult to predict: CNN-, YOLO-, and SSD-based detectors deliver the required precision and latency, color–thermal fusion handles low-light scenes, and spatial–temporal models couple detection with motion prediction to anticipate crossing behavior.

Across all four layers, perception is benchmarked on large-scale driving datasets, KITTI [], the Waymo Open Dataset [], and nuScenes [] for 2D/3D detection, Cityscapes [] and BDD100K [] for segmentation, dedicated lane benchmarks for lane detection, and CityPersons [] for pedestrians, and scored with mean Average Precision (mAP) and the nuScenes Detection Score (NDS), mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU), and F1/accuracy, respectively (Table ). Increasingly these metrics are reported on adverse-weather and out-of-distribution splits, precisely to measure behavior within and beyond the declared ODD.

If perception answers what is around the vehicle, localization and mapping answer where the vehicle is and what the persistent structure of the world is. The two are tightly coupled: a metric, HD-map-anchored pose lets perception outputs be expressed in a stable world frame that planning can rely on, and the map itself is built and maintained from the same sensor streams. As Figure shows, the problem decomposes into pose estimation against a known map (localization), the construction of that map (3D mapping and reconstruction), and the joint solution of both when no map exists (SLAM), with multi-sensor fusion the common thread that holds accuracy together when any single modality degrades.

Pose and map are parallel products of joint estimation; only verified loop constraints return to the estimator. Recall@
