para.p: Localization has moved from GPS-dependent positioning to learned matching of live camera or LiDAR observations against a pre-built map, reaching centimeter-level accuracy even in GPS-denied urban canyons; semantic cues such as roads and buildings further let a vehicle re-localize in changed environments without full remapping. Because no single sensor is reliable across occlusion, weather, and GPS dropout, sensor-fusion localization is the dominant paradigm: probabilistic estimators (particle filters, Kalman filters, and NDT scan matching) reconcile GNSS, IMU, and LiDAR, while learned vision–radar fusion compensates for modality-specific weaknesses in rain, fog, and glare. The recurring bottlenecks here are cross-sensor spatial/temporal synchronization and fault tolerance, which motivate Bayesian uncertainty weighting and online-adaptive fusion that recalibrates as conditions change.

3D mapping and reconstruction supply the persistent representation that localization matches against, turning LiDAR and stereo streams into metric models; for the place-recognition and loop-closure that keep maps globally consistent, transformer descriptors such as SeqOT [] match sequential LiDAR scans faster than the sensor frame rate, trained on richly annotated corpora such as ApolloScape []. The open problems are the cost of processing dense point clouds at city scale and the handling of occluded or incomplete returns, which favor incremental map updating over full re-mapping. When the map is unavailable, SLAM solves localization and mapping jointly, which is critical in GPS-denied corridors; modern driving-oriented vSLAM hybridizes classical geometry with learned features (for example, extending ORB-SLAM [] with learned features, semantic labels, and learned depth to favor stable landmarks) and recovers from drift through loop closure with bundle adjustment.

These capabilities are evaluated on KITTI Odometry [], Oxford RobotCar [], and ApolloScape [] for long-horizon SLAM and place recognition, on nuScenes [] and Waymo [] for map-relative pose, and on Argoverse [] for the trajectory forecasting that localization feeds, e.g., , with the Motion Transformer [] (Table ). The standard metrics, i.e., , Absolute and Relative Pose Error (ATE/RPE), recall@
N
for loop closure, and minADE/minFDE for forecasting, are reported under GPS-denied, adverse-weather, and sensor-degradation conditions to stress exactly the robustness the fusion machinery is built to provide.

Decision making and control is the action end of the pipeline: it consumes the scene model from perception and the pose from localization, predicts how the scene will evolve, and commits to the steering, acceleration, and braking that close the loop, drawing on the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter . As Figure indicates, two architectural philosophies dominate, differing in how much of the perceive-to-act mapping is learned end-to-end versus decomposed into interpretable modules, and they are increasingly converging.

figure.toccaption: 9.10Three alternative architectures for driving decision and control: (1) modular pipelines with an explicit BEV scene, (2) end-to-end sensor-to-control learning, and (3) hybrids with inspectable scene or trajectory intermediates and explicit constraint checks.

caption.text: Three alternative architectures for driving decision and control: (1) modular pipelines with an explicit BEV scene, (2) end-to-end sensor-to-control learning, and (3) hybrids with inspectable scene or trajectory intermediates and explicit constraint checks.

para.p: The first philosophy is learning-based decision making, centered on (deep) reinforcement learning, which acquires driving policies through trial-and-error interaction and is well suited to the sequential, interactive nature of driving. Representative methods illustrate its design axes: the stochastic latent actor-critic (SLAC) [] learns compact latent states from high-dimensional images, PPO [] within a nonlinear control framework handles sharp turns and obstacle avoidance, and the DeepSet-Q architecture [], building on permutation-invariant set encoders [], ingests a variable number of surrounding agents for high-level lane-change decisions. Hybrids with explicit planning, such as Monte Carlo tree search guided by DRL or scene-representation transformers that forecast neighbor intentions, improve sample efficiency and situational awareness in dense traffic. The binding difficulty is that safety-critical episodes are rare in logged data, which pushes the field toward high-fidelity simulation for rare-event coverage and toward encoding hard safety constraints directly in the policy rather than trusting the reward signal alone. The second philosophy, end-to-end decision making, learns the mapping from sensors to trajectory or control directly, removing hand-designed interfaces between modules. Early instances learned state-to-action policies with DDPG [] in simulators such as TORCS, and multi-task backbones such as HybridNets [] share computation across detection and segmentation without yet closing the loop to control. Current systems are trained by imitation on large driving logs: TransFuser [] fuses camera and LiDAR features with transformer attention and predicts waypoints for a closed-loop agent, and UniAD [] chains tracking, mapping, motion forecasting, and occupancy prediction through query interfaces inside one network optimized for planning. Driving world models such as GAIA-1 [] generate future multi-view scenes conditioned on ego actions, giving such policies a learned simulator for training and evaluation. Opacity is the price of end-to-end training: attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) [] support interpretation but do not by themselves establish safety or regulatory compliance, which is why hybrid designs keep inspectable scene or trajectory intermediates together with explicit constraint checks, whose guarantees extend only as far as the modeled constraints.

Closed-loop driving policies are evaluated chiefly in simulation, i.e., , the CARLA urban simulator [] (NoCrash, Longest6), the nuPlan planning benchmark [], and highway-interaction simulators built on HighD/INTERACTION (Table ), because rare, safety-critical events cannot be exercised safely on public roads. The headline metrics are the CARLA Driving Score (route completion penalized by infractions), collision and intervention rates, and route completion, complemented by comfort proxies such as jerk and, for the open-loop forecasting sub-problem, minADE/minFDE.

para.p: The systems on the road today populate a deployment ladder whose rungs are the SAE levels of Figure , but what separates one rung from the next is rarely a single breakthrough in perception accuracy. It is, instead, two coupled engineering choices: how wide an Operational Design Domain (ODD) the system claims, and where legal responsibility for the driving task sits. Three tiers are in genuine production, i.e., , supervised Level 2 assistance, certified Level 3 “eyes-off” automation, and driverless Level 4 robotaxis, and, as the following progression shows, moving up the ladder consistently means adding sensing and compute redundancy while narrowing the domain in which the autonomy guarantee holds.

The defining property of Level 2 is that the system performs continuous lateral and longitudinal control, yet the human remains the legal driver and the immediate fallback; consequently, every Level 2 product is fundamentally an exercise in bounding the ODD and enforcing driver attention rather than in achieving autonomy, and the deployed systems differ mainly in how they strike that balance. One design philosophy gates hands-free operation to pre-validated, HD-mapped limited-access highways and polices it with in-cabin driver monitoring: GM Super Cruise 17 footnote 17 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 17 footnote 17 https://www.gm.com/innovation/autonomous-driving, Ford/Lincoln BlueCruise 18 footnote 18 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 18 footnote 18 https://www.lincoln.com/technology/bluecruise/, and BMW Driving Assistant Professional 19 footnote 19 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 19 footnote 19 https://www.bmwgroup.com/en/news/general/2023/driver-assistance-systems.html all keep the vehicle centered, regulate following distance, and offer assisted lane changes, but escalate alerts and disengage the moment attention drifts or the car leaves a supported segment; their reliability is a direct product of this deliberately narrow envelope. A second philosophy trades map dependence for scale: Tesla Autopilot 20 footnote 20 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 20 footnote 20 https://www.tesla.com/en_gb/support/autopilot and FSD (Supervised) 21 footnote 21 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 21 footnote 21 https://www.tesla.com/en_gb/fsd rely on a camera-first vision stack refined through fleet-wide over-the-air training, which extends assistance to a far broader and less-bounded set of scenarios but, lacking comparable geofencing, still demands constant supervision and degrades on poor markings, construction zones, and adverse weather. At the conservative end, Toyota Safety Sense declines hands-free operation altogether, functioning as an always-on crash-avoidance layer (automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping, and adaptive cruise) that intervenes only to prevent or mitigate collisions. Despite these differing emphases, the binding limitation is identical across all of them: a bounded ODD coupled with a mandatory human fallback, and it is precisely that fallback which the next tier begins to remove.

Level 3 is the first tier at which, inside a defined envelope, the driver may legally divert attention and the manufacturer assumes liability for the driving task. This shift in responsibility, rather than any new perception capability, is what dictates the engineering. Mercedes-Benz Drive Pilot 22 footnote 22 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 22 footnote 22 https://www.mercedes-benz.co.uk/passengercars/technology/autonomous-driving.html and Honda Traffic Jam Pilot 23 footnote 23 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 23 footnote 23 https://global.honda/en/tech/Traffic_Jam_Pilot_TJP/ purchase the “eyes-off” guarantee by pairing complementary sensing (cameras, radar, and LiDAR with high-precision, HD-map-anchored localization) with redundant braking, steering, and power paths that retain control through a single-component failure. Both, tellingly, keep the envelope deliberately small (low-speed or traffic-jam flow on mapped, divided highways), and both center on the same safety mechanism: as conditions approach the ODD boundary, the system issues a timed takeover request and, absent a driver response, executes a minimal-risk maneuver such as a controlled stop with hazard signals. The narrowness of the Level 3 envelope is therefore not a marketing concession but the direct cost of guaranteeing safe behavior once the human is no longer continuously in the loop: a cost the next tier pays in full by removing the driver entirely.

Level 4 removes the human from the loop entirely within a geofence: there is no driver to hand back to, so the vehicle must resolve every in-domain situation itself or bring itself to a safe state, with remote operators supplying only high-level guidance rather than moment-to-moment control. To meet this far stricter bar, Waymo One 24 footnote 24 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 24 footnote 24 https://waymo.com/ and Baidu Apollo Go 25 footnote 25 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 25 footnote 25 https://www.apollogo.com/ converge on essentially the same recipe: a dense, overlapping multi-sensor suite (lidar, radar, and camera vision) for redundant coverage, HD-map-anchored localization, and conservative prediction-and-planning that favors lawful, cautious maneuvers through dense urban traffic. Each makes the problem tractable not by claiming universal competence but by tightly restricting where and when it operates and validating performance city by city before extending the geofence. Across the three tiers, every step up the ladder buys wider autonomy by narrowing the operating domain and adding redundancy, until at Level 4 the system finally internalizes the fallback that Levels 2 and 3 delegated to the driver.

Every tier of the deployment ladder works because it limits where it operates, and general, trustworthy autonomy requires lifting those limits. Four threads, each cutting across perception, localization, and decision, stand in the way: justifying life-critical decisions (safety and explainability), dependable behavior across the long tail of road, weather, and traffic conditions (resilience and robustness), adaptation to genuinely novel situations from little prior data (unfamiliar road scenarios), and continual learning on deployed vehicles without eroding mastered behavior (enhanced autonomy in complex scenarios).

Because driving decisions are life-critical, the inability to explain why a model selected a given maneuver is a first-order obstacle to certification and public trust. Post-hoc attribution methods such as layer-wise relevance propagation [] and Shapley-value attribution expose which inputs drove a decision, supporting both engineering debugging and regulatory audit, while causal-inference models go further by separating mere correlation from the actual influence of factors such as road state and a maneuver’s effect on surrounding agents. The unresolved difficulty is that these explanations remain largely retrospective and local to individual decisions; converting them into guarantees that provably hold across the full operating domain is still an open problem.

Robustness to the long tail of driving conditions is commonly pursued through curriculum learning, where a policy is trained on a graded sequence from simple navigation to dense mixed-traffic interaction, which improves sample efficiency and training stability relative to confronting hard cases directly. Its effectiveness, however, hinges on a scenario curriculum that faithfully spans the deployment distribution and on objectives that keep safety and comfort constraints satisfied at every difficulty level. The practical risk is that, absent a benchmark which deliberately surfaces rare but critical events, strong curriculum performance on common scenes can mask failures precisely on the cases that determine real-world safety.

A distinct difficulty is generalization to genuinely novel situations (an unseen sign, an irregular work zone, an atypical vehicle) where data-hungry models degrade but human drivers adapt from a single exposure. Approaches that target this gap include probabilistic program induction in a Bayesian framework, which represents a new concept as a compact program inferred from few examples, and the injection of compositional, causal, and meta-learning priors so that, for instance, a system can infer that a fallen obstacle will trigger sudden lane changes in adjacent traffic. The standing obstacle is validating such few-shot behavior to a safety standard, since the very rarity of these events makes their failure modes hard to measure and certify.

Sustained operation in changing environments motivates lifelong learning [], in which a deployed system keeps acquiring new knowledge (a new traffic pattern or road layout) without retraining from scratch and without overwriting prior competence. The central technical barrier is catastrophic forgetting, which is addressed by memory-augmented architectures and continual-learning regularizers that protect previously learned parameters, together with transfer mechanisms that reuse knowledge across tasks and cities. The harder, still-open requirement is to perform such updates on-vehicle under real-time and verification constraints, so that an update improving one scenario cannot silently regress a safety-critical behavior elsewhere.

Wearable devices have become a central sensing modality for embodied and spatial intelligence, delivering continuous, fine-grained measurements of human motion, physiology, and physical interaction. Because they are worn on or integrated into the body, they access proprioceptive and kinesthetic cues, joint rotations, muscle activations, contact forces, and locomotion patterns, which exteroceptive sensors such as RGB-D cameras or LiDAR cannot capture directly. We use the term broadly, covering inertial measurement units (IMUs), surface electromyography (EMG) sensors, smart textiles, haptic interfaces, and wearable cameras: body-mounted technologies that together model human dynamics and embodied interaction in real-world settings. It is this egocentric, body-centric vantage point that makes wearables valuable for spatial intelligence, letting a system reason about how a person moves through, reads, and acts upon their surroundings, and it has driven rapid adoption across health monitoring, sports analytics, rehabilitation [], industrial safety, and human–robot collaboration.

The signals wearables provide are especially valuable because they are anticipatory. Joint kinematics and muscle activity reveal what a person is doing and, crucially, what they are about to do next, which is what underpins intent recognition, action forecasting, and safe coordination in shared spaces. Wearable IMU arrays, for example, recover whole-body skeletal motion in cluttered or occluded settings where optical capture breaks down [], and EMG surfaces pre-activation patterns that precede any visible movement [].

These devices are often bracketed with head-mounted XR hardware, yet their role in spatial intelligence differs in kind. XR headsets integrate sensing and display for immersive visualization and mixed-reality interaction, leaning on outward-facing cameras for SLAM and environment mapping. The wearables treated here look inward instead, supplying the biomechanical and physiological state, high-frequency, continuous, and on-body, that an XR headset does not observe.

The spatial-intelligence capabilities that wearables ultimately serve, pose estimation, action recognition, localization, and trajectory prediction, are formulated in Part III (spatial perception in Chapter , spatial reasoning in Chapter ). This section does not re-derive them; it concentrates on the body-centric sensing layer, the devices that acquire embodied signals, the systems assembled around them, and the tasks, methods, and failure modes that surface once spatial intelligence must be grounded in continuous on-body measurement, spanning long-horizon activity and gait analysis, intention prediction for human–robot collaboration, and real-time safety in industrial and logistics settings.
Body-centric sensing spans a diverse device ecosystem, summarized in Table .

Inertial measurement units (accelerometers, gyroscopes, and often magnetometers) are the most widely deployed body-worn sensors. Consumer watches and bands such as the Apple Watch 26 footnote 26 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 26 footnote 26 https://www.apple.com/watch/, Samsung Galaxy Watch 27 footnote 27 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 27 footnote 27 https://www.samsung.com/global/galaxy/galaxy-watch/, Fitbit 28 footnote 28 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 28 footnote 28 https://www.fitbit.com/, and Xiaomi Band stream inertial data for activity and gait monitoring, while research and industrial systems place IMUs at specific anatomical sites and fuse them into full-body kinematics []; because they need no line of sight, they keep working under occlusion and poor lighting. Full-body motion-capture suits such as Xsens 29 footnote 29 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 29 footnote 29 https://www.movella.com/products/xsens, Rokoko Smartsuit Pro 30 footnote 30 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 30 footnote 30 https://www.rokoko.com/, and Noitom 31 footnote 31 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 31 footnote 31 https://www.noitom.com/ combine many IMUs, sometimes with pressure or stretch sensors, into accurate skeletal pose outside the studio, which has made them standard in biomechanics, sports, robotics, and character animation []. Smart clothing embeds conductive fabrics, stretch sensors, or distributed pressure sensors in garments for unobtrusive, long-duration monitoring of posture, joint angles, and whole-body contact [], and physiological sensors (heart rate, galvanic skin response, respiration), foot-mounted inertial or pressure sensors, and ear-worn IMUs add workload, ground-contact timing, and head orientation [].

Electromyography (EMG) armbands and high-density arrays sense the muscle activations that precede visible movement, giving early cues for gesture recognition and intent estimation [], and combining EMG with inertial data makes them more robust to arm posture and fatigue []. Wearable cameras add the exteroceptive, first-person view: egocentric RGB, depth, or fisheye streams supply scene geometry and activity context that can be fused with on-body signals []. Two device families also act on the body. Haptic gloves such as HaptX 32 footnote 32 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 32 footnote 32 https://haptx.com/ and SenseGlove 33 footnote 33 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 33 footnote 33 https://www.senseglove.com/ and haptic vests such as bHaptics 34 footnote 34 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 34 footnote 34 https://www.bhaptics.com/ return tactile, vibration, or force feedback during manipulation, teleoperation, and training [], and exoskeletons combine IMUs, torque and force sensors, and joint encoders with actuation, estimating user intent in real time to assist or rehabilitate movement [], which makes them a direct test of embodied spatial intelligence.

para.p: Taken together, the devices above form the front end of a single body-centric perception-to-action loop that defines the wearable AI system as a whole. Raw on-body signals are first sensed (inertial, neuromuscular, tactile, and egocentric-visual streams), then modeled into geometric and biomechanical state (joint kinematics, body pose, contact forces), interpreted and predicted into higher-level behavioral and intentional descriptions (activities, gestures, short-horizon motion forecasts), and finally fed back to the wearer or to a collaborating agent through action channels (haptic cues, exoskeleton assistance, safety alerts, or shared-control commands). The loop then closes: the consequences of feedback alter the wearer’s motion, which the sensors observe anew.

Figure schematizes this loop and situates the three pivotal tasks that organize the remainder of this section as complementary stages of it. Pivotal Task-1 (Embodied Motion Sensing and Pose Reconstruction) occupies the sense-to-model stage, turning body-centric signals into stable geometric descriptions of motion. Pivotal Task-2 (Behavioral Understanding and Intention Modeling) occupies the interpret-and-predict stage, mapping reconstructed motion and neuromuscular cues to recognized activities and anticipated actions. Pivotal Task-3 (Safe Collaboration and Embodied Interaction) closes the loop at the action stage, converting interpreted human state into coordinated, safe, and assistive responses in shared physical environments. Because all three stages must run under the power, compute, and reliability constraints of body-worn hardware, lightweight on-device inference is a cross-cutting concern that recurs throughout.

subsection.title: 9.3.4Pivotal Task-1: Embodied Motion Sensing and Pose Reconstruction

para.p: The first stage of the wearable loop turns raw body-centric signals into a geometric description of how the wearer moves. It is a bottom-up reconstruction problem: per-segment inertial and biomechanical measurements must yield joint angles, segment velocities, and ultimately a full-body pose that remains stable over long horizons and in settings where exteroceptive capture fails. This task subsumes full-body skeletal pose estimation, fine-grained limb tracking, real-world locomotion and gait analysis, and body-centric localization in GPS-denied spaces; the underlying pose-estimation formulations are developed in Chapter , so the emphasis here is on reconstruction from on-body sensing. Figure illustrates this reconstruction stack from segment-level signals to full-body pose.

figure.toccaption: 9.12Motion sensing and pose reconstruction from body-worn IMUs: estimators supported by a parametric body model recover root-relative full-body pose, while visual–inertial fusion anchors a world-frame trajectory. Contact or zero-velocity updates apply only when their assumptions hold, and metric scale requires sufficient observability; signals and trajectories are illustrative.

caption.text: Motion sensing and pose reconstruction from body-worn IMUs: estimators supported by a parametric body model recover root-relative full-body pose, while visual–inertial fusion anchors a world-frame trajectory. Contact or zero-velocity updates apply only when their assumptions hold, and metric scale requires sufficient observability; signals and trajectories are illustrative.

para.p: From signals to kinematics. Reconstruction begins with kinematic and dynamic modeling, which provides the physical grounding for interpreting inertial and pressure-based signals. Forward and inverse kinematics infer joint angles and segment orientations from inertial measurements, compensating for drift and sensor noise through optimization-based filtering and biomechanical constraints. Classical recursive estimators such as extended and unscented Kalman filters incorporate kinematic priors and temporal smoothness to improve stability in real-world settings [], while articulated-body dynamics and parametric body models such as SMPL [] enforce anatomical plausibility for complex motions such as rapid locomotion or limb coordination. Multi-IMU fusion against musculoskeletal models extends these ideas to full-body pose estimation in challenging environments where optical motion-capture systems fail [], and recent systems fold in physics-based dynamics and inter-sensor ultra-wideband ranging to tighten accuracy and suppress jitter [].

Learning-based reconstruction and sensor fusion. Where analytic models struggle with sparse or noisy sensing, data-driven approaches learn the mapping from raw inertial streams to pose directly [], and sensor fusion integrates heterogeneous modalities for drift-compensated estimates. IMU-and-vision fusion resolves ambiguities in inertial tracking by leveraging environmental context from egocentric cameras [], while drift-compensation techniques, including zero-velocity updates and constraint-based corrections, stabilize long-horizon wear. For body-centric localization, sparse-sensor systems couple inertial pose estimation with simultaneous localization and mapping, so that the wearer’s global trajectory is recovered together with body pose rather than left to drift freely []; visual-inertial odometry that fuses the same inertial signals with first-person imagery offers a complementary route through GPS-denied indoor spaces, assessed on dedicated benchmarks [].

Benchmarks and evaluation. The kinematic, learning-based, and fusion methods above are measured against the same yardsticks: large-scale motion-capture corpora such as AMASS [], which provides a canonical surface-and-skeleton reference for full-body pose, alongside dedicated inertial-pose datasets for sparse-IMU reconstruction [], while body-centric localization is assessed separately on visual-inertial odometry benchmarks []. Reconstruction quality is reported as mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) and joint-angle error, and localization as absolute trajectory error and accumulated drift (Table ). Read against the needs of real deployment, these numbers reveal a clear gap. On curated benchmarks, sparse-IMU systems now recover root-relative full-body pose to within roughly five centimeters of optical ground truth [], but global translation still drifts over long sequences unless it is anchored by SLAM or ranging [], and even the root-relative accuracy falls off in the wild, where fast or unseen motions and loose sensor placement push errors past the tolerance that downstream control or clinical gait analysis can absorb. The pose the next stage consumes is thus dependable on average yet brittle at exactly the fast, atypical movements that matter most.

subsection.title: 9.3.5Pivotal Task-2: Behavioral Understanding and Intention Modeling

para.p: Once motion has been reconstructed, the second stage of the loop interprets it: recognizing what the wearer is doing and anticipating what they will do next. Continuous neuromuscular and inertial cues feed activity recognition and segmentation and then short-horizon intention prediction, even in daily-life settings where visual systems face severe occlusion or field-of-view limits. Because the recognition and reasoning formulations themselves are treated in Chapter , the focus here is on how high-frequency wearable streams are modeled to support behavioral inference. Figure sketches the path from multimodal time-series and body-graph representations to recognized activity and predicted intent.

figure.toccaption: 9.13Behavioral understanding and intention modeling: IMU and EMG sequences and a kinematic body graph pass through temporal and graph encoders, fused by attention to recognize current activity and forecast short-horizon intent. The EMG pre-activation inset draws anticipatory cues from the observed stream, not from future measurements.

caption.text: Behavioral understanding and intention modeling: IMU and EMG sequences and a kinematic body graph pass through temporal and graph encoders, fused by attention to recognize current activity and forecast short-horizon intent. The EMG pre-activation inset draws anticipatory cues from the observed stream, not from future measurements.

para.p: Sequence models for wearable time-series. The availability of large-scale wearable recordings has driven deep models tailored to high-frequency temporal streams from IMU, EMG, and multimodal sensors. Recurrent networks, temporal convolutional networks, and Transformers are widely applied to gait classification, gesture recognition, and activity segmentation []: temporal convolutions capture multi-scale dependencies for long-horizon pattern detection [], while attention-based architectures learn complex correlations across sensor channels []. Because labeled wearable data are scarce and expensive, self-supervised pretraining on unlabeled motion recordings has become the dominant route to transferable representations []: masked-reconstruction encoders such as LIMU-BERT learn compact IMU features from raw streams [], and multimodal contrastive objectives such as IMU2CLIP align inertial signals with video and language, pointing toward wearable foundation models that generalize across tasks and users [].

Graph-based body representations. Because human anatomy is structured as a kinematic tree, graph neural networks offer a natural representation for wearable-derived motion [], encoding relational dependencies between joints and limbs directly in graph space. Such formulations fuse IMU placements across body segments, propagate temporal features along skeletal edges, and remain robust to missing or corrupted sensor channels; combining graph convolution with temporal attention jointly models spatial structure and temporal evolution for activity recognition and biomechanical analysis [].

Neuromuscular cues and multimodal fusion for intent. Beyond recognizing observed motion, EMG-based wearables detect subtle neuromuscular activations that precede visible movement [], providing predictive cues for early intention estimation and responsive human-robot collaboration. Fusing EMG with inertial data sharpens fine-grained gesture and anticipatory-command decoding [], while fusing IMU with egocentric video grounds activity recognition in environmental context []. A recent milestone shows how far this can scale: a surface-EMG wristband trained across more than a thousand users decodes gestures, clicks, and handwriting from neuromuscular signals alone and, critically, generalizes to new wearers without per-user calibration [], addressing the inter-user variability that has long limited EMG interfaces. Physiological and pressure cues additionally support inference of fatigue, balance, and abnormal gait over extended periods.

Benchmarks and evaluation. Taking the reconstructed motion of the previous stage as input, the sequence, graph, and fusion models above are evaluated on wearable human-activity-recognition corpora [], EMG gesture datasets [], and egocentric activity datasets such as Ego4D [] and EPIC-KITCHENS [], with recognition reported as accuracy and macro-F1 and intention prediction as anticipation accuracy and prediction lead time (Table ). Here the gap to maturity is one of generalization rather than peak score. Balanced locomotion corpora such as PAMAP2 are close to saturated, yet the same architectures score markedly lower on cluttered, null-dominated sets such as Opportunity and lose accuracy again under cross-user and cross-environment evaluation; reliable intention forecasting, meanwhile, still extends only to short, well-rehearsed horizons. This falls well short of the open-world, anticipatory understanding that the safe-collaboration stage below depends on, where the system must read unfamiliar users in unfamiliar settings.

subsection.title: 9.3.6Pivotal Task-3: Safe Collaboration and Embodied Interaction

para.p: The third stage closes the loop, converting interpreted human state into coordinated, safe, and assistive responses in shared physical environments. Contact- and force-level sensing of human–environment interaction supports real-time inference of effort and hazard, which in turn drives feedback for collaboration and shared autonomy. The collaboration and shared-control reasoning that this task builds on is developed in Chapter and, for the manipulation setting specifically, in Section ; here the emphasis is on the wearable feedback and safety layer. Figure depicts this closing stage, from contact sensing to coordinated safety response.

figure.toccaption: 9.14Safe human–robot collaboration with wearables: fused contact, force, and proximity signals, together with intent forecasts (T2) and robot motion context, drive motion prediction and risk evaluation, which select glove, exoskeleton, or cobot responses. Prediction envelopes and risk thresholds are schematic, not measured safety guarantees.

caption.text: Safe human–robot collaboration with wearables: fused contact, force, and proximity signals, together with intent forecasts (T2) and robot motion context, drive motion prediction and risk evaluation, which select glove, exoskeleton, or cobot responses. Prediction envelopes and risk thresholds are schematic, not measured safety guarantees.

para.p: Sensing interaction and effort. Haptic and tactile wearables capture contact forces, surface interactions, and manipulative behaviors, supplying the signals needed to model human–environment interaction and object handling []. Exoskeletons equipped with torque and force sensors use these signals to infer user effort and detect hazardous conditions, adjusting assistive strategies accordingly []; probabilistic fusion that integrates biomechanical priors and uncertainty estimates is central to robustness in such safety-critical settings.

Coordination, safety, and feedback. In industrial and shared-autonomy scenarios, on-body inertial and proximity sensors contribute to safety monitoring by detecting collision risks, unsafe postures, and sudden motion anomalies, while haptic channels return spatial alerts and force feedback that close the sensorimotor loop []. Combined with the intention forecasts of Pivotal Task-2, these signals form the basis for predictive safety mechanisms and shared-control frameworks that anticipate human motion rather than merely reacting to it.

On-device constraints. Because feedback must be timely, the action stage is where the wearable system’s power, memory, and compute limits bite hardest. Model compression (pruning, quantization, and distillation) [] and edge-optimized architectures [] enable real-time inference on wearable microcontrollers or smartphone-class processors, and on-device adaptation mitigates inter-user variability without relying on remote servers, keeping safety-critical computation local and low-latency.

Benchmarks and evaluation. Closing the loop, the interaction-sensing, safety, and on-device methods above are assessed on human-object-interaction datasets such as HOI4D [] and, for assistive control, on exoskeleton and teleoperation testbeds, with metrics spanning contact- and force-estimation error, collision-avoidance and safety-violation rates, and intention-anticipation lead time (Table ). Evaluation here is the least mature of the three stages: it remains fragmented across hardware-specific testbeds with few shared protocols, so reported gains are hard to compare and seldom stress real safety guarantees. Current systems perform convincingly in instrumented demonstrations, but closed-loop, certified safety under the full variability of human partners, the bar that genuine shared autonomy must clear, is still an open target rather than a measured result. The robustness, generalization, and safety gaps that recur at each stage of the loop are what the challenges below take up directly.

table.toccaption: 9.4Representative benchmarks for wearable spatial-intelligence tasks, grouped by pivotal task.

caption.text: Representative benchmarks for wearable spatial-intelligence tasks, grouped by pivotal task.

para.p: Commercial wearables have converged on the head and the wrist, and what separates current products is less their sensors than where perception runs and whether anything is shown back to the wearer. Full augmented-reality headsets are covered with the XR platforms in Section ; here the focus is on everyday-wearable glasses, neural input bands, and the research platforms and chips behind them.

AI glasses without a display. By volume, the dominant wearable AI device is a pair of ordinary-looking glasses carrying a camera, microphones, open-ear speakers, and an IMU, with a multimodal assistant running on the paired phone or in the cloud. Meta’s line with EssilorLuxottica 35 footnote 35 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 35 footnote 35 https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/ defines the category: the second-generation Ray-Ban Meta (2025) records 3K video from a 12-megapixel camera and runs up to eight hours per charge, and the Oakley Meta Vanguard adapts the design to sport with a 122-degree camera. Display-less models made up 96% of AI-glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, almost all of them Meta’s 36 footnote 36 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 36 footnote 36 Counterpoint Research, global AI glasses shipments, H1 2026., while Xiaomi’s AI glasses (2025) and Alibaba’s Qwen-based Quark AI glasses 37 footnote 37 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 37 footnote 37 https://www.quark.cn/ (November 2025) lead a fast-growing Chinese segment. Google and Samsung previewed Gemini-based Android XR glasses 38 footnote 38 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 38 footnote 38 https://www.android.com/xr/ with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker in May 2026, with the first display-less models due in the fall. Spatially, these devices answer questions about what the wearer is looking at one camera frame at a time; most keep no persistent map of the surroundings, so the continuous body and scene tracking of Pivotal Tasks 1 and 2 is still largely absent from shipping products.

Display glasses and neural input. Adding a display makes the glasses an interface, and input then becomes the hard problem. Meta Ray-Ban Display 39 footnote 39 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 39 footnote 39 https://www.meta.com/ai-glasses/meta-ray-ban-display/ (September 2025) puts a small monocular display, with a 20-degree field of view, in the right lens and ships with the Meta Neural Band, a surface-EMG wristband that decodes finger gestures and handwriting; it is the commercial form of the generic neuromotor interface described in Pivotal Task-2 []. In waveguide display glasses, Rokid 40 footnote 40 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 40 footnote 40 https://global.rokid.com/ led shipments in the first half of 2026, ahead of Meta and Even Realities 41 footnote 41 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 41 footnote 41 https://www.evenrealities.com/, whose glasses favor a minimal text display over cameras.

Research platforms and on-glass compute. Much of the egocentric data behind the methods of this section was recorded on research glasses rather than consumer products. Meta’s Project Aria [] 42 footnote 42 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 42 footnote 42 https://www.projectaria.com/ provides glasses with RGB, tracking, and eye-tracking cameras, IMUs, and spatial microphones, together with machine-perception services for trajectories, eye gaze, and hand tracking; its second generation (2025) adds a heart-rate sensor and a contact microphone in the nosepad, alongside on-device perception. The platform underlies Aria Digital Twin []; Ego-Exo4D [], which pairs egocentric Aria recordings of skilled activities with synchronized exocentric cameras over 1,422 hours; and Nymeria [], which adds full-body ground-truth motion from a motion-capture suit to 300 hours of everyday activity, the kind of supervision the pose reconstruction of Pivotal Task-1 needs. Ego4D [] gathered its 3,670 hours from several head-mounted cameras, and remains the main benchmark for egocentric activity understanding. On the compute side, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon AR1+ Gen 1 43 footnote 43 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 43 footnote 43 https://www.qualcomm.com/products/mobile/snapdragon/xr-vr-ar (2025) runs a one-billion-parameter language model on the glasses without a phone, a first step toward the on-device inference that the latency and power constraints of Pivotal Task-3 call for.

Wearable sensing is coupled to the dynamics and variability of the human body in a way that external sensing is not, and that coupling is the source of its hardest problems. The four below track the loop of the System Overview: signal quality at the sense stage, robustness under partial observation, fusion across heterogeneous modalities, and generalization across users.

On-body signals are inherently unstable. IMU drift, EMG noise, and calibration shifts arise continuously from motion artifacts, sensor displacement, and soft-tissue deformation, and they strike precisely the quantities that pose estimation, trajectory tracking, and dynamics reconstruction integrate over time, so small per-step errors compound into large ones across a long recording.

Sensing is rarely continuous in practice. Sweat, motion, and wireless dropouts cause brief losses of contact and stretches of degraded signal, leaving the system to reconstruct reliable motion from partial and sometimes corrupted segment-level data, a demand that clean-benchmark evaluation rarely exercises.

The modalities that make wearables powerful are also mismatched. IMU, EMG, pressure, and egocentric-visual streams differ in sampling rate, latency, noise, and coordinate frame, and fusing them under real-world variability, without letting one noisy channel corrupt the whole estimate, remains an open integration problem rather than a solved preprocessing step.

Finally, the body itself is the confound. Anatomy, muscle-activation patterns, and movement style vary enough between people that a model tuned on a small or homogeneous population transfers poorly, and the effect is sharpest exactly where wearables matter most, in motion reconstruction, intent prediction, and gait analysis, where individual biomechanics dominate the sensor signature. Personalization, domain adaptation, and larger, more diverse training corpora are the levers for closing this gap, and how far they succeed will decide whether wearable spatial intelligence moves from convincing demonstrations to dependable deployment.

Aerial agents (satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)) acquire rich, dynamic, large-scale observations from the sky and near space and, increasingly, perceive, decide, and act on them autonomously through onboard processing and adaptive control (Table ). The aerial domain is a demanding testbed for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part : it stresses perception across extreme scale and viewpoint changes (Chapter ) and decision-making under partial observability and tight latency budgets (Chapter ), across platform tiers that differ in altitude, resolution, endurance, and latency by orders of magnitude.

Satellites supply the global tier. Navigation constellations, namely GPS [] within the broader Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), Russia’s GLONASS [], the European Union’s Galileo, and China’s BeiDou [], provide the positioning, navigation, and timing on which vehicles [], smartphones [], network synchronization [], and every lower aerial tier rely. Earth-observation satellites operate continuously over years, which suits long-term, wide-area monitoring that neither ground sensors nor short-endurance UAVs can provide: seasonal vegetation dynamics [], wildlife migration [], river-basin ecosystem health [], deforestation [], desertification [], biodiversity loss [], and climate indicators such as land surface temperature, ocean color, and atmospheric composition [], together with ecological conservation [], multispectral and hyperspectral resource discovery [], precision agriculture [] and crop-yield estimation [], and the detection of algal blooms [] and pollutant leakage [].

table.toccaption: 9.5Comparison of satellite, HAPS, and UAV platforms.

caption.text: Comparison of satellite, HAPS, and UAV platforms.

para.p: Differently, UAVs, commonly known as drones, have gained widespread popularity due to their agility, low operational cost, and capability for autonomous operation. Equipped with onboard sensors and processing units, UAVs can perceive their surroundings, plan flight paths, and adapt to dynamic conditions in real time. This unique perspective allows UAVs to capture high-resolution imagery and video from flexible vantage points, enabling frequent revisits and reduced occlusions in complex environments. Compared to satellites, UAVs excel in capturing fine-grained, localized data, and can be rapidly deployed to areas of interest, including hazardous or otherwise inaccessible regions. They now serve aerial photography [], cinematography [], environmental mapping [], precision agriculture [], geolocalization [], and last-mile delivery [].

Filling the altitude gap between satellite systems and UAVs, emerging platforms such as stratospheric balloons, solar-powered high-altitude platform stations, and small satellite constellations (e.g., , CubeSats []) are increasingly being integrated into aerial observation networks. These high-altitude platform stations (HAPS) offer complementary advantages: HAPS [] provide persistent regional coverage with higher spatial resolution than satellites, while orbital systems [] enable global, long-term monitoring at varying temporal and spectral scales. Together, they form a multi-tiered aerial ecosystem capable of capturing heterogeneous multimedia data, from visible and thermal imagery to hyperspectral and LiDAR scans, across spatiotemporal scales unattainable by any single platform alone. For instance, solar-powered HAPS such as Airbus Zephyr [] or HAWK30 by AeroVironment/HAPSMobile [] can operate autonomously in the stratosphere (about 20 km altitude) for weeks, offering persistent observation and communication relay services with sub-meter resolution, which is superior to most Earth observation satellites and at lower cost than maintaining UAV fleets.

A growing trend is the coordination of heterogeneous aerial agents into cooperative networks, where satellites offer global context, HAPS serve as communication relays or edge computing nodes, and UAVs execute localized missions, enabling real-time, closed-loop intelligence. The utility of these systems is further amplified by advances in artificial intelligence, including machine learning, computer vision, big data analytics, and transfer learning []. These technologies empower intelligent processing of massive aerial datasets, enabling automated image and video analysis [], real-time object detection and tracking [], predictive modeling for urban dynamics [], natural language-based control interfaces [], and city-scale digital twin simulations []. Data privacy, airspace integration, energy efficiency, and operational robustness remain open, and are taken up in the Challenges below.

An aerial agent realizes a sensing-to-action loop that spans the multi-tier ecosystem of Table : satellites supply global context and positioning, HAPS act as persistent regional relays and edge-computing nodes, and UAVs execute localized, low-latency missions at the point of interest. Across this stack, spatial intelligence is exercised through three complementary stages, which constitute the pivotal tasks of this section. Cross-view perception anchors aerial and ground observations to a common geographic frame, so that what a drone sees can be matched to a map or a street-level query (Pivotal Task-1); remote-sensing detection and environmental understanding turn that imagery into structured scene knowledge about objects, layouts, and human activity (Pivotal Task-2); and autonomous navigation and decision making convert perception into flight plans and control actions in unseen environments (Pivotal Task-3). Figure sketches this pipeline, with a feedback path from action back onto sensing that ties the three stages into one closed loop rather than a feed-forward chain.

subsection.title: 9.4.3Pivotal Task-1: Ground-Air Collaborative Perception and Visual Geolocalization

para.p: A foundational requirement of any aerial system is to place its observations on the map: the integration of ground-level and aerial views for cross-modal understanding enables visual geolocalization, determining the geographic location of a query image by matching it against a reference database. This task anchors the perception stage of the system and is particularly challenging due to the large modality gap between ground street-view images and overhead (aerial or satellite) imagery, an instance of the cross-view correspondence problem treated more generally in Chapter . For instance, the University-1652 dataset [] has become a benchmark for this task, offering ground, drone and satellite image triplets of campus buildings, thus facilitating research on cross-view matching and localization. Such capabilities are critical for urban search-and-rescue, augmented reality, and infrastructure monitoring, where precise alignment between ground observations and aerial maps is essential. Progress has come from bridging the modality gap, encoding spatial structure into a viewpoint-invariant representation, and exploiting multiple views per location (Figure ).

Bridging the modality gap. Most extant research frames geolocalization as a cross-view image retrieval problem, where the core challenge is to learn a viewpoint-invariant representation that effectively bridges the disparity between images captured from different perspectives. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the widespread application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) for extracting robust visual features. One prominent line of inquiry employs metric learning to construct a shared latent space for images acquired from diverse platforms. Workman et al. [] show that a CNN pre-trained on the Places dataset [] can, by itself, yield highly discriminative features without explicit fine-tuning for the task. The integration of contrastive loss, which minimizes the distance between positive pairs in the feature space, further enhances geolocalization performance []. Liu et al. [] introduce the Stochastic Attraction and Repulsion Embedding (SARE) loss, which minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the learned and actual data distributions, and more recently Deuser et al. [] show that hard negative sampling strategies also significantly influence the final discriminative power.

Encoding spatial structure. Another significant body of work addresses the problem of spatial misalignment in ground-to-aerial matching, injecting geometric priors into the representation. Vo et al.evaluate various network architectures and propose an orientation regression loss to train an orientation-aware network []. Zhai et al. [] utilize semantic segmentation maps to facilitate semantic alignment, while Hu et al. [] incorporate a NetVLAD layer to extract more discriminative features. Subsequently, Liu et al. [] propose a Siamese Network to explicitly integrate spatial cues, such as orientation maps, into the training process, and Shi et al. [] introduce a spatial-aware layer to improve localization performance. Given that each location has multiple training images from different viewpoints, Zheng et al. [] train a multi-branch CNN as a base model. Building upon this multi-branch architecture, Wang et al. [] further partition the feature map into multiple segments to improve matching discriminability, while Lin et al. [] incorporate keypoint detection into the learning process. More recently, researchers resort to ViT structures: L2LTR [] adopts a hybrid CNN-ViT architecture, leveraging CNNs to extract high-level semantic features and ViTs to encode them into global representations; GeoDTR [] further enhances geometric reasoning by introducing a ViT-based layout extractor that generates geometry-aware attention maps; and TransGeo [] advances the paradigm with a two-branch ViT model and a two-stage coarse-to-fine learning strategy.

para.p: From image pairs to multi-view benchmarks. The maturation of these methods is closely tied to the datasets that score them (see Table ). The majority of prior geolocalization datasets are based on image pairs, designed for matching images from two distinct platforms such as terrestrial cameras and satellites. One of the earliest contributions [] leverages public sources to create 78,000 image pairs spanning a 45-degree bird’s-eye perspective and the ground. In a similar vein, Tian et al. [] compile image pairs for urban localization, positing that buildings are crucial for this task and thus incorporating building detection into their pipeline. The CVUSA [] and CVACT [] datasets instead address matching panoramic ground-view images with satellite-view images, which is particularly useful for user localization when GPS data is unavailable. A key distinction is one of objective: the latter two focus on localizing the user who captures the photograph, while the former focus on localizing a specific target within the image, so that multiple views of the target are more beneficial for the target-localization datasets (Lin et al., Tian et al.) because they encourage the model to learn the target’s structure. However, most existing datasets typically provide only two views of a given location. The University-1652 dataset [] addresses this by including a greater number of views per target, thereby fostering more robust viewpoint-invariant features; SUES-200 [] follows a similar multi-view strategy with drone-captured real-world data. Wang et al. [] further extend University-1652 to multi-weather evaluation (rain, fog, and other complex conditions), while Chu et al. [] introduce linguistic annotations and a language-based query setting for a more intuitive user experience.

Metrics. These benchmarks are scored by retrieval metrics that reflect their gallery structure. Several datasets [] adopt Recall@K, defined as 1 if a correct match appears within the top K retrieved images; Recall@K is highly sensitive to the rank of the first correct match and is best suited for test sets containing only a single ground-truth match in the gallery. In contrast, datasets such as University-1652 [] and SUES-200 [] include multiple ground-truth matches from various viewpoints, where Recall@K fails to comprehensively reflect retrieval performance; they therefore also employ Average Precision (AP), as used by Lin et al. [] and Tian et al. []. AP, defined as the area under the Precision-Recall (PR) curve, considers all ground-truth images in the gallery, and recent evaluations usually report both Recall@K and the mean Average Precision (mAP) across all queries.

subsection.title: 9.4.4Pivotal Task-2: Remote Sensing Detection and Environmental Understanding

para.p: Once observations are geolocalized, the next stage turns aerial imagery into structured scene knowledge. Aerial platforms are integral to large-scale environmental monitoring and public safety, facilitating fine-grained object detection in complex scenes, a specialization of the detection and segmentation machinery of Chapter to the aerial viewpoint. Prominent datasets such as DOTA [], DOTA-v2 [], and VisDrone [] provide comprehensive annotations for detecting various objects, including vehicles and pedestrians, under a wide range of weather, illumination, and scale conditions. These benchmarks have spurred the development of robust detection models specifically engineered to address challenges inherent to aerial perspectives, such as extreme aspect ratios, dense object clustering, and diminutive object sizes. A significant application is found in UAV-based wildlife monitoring, where systems are deployed for animal census in conservation areas [], highlighting the utility of aerial technologies in promoting ecological sustainability. Figure relates the aerial-specific difficulties of orientation, scale, and density to the detectors built for them and to the human-centric understanding that aerial video enables.

para.p: Beyond object detection, as shown in Table , with the proliferation of UAVs in smart-city and other human-centric applications, human behavior understanding [] has emerged as a critical and formidable research challenge, including person re-identification and action recognition. For instance, the UAV person re-identification (re-ID) task [] is designed to address cross-drone identity matching amid substantial viewpoint and illumination variations, thereby motivating the creation of view-invariant feature representations. In conjunction with resources like VisDrone, which contains multi-target tracking sequences from mobile UAVs, these datasets facilitate the design of intelligent video analytics systems capable of performing long-term human behavior analysis and anomaly detection in dynamic environments.

para.p: Remote sensing object detection is primarily challenged by the prevalence of arbitrarily oriented objects and substantial scale variations [], and existing research can be broadly organized along two corresponding fronts. Detection of arbitrarily oriented objects. A significant line of work focuses on developing specialized oriented object detection (OOD) methods. Early approaches often augment horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) with an angle parameter, employing techniques such as feature refinement in the detector neck [], extraction of rotated regions of interest (RoIs) [], or designing specific OOD heads []. However, these methods frequently suffer from boundary discontinuity and representation ambiguity due to their reliance on angle parameters. To mitigate these issues, subsequent research has explored more flexible object representations: some methods describe oriented objects using points [] or gliding vertexes [], while others model them with Gaussian distributions [] and design corresponding loss functions []. Handling substantial scale variations. Another research direction designs specialized backbones and feature extraction strategies to cope with large scale variations in remote sensing images (RSIs). A common strategy is multi-scale feature learning, achieved through data augmentation [], multi-scale feature integration [], enhanced feature pyramid networks (FPNs) [], or multi-scale anchor generation []. Other works focus on ensuring equivalent receptive fields for objects of different orientations []. More recently, some methods [] have employed large kernel convolutions [] to enlarge the spatial receptive field for large objects, though this can introduce background noise for smaller ones, while others harness multi-scale convolution kernels and attention to address scale variance [].

These method fronts are evaluated on a complementary set of benchmarks and metrics. The VisDrone dataset [] provides a comprehensive benchmark for drone-captured imagery, featuring urban and rural scenes with challenges like varying altitudes and occlusions; DOTA-v2 [] focuses on oriented object detection in high-resolution satellite images, emphasizing rotated bounding boxes for objects like planes and ships; and UAV-Human [] targets human behavior understanding from UAVs, with multi-modal sequences for pose and action analysis. Complementary datasets, such as UAVDT [] for traffic surveillance and iSAID [] for instance segmentation, broaden the scope of aerial detection tasks and collectively enable cross-dataset fine-tuning to mitigate domain gaps. Evaluation extends standard metrics to address orientation, scale, and density: the primary metric, mean Average Precision (mAP), is computed as the area under the precision-recall curve, typically at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5) or across 0.5:0.95 for stricter assessment [], and for oriented detection, as in DOTA-v2, rotated IoU variants ensure alignment with object headings []. Per-class and per-size Average Precision exposes imbalances, and small objects (
<
× 32 32
pixels) remain the main source of error on drone imagery []. Additional metrics include precision, recall, and F1-score to assess false positives (e.g., , background clutter) and misses (e.g., , occlusions), while Frames Per Second (FPS) is critical for real-time UAV deployment, targeting 30+ FPS []. Video-specific metrics like Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) are used for dynamic scenes in datasets like UAV-Human []. Modern real-time detectors of the YOLO family [] are increasingly adapted to the aerial setting, though aggregated aerial mAP still trails their COCO-level performance owing to small-object and orientation hardness, keeping open gaps such as multi-modal fusion and zero-shot adaptation active.

subsection.title: 9.4.5Pivotal Task-3: Autonomous Aerial Navigation and Decision Making

para.p: The final stage closes the loop, converting perception into action. Traditional UAV geolocalization addresses basic aerial navigation by matching a query (e.g., , a satellite image or textual description) to a database of historical flight paths or geographic points []. However, a critical distinction exists between such perception-oriented tasks and the overarching goal of autonomous navigation: the latter requires complex decision-making and control to bridge perception to action, drawing on the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter . In practical scenarios, the objective is often for an aerial agent to autonomously locate a destination, particularly an unexplored target, through environmental exploration and, when available, collaboration with a map. This goal introduces significant challenges in generalization to unseen environments, including novel objects, unmapped regions, and interaction with the environment. For instance, recent benchmarks adapted from general Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) have begun to address this by requiring models to output a detailed flight plan with 6-DoF control signals []. Figure follows the problem from the perception-to-action gap to foundation-model-driven VLN and multi-agent extensions.

para.p: From visual perception to language-guided planning. Recent years have witnessed significant progress in UAV navigation, with a primary focus on visual perception [] and collision avoidance []. Building on this aerial-perception foundation, Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) for UAVs remains an emerging area of research. To address it, recent efforts have leveraged Large Multi-modal Models (LMMs) to harness general knowledge for navigation planning: STMR [] builds upon AerialVLN [] with a zero-shot LLM-based framework utilizing a Semantic-TopoMetric Representation for enhanced spatial reasoning. A parallel line reframes UAV autonomy as a full agentic loop rather than one-shot instruction following. AeroVerse [] assembles a simulator, real-virtual pre-training corpora, and five downstream tasks, i.e., , scene awareness, spatial reasoning, navigational exploration, task planning, and motion decision, to train aerospace embodied world models, and proposes SkyAgentX as a unified perception-reasoning-navigation-planning agent; AirVista-II [] pursues zero-shot dynamic-scene semantic understanding via agent-based task scheduling and adaptive keyframe selection; and PRPSearcher [] casts aerial visual object search over the CityAVOS benchmark as a perception-reasoning-planning problem solved by a multimodal LLM agent. Complementary systems such as NeLV [] operationalize the language-to-flight pipeline end to end, chaining an LLM parser, route and path planners, and a control platform across short-, medium-, and long-range missions. Beyond single-agent setups, some works have begun to explore multi-drone systems; for instance, Wu et al. [] deploy two drones flying at different altitudes to facilitate planning.

Datasets and simulators. As shown in Table , several foundational frameworks and datasets have been established. One of the early works, i.e., , UAVA [], leverages the panorama images in the Matterport3D dataset [] to render the indoor environment, while harnessing the camera viewpoints as physically available flight anchors to generate trajectories. AerialVLN [] introduces a large-scale dataset with an effective baseline, and further infrastructure contributions include datasets such as CityNav [], AVDN [], and OpenFly []. Notably, UAV-Need-Help [] provides a realistic UAV dynamics simulator, i.e., , OpenUAV, alongside its evaluation protocol; OpenUAV is further used in HaL-13k [] to simulate two drones at different altitudes. Additional observation agents, such as road infrastructures and vehicles with depth sensing, have also been incorporated to enrich environmental understanding [].

Metrics. Evaluation metrics for UAV aerial navigation, especially VLN, measure how well a model navigates a drone based on visual inputs and language instructions. Common metrics include Success Rate (SR), which checks if the UAV reaches the target location within a specified distance, and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), which balances success with how efficiently the drone travels (shorter paths score higher). Path Length (PL) measures the total distance traveled, while Navigation Error (NE) calculates the distance between the final position and the goal. Together these metrics assess both accuracy (reaching the target) and efficiency (taking an optimal route), providing a clear way to compare model performance across datasets like UAVA, AerialVLN, and CityNav.

Beyond the methods and benchmarks above, the aerial domain rests on a real-world layer of simulators, platforms, and infrastructure that turns research prototypes into deployable systems; we group it into three tiers.

Simulation environments and benchmarks. Because flight data is costly and safety-critical to collect, high-fidelity simulation underpins much of the field. The OpenUAV simulator released with UAV-Need-Help [] supplies realistic UAV dynamics and a continuous 6-DoF evaluation protocol, and is reused to simulate multi-altitude drone teams in HaL-13k []; OpenFly [] targets large-scale real-to-sim transfer across diverse scenes; and AerialVLN [] pairs a city-scale synthetic environment with a navigation baseline. Photorealistic indoor rendering for UAV tasks is provided through Matterport3D [] in UAVA [], while V2X-style multi-agent simulation combines CARLA and Microsoft AirSim 44 footnote 44 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 44 footnote 44 https://microsoft.github.io/AirSim/ in AirV2X [].

Commercial platforms and vendors. On the hardware side, consumer and enterprise drones from DJI 45 footnote 45 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 45 footnote 45 https://www.dji.com/ (whose Matrice series collects datasets such as UAV-Human) and autonomy-focused vendors such as Skydio 46 footnote 46 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 46 footnote 46 https://www.skydio.com/ dominate the UAV tier. In the stratospheric tier, solar-powered HAPS such as Airbus Zephyr [] and AeroVironment/HAPSMobile’s HAWK30 [] provide persistent regional coverage, complemented by small-satellite constellations built on CubeSat platforms [] and broader HAPS programs [].

Connectivity and positioning infrastructure. Aerial autonomy ultimately depends on shared positioning and communication backbones: the GNSS constellations introduced above (GPS [], GLONASS [], Galileo, and BeiDou []) supply global timing and localization, while space-based broadband relays such as Starlink [] and orbital observation systems [] increasingly serve as the connectivity layer for coordinated, real-time aerial operations.

Aerial autonomy is limited less by any single model than by the gaps between platforms, scales, and operating conditions. Four threads follow the pipeline in order: fusing heterogeneous platforms into a coherent situational model, perceiving small objects and complex activities reliably, navigating unseen and GPS-denied environments, and meeting the ethical and operational constraints under which any of this can be deployed.

A primary obstacle lies in integrating aerial agents with heterogeneous platforms for robust environmental perception. Coordinating a UAV with ground-based sensors or satellite systems to construct a cohesive situational-awareness model remains complex, particularly in dynamic or cluttered settings where the platforms differ in resolution, latency, and viewpoint (Table ). Reconciling these asynchronous, multi-resolution streams into a single consistent representation, without one modality’s noise corrupting the fused estimate, is the standing difficulty, and it motivates the V2X-style cooperative-perception efforts that incorporate road infrastructure and ground vehicles as additional observers.

Aerial perception is defined by extremes of scale and density. The recognition of small objects, such as identifying debris in disaster zones or distinguishing wildlife in ecological surveys, demands high-resolution imaging and detectors robust to dense clustering, which often strain onboard computational resources. Understanding complex activities, such as discerning human behavior during search-and-rescue missions, compounds the problem by requiring nuanced spatio-temporal and contextual analysis that current systems struggle to deliver consistently. Closing this gap calls for detectors and activity models that remain accurate at extreme scale variation while fitting a UAV’s tight compute and power budget.

paragraph.title: Navigation in Unseen and GPS-denied Environments.

para.p: Autonomous operation in unseen or GPS-denied environments, such as dense urban canyons or subterranean spaces, further complicates the action stage, as agents must rely on real-time mapping and obstacle avoidance without pre-existing data. The core requirement is generalization: a navigation policy must extend to novel objects, unmapped regions, and genuinely interactive scenarios, rather than replaying matched trajectories. This is precisely the gap that foundation-model-driven VLN and multi-altitude cooperative planning aim to narrow, but validating such behavior to a safety standard in the open world remains open.

Beyond perception and navigation, several ethical and operational challenges persist. Data-privacy concerns arise when aerial agents capture high-fidelity multimedia data, potentially compromising individual rights without stringent safeguards, motivating privacy-preserving approaches such as federated learning. Airspace integration poses another hurdle, as regulatory frameworks struggle to accommodate the proliferation of aerial agents alongside traditional aviation, necessitating harmonized protocols to ensure safety. Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck, since prolonged missions demand lightweight yet powerful power sources and motivate renewable solutions such as solar-powered propulsion. Finally, operational robustness is challenged by environmental uncertainties, such as extreme weather or electromagnetic interference, that can disrupt system reliability. Advances in artificial intelligence and sensor fusion that address these constraints, rather than perception accuracy alone, are what will let aerial agents move from bounded demonstrations toward dependable, large-scale deployment.

Warehouse and industrial logistics is one of the most mature real-world testbeds for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part : it demands perception-to-action pipelines that interpret complex, dynamic environments such as dense shelving systems populated with diverse stock keeping units (SKUs), pallets, forklifts, and human workers. These systems construct and maintain spatial memory representations (semantic maps, object and pose states) to support downstream planning and manipulation for tasks including inventory counting, order picking, pallet handling, and coordinated fleet operations. Perception and reasoning themselves are treated in Chapter and Chapter ; logistics adds throughput targets, engineered but crowded layouts, and people sharing the floor with fleets of robots. Performance is judged in terms of throughput, order accuracy, safety, and operational cost, especially under high SKU diversity, visual clutter, elongated aisles, and human-robot collaboration. Dense shelving and manipulation in clutter remain the hardest cases, as the Amazon Picking Challenge made plain [], and they demand that perception, pose estimation, mapping, and multi-agent planning be integrated rather than tuned in isolation.

figure.toccaption: 9.19Spatial intelligence for warehouse and industrial logistics: RGB-D, LiDAR, and RFID observations support five complementary capabilities for picking and pallet transport, and execution outcomes update maps and plans. Scene images and diagrams are illustrative.

caption.text: Spatial intelligence for warehouse and industrial logistics: RGB-D, LiDAR, and RFID observations support five complementary capabilities for picking and pallet transport, and execution outcomes update maps and plans. Scene images and diagrams are illustrative.

para.p: The complete warehouse automation pipeline, sketched in Figure , integrates five complementary capabilities into a closed loop. Perception converts raw multi-sensor streams into semantic object information (what is present, where, and in what pose); localization and mapping grounds that information in a metric spatial map and keeps it consistent over time; reasoning and planning consume these representations to allocate tasks and generate optimized fleet schedules; manipulation and control physically execute the resulting picking and transport actions; and a human-robot collaboration and safety layer adapts behavior dynamically in mixed human-robot environments. Integration is achieved via middleware such as ROS 2 and industrial protocols like Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC-UA), while digital twin platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse 47 footnote 47 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 47 footnote 47 https://www.nvidia.com/en-gb/omniverse/ support simulation and validation before deployment. The five capabilities are the pivotal tasks below, taken in pipeline order.

Perception constitutes the sensory foundation of the pipeline: it transforms raw sensor data into actionable knowledge, reusing the detection, segmentation, and pose-estimation machinery of Chapter but specializing it to the warehouse Operational Design Domain. Core capabilities include detecting and classifying objects (packages, pallets, tools), estimating their 3D poses, and tracking their motion and state over time. Unlike outdoor environments, warehouses impose distinct perceptual challenges: dense clutter, heavy occlusion, visually similar items, reflective packaging, narrow aisles, and continually changing layouts, which together make robust perception a central and ongoing research focus []. para.p: Detection and recognition form the base layer. Convolutional and transformer-based architectures, i.e., , YOLO [], RetinaNet [], and the transformer-based DETR with deformable attention [], have steadily improved accuracy and efficiency under clutter, and are scored on COCO [], whose mean Average Precision (mAP) broken down by object size is particularly informative for the small-SKU and barcode-label cases that dominate warehouse failure modes. Pose estimation lifts these 2D detections into the metric space that manipulation requires: PoseCNN [], DenseFusion [], and CosyPose [] fuse visual and geometric cues to infer six-degree-of-freedom (6D) orientation and position even under occlusion, and are evaluated on YCB-Video [] for textured household and industrial objects and on T-LESS [] for textureless, industry-relevant parts, with Average Distance (ADD) the standard accuracy measure and MOTA/MOTP reporting tracking quality in dynamic scenes. The Amazon Picking Challenge [] couples perception with manipulation in real warehouse scenarios, stressing generalization across novel object sets and thereby anticipating the manipulation task of § below. Representative benchmarks across the section are consolidated in Table . In industrial practice, perception pipelines are increasingly standardized and modularized; the deployed software stacks that realize them are surveyed in the Established Tools and Systems subsection.

If perception answers what is around the robot, localization and mapping answer where the robot is and what the persistent structure of the warehouse is, forming the spatial backbone on which fleet coordination rests and drawing on the same scene-construction techniques as Chapter . Automated guided vehicles (AGVs) and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) require centimeter-level accuracy to navigate narrow aisles, dock precisely at shelves, and operate safely alongside workers. The problem is conceptually the SLAM problem of autonomous driving, yet it faces warehouse-specific constraints: highly repetitive structures (rows of identical shelves), dynamic obstacles (workers, pallets, forklifts), and low-light or GPS-denied indoor conditions.
