para.p: A family of SLAM algorithms has been tailored to these conditions. ORB-SLAM3 [] extends visual SLAM with inertial and multi-camera support for accurate visual-inertial localization; LIO-SAM [] provides real-time LiDAR–IMU fusion through factor-graph optimization that stays robust under fast motion and partial occlusion; and RTAB-Map [] supports online RGB-D mapping and loop-closure detection with memory management suited to long-term operation, all expressible within the unified factor-graph framework of GTSAM []. Multi-modal fusion is the common thread that holds accuracy together when any single modality degrades, and is also the dominant emerging research direction, alongside learning-based estimation (neural depth prediction, differentiable bundle adjustment, and learned place-recognition embeddings) and the migration of SLAM computation to the edge for fleet-scale latency. These capabilities are evaluated on KITTI [] for outdoor visual and LiDAR odometry and loop closure, on the indoor visual-inertial EuRoC MAV dataset [] whose challenging motion and illumination mirror warehouse conditions, and on the high-fidelity Replica reconstructions [] for dense mapping and semantic labeling, with Absolute and Relative Pose Error (APE/RPE) and loop-closure precision/recall the standard metrics and, for warehouse use, semantic-zone IoU and map completeness (Table ).

caption.text: Two families for warehouse reasoning and planning over shared task, fleet, and map inputs: combinatorial optimization (assignment and routing) and learning-based coordination (per-agent policies), optionally combined in hierarchical or hybrid designs. Allocations, paths, and schedules are illustrative.

para.p:
Reasoning and planning form the decision-making core of warehouse automation, transforming the perceptual and localization outputs into task assignments and motion plans, and instantiating the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter . This layer determines which robot executes which task, how tasks are sequenced, and how routes and schedules are optimized for safe, efficient, coordinated operation. In contrast to autonomous driving, where planning typically focuses on individual vehicles, warehouse reasoning must address multi-agent coordination across fleets of dozens or hundreds of robots in constrained indoor space [], maximizing throughput and minimizing latency while maintaining safety under dynamic obstacles, human interactions, and stochastic task arrivals. Formally, the perceived states
G t
, a task list
T
, the fleet state
F t
(positions, capabilities, battery levels), and the warehouse map
M t
are mapped to a task-allocation matrix
A
, optimized motion paths
R
, and temporal schedules
π
that jointly specify when and how tasks execute. Figure contrasts the two solution families.

The first family is combinatorial optimization. Traditional methods (the Hungarian algorithm, branch-and-bound, and mixed-integer linear programming) remain widely used for task allocation and scheduling in small- to medium-scale deployments, while Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulations [] and their multi-depot and time-window variants are central to modeling fleet movement. The second family is learning-based coordination: reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent RL (MARL) handle dynamic environments and real-time uncertainty [], with toolkits such as Google OR-Tools [] and PyMARL enabling rapid experimentation across both families. Emerging research couples the two: hierarchical and hybrid frameworks combine symbolic reasoning with learned components, graph neural networks and differentiable optimization accelerate multi-agent coordination and transfer policies across layouts, and digital-twin integration enables simulation-informed, predictive re-planning, increasingly under multi-objective criteria that balance throughput, energy, and human safety. Planning systems are benchmarked on Solomon’s VRP suite [] for static routing and scheduling and on the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) [] for continuous-space motion planning, complemented by synthetic multi-robot testbeds; common metrics are throughput (items/hour), task-completion latency, total travel distance or time, collision rate, and re-planning latency (Table ).

Manipulation constitutes the physical execution layer, enabling robots to interact directly with objects, containers, and infrastructure such as bins, shelves, and conveyors. In industrial logistics this typically involves robotic arms performing grasping, placing, sorting, or palletizing, as well as AGVs docking to pallets or workstations. Manipulation bridges high-level symbolic or geometric plans with continuous motor control, and therefore demands both precision and robustness to the inherent variability in packaging, geometry, and material properties []; the grasping and control techniques here connect directly to the robotic-manipulation treatment of § and the planning paradigms of Chapter . Formally, estimated object poses
p i
and task descriptions (grasp targets, placement goals, trajectory constraints) are mapped to low-level motor commands
u t
that ensure stable grasping, precise placement, and compliant, collision-free motion. Figure contrasts modular grasp-and-plan systems with learned visuomotor control.

figure.toccaption: 9.23Warehouse manipulation through (a) a modular route, where grasp candidates scored by analytic metrics and learned quality (Dex-Net) feed sampling-based planning (RRT*) and trajectory tracking, and (b) learned visuomotor control from camera observations. Action spaces vary across systems, and the routes can be combined.

caption.text: Warehouse manipulation through (a) a modular route, where grasp candidates scored by analytic metrics and learned quality (Dex-Net) feed sampling-based planning (RRT*) and trajectory tracking, and (b) learned visuomotor control from camera observations. Action spaces vary across systems, and the routes can be combined.

para.p: Grasp synthesis anchors the methodology: Dex-Net combines synthetic grasp data and analytic robustness metrics to train a grasp-quality predictor for candidate selection [], while learned visual control can predict grasp success from camera images and candidate task-space motions, then select actions for adaptive manipulation []. Motion planning then realizes the chosen grasp: sampling-based algorithms such as RRT* [] remain fundamental for generating collision-free trajectories in high-dimensional configuration spaces, exposed through frameworks like MoveIt []. These capabilities are benchmarked on the Amazon Picking Challenge [], which established a standardized testbed for picking under clutter and uncertainty, and on the YCB Object and Model Set [], a diverse collection of everyday items with physical models for grasping and manipulation; grasp success rate, cycle time per pick, placement accuracy, and task-completion rate are the headline metrics (Table ). Hybrid control frameworks that combine analytical models with data-driven adaptation are emerging as the practical route to generalizing across variable geometries and grasp contexts, complemented by tactile sensing and force control for slip detection and contact regulation.

Even in highly automated warehouses, human workers remain indispensable for complex, dexterous, or exception-handling tasks that require contextual understanding and flexible decision making, so the final stage of the pipeline is safe and efficient human-robot collaboration (HRC). HRC systems must balance productivity with stringent safety guarantees, enabling mixed teams (robots handling repetitive or heavy-load work, humans managing fine-grained, judgment-based activities) to share workspaces without physical or operational interference []. The task maps multimodal human-detection and intent signals (pose, gesture, gaze, and trajectory data from vision, LiDAR, wearables, or motion capture) to adaptive robot behaviors such as dynamic speed modulation, path re-routing, stop-and-wait actions, or task reallocation in response to predicted human movement. Figure sketches this predict-then-adapt loop.

figure.toccaption: 9.24The human–robot collaboration loop: multimodal human sensing and intent recognition inform proximity-aware planning, which selects slowing, rerouting, or stopping. Clearance regions and routes are illustrative, not certified safety zones.

caption.text: The human–robot collaboration loop: multimodal human sensing and intent recognition inform proximity-aware planning, which selects slowing, rerouting, or stopping. Clearance regions and routes are illustrative, not certified safety zones.

para.p: Intent recognition lets robots anticipate human motion: sequence models based on hidden Markov models or recurrent networks predict trajectories and proactively adjust behavior [], while proxemics-aware planning maintains socially acceptable distances and re-routes trajectories under human proximity [], with multimodal sensing (vision-based detection fused with wearable or RFID localization) improving reliability. These principles are embodied in force- and speed-limited collaborative robots and safety-rated AMRs (see Established Tools and Systems), governed by international standards such as ISO 10218 and ISO/TS 15066. Evaluation combines quantitative safety metrics with qualitative interaction assessment: human-motion corpora such as Human3.6M [] supply sequences for intent prediction, and key indicators include intervention frequency (safety-triggered stops per hour), near-miss rate, human-detection accuracy, and compliance with ISO-defined safety zones.

table.toccaption: 9.9Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in warehouse and industrial logistics, spanning the five pivotal tasks.

caption.text: Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in warehouse and industrial logistics, spanning the five pivotal tasks.

para.p: The pivotal tasks above are realized in production through a layered ecosystem of simulators, middleware, optimization services, and robot hardware that together constitute the real-world delta over the methods of Part .

Simulation and middleware form the integration substrate. Digital-twin and physics platforms such as NVIDIA Omniverse Isaac Sim [] and Gazebo provide realistic environments for developing and validating perception, localization, and planning pipelines before deployment, while perception SDKs such as NVIDIA Isaac, the Intel RealSense SDK, and Zebra RFID/barcode platforms supply end-to-end sensing support in real facilities. Interoperability across heterogeneous hardware is provided by ROS [], ROS 2, and ROS-Industrial, with commercial localization stacks such as SLAMcore 48 footnote 48 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 48 footnote 48 https://www.slamcore.com/ and BlueBotics ANT 49 footnote 49 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 49 footnote 49 https://bluebotics.com/ delivering optimized multi-sensor fusion, map management, and fleet coordination for AGVs and AMRs.

Warehouse management and fleet orchestration sit at the enterprise layer. Large-scale optimization services such as SAP Extended Warehouse Management 50 footnote 50 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 50 footnote 50 https://www.sap.com/products/scm/extended-warehouse-management.html, Blue Yonder WMS 51 footnote 51 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 51 footnote 51 https://blueyonder.com/, and Manhattan Associates 52 footnote 52 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 52 footnote 52 https://www.manh.com/ integrate task allocation and scheduling with enterprise resource planning, while open toolkits such as Google OR-Tools [] and PyMARL support the underlying combinatorial and learning-based planners.

Robot hardware and manipulation close the loop physically. High-throughput pick-and-place arms from ABB 53 footnote 53 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 53 footnote 53 https://new.abb.com/products/robotics, FANUC 54 footnote 54 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 54 footnote 54 https://www.fanuc.com/, and KUKA 55 footnote 55 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 55 footnote 55 https://www.kuka.com/ are widely deployed and integrated through ROS-based middleware, mobile manipulators such as those from Fetch Robotics 56 footnote 56 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 56 footnote 56 https://fetchrobotics.com/ unify navigation and grasping, and motion-planning frameworks such as MoveIt [] and NVIDIA cuMotion provide inverse kinematics and trajectory optimization. For shared workspaces, collaborative robots from Universal Robots 57 footnote 57 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 57 footnote 57 https://www.universal-robots.com/ and AMRs from Locus Robotics 58 footnote 58 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 58 footnote 58 https://locusrobotics.com/ provide the safety-rated platforms on which the HRC layer is built.

Deployed warehouse systems work because they fix the SKU sets, layouts, and operating conditions they handle, and each stage of the pipeline has its own obstacle to relaxing those limits: small-object and cluttered perception, perceptual aliasing in repetitive aisles, multi-agent scalability under uncertainty, manipulation of variable objects, and the safety–throughput trade-off in human–robot collaboration.

Barcode labels and compact SKU packages often occupy only a few pixels in high-resolution images, leading to frequent misdetections, while occlusion and clutter compound the difficulty as items overlap within bins and shelves. A further persistent issue is domain shift: models trained on synthetic or generic data degrade under real-world variation in lighting, reflective surfaces, and packaging. Research responses include domain adaptation and self-supervised learning for generalization [], active perception that deliberately adjusts viewpoints or sensing to resolve occlusion [], and continual learning that lets perception adapt over time without exhaustive retraining, increasingly combined with multi-sensor fusion and neuro-symbolic representations for higher-level causal and semantic reasoning.

Localization and mapping are degraded by dynamic obstacles (humans, forklifts) that generate transient or misleading landmarks corrupting loop-closure hypotheses [], and above all by perceptual aliasing: repetitive shelving and low-texture surfaces produce ambiguous place recognition and false data associations in feature-based SLAM []. High-speed AGV and AMR operation further demands low-latency, sub-centimeter pose updates that sensor delays, occlusion, and monocular scale drift can readily violate. Robust multi-modal fusion, learning-based estimation, and tighter integration of SLAM with semantic perception and digital twins are the leading mitigations.

paragraph.title: Scalability and Uncertainty in Multi-agent Planning.

para.p: The combinatorial complexity of multi-robot coordination grows exponentially with the number of agents and tasks, rendering exact optimization intractable for large fleets, while real-world uncertainty (new order arrivals, blocked aisles, unpredictable human movement) necessitates adaptive re-planning and decentralized decision making under partial observability []. Hierarchical and hybrid planners, graph-neural and differentiable coordination, and simulation-informed multi-objective optimization are the active directions toward scalable, resilient fleet behavior.

paragraph.title: Manipulation of Variable and Deformable Objects.

para.p: Many SKUs exhibit deformable, reflective, or transparent surfaces that interfere with perception and grasp stability [], and deformable handling remains especially difficult because grasp dynamics and contact points resist rigid-body modeling []. Tactile sensing and force control improve slip detection and grasp robustness but face cost and calibration barriers in industrial deployment, motivating hybrid control that combines analytical models with data-driven adaptation for generalization across geometries and grasp contexts.

Robust human detection under occlusion, variable lighting, and cluttered aisles continues to hinder reliable intent estimation [], and the trade-off between throughput and safety remains unresolved: conservative margins reduce efficiency while aggressive planning risks unsafe interaction []. Emerging work emphasizes predictive and explainable safety models that justify decisions in human-interpretable terms, and adaptive safety frameworks that fuse learned intent models with certified control policies for dynamic risk assessment and shared autonomy on the warehouse floor.

Virtual realities are the media in which spatial intelligence becomes constitutive rather than optional: an extended-reality (XR) device cannot draw a single pixel until it knows where it is, what surrounds it, and where the user is looking and reaching. This makes XR the most demanding real-time deployment target for the perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities of the previous part, specialized to run egocentrically, on-device, and within a hard latency budget.

Beneath everything in XR sits the platform itself, the runtime that localizes the device, maps and registers the surrounding world, senses the user’s body, and composites the result in real time; layered on top is the application that has driven the medium hardest, entertainment, spanning live AR and VR experiences and virtual production as well as the offline, high-fidelity reconstruction and performance capture that supply them with authored content.

Augmented, virtual, and mixed reality (collectively, extended reality or XR) form a continuum of media in which a head-worn display couples the user’s egocentric viewpoint to a computational world that is registered to, or substituted for, the physical surroundings. What distinguishes XR from screen-based media is that spatial intelligence is not an optional feature but a constitutive requirement: before any pixel can be drawn, the system must know where the headset is, what geometry surrounds it, and where the user is looking and reaching. XR is therefore the most demanding real-time deployment target for the spatial capabilities surveyed in Part . The perception machinery (detection, depth, pose, reconstruction) of Chapter , the spatial reasoning and planning of Chapter , and the neural reconstruction and rendering of Chapter all reappear here, but specialized to run egocentrically, on-device, and within a hard latency budget.

This section treats the XR medium itself as a spatial-computing platform: the runtime engine that localizes the device, maps and registers the world, senses the user’s body, and presents a composited result. The neighboring section on entertainment (§) builds on top of this engine, treating entertainment as an application domain: its real-time AR/VR experiences and virtual production, together with the offline, high-fidelity reconstruction and performance capture that supply them with authored content; here we focus on the platform that makes such experiences run at interactive rates. Concretely, a headset must continuously answer three coupled questions, i.e., , where am I (6-DoF self-localization), what is around me (geometry and semantics), and how do I fuse virtual content into that reality so that it appears physically present, while simultaneously sensing the user and refreshing the display. Early systems answered the localization question with outside-in tracking, using external base stations or cameras (SteamVR Lighthouse, the original Oculus constellation), but the dominant modern paradigm is inside-out tracking, in which visual–inertial SLAM runs entirely on the device, as in Meta Quest, Apple Vision Pro, and Microsoft HoloLens. The three pivotal tasks below correspond to the stages of this loop.

figure.toccaption: 10.1Spatial intelligence for XR as a closed real-time loop: world-facing sensing, tracking and mapping, and registration (T1), user-facing input (T2), and rendering and display (T3). The latency values are illustrative end-to-end targets, not per-stage budgets.

caption.text: Spatial intelligence for XR as a closed real-time loop: world-facing sensing, tracking and mapping, and registration (T1), user-facing input (T2), and rendering and display (T3). The latency values are illustrative end-to-end targets, not per-stage budgets.

para.p:
As sketched in Figure , an XR device closes a tight real-time loop. Egocentric sensors first sense the device and the user (outward cameras and an inertial measurement unit for head pose; inward-facing cameras for eyes and outward- or downward-facing cameras for hands and body). The system then tracks and maps the environment, recovering a 6-DoF pose and a persistent geometric model, and registers virtual content into that model with correct anchoring, occlusion, and lighting. Finally, it renders and displays the composite back through the headset optics, after which the user moves and the loop repeats. The pipeline shares an end-to-end motion-to-photon budget; roughly
20
ms at a display refresh of
90
Hz or higher are the commonly cited targets, though the right values depend on device and application, and exceeding them degrades presence and comfort. The three pivotal tasks map onto this loop directly: Task-1 is the world-facing engine (track, map, register), Task-2 is the user-facing input (egocentric sensing and interaction), and Task-3 is the user-facing output (display and rendering).

subsection.title: 10.1.3Pivotal Task-1: Spatial Tracking, Mapping, and Registration

para.p: The first task is the medium’s spatial backbone: it answers where the device is, what surrounds it, and how virtual content is pinned to the world so convincingly that the illusion holds. It proceeds in three steps: localize the device, model the environment, and register synthetic content into that model. Figure sketches this progression from inside-out tracking to a persistent scene map and finally to anchored, occluded, and relit virtual content.

figure.toccaption: 10.2The XR world-facing engine: (a) inside-out visual–inertial tracking of 6-DoF pose, (b) mapping of geometry, semantic labels, and persistent anchors, and (c) registration of virtual content with depth-tested occlusion and matched lighting. The room and shading are illustrative, not measured reconstructions.

caption.text: The XR world-facing engine: (a) inside-out visual–inertial tracking of 6-DoF pose, (b) mapping of geometry, semantic labels, and persistent anchors, and (c) registration of virtual content with depth-tested occlusion and matched lighting. The room and shading are illustrative, not measured reconstructions.

para.p: Inside-out 6-DoF tracking. The foundational layer estimates the headset’s six-degree-of-freedom pose at high rate by fusing visual features with inertial measurements. Feature-based visual SLAM with loop closure and relocalization remains the academic standard, exemplified by the ORB-SLAM lineage and its visual-inertial extension ORB-SLAM3 [], while tightly-coupled visual–inertial odometry such as VINS-Mono [] underpins many mobile and headset stacks; direct (photometric) methods such as DSO [] and the earlier LSD-SLAM [] offer an alternative that does not depend on sparse keypoints. More recent learned dense systems, including DROID-SLAM [] and transformer-based geometric matchers [], trade computation for robustness in low-texture and fast-motion regimes. These methods are evaluated chiefly on EuRoC [] and TUM-VI [], with absolute trajectory error (ATE) as the headline metric, but the binding constraints in XR are drift accumulation, recovery from tracking loss (the kidnapped-device problem), and the power and thermal envelope of on-device inference.

Spatial mapping and scene understanding. The tracked stream is consolidated into a usable model of the environment: dense depth and mesh, planar surfaces (floor, wall, table), and semantic labels. Real-time volumetric fusion in the KinectFusion tradition [] provides the geometric substrate, on top of which plane and mesh extraction expose the surfaces that gameplay and user interfaces attach to. (The offline, high-fidelity reconstruction of such scenes as navigable content is treated in § and Chapter ; here the map is a means to localization and registration, not an end in itself.) Semantic and instance understanding is benchmarked on indoor datasets such as ScanNet [] and Matterport3D [], with mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) for segmentation, and increasingly on mobile-captured data with laser ground truth such as ARKitScenes [] and high-quality reconstructions such as Replica [] for depth and geometry evaluation.

Persistent and shared anchors. For content to survive across sessions and to be experienced jointly by co-located users, the map must be persistent and shareable. Cloud-hosted and peer-to-peer world maps let a device relocalize against a previously built model, and at city scale a Visual Positioning System anchors content to real landmarks in well-mapped areas. The open problems are relocalization under appearance change (lighting, season, rearranged furniture), the memory footprint of on-device maps, and the privacy implications of uploading scans of private spaces, a thread we return to in the challenges.

Registration and realistic compositing. Finally, virtual content must be registered both geometrically and photometrically so that it appears to occupy the scene. Geometric registration pins objects to anchors and planes in the SLAM frame; depth-based occlusion lets real geometry correctly hide virtual pixels, as in the per-pixel depth produced for mobile interaction by DepthLab and the ARCore Depth API []; and lighting estimation predicts the dominant light direction and an ambient environment map from a single image so that virtual objects are shaded and shadowed consistently []. Small errors here are perceptually unforgiving: a few centimeters of depth error at an object boundary, or a mismatched shadow, immediately reveals the composite as synthetic, which is why robust occlusion and real-time inverse lighting remain active research problems.

subsection.title: 10.1.4Pivotal Task-2: Egocentric Human Sensing and Spatial Interaction

para.p: The second task closes the loop from the user’s body back into the system: it senses the hands, eyes, and posture from inside-out cameras and turns those signals into spatial intent. Low-level egocentric estimates of hands, gaze, and body are fused into selection, manipulation, and locomotion. As Figure indicates, the same headset sensors that localize the device are repurposed to track the user, and the resulting estimates drive a gaze-and-gesture interaction model.

figure.toccaption: 10.3Egocentric human sensing for XR interaction: (a) articulated hand tracking, (b) gaze from inward-facing eye cameras, (c) full-body pose inferred from three tracked points, and (d) gaze-plus-pinch selection, in which gaze supplies the target and a pinch confirms it.

caption.text: Egocentric human sensing for XR interaction: (a) articulated hand tracking, (b) gaze from inward-facing eye cameras, (c) full-body pose inferred from three tracked points, and (d) gaze-plus-pinch selection, in which gaze supplies the target and a pinch confirms it.

para.p:
Hand tracking. Articulated 3D hand pose (commonly
21
joints, often a full mesh) is regressed from headset cameras under heavy self-occlusion and truncation. The standard hand model is MANO [], and on-device pipelines such as MediaPipe Hands [] combine a palm detector with a landmark regressor to run in real time. Methods are benchmarked on FreiHAND [] and the two-hand InterHand2.6M [], with 3D mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) in millimeters as the headline metric; robust two-hand interaction and egocentric truncation remain the hard cases.

Eye and gaze tracking. Estimating 3D gaze from infrared eye images serves three roles: calibration, gaze as a pointing modality, and as the driver for foveated rendering (Task-3). Appearance-based estimation in the iTracker and GazeCapture tradition [] established that gaze can be regressed from commodity cameras, and headset-specific datasets such as OpenEDS [] provide near-eye infrared imagery with dense eye-region segmentation, with the later OpenEDS2020 track adding gaze prediction (angular error in degrees). The decisive interaction consequence is that gaze targets quickly but lacks a natural trigger, a long-standing difficulty known as the Midas-touch problem, which motivates the gaze-plus-pinch pattern discussed below.

Full-body pose from sparse signals. Driving a full-body avatar from a headset and two controllers is an underconstrained inverse problem, since the lower body is unobserved and must be synthesized. Recent methods infer plausible full-body motion from these three tracked points, including the transformer-based AvatarPoser [] and the diffusion-based AGRoL [], while a parallel line recovers pose from sparse body-worn inertial sensors, as in DIP [], TransPose [], and the physics-aware PIP []. These models are trained on large motion corpora such as AMASS [] and evaluated with MPJPE and temporal jitter. This sparse, live setting is distinct both from the wearable-IMU body sensing of § (which instruments the body more densely) and from the studio performance capture that drives authored avatars in §; the XR-specific challenge is plausibility from radically incomplete observation.

Multimodal interaction and locomotion. The recovered signals are fused into spatial actions. The foundational idea of combining a deictic gesture with a complementary modality dates to Bolt’s “Put-That-There” [], and the modern instantiation decouples targeting from confirmation: the eyes select while a hand pinch or a voice command commits, sidestepping the Midas-touch problem. Locomotion through a virtual space larger than the physical room is handled by redirected walking, which applies imperceptible rotational and translational gains to steer the user within a confined area [], with teleportation as the common non-natural fallback. Spatial user interfaces, in turn, must choose a reference frame (world-locked, body-locked, or head-locked) and increasingly anchor panels to scene semantics so that content lands on appropriate surfaces. Learning these interaction behaviors at scale is increasingly grounded in large egocentric corpora such as Ego4D [], which supply the first-person video of hands, objects, and activities that egocentric-understanding models are trained and benchmarked on.

subsection.title: 10.1.5Pivotal Task-3: Spatial Display and Real-Time Rendering

para.p: The third task presents the composited world back to the user within the perceptual budget that the previous two stages must respect. Three questions decide it: where to spend rendering effort, how to hide system latency, and how to display the result comfortably. Figure previews this pipeline, from gaze-contingent shading through latency compensation to the optics that place the image before the eye.

figure.toccaption: 10.4The XR display and rendering pipeline: (a) gaze-contingent foveated rendering, (b) late reprojection of a rendered frame to the latest pose, and (c) alternative video-passthrough and optical see-through display paths. The motion-to-photon target is illustrative and applies end to end.

caption.text: The XR display and rendering pipeline: (a) gaze-contingent foveated rendering, (b) late reprojection of a rendered frame to the latest pose, and (c) alternative video-passthrough and optical see-through display paths. The motion-to-photon target is illustrative and applies end to end.

para.p: Foveated rendering. Because acuity falls off sharply outside the fovea, rendering effort can be concentrated at the gaze point. Foveated 3D graphics established multi-resolution shading driven by eye tracking [], and subsequent work added temporal stability and contrast preservation to make the quality reduction imperceptible []. Eye-tracked foveated rendering now ships on consumer headsets, materially reducing shading cost on thermally constrained hardware.

Latency compensation. Even an efficient renderer cannot meet the motion-to-photon budget on every frame, so the last stage warps the rendered image to the most recent head pose. Asynchronous time warp applies a rotational reprojection at display refresh, asynchronous space warp adds depth-aware frame extrapolation, and head-mounted optical-see-through systems use per-pixel late-stage reprojection []. These techniques keep the world stable under fast head motion and are essential to comfort.

Passthrough versus optical see-through. Two display regimes trade off differently. Video passthrough mixed reality (as on Meta Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro) renders the real world from cameras, granting full control over occlusion and relighting at the cost of camera-to-display latency, parallax, and limited dynamic range; optical see-through (as on HoloLens 2 and Magic Leap 2) presents the real world with zero latency at its true focal depth (though the virtual overlay still incurs render latency and a fixed focal plane) but cannot occlude real light or match real-world brightness. The choice propagates back into the registration problem of Task-1.

Depth-correct rendering and visual comfort. Conventional stereo displays fix the focal plane while vergence varies with content, producing the vergence-accommodation conflict and the eye strain that limits session length. Varifocal, light-field, and holographic near-eye displays aim to restore correct focus cues [], but remain largely at the prototype stage.

Neural rendering for telepresence. Finally, photoreal social presence requires driving a faithful avatar of a remote user from headset-mounted cameras that see only oblique crops of the face. The codec-avatar line, beginning with deep appearance models [], learns a person-specific decoder that is driven on-device, a direct specialization of the neural rendering of Chapter to the constrained, real-time XR setting.

table.toccaption: 10.1Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in XR, spanning the three pivotal tasks.

caption.text: Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in XR, spanning the three pivotal tasks.

para.p: A mature ecosystem implements these tasks across mobile AR, standalone headsets, and the web, and it is organized into developer frameworks, cross-platform standards, hardware, and the companies that drive them.

SDKs and standards. At the device level, Apple’s ARKit 1 footnote 1 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 https://developer.apple.com/augmented-reality/ and Google’s ARCore 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://developers.google.com/ar expose plane detection, anchors, depth, light estimation, and people occlusion, with ARCore’s Geospatial API localizing against world imagery for outdoor anchoring; Vuforia 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://developer.vuforia.com specializes in robust image and object targets for industrial AR. Cross-engine abstraction layers such as Unity AR Foundation 4 footnote 4 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 4 footnote 4 https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.xr.arfoundation@6.0/ and the Meta Presence Platform and Spatial SDK 5 footnote 5 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 5 footnote 5 https://developers.meta.com/horizon/develop/spatial-sdk present the common subset (planes, anchors, meshes, occlusion, hand and body tracking) over multiple devices, while 8th Wall and WebXR 6 footnote 6 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 6 footnote 6 https://immersiveweb.dev bring markerless AR into the browser. These abstractions matter because XR content is expensive to author and must migrate across devices and sessions; this is the role of cross-platform standards, principally OpenXR 7 footnote 7 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 7 footnote 7 https://www.khronos.org/openxr/ as a unifying runtime API and glTF together with OpenUSD and USDZ 8 footnote 8 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 8 footnote 8 https://openusd.org as asset and scene-description formats. Without a shared runtime and shared asset formats, the ecosystem fragments into incompatible walled gardens.

Hardware. Current headsets divide along the passthrough versus optical-see-through axis. Apple Vision Pro 9 footnote 9 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 9 footnote 9 https://www.apple.com/apple-vision-pro/ (2024) and Meta Quest 3 and 3S 10 footnote 10 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 10 footnote 10 https://www.meta.com/quest/ use high-resolution video passthrough, with the Quest line the consumer volume leader; Microsoft HoloLens 2 11 footnote 11 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 11 footnote 11 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/hololens/ (optical see-through, with production ended in 2024) and Magic Leap 2 12 footnote 12 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 12 footnote 12 https://www.magicleap.com target enterprise, and Varjo 13 footnote 13 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 13 footnote 13 https://varjo.com and Pico 14 footnote 14 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 14 footnote 14 https://www.picoxr.com serve high-fidelity simulation and the Asian consumer market respectively. Lightweight true-AR glasses, such as Snap Spectacles 15 footnote 15 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 15 footnote 15 https://www.spectacles.com and Meta’s Orion and Project Aria research prototypes, signal the all-day-glasses horizon toward which the field is converging.

Companies and platforms. Meta leads consumer volume and the most aggressive glasses research bet; Apple defines the premium spatial-computing tier and the USD content pipeline; Google supplies world-scale localization through ARCore and Android XR; Microsoft has pivoted from first-party HoloLens hardware toward OpenXR software and enterprise cloud services; Niantic 16 footnote 16 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 16 footnote 16 https://www.nianticspatial.com operates a city-scale Visual Positioning System for persistent, multi-user AR; and Snap, Varjo, and ByteDance’s Pico round out the social-AR, high-fidelity, and consumer-standalone niches.

XR runs every spatial capability egocentrically and on-device under a perceptual real-time budget, and its open problems follow from that constraint: holding the motion-to-photon budget, fitting perception into the compute and thermal envelope of glasses, keeping tracking and registration robust in the wild, sharing persistent maps without compromising privacy, and making extended wear visually comfortable.

Meeting the motion-to-photon targets of the System Overview is increasingly difficult as pipelines add wireless or split rendering, cloud offload, and learned perception in the loop, each of which contributes its own delay that the reprojection stage of Task-3 can only partially mask.

All-day glasses face a hard energy and heat envelope: a lightweight form factor leaves little room for the silicon that SLAM, hand and eye tracking, and scene understanding demand. The frontier is partitioning perception across on-device accelerators, companion devices such as wristbands or pucks, and edge offload, without violating the latency or thermal budget.

paragraph.title: Robust Tracking and Registration in the Wild.

para.p: Visual–inertial SLAM and relocalization degrade in dynamic scenes, textureless rooms, repetitive structures, low light, and outdoors, exactly the conditions that curated benchmarks such as EuRoC and ScanNet underrepresent []. Persistent Visual Positioning Systems push toward city-scale anchoring, but globally drift-free, cross-device localization, together with convincing occlusion and lighting registration, remains unsolved.

Co-located multi-user AR requires a shared, persistent spatial map, an “AR cloud”, which collides directly with privacy: always-on egocentric cameras continuously scan private spaces and bystanders. Designing maps that support shared anchoring while minimizing the retention of raw imagery, and that admit meaningful consent, is both a research and a policy frontier.

Beyond latency, fixed-focus stereo optics decouple vergence from accommodation, causing eye strain that limits session length, and poorly designed locomotion induces cybersickness. Varifocal and holographic displays, gaze-contingent depth-of-field, and accurate interpupillary-distance matching are promising but immature, leaving comfort a gating factor for mainstream adoption.
Because XR subjects the perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities of Part to egocentric, on-device, real-time constraints, it exposes failure modes that offline settings rarely reveal.

In entertainment, spatial intelligence is exercised chiefly as the ability to perceive and reconstruct 3D environments, objects, and human bodies, and to embed virtual content into the physical world so that it is geometrically and physically consistent. Spatial entertainment (AR games, VR experiences, location-based attractions, and virtual production for film) differs from screen-based media in that it must compute camera pose, scene geometry, and user state continuously and within strict latency limits, without sacrificing aesthetic quality or narrative coherence; the perception and reconstruction machinery involved is treated in Chapter and Chapter .

The field has followed the same arc as the capabilities it borrows: commodity depth sensing made real-time dense mapping practical for AR games, neural radiance and Gaussian representations made captured sets photoreal and navigable, parametric body models made full-body avatars routine, and world-scale visual positioning let location-based games such as Pokémon GO anchor characters to real landmarks across sessions and players. Each of these threads returns in the pivotal tasks below.

figure.toccaption: 10.5Spatial intelligence for entertainment as a real-time closed loop: sensor inputs feed world reconstruction, performance capture, and content authoring, whose composited render is presented back to the user.

caption.text: Spatial intelligence for entertainment as a real-time closed loop: sensor inputs feed world reconstruction, performance capture, and content authoring, whose composited render is presented back to the user.

para.p: Entertainment sits on top of the XR platform of §: it does not re-implement that runtime but builds on it, and its distinctive demand is production-quality spatial content, whether rendered live or authored offline. The domain spans two regimes. Real-time interactive experiences (AR games, VR titles, location-based attractions, and live virtual production) close the tight sensing-to-display loop sketched in Figure , whereas offline high-fidelity creation (scanning sets, capturing performers, building volumetric footage) supplies those experiences with assets. Across both, three spatial tasks recur as the frequent bottlenecks. World reconstruction builds the geometric and radiance model of the environment, supplying localization and occlusion for live experiences and navigable captured content for authored ones; embodied performance capture digitizes the user or performer into a controllable avatar; and spatial content authoring decides where virtual elements appear and how cameras move so that the result is both consistent and expressive. The interactive regime runs all three under hard latency budgets, while offline authoring trades that latency for fidelity.

subsection.title: 10.2.3Pivotal Task-1: World Reconstruction and Spatial Mapping

para.p: The first task builds and maintains an accurate, consistent model of the environment that supports localization, occlusion, and physics for live experiences and navigable content for authored ones, specializing the dense-reconstruction and scene-understanding techniques of Chapter and Chapter to interactive rates. Where § treated mapping as a means to on-device localization, here the reconstruction is itself the deliverable: the navigable set or stage that players and film-makers inhabit. Figure contrasts geometric fusion, neural and point-based scene representations, and world-scale localization as complementary capabilities rather than obligatory sequential stages.

figure.toccaption: 10.6Complementary capabilities for entertainment reconstruction, not sequential stages: (a) TSDF fusion of posed RGB-D frames into a mesh, (b) radiance-field or 3D Gaussian appearance models for view synthesis, and (c) visual positioning for persistent place-based content. Samples, surfaces, and place markers are schematic.

caption.text: Complementary capabilities for entertainment reconstruction, not sequential stages: (a) TSDF fusion of posed RGB-D frames into a mesh, (b) radiance-field or 3D Gaussian appearance models for view synthesis, and (c) visual positioning for persistent place-based content. Samples, surfaces, and place markers are schematic.

para.p: Geometric reconstruction forms the base: geometric SLAM and dense methods fuse depth or RGB data into volumetric maps, as in KinectFusion [] and the reconstructions underlying datasets such as ScanNet [], while DynamicFusion extends this to moving users by tracking non-rigid deformations []. Neural and point-based representations such as NeRF, instant-NGP, and 3D Gaussian Splatting then represent scene radiance to produce compact, high-fidelity reconstructions that render at interactive rates []; dynamic and 4D extensions that deform or time-index the primitives carry this to moving scenes, so a performance or an entire set can be captured as free-viewpoint volumetric video for later replay []. At global scale, visual positioning systems (VPS) combine local reconstructions into a worldwide map that lets a mobile device localize from a single image, as in Niantic’s Lightship platform. These methods are evaluated on indoor datasets such as ScanNet and Matterport3D, which provide large-scale reconstructions with semantic labels for scene understanding [], and on NeRF-style view-synthesis benchmarks (e.g., , synthetic Blender scenes) for photometric fidelity; the latter, however, rarely capture entertainment-specific constraints such as rapid camera motion or cluttered living rooms, so practitioners often fall back on custom internal datasets (Table ). The standard metrics are absolute trajectory error (ATE) for localization, surface reconstruction error for geometry, and PSNR/SSIM for neural rendering [], but in entertainment these are complemented by interaction-centric measures: the accuracy of occlusion masks, the physical plausibility of collisions, and user reports on realism (for instance, whether a virtual character convincingly hides behind a sofa).

subsection.title: 10.2.4Pivotal Task-2: Embodied Performance Capture and Avatar Control

para.p: The second task estimates full-body pose, shape, and facial expression to drive avatars in real time, specializing the human pose and motion machinery of Chapter (and the motion-generation methods of Chapter ) to live interaction. Unlike the sparse three-point body tracking of §, driven from a headset and two controllers, entertainment capture targets studio-grade, fully-observed performance. As Figure indicates, approaches range from skeleton-based joint prediction to surface-based model fitting and full volumetric capture.

figure.toccaption: 10.7Three routes to performance capture, each able to drive avatar playback or control: (a) skeleton joints retargeted to a rig, (b) a parametric surface (SMPL) driving a body mesh, and (c) volumetric capture for reconstructed or animatable appearance. Performer illustrations and motion traces are qualitative, not measured scores.

caption.text: Three routes to performance capture, each able to drive avatar playback or control: (a) skeleton joints retargeted to a rig, (b) a parametric surface (SMPL) driving a body mesh, and (c) volumetric capture for reconstructed or animatable appearance. Performer illustrations and motion traces are qualitative, not measured scores.

para.p: Skeleton-based methods predict joint positions from sensors, while surface-based approaches fit parametric models such as SMPL directly to video [], with datasets like Human3.6M and AMASS supplying the supervised motion priors that make this robust []. Volumetric capture systems such as Holoportation go further, streaming textured 3D avatars into VR/AR scenes by combining reconstruction with tight time synchronization []. More recent Gaussian-splatting avatars learn drivable, photorealistic humans from multi-view capture, with rigged 3D Gaussians giving expressive control over head avatars [] and pose-dependent Gaussian maps modeling full-body avatars with dynamic clothing [], narrowing the gap between a captured performance and a real-time renderable asset. These capabilities are benchmarked chiefly on Human3.6M, which offers millions of 3D poses with calibrated cameras [], and on AMASS, which provides over forty hours of motion data for learning priors []; commercial scenarios remain underrepresented, however, since common cases such as players using controllers in small rooms or performers in costumes lack sufficient public benchmark data (Table ). Quantitative evaluation uses metrics like mean per-joint position error (MPJPE), but for interactive entertainment latency and temporal stability are decisive, as even minor jitter breaks the sense of embodiment, and user studies show that enjoyment depends on the alignment between perceived and actual motion []; production systems therefore pair algorithmic metrics with feedback from expert animators.

subsection.title: 10.2.5Pivotal Task-3: Spatially-Aware Content Authoring and Virtual Production

para.p: The third task helps creators decide where virtual elements appear and how cameras move, turning the reconstructed world and captured performers into a coherent, expressive scene, and connecting to the spatial-reasoning and planning paradigms of Chapter . Figure previews the spectrum from SDK-level authoring primitives to camera-tracked LED-wall virtual production and AI-assisted cinematography.

figure.toccaption: 10.8Three related spatial authoring capabilities: (a) engine primitives (detected planes and persistent anchors) for asset placement, (b) virtual production, where tracked camera pose updates the LED-wall perspective, and (c) camera planning from narrative and scene constraints to a shot plan. The scene, camera path, and shot settings are illustrative.

caption.text: Three related spatial authoring capabilities: (a) engine primitives (detected planes and persistent anchors) for asset placement, (b) virtual production, where tracked camera pose updates the LED-wall perspective, and (c) camera planning from narrative and scene constraints to a shot plan. The scene, camera path, and shot settings are illustrative.

para.p: Engine-level authoring provides designers with high-level primitives such as plane detection and anchors through AR SDKs in real-time engines like Unity and Unreal. Virtual production links physical cameras to 3D scenes on LED walls so that lighting and parallax respond correctly to camera movement, and intelligent cinematography research is exploring AI-assisted camera planning that respects film grammar while adapting to dynamic user actions []. Standardized benchmarks for spatial authoring are rare: some studies evaluate camera planning on synthetic storyboards, but most assessment happens internally at studios, and virtual-production workflows are typically tested on complex reference sequences rather than public datasets, which makes objective comparison of authoring tools difficult (Table ). Evaluation accordingly mixes system metrics such as rendering latency with expert judgment on cinematic quality, with intelligent-cinematography studies often convening expert panels to analyze framing and continuity []; for AR/VR tools usability is paramount, and HCI evaluations measure how quickly a user completes a level-design task or how rich the resulting spatial layouts are under different tool abstractions. Generative world models are beginning to bypass authoring by synthesizing playable worlds directly: GameNGen [] simulates the game DOOM interactively in real time with a diffusion model, and Genie 3 [] generates navigable environments that respond to user actions, so that creating content starts to mean conditioning a world model (§).

table.toccaption: 10.2Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in entertainment, spanning the three pivotal tasks.

caption.text: Representative benchmarks for spatial intelligence in entertainment, spanning the three pivotal tasks.

para.p: A robust set of tools implements these tasks for games, film, and live events. At the engine level, Unity’s AR Foundation 17 footnote 17 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 17 footnote 17 https://docs.unity3d.com/Packages/com.unity.xr.arfoundation offers a unified API over ARKit, ARCore, and other SDKs, exposing essential features such as point clouds and depth meshing, while Google’s ARCore Geospatial API 18 footnote 18 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 18 footnote 18 https://developers.google.com/ar/develop/unity-arf/geospatial/developer-guide adds global localization, allowing applications to attach anchors to outdoor landmarks with meter-level accuracy. These abstractions let designers build AR gameplay around real-world surfaces without managing low-level sensor fusion.

Niantic’s Lightship platform packages spatial mapping and multiplayer synchronization into turnkey services: Reality Blending 19 footnote 19 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 19 footnote 19 https://nianticlabs.com/news/realityblending-announcement in Pokémon GO uses learned depth to let virtual creatures move behind real-world obstacles, and Pokémon Playgrounds 20 footnote 20 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 20 footnote 20 https://nianticlabs.com/news/pokemon-playgrounds extends this to persistent AR, where players leave virtual items at specific locations for others to find, with Niantic’s Visual Positioning System (VPS) keeping that content anchored consistently across users and times.

In VR gaming, consumer headsets with inside-out tracking enable room-scale interaction; games like Beat Saber use precise 6-DoF tracking to create rhythm gameplay that doubles as exercise, and studies show a strong link between spatial design choices and player exertion, underscoring the connection between tracking quality and user experience []. Virtual production stages have likewise transformed film and sports broadcasting: productions such as The Mandalorian (built on ILM’s StageCraft) and sports studios such as ESPN’s Catalyst Stage 21 footnote 21 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 21 footnote 21 https://espnpressroom.com/us/press-releases/2023/06/catalyst-stage-disneys-new-immersive-espn-studio-opens-storytelling-and-production-frontiers/ use LED volumes driven by tracked cameras, where spatial intelligence involves calibrating physical cameras to digital scenes and maintaining low-latency tracking. Finally, neural capture tools inspired by NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting are entering the pipeline, letting artists scan a location with a phone and import navigable 3D assets into game engines []; while this bridges scouting and production, it introduces new challenges around lighting control and integration.

Entertainment asks for production-quality spatial content at interactive rates, and its open problems stem from that demand. The tension between real-time performance and visual fidelity is the most immediate; close behind come robustness once the system leaves controlled spaces, the cognitive load that authoring places on creators, and the human-factors and ethics questions that surface the moment these systems scan real users and real rooms.

Neural representations have improved visual quality, but many methods remain too computationally heavy for mobile or standalone VR. While techniques such as 3D Gaussian Splatting achieve real-time rendering on high-end hardware [], porting them to thermally constrained devices is difficult, and entertainment applications must additionally handle variable network conditions while guaranteeing stable frame rates, since frame drops that are acceptable in research benchmarks can cause physical discomfort in VR.

Existing benchmarks such as ScanNet focus on standard indoor spaces, yet entertainment experiences often occur in unpredictable environments such as festivals, dim clubs, or crowded stadiums. World-scale AR platforms address this by training on millions of crowdsourced scans, which raises questions about coverage bias (particularly toward urban areas) and the difficulty of maintaining maps as the world changes; designing models that remain robust under these shifts is an open research area.

Although modern SDKs are powerful, creating high-quality spatial experiences imposes a high cognitive load, as creators must simultaneously manage geometry, interaction, cinematography, and technical constraints. Intelligent-cinematography tools attempt to assist by suggesting camera paths [], but these are not yet standard in creative workflows; there is a pressing need for tools that let designers specify high-level intentions (for example, “the character should hide behind the sofa”) which the system then realizes via underlying planning modules.

Spatial systems frequently scan users and private spaces. While datasets like AMASS demonstrate the utility of large-scale motion capture, collecting similar data in the wild raises privacy concerns, and from an HCI perspective issues such as cybersickness and fatigue limit the duration of VR and AR sessions, while physically active titles introduce comfort and safety considerations that spatial layout must respect. Addressing these problems requires a collaborative approach spanning algorithm design, user-feedback systems, and clear data governance.

Geo-spatial systems operate on spatial structure at the scale of assets, cities, and the planet, where the task is to build a faithful model of a physical system and keep it aligned with live observation. This chapter applies the spatial intelligence of the previous part to that task, across three settings that share the same closed loop between model and world but differ in scale and stakes.

The digital twin binds a metric, physically grounded replica to a specific asset through a live bidirectional loop, so that the physical system and its model track each other. GeoAI widens the frame to the planet, where streams of Earth-observation data drive perception and decision-making over terrain, infrastructure, and environmental change. Aerospace systems carry the same loop off the planet, where a spacecraft or rover must perceive, reason about, and act on its surroundings with little or no ground support.

A digital twin is a 3D representation faithful enough to stand in for its physical counterpart in analysis and operation. Building one requires more than accurate geometric reconstruction and photorealistic appearance under varying illumination; it requires realistic modeling of physical properties and interaction, so that the replica behaves as the original would. What separates a digital twin from any other 3D asset, however, is not fidelity alone but coupling. Following the now-standard taxonomy of Kritzinger et al. [], a digital model carries no automated data exchange with the physical object, a digital shadow carries an automated one-way flow from the physical to the virtual, and only a digital twin closes the loop with an automated, bidirectional flow: the virtual model is continuously synchronized to the physical asset, simulated forward to predict, and used to act back upon it.

A digital twin therefore reuses, but specializes, much of the machinery surveyed earlier in this handbook. The perception stack of Chapter supplies the captures from which a twin is built, and the neural reconstruction and generation methods of Chapter supply its geometry and appearance; what the twin adds is metric accuracy, physical grounding, and a persistent correspondence to a specific real object over its lifecycle. Entertainment (§) builds the same high-fidelity captures as creative content; here they become an operational engineering model wired to a live counterpart, and the city- and planet-scale twins that recur below connect to the GeoAI methods of §. The concept itself traces from Grieves’ product-lifecycle lectures, formalized with Vickers [], through its aerospace codification for NASA and U.S. Air Force vehicles [], to its industrial maturation [], where the five-dimension model of Tao et al.makes the data connections between physical entity, virtual entity, and services a first-class element of the architecture.

Figure draws the twin as a closed loop around its physical asset. Sensing (images, LiDAR, RGB-D scans, onboard IoT telemetry) feeds the construction of a replica that carries geometry, appearance, materials, and physical properties; the replica is simulated forward, kept synchronized by live data assimilation, and queried to predict, and its decisions operate the asset, which is then sensed anew. The three pivotal tasks map onto this loop directly. Task-1 builds the twin (sense and construct), Task-2 makes it behave (model and simulate), and Task-3 keeps it synchronized and turns it to use (assimilate, predict, and act). Table collects the benchmarks on which the first two are evaluated; synchronization has no shared benchmark.

figure.toccaption: 11.1The digital twin as a closed loop around its physical asset: construction (T1) and modeling (T2) establish the replica, synchronization (T3) corrects its state from live observations, and forecasts drive decisions through a control path separate from the observation path.

caption.text: The digital twin as a closed loop around its physical asset: construction (T1) and modeling (T2) establish the replica, synchronization (T3) corrects its state from live observations, and forecasts drive decisions through a control path separate from the observation path.

para.p: The first task builds the twin from sensor captures, and it must deliver four properties that a generic one-shot reconstruction does not guarantee. The twin must be metric (correct at real-world scale), relightable (its appearance separable from capture-time illumination), physically grounded (carrying mass, material, and friction), and actionable (its movable parts and joints encoded so a simulator can drive it). Figure sketches the progression from raw captures through geometry and material recovery to a simulatable model.

figure.toccaption: 11.2Three components of high-fidelity twin construction: (a) metric geometry from multi-view, LiDAR, or RGB-D capture; (b) relightable material channels separated from illumination; and (c) physical articulation, here a prismatic drawer joint with mass and friction. Material swatches and mesh overlays are schematic.

caption.text: Three components of high-fidelity twin construction: (a) metric geometry from multi-view, LiDAR, or RGB-D capture; (b) relightable material channels separated from illumination; and (c) physical articulation, here a prismatic drawer joint with mass and friction. Material swatches and mesh overlays are schematic.

para.p: Geometry and appearance acquisition. The earliest replicas were built by photogrammetry: multiple overlapping photographs of an object, terrain, or structure are captured, and a Structure-from-Motion algorithm recovers camera poses and a sparse metric point cloud, as systematized in COLMAP [], after which dense multi-view stereo and meshing produce a surface. Real-time RGB-D fusion in the KinectFusion tradition [] yields metric, watertight geometry over the observed region, and neural implicit-surface methods such as NeuS [] and the detail-preserving Neuralangelo [] recover watertight meshes as the zero-level-set of a learned signed-distance field. A second family optimizes for view synthesis rather than surface quality: NeRF [], its hash-grid acceleration Instant-NGP [], and the explicit, real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting [] render novel views with high fidelity but historically produced no clean surface and bake appearance into the representation; surface-aligned variants such as SuGaR [] and 2D Gaussian Splatting [] narrow this gap by extracting watertight meshes directly from a Gaussian field. Because a twin requires metric scale and an extractable surface, the photogrammetric and implicit-surface lines are load-bearing, with meshing operators such as Poisson surface reconstruction [] and Marching Cubes [] converting a field or point set into geometry; the radiance-field family enters as an appearance and speed substrate, treated in full in Chapter .

Inverse rendering and relightable materials. A captured asset whose appearance is baked at scan time only reproduces the object under the one illumination it was scanned in, because each pixel entangles albedo, geometry, and lighting. A twin, by contrast, lives in a simulator where viewpoint and illumination change every frame, so its construction must recover separated physically based rendering (PBR) channels (albedo, roughness, normals) together with an estimate of the environment lighting. Inverse-rendering methods supply exactly this factorization: NeRFactor decomposes a captured radiance field into shape, reflectance, and a single environment light [], while the differentiable, engine-ready NVDiffRec jointly extracts a triangle mesh, an SVBRDF, and a lighting estimate directly optimizable for downstream rendering []. The same factorization has been ported onto explicit Gaussians, as in Relightable 3D Gaussians, which attaches normals and a BRDF to each primitive and ray-traces shadows for real-time relighting []. Relightability is what lets a twin be composited under novel lighting and rendered consistently inside a physics or sensor simulation.

Physical-property and articulation estimation. A static mesh is viewable but not operable: it has no notion of which surfaces move, with what effort, or under what dynamics. Closing this gap requires a movable-part inventory and the kinematic joints (revolute or prismatic, with axes and limits) that a physics engine can integrate, together with physical parameters such as mass and friction. Ditto recovers part geometry and an articulation model jointly from before-and-after observations of an interaction [], and URDFormer predicts a full URDF, the standard interactive description, from a single real image, turning a photograph into a simulatable articulated twin []. Dynamical parameters can be identified directly in a differentiable field representation, as in PAC-NeRF, which estimates geometry and physical parameters together through a differentiable material-point simulator [], and PhysGaussian, which integrates Newtonian dynamics into a Gaussian representation so that what is reconstructed can also be simulated []. Such methods lean heavily on articulated-object datasets, principally the PartNet-Mobility models exposed through the SAPIEN simulator [], the fine-grained part hierarchy of PartNet [], and the cross-category, actionable parts of GAPartNet []. The resulting articulated, parameterized model is the input to the behavioral simulation of Task-2.

Datasets and metrics. Construction quality is measured against scanned-object and scene corpora (Table ). At the object level, the recent Digital Twin Catalog provides a large set of digital-twin-quality scans with millimeter geometry, photorealistic materials, and an explicit relighting evaluation [], complementing the real-scanned OmniObject3D [], the simulation-ready Google Scanned Objects [], the artist-authored, PBR-annotated ABO [], the large Objaverse collection [], and the in-the-wild Common Objects in 3D []. At the scene level, twins are evaluated on ScanNet [], Matterport3D [], the photorealistic Replica reconstructions [], and the commodity-LiDAR ARKitScenes [], with metric-geometry benchmarks such as Tanks and Temples supplying laser-scan ground truth []. Geometry is reported with Chamfer distance, F-score at a stated threshold, and normal consistency; appearance with PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; and, for twins specifically, an added relighting error that penalizes appearance that fails to transfer across illumination.

subsection.title: 11.1.4Pivotal Task-2: Physics-Based Modeling and Behavioral Simulation

para.p: The second task makes the constructed replica behave. Geometry is not behavior: a twin must reproduce its asset’s dynamics, not merely its shape, so the static model of Task-1 is coupled to a physics, behavioral, or surrogate engine and run forward as an executable model whose parameters are fit to the real asset (Figure ).

para.p: Physics engines. The behavioral substrate of a twin is a simulator that integrates its dynamics. MuJoCo provides accurate rigid-body contact dynamics and is the de facto standard for model-based control []; the open-source PyBullet offers a widely used free alternative spanning rigid and soft bodies []; and SAPIEN specializes in part-level interaction with large articulated objects [], the natural runtime for the actionable twins of Task-1. GPU-accelerated platforms couple photorealistic rendering with physics at scale, exemplified by NVIDIA Isaac Sim 1 footnote 1 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim on the Omniverse stack and its successor Isaac Lab 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab, with newer GPU-first simulators such as Genesis 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://genesis-embodied-ai.github.io/ and the accelerator-native MuJoCo MJX pushing throughput further; deformable phenomena such as cloth and fluids are handled by unified particle and material-point (MPM) solvers.

Differentiable simulation and system identification. A twin is only behaviorally faithful if its physical parameters match the real asset, which makes parameter estimation central. Differentiable simulators expose gradients of simulated outcomes with respect to physical parameters, turning system identification into gradient-based optimization: DiffTaichi compiles differentiable physical simulators from high-level code [], Brax provides massively parallel differentiable rigid-body dynamics on accelerators [], and gradSim couples differentiable simulation with differentiable rendering to backpropagate from video pixels all the way to mass, friction, and elasticity []. A twin can thus be calibrated to its counterpart from observation rather than hand-tuned.

Surrogate and physics-informed models. High-fidelity simulation is often too slow to run in the synchronization loop of Task-3, so twins frequently substitute a reduced or learned surrogate. Physics-informed neural networks embed governing partial differential equations directly in the training loss, solving forward and inverse problems with scarce data [], a strategy situated within the broader programme of physics-informed machine learning []. Reduced-order modeling, identified early as a key enabling technology for digital twins, compresses a high-fidelity simulation to real-time evaluation [], and the hybrid-twin paradigm couples such a physics-based reduced model with a data-driven correction term to absorb unmodeled effects [].

Real-to-sim for policy learning. A faithful behavioral twin is also the substrate on which robot policies are trained and validated before deployment, which connects this task to the manipulation methods of § and the reasoning of Chapter . The reality gap between simulation and the physical world is bridged by randomizing visual appearance [] and dynamics [] during training, and recent real-to-sim-to-real pipelines build a twin of the workspace from a quick scan and use it to robustify learned policies, as in RialTo []. A complementary line argues that an exact twin is not always necessary: ACDC instead generates geometrically and semantically similar “digital cousins,” trading exact correspondence for robustness and zero-shot transfer [], sharpening by contrast what a true digital twin provides.

subsection.title: 11.1.5Pivotal Task-3: Real-Time Synchronization and Predictive Operation

para.p: The third task is the one that earns the name twin: it maintains the automated bidirectional coupling between model and asset that defines a twin [], and turns that coupling to use. Figure previews the pipeline, from a live sensor stream through data assimilation to prediction and a control signal fed back to the physical asset.

figure.toccaption: 11.4Real-time synchronization and predictive operation: (a) live measurements from the physical asset are (b) assimilated with the model prior into a posterior state of (c) the synchronized twin, which feeds forecasts, what-if, anomaly, and useful-life outputs. The upper feedback path propagates the updated state into the next model prior; the lower path returns decisions or controls to the physical asset. Dashed forecast branches are possible futures, not observed trajectories; all analytical outputs are schematic.

caption.text: Real-time synchronization and predictive operation: (a) live measurements from the physical asset are (b) assimilated with the model prior into a posterior state of (c) the synchronized twin, which feeds forecasts, what-if, anomaly, and useful-life outputs. The upper feedback path propagates the updated state into the next model prior; the lower path returns decisions or controls to the physical asset. Dashed forecast branches are possible futures, not observed trajectories; all analytical outputs are schematic.

para.p: Data assimilation and state estimation. Keeping the twin synchronized is a state-estimation problem: the model’s latent state must be continually corrected toward the incoming measurements. The classical recursive estimator is the Kalman filter [], and for the nonlinear, high-dimensional systems typical of physical twins the ensemble Kalman filter provides a Monte-Carlo data-assimilation scheme that propagates an ensemble of states to forecast error statistics []. At the level of an entire engineered system, a probabilistic graphical model casts data-driven model adaptation as Bayesian state estimation with end-to-end uncertainty quantification [], so that predictive twins can be assembled and updated at scale and their predictions carry calibrated confidence rather than point estimates.

Predictive operation across domains. The synchronized twin is queried to anticipate rather than merely to monitor, and the applications follow the asset. In manufacturing, the twin couples machine geometry to live telemetry for prognostics and health management, estimating remaining useful life and scheduling maintenance before failure []. At urban scale, a city digital twin fuses a semantically rich 3D model with sensor and simulation layers to support planning and what-if analysis, as in the Herrenberg study [] and national programmes built on CityGML foundations [], a layer that connects directly to the GeoAI methods of §. In healthcare, patient-specific anatomical twins driven by physiological models support precision diagnosis and treatment planning, with cardiology an early exemplar [] and a growing body of work surveyed across the field []; the medical twin is developed in §. In aerospace, where the paradigm was first codified, a structural twin mirrors an as-flown airframe to predict fatigue []; and in agriculture, field and crop twins fuse geospatial layers with growth models for precision management [].
