para.p: Many key quantities in physical systems are available only through sparse and noisy observations, and representation and reconstruction recover continuous spatial fields from such data, the input to law discovery and control. Embedding physical priors such as governing partial differential equations and symmetry constraints keeps these reconstructions physically consistent in low-data regimes.

A classical task is physical field reconstruction, which aims to recover continuous physical fields such as temperature, pressure, and velocity from sparse sensor readings or boundary measurements; the central challenge lies in ensuring the physical plausibility of the solution under the ill-posed conditions caused by insufficient observations. Physics-informed neural networks are a classical approach for this task [], embedding partial differential equations such as the Navier–Stokes equations as soft constraints in the loss function and computing physical residuals via automatic differentiation, which enables accurate reconstruction of fluid and thermal fields in data-scarce settings; the same networks serve as real-time surrogates in digital twins (§). Neural fields implicitly represent continuous physical fields by using coordinate-based networks that map spatial locations to physical quantities. Sitzmann et al. [] proposed SIREN, which employs periodic activation functions to capture high-frequency spatial details with high fidelity and has been applied to solving Poisson equations and reconstructing wave fields. The general machinery of coordinate-based neural representation is developed in Chapter .

Inverse scattering aims to infer the internal structure or material parameters of an object from measured wave-scattering data, and it remains a canonical ill-posed problem in electromagnetics and acoustics []. Wei and Chen proposed deep-learning schemes [] for full-wave nonlinear inverse scattering that directly invert dielectric-permittivity profiles from scattered fields, thereby moving beyond linearized Born-type approximations in practical reconstructions. SwitchNet [] introduced a unified neural architecture that learns both the forward map from scatterers to scattered fields and the inverse map from measurements to scatterer profiles, using a switching layer that exploits low-rank structure to reduce model complexity and facilitate training. Physics-guided losses that inject multiple-scattering near-field priors into the objective further improve robustness.

Law discovery aims to learn the generative structures or explicit laws that govern the evolution of physical systems from observational data, emphasizing the automatic extraction of conservation laws, symmetries, and interpretable mechanisms beyond accurate prediction. Hamiltonian Neural Networks [] directly learn the Hamiltonian of a system, thereby enforcing energy conservation and symplectic structure at the model level and providing a principled foundation for interpretable dynamical modeling. Lagrangian Neural Networks [] parameterize arbitrary Lagrangians with neural networks, learning energy conserving dynamics without canonical coordinates, as validated on the double pendulum and a relativistic particle. Cranmer et al. [] combine graph networks with symbolic regression on their internal representations, recovering known force laws and Hamiltonians, and applying the approach to cosmology. The SINDy algorithm [] employs sparse regression to identify governing differential equations directly from time-series data, enabling data-driven discovery of interpretable physical laws.

Efficient physical solvers focus on predicting the spatio-temporal evolution of physical systems under known governing equations or interaction rules, with the goal of achieving fast and scalable computation while preserving physical consistency beyond the limits of traditional numerical methods. The Fourier Neural Operator [] learns mappings between function spaces rather than individual discretized instances, enabling trained models to predict the evolution of partial differential equations at arbitrary spatial resolutions without relying on a fixed computational grid. DeepONet [], grounded in the universal approximation theorem for operators, learns nonlinear mappings from input functions to output functions and thereby approximates the solution operators that govern physical systems. Interaction Networks [] introduced the relational reasoning architecture that learns physical interactions between objects, laying the foundation for graph-based physical simulation. The Graph Network Simulator [] employs graph neural networks to model spatial interactions among particles or objects, achieving high-fidelity simulations of fluids, rigid bodies, and deformable materials, and MeshGraphNets [] extend graph-based models to unstructured meshes, allowing efficient simulation of continuum mechanics on irregular geometries. For the classical challenge of turbulence modeling, Mohan et al. [] proposed spatio-temporal deep-learning models with physics-informed diagnostics that improve the prediction accuracy of three-dimensional turbulent flows, and Lusch et al. [] developed a deep-learning framework for universal linear embeddings of nonlinear dynamics, enabling low-dimensional representations and long-term prediction of nonlinear fluid systems. Neural representations of the many-body wavefunction are treated with electronic structure in the chemistry subsection.

Optimization and control in physical systems seek optimal trajectories, shapes, or control policies under governing physical laws and environmental constraints. Differentiable physics formulates physical simulators as differentiable operators, enabling gradient-based optimization over control inputs, design variables, and physical parameters, and providing a unified framework for optimal control, system identification, and design. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations [] provide a differentiable formulation of continuous-time dynamical systems by parameterizing the vector field with a neural network and enabling gradient computation through adjoint sensitivity analysis, serving as a flexible building block for learning and control in continuous time. ChainQueen [] demonstrates differentiable simulation of soft and deformable bodies based on the moving least squares material point method, enabling gradient-based optimization in high-degree-of-freedom systems with contact and supporting applications in soft-robot control and co-design. DiffTaichi [] generalizes this paradigm through a differentiable programming framework for high-performance physical simulation, allowing efficient construction of differentiable solvers and gradient-driven optimization for fluid control, shape optimization, and material-parameter estimation; the same tools calibrate digital twins (§). In practice, a mature software substrate of differentiable and physics-informed libraries, such as DeepXDE 19 footnote 19 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 19 footnote 19 https://github.com/lululxvi/deepxde and NVIDIA Modulus 20 footnote 20 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 20 footnote 20 https://developer.nvidia.com/modulus for operator and PINN training, and JAX-MD 21 footnote 21 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 21 footnote 21 https://github.com/jax-md/jax-md and DeePMD-kit 22 footnote 22 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 22 footnote 22 https://github.com/deepmodeling/deepmd-kit for differentiable and learned-potential molecular dynamics, turns this triad into runnable physics.

Chemistry is intrinsically spatial: a molecule or a material is a three-dimensional arrangement of atoms together with an electronic field over it, and its behavior, whether energy, reactivity, or a bulk property, is a function of that geometry under strict symmetry. Physical observables must be invariant or equivariant to the Euclidean group of rotations, translations, and reflections and to permutations of identical atoms; for crystalline solids they must also respect periodic lattice symmetry, and for electrons they must obey antisymmetry under exchange. Spatial intelligence in chemistry is therefore largely the art of building these symmetries into models that represent atomic and electronic structure, simulate its dynamics, and generate new structure under chemical feasibility. Figure previews this triad from an equivariant representation of a 3D structure to a learned-potential simulation and a 3D generative design.

para.p: The central representational problem of chemistry is to map a 3D atomic geometry to energies, forces, and properties while respecting symmetry, and successive representations have captured progressively more of that geometry. Geometry-grounded potentials. The Behler–Parrinello neural network potential founded the area by decomposing the total energy into atomic contributions computed from rotation-, translation-, and permutation-invariant symmetry functions of each atom’s local environment []. SchNet [] replaced hand-designed descriptors with continuous-filter convolutions over interatomic distances, giving a smooth invariant representation for energy and force prediction, while DimeNet [] added directional message passing that encodes bond angles through spherical harmonics, moving beyond pairwise distances to angular structure, and PaiNN [] extended message passing to rotationally equivariant vector features for tensorial properties and spectra. The Deep Potential model [] preserves all natural symmetries at linear cost, and the ANI potentials [] demonstrated transferable organic-chemistry accuracy at force-field cost. Equivariant interatomic potentials. The decisive recent step was to carry geometric tensors, not merely invariant scalars, through the network. NequIP [] introduced E(3)-equivariant convolutions over geometric tensors and achieved striking data efficiency, often requiring orders of magnitude less training data; Allegro [] made the representation strictly local and thereby scalable to 100 million atoms, and MACE [] used higher body-order equivariant messages to reach high accuracy in only two message-passing layers. A further shift is from per-system fits to universal potentials that span the periodic table: M3GNet [] couples a graph network with explicit three-body interactions trained on materials relaxations, and CHGNet [] augments the 3D-structure graph with atomic magnetic moments to capture electronic degrees of freedom alongside geometry. These equivariant backbones share machinery with the geometric representations of Chapter . Neural electronic structure. At the quantum scale the spatial object is the many-electron wavefunction itself. Neural quantum states parameterize that wavefunction with a neural network over spin configurations [], and deep variational ansätze such as FermiNet [] and PauliNet [] operate directly on 3D electron coordinates while enforcing exact antisymmetry, solving the electronic Schrödinger equation to chemical accuracy from nuclear positions alone.

The potentials of the previous thread are also the simulators: once a model maps a 3D configuration to energies and forces, it drives molecular dynamics at a fraction of the cost of first-principles calculation, and the same representations predict quantum properties such as energies, dipoles, and frontier-orbital gaps directly from coordinates. The gradient-domain machine-learning force field made this explicit by exploiting energy conservation and the geometry of conformations, and it established the widely used MD17 trajectory benchmark of energies and forces for small molecules []. Heterogeneous catalysis pushes the same energy-and-force prediction task to a far larger and more diverse chemical space, spanning many combinations of metal surfaces and adsorbates. GemNet-OC [] extends directional message passing to this setting, delivering accurate energies and forces across the surfaces and adsorbates of the Open Catalyst datasets. In parallel, structure-to-property prediction is standardized on QM9 [], a dataset of roughly 134,000 small organic molecules with density-functional geometries and quantum properties, on which the equivariant networks above are routinely evaluated by the mean absolute error of predicted properties. This ecosystem rests on open toolkits, including the equivariant-network library e3nn 23 footnote 23 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 23 footnote 23 https://e3nn.org/, the atomistic-simulation environment ASE 24 footnote 24 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 24 footnote 24 https://wiki.fysik.dtu.dk/ase/, and the quantum-chemistry package PySCF 25 footnote 25 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 25 footnote 25 https://pyscf.org/, together with universal-potential foundation models such as MACE-MP, and on reference corpora such as the Materials Project [], the Open Catalyst dataset [], and the MoleculeNet benchmark suite [].

The inverse of property prediction is design: generating new 3D structures that satisfy desired properties under chemical feasibility, by sampling on the appropriate geometric manifold rather than enumerating candidates. G-SchNet [] autoregressively places atoms in 3D Euclidean space with each placement respecting the rotational invariance and local symmetry of those already placed, the first strong 3D-native generator. Diffusion models then became the dominant paradigm: the equivariant diffusion model [] jointly denoises atom coordinates and types under E(3) equivariance, GeoDiff [] generates conformers from the molecular graph through roto-translation-equivariant Markov kernels that induce an invariant distribution, and torsional diffusion [] restricts the process to the hypertorus of torsion angles, the true intrinsic conformational degrees of freedom, achieving state-of-the-art conformer quality on GEOM-Drugs [] at a fraction of the cost. For crystalline materials, CDVAE [] generates stable structures under periodicity and SE(3) invariance and supports inverse design by optimizing target properties in latent space. The line has since moved to diffusion directly on the periodic structure: DiffCSP [] jointly denoises lattice and fractional coordinates under periodic equivariance for crystal structure prediction, and MatterGen [] scales this into a property-conditioned foundation model for inorganic materials design, with generated candidates validated by experimental synthesis. The general diffusion machinery underlying these models is developed in Chapter ; what is chemistry-specific is the constraint manifold (valence and bonding feasibility, energy-minimum geometries, lattice periodicity) on which generation must take place.

At the molecular, cellular, and tissue scale of basic biology the object of interest is again a three-dimensional structure: a protein fold, a molecular complex, a spatial map of gene expression, or the wiring of a neural circuit, and in each case function follows from spatial form. Spatial intelligence here recovers that structure from indirect measurement, models how biomolecules interact and move, and designs new structure. Figure previews the triad from structure recovery through interaction modeling to generative design.

figure.toccaption: 12.8The life-science triad: (1) complementary sequence-to-structure prediction and cryo-EM projection-to-density reconstruction, (2) ligand binding-pose geometry with translation, rotation, and bond torsion, and (3) de novo backbone generation followed by sequence design. These are complementary capabilities, not an obligatory serial pipeline. Protein, pocket, and density renderings, noisy projection examples, and sequence fragments are schematic; they do not constitute experimentally validated structures or designs.

caption.text: The life-science triad: (1) complementary sequence-to-structure prediction and cryo-EM projection-to-density reconstruction, (2) ligand binding-pose geometry with translation, rotation, and bond torsion, and (3) de novo backbone generation followed by sequence design. These are complementary capabilities, not an obligatory serial pipeline. Protein, pocket, and density renderings, noisy projection examples, and sequence fragments are schematic; they do not constitute experimentally validated structures or designs.

para.p: The defining achievement of spatial intelligence in biology is the recovery of 3D structure from indirect signals. Protein structure prediction maps a one-dimensional sequence to a three-dimensional fold. The original AlphaFold predicted inter-residue distance distributions as a learned potential to fold the chain [], and AlphaFold2 [] reached near-experimental accuracy through an end-to-end architecture that reasons explicitly over residue frames and pairwise geometry, the exemplar of spatial intelligence in the natural sciences. AlphaFold3 [] generalized this to the joint structure of proteins, nucleic acids, and small molecules through a diffusion decoder; RoseTTAFold [] let one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional information flow between tracks, and ESMFold [] showed that atomic-level structure emerges from a protein language model without explicit alignments, enabling metagenomic-scale folding. Cryo-electron microscopy solves the inverse problem of reconstructing a 3D density map from many noisy 2D projections. RELION cast this as Bayesian refinement [], CryoSPARC enabled rapid ab-initio reconstruction without a starting model [], and cryoDRGN used a coordinate-based neural decoder to reconstruct continuous distributions of conformations and thereby resolve molecular heterogeneity and motion []. Spatial transcriptomics places gene expression back into tissue space. The founding barcoded-array assay preserved the positional information of the transcriptome in tissue sections []; Tangram learns a spatial mapping that aligns dissociated single cells onto a spatial reference [], and novoSpaRc reconstructs spatial arrangement from expression alone through optimal transport, assuming that expression-similar cells lie physically close []. Connectomics reconstructs neural wiring from electron-microscopy volumes, where flood-filling networks iteratively trace the 3D morphology of individual neurites through the volume [].

Beyond static structure, spatial intelligence models how biomolecules bind and interact. Molecular docking predicts the 3D pose in which a ligand binds a protein, and recent methods treat it as a geometric problem on the natural manifold of poses. DiffDock [] formulates docking as diffusion over the product space of ligand translation, rotation, and torsion, sampling binding poses in their intrinsic degrees of freedom, while EquiBind [] regresses the binding location and pose in a single shot using an SE(3)-equivariant network whose equivariance encodes the rotational and translational symmetry of the binding geometry. Protein–protein and complex geometry is predicted by extending folding models to multiple chains [], and AlphaFold3 above provides a generative alternative for protein–ligand and protein–nucleic-acid complexes. The dynamics of biomolecules in turn rest on the learned interatomic potentials of the chemistry subsection, which accelerate the molecular dynamics that sample conformational change.

The generative leg designs new 3D biological structure. RFdiffusion [] adapts structure-denoising diffusion to generate novel protein backbones conditioned on functional and geometric constraints such as motif scaffolding, binders, and symmetric assemblies, and ProteinMPNN [] solves the inverse-folding problem of designing an amino-acid sequence that folds into a given 3D backbone, the standard partner to backbone generation. Chroma [] couples equivariant graph networks with a diffusion process to sample novel all-atom structures and sequences steerable toward desired properties, illuminating regions of protein space never explored by evolution. As in chemistry, the underlying diffusion machinery is that of Chapter ; what is biology-specific is that the generated geometry must be foldable and functional, which is why design is paired with structure prediction and, ultimately, wet-lab validation. The field is supported by open infrastructure, including the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database and AlphaFold3 server 26 footnote 26 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 26 footnote 26 https://alphafoldserver.com/, the ESM Metagenomic Atlas 27 footnote 27 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 27 footnote 27 https://esmatlas.com/, and the open-source folding stack OpenFold 28 footnote 28 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 28 footnote 28 https://github.com/aqlaboratory/openfold, together with reference corpora such as the Protein Data Bank, the CASP blind-assessment benchmark [], and the PDBBind docking benchmark [].

para.p: A learned model of nature has to respect the symmetries and conservation laws of its domain and remain correct outside the data it was fitted to. The six problems below follow from that requirement: how to build symmetry in, how to bridge scales, how to solve ill-posed inverse problems, how to learn from scarce and expensive labels, how to generalize to genuinely new systems, and how to make predictions physically consistent and trustworthy.

Physical observables are constrained by symmetry: Euclidean invariance and equivariance, permutation of identical particles, antisymmetry of electrons, and periodicity of crystals. Whether to build these symmetries into the architecture or to learn them from data is the central design tension, trading the cheaper but less expressive invariant features [] against the richer but costlier equivariant tensor features [], and it recurs from interatomic potentials to protein structure.

Spatial structure in nature spans many orders of magnitude, from electrons and atoms to molecules and materials, and from biomolecules through cells to tissue. Learned potentials now reach a hundred million atoms [], still far below cellular scale; no single representation natively bridges electronic-structure accuracy and mesoscale reachability, and the handoffs between scales, through coarse-graining or learned-potential dynamics, are lossy and remain only partially solved.

Much of natural science is an inverse problem in which a high-dimensional spatial field must be recovered from sparse, indirect, and noisy measurements: field reconstruction from a few sensors, inverse scattering [], and the recovery of 3D density from 2D cryo-electron-microscopy projections [] all share this under-determined character and demand strong learned priors to yield a unique and physical solution.

paragraph.title: Data Scarcity and the Cost of Ground Truth.

para.p: High-fidelity labels are expensive: accurate energies and forces require costly quantum-chemistry calculations, which is why force-field benchmarks such as MD17 cover only small molecules [], and validated 3D biological structures require slow experiments, so the space of trustworthy training data is small relative to the space of possible systems. This drives the field’s emphasis on data efficiency, multi-fidelity learning, and physics-guided objectives.

Models must extrapolate to unseen chemistry, novel protein folds, off-equilibrium and reactive geometries, and configurations far from those they were trained on. Discovery is by definition out of distribution, so leaderboard accuracy says little about it; this is why generative materials design is now judged by whether its candidates can actually be synthesized [].

Predictions that violate conservation laws or come without calibrated uncertainty cannot support a scientific conclusion. Building conservation into the model, as Hamiltonian networks do for energy [], and quantifying confidence are what let a learned model extend the scientific record rather than interpolate it.

Intelligent Assistance is the assistant-facing application of spatial intelligence: an agent must perceive a user’s lived environment, remember its changing state, ground natural instructions in that state, and act in ways that are useful, legible, and safe. Unlike a task-specific robot in a factory, vehicle, or clinic, a personal assistant operates in homes, offices, streets, and wearable or XR interfaces where the scene is private, cluttered, and shaped by individual routines. This chapter therefore treats assistance as a persistent human-centered loop over spatial memory, language grounding, action, and feedback. The same spatial model supports tidying and search, close collaboration, and accessibility support for vulnerable users, but each setting changes how much the assistant must model the person as well as the place.

An intelligent assistant is a generalist embodied agent that shares the user’s own private, unstructured world and acts on the user’s behalf. Unlike the domain agents of the preceding chapters, which are optimized for a bounded operational envelope (a road network, a warehouse aisle, an operating theater), the assistant must function inside the open-ended geometry of a home, an office, or a sidewalk, in the continuous physical presence of the person it serves. Its defining spatial challenge is therefore not a new perception, reasoning, generation, or memory primitive: those capabilities are surveyed in Chapter (perception), Chapter (reasoning), Chapter (generation), and Section (retrieval- and memory-augmented spatial reasoning). The challenge here is rather to build and maintain a persistent, personalized, and queryable spatial-semantic model of the user’s environment, to ground human intent onto that model, and to act on it legibly and safely while a person occupies the same space.

Three properties separate the assistant from the embodied agents discussed elsewhere in this part. The environment is the user’s own, so the assistant cannot assume an engineered layout and must instead generalize across the long tail of real homes. It is also personalized: the same instruction (“tidy up,” “take me to the exit”) resolves to different geometric goals for different users, so the spatial model must absorb individual preference. And because the human is always co-present, otherwise routine motion becomes a social act that must be predictable, comfortable, and safe. These three demands (an unengineered space, an individual user, and a person sharing that space) recur across every regime in which the assistant operates.

Across these settings, every assistant closes the same loop. It perceives the environment and the user, represents what it perceives in a persistent spatial-semantic memory, grounds a natural-language or gestural instruction onto that memory, reasons about a goal-directed plan, acts on the physical or informational world, and observes the human’s feedback, which re-grounds the next interaction. The persistent memory is the part that distinguishes an assistant from a single-shot perception or manipulation system: because the assistant lives in one place over long horizons, it can accumulate a map of where objects belong, where the user tends to be, and how the user prefers tasks to be performed. Long-horizon mobile-manipulation benchmarks such as EMMOE instantiate one slice of this loop (language-conditioned planning and action in open environments) but still leave persistent personalization, memory update, and human feedback as broader assistant-level requirements []. Figure schematizes the loop, with the spatial-semantic memory at its center and the human present at every stage.

figure.toccaption: 13.1The intelligent-assistant loop. Alternative outputs illustrate household management, shared-space collaboration, and audio/haptic assistance. para.p: The assistant is deployed in three escalating regimes of human-proximity, which organize the remainder of this chapter. In the first, the assistant acts on the space while the human is a beneficiary at a distance: it tidies, fetches, and searches. In the second, the assistant acts alongside the human as a partner that must move and manipulate in shared space without intruding. In the third, the assistant acts for a vulnerable human, standing in for an impaired capability under hard safety, privacy, and accessibility constraints. The three regimes share the loop above but place progressively more weight on modeling the person rather than the place; Table collects benchmarks for all three.

The most autonomous regime asks the assistant to maintain the physical state of a human environment with little real-time supervision. A persistent model of the dwelling supports two complementary operations: grounding instructions for physical action, and retrieving remembered evidence to answer queries. New observations update the model, including after an action changes the environment. Figure separates these action and recall branches around their shared home memory.

Representing the home. Everything downstream depends on a queryable model of the space, which extends the scene-understanding methods of Chapter into a persistent, semantically indexed memory. The memory architectures themselves are treated in Section ; here they are the infrastructure that lets an assistant know not only where surfaces are, but what and whose. The 3D scene graph [] introduced a hierarchical structure that unifies objects, rooms, and cameras with the underlying geometry, and Hydra [] brought such graphs into real-time, loop-closure-optimized robot perception so that the memory stays current as the assistant moves. To make the memory addressable by free-form language, ConceptFusion [] builds an open-set, multimodal 3D map that answers text, image, or click queries, and ConceptGraphs [] fuses foundation-model outputs across views into a captioned, language-queryable 3D scene graph suitable for planning. This open-vocabulary memory is what lets an assistant act on objects it was never explicitly trained to recognize.

figure.toccaption: 13.2Managing the physical environment through a shared home memory. Observations maintain room, object, and relation records; grounded instructions drive manipulation, while queries independently retrieve last-seen evidence. Physical outcomes are re-observed to update memory.

caption.text: Managing the physical environment through a shared home memory. Observations maintain room, object, and relation records; grounded instructions drive manipulation, while queries independently retrieve last-seen evidence. Physical outcomes are re-observed to update memory.

para.p: Acting on the space: tidy-up and rearrangement. Restoring order is the canonical management task, framed by Batra et al.[] as bringing an environment from an arbitrary configuration into a target spatial state. The benchmark substrate includes the Visual Room Rearrangement (RoomR) challenge [], which asks an agent to observe a goal arrangement and then reset one to five displaced objects, and Housekeep [], which removes the explicit goal and instead judges placements against human preferences over nearly two thousand objects. Method work has moved from fixed rules to learned commonsense priors. TIDEE [] tidies a never-before-seen room from pixels using a visuo-semantic out-of-place detector and an associative memory of where receptacles tend to be, and TidyBot [] makes the placement preference-aware, using few-shot summarization with a large language model to generalize a particular user’s tidying rules from a handful of examples. The shift these systems mark, from a universal notion of tidiness to one conditioned on the resident, is exactly the personalization property that defines the assistant.

Acting on the space: open-vocabulary mobile manipulation. Tidying a real home requires picking and placing arbitrary objects at arbitrary locations, the task formalized as open-vocabulary mobile manipulation by HomeRobot [], which pairs a simulation and real benchmark with a software stack for the Hello Robot Stretch. Notable deployment evidence comes from OK-Robot [], which combines a phone-scanned dense vision-language map with off-the-shelf navigation and grasping to achieve zero-shot pick-and-drop across ten real homes, and from Mobile ALOHA [], which shows that low-cost whole-body teleoperation plus imitation learning can acquire dexterous bimanual household skills. These systems lean directly on the manipulation primitives of Section , increasingly instantiated as generalist vision-language-action policies (e.g., , OpenVLA [],
π 0
[]) that fold perception, grounding, and control into one model; the assistant contribution is to drive them in unstructured homes from open-vocabulary goals rather than in an engineered cell. Commercial and pre-commercial examples illustrate the same pressure from different directions: mapping vacuum robots such as iRobot’s Roomba, which build semantic room maps for targeted cleaning, 1 footnote 1 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 https://www.irobot.com represent the mature narrow end, while emerging home-humanoid platforms such as 1X’s Neo 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://www.1x.tech/neo and Figure 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://www.figure.ai show how the field is attempting, so far without a general-purpose result, to generalize mobile manipulation into domestic settings.

Searching and recalling the model. The dual of acting on the space is querying it: an assistant is, among other things, a search engine for the physical world that answers “where did I leave my keys?” Object-goal navigation supplies the active half, with goal-oriented semantic exploration (SemExp) [] building an episodic semantic map and a policy that exploits object co-occurrence to find a target efficiently rather than searching blindly. Embodied question answering [] couples navigation with answering, and its open-vocabulary successor OpenEQA [] spans both an episodic-memory setting, in which the assistant must recall what it has already seen, and an active-exploration setting, over more than a hundred real environments. For wearable assistants that record the user’s day, the same recall problem becomes natural-language search of long egocentric video, the episodic-memory task defined by Ego4D []. This is the application-facing counterpart of the memory-augmented reasoning systems in Section .

As the distance between assistant and human shrinks, spatial intelligence must become social intelligence. The assistant must model the human as a co-located agent with intent, viewpoint, and comfort zones, not as a moving obstacle or a bare command source, and act predictably and collaboratively. Running through every part of this task is the reconciliation of reference frames: the assistant’s own egocentric view, the human’s egocentric view, and a shared allocentric map must be kept aligned.

Dashed rings indicate comfort regions, and dashed sight lines associate views with shared objects.

caption.text: Collaborating in shared space: (a) person- and context-dependent comfort zones and (b) aligned robot/human views inform an interaction-aware plan; (c) navigation and handover illustrate alternative behaviors. Dashed rings indicate comfort regions, and dashed sight lines associate views with shared objects.

para.p: Socially-aware navigation. Moving through a populated space is not collision avoidance; it is adherence to the unwritten contracts of proxemics. The classical account is the social force model [], which casts pedestrian motion as attraction to a goal under repulsion from others, operationalizing Hall’s anthropological zones of personal space. Data-driven successors learn the interaction directly: Social LSTM [] couples per-person recurrent predictors through a social-pooling layer to forecast jointly plausible trajectories, and deep reinforcement-learning planners such as the attention-based crowd-robot model [] weigh neighbors to navigate dense crowds while avoiding the “freezing robot” failure that purely reactive planners suffer []. Progress is measured on human-demonstration corpora such as SCAND [], which records hours of socially compliant teleoperation for imitation and inverse reinforcement learning. The trend is toward anticipatory planning, in which the assistant infers the human’s intended path and yields proactively, and toward learnable cost functions that adapt passing distances to individual or cultural preference rather than enforcing one universal margin.

Grounded instruction following and spatial dialogue. A collaborating assistant must resolve spatial language against what it sees, including the deictic references (“put it next to the other bowl,” “the one over there”) that pervade human speech. Vision-and-language navigation, introduced with the Room-to-Room benchmark [], established the problem of following natural-language route instructions in photorealistic buildings; ALFRED [] extended it to long-horizon household tasks with irreversible state changes, and TEACh [] cast the task as a two-agent dialogue in which a commander and follower must build shared spatial reference over multiple turns. Resolving a referring expression to a specific object in a cluttered 3D scene is studied directly by ScanRefer [] and ReferIt3D [], whose same-class distractors force the model to rely on spatial relations rather than appearance. These benchmarks build on the reasoning capabilities of Chapter ; the assistant requirement is to maintain a spatial working memory that links current observations to earlier instructions so that deixis can be resolved.

Shared autonomy and collaboration. When full autonomy is brittle, the assistant acts as a third hand under shared control. The defining formulation is shared autonomy via hindsight optimization [], in which the robot infers a distribution over the user’s spatial goal and assists toward it without committing to a single confident prediction, formalizing the earlier policy-blending account of arbitration between human and robot intent []. Equally important is making the assistant’s own motion readable: legible motion [] shapes a reaching trajectory so a human can quickly infer its intended target, which is what allows close-quarters collaboration to feel safe. Physical handovers, where giver and receiver must coordinate in space and time [], are the elementary collaborative act on which assistive manipulation is built.

Perspective-taking and egocentric grounding. Many assistants observe the world from a wearable, first-person viewpoint, so the frame-alignment problem becomes explicit. Ego4D [] and its successors anchor egocentric perception at scale, and dedicated capture platforms such as Project Aria 4 footnote 4 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 4 footnote 4 https://www.projectaria.com supply the calibrated multi-sensor first-person stream such assistants run on, while spatial-VQA backbones such as SpatialVLM [] give a vision-language model the quantitative 3D reasoning (distances, sizes, directions) needed to answer spatial questions about the user’s scene. The hardware and pose-estimation side of wearable sensing is treated in Section , and the augmented-reality runtime that renders guidance into the user’s view is treated in Section ; here the contribution is the reasoning that converts a first-person observation into a collaborative action in the human’s frame. Embodied-AR applications make this alignment problem explicit when directions, warnings, or manipulation cues must be registered into the user’s view []. Figure illustrates the elements of this regime.

The highest-impact regime uses spatial intelligence to compensate for a sensory, cognitive, or motor impairment, acting as a prosthesis for the user’s perception or agency. The assistant translates the environment into a queryable, navigable, and actionable representation and delivers it through a channel the user can still use (audio, haptics, or physical action). Because the loop closes around a vulnerable person in their own home, safety, privacy, and personalization are design constraints from the start.

para.p: Assistance for the blind and visually impaired. For blind and low-vision users, spatial intelligence turns an unknown and hazardous environment into a queryable one. The oldest strand is sensory substitution, exemplified by the vOICe [], which sonifies the spatial structure of an image into sound. The modern strand is conversational visual question answering: VizWiz [] introduced a deployed system in which a blind user photographs their surroundings and asks a spoken question, and the VizWiz Grand Challenge [] turned the resulting real-world distribution, including blurry and unanswerable images, into the reference benchmark for assistive VQA. Indoor wayfinding is addressed by smartphone navigation aids such as NavCog [], which deliver turn-by-turn audio guidance from accurate beacon-based localization, and by three-dimensional spatial audio that places points of interest around the user. Commercial assistive applications include Microsoft’s Seeing AI for scene and text narration 5 footnote 5 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 5 footnote 5 https://www.seeingai.com, Be My Eyes for volunteer- and model-mediated visual assistance 6 footnote 6 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 6 footnote 6 https://www.bemyeyes.com, and wearable systems from OrCam 7 footnote 7 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 7 footnote 7 https://www.orcam.com, Envision 8 footnote 8 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 8 footnote 8 https://www.letsenvision.com, and biped.ai 9 footnote 9 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 9 footnote 9 https://biped.ai for scene description and obstacle warning. These tools move from passive obstacle warning to active interrogation, in which the user asks “is there a free seat?” or “read the sign on the door” and the assistant retrieves the answer.

Cognitive and mobility assistance. For users with cognitive decline or limited mobility, spatial assistants provide external scaffolding for the activities of daily living. Ambient assisted living systems such as the CASAS smart home [] instrument a dwelling to track the resident’s location and activity, learning the spatio-temporal patterns whose violation (a fall, a missed meal) signals a need to intervene; wearable accelerometry supplies the canonical fall-detection paradigm [].

Where monitoring gives way to physical action, the assistant becomes a shared-control effector. Smart wheelchairs [] and wheelchair-mounted assistive arms use collaborative control to enforce spatial safety zones, for example forbidding a chair from driving down a staircase, so that the user retains mobility without constant supervision; the goal-arbitration that underlies such control is the same shared-autonomy machinery introduced above, here cast as a decision-theoretic problem []. Assistive feeding [] shows how fine spatial reasoning (where to acquire a bite, how to transfer it to the user’s mouth) becomes a caregiving act. The platform lineage runs from Robots for Humanity [], which let a man with quadriplegia perform self-care through a teleoperated PR2, to the affordable Stretch mobile manipulator [], with physics-based simulation of caregiving tasks consolidated in Assistive Gym []. Commercial assistive hardware in this space includes the Kinova JACO arm 10 footnote 10 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 10 footnote 10 https://www.kinovarobotics.com and the Obi feeding device 11 footnote 11 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 11 footnote 11 https://meetobi.com. This regime overlaps the clinical setting of Section , but the boundary is clear: there the focus is diagnosis and surgical intervention, whereas here it is daily living in the home. Figure summarizes the compensation principle.

para.p: Deployed assistants have so far approached the persistent, personalized spatial model of this chapter from opposite ends: software agents know a great deal about the user but nothing about the user’s space, while home robots occupy the space but act with limited autonomy.

Personal agents. The most widely used assistants now act on a user’s behalf in the digital world. OpenAI’s ChatGPT agent 12 footnote 12 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 12 footnote 12 https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-agent/ (July 2025) runs on its own virtual computer, browsing and filling in forms across multi-step tasks and asking permission before consequential actions. Meta’s Muse 13 footnote 13 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 13 footnote 13 CNBC, 8 September 2026. (September 2026), billed as a personal agent for everyday users, likewise runs in an isolated virtual machine and handles errands such as shopping and travel booking, and its request for access to email, calendars, and payments made privacy the main point of public debate around its launch. Voice assistants are being rebuilt on the same models: Amazon’s Alexa+ 14 footnote 14 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 14 footnote 14 https://www.aboutamazon.com, generally available in the United States since February 2026, adds generative dialogue to the smart-home control that Alexa already provided, and Apple’s Siri 15 footnote 15 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 15 footnote 15 https://www.apple.com/siri/ is being rebuilt on Google’s Gemini models, adding personal context and on-screen awareness. For spatial intelligence, these agents matter mainly as the layer that holds personal context and preference; apart from smart-home control, none of them maintains a model of the physical home.

Camera-grounded assistants. A second line brings the physical world into the conversation through a camera. Gemini Live’s camera mode 16 footnote 16 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 16 footnote 16 https://gemini.google/, the product form of Google’s Project Astra, lets a user point a phone at the surroundings and ask about what it sees, and Meta AI on camera glasses does the same from the wearer’s viewpoint (Section ). These systems answer spatial questions about the current view, and the assistive applications of Pivotal Task-3 build on the same capability, but they keep at most a short history of what they have seen, so the long-horizon spatial memory this chapter calls for remains outside them.

Home robots. Embodied assistants remain the least mature tier. Beyond mapping vacuums, the home humanoids introduced under Pivotal Task-1 are moving toward sale: 1X opened preorders for NEO in October 2025, at $20,000 or a monthly subscription, with first deliveries promised for 2026 and with remote operators teleoperating tasks that its onboard autonomy cannot yet complete, and Figure’s third-generation humanoid, Figure 03 (2025), is designed for homes and driven by its Helix vision-language-action model. The reliance on teleoperation shows how far these products are from the autonomous, open-vocabulary mobile manipulation of Pivotal Task-1, and it raises the in-home privacy question discussed below.

The three regimes share a common obstacle: the assistant must be reliable in the one setting that resists engineering, namely a real person’s private and unstructured life. The challenges below are ordered from the perceptual frontier (generalization, memory) through the human frontier (personalization, social safety) to the deployment frontier (privacy, compute, trust), and each cuts across all three pivotal tasks above. Governance benchmarks for embodied agents have begun to measure the deployment end directly, testing whether a system stays controllable, recoverable, and auditable under perturbation rather than only whether it completes tasks [].

Generalization to unstructured homes. An assistant cannot be retrained per household, yet homes vary without bound in layout, lighting, and contents. Zero-shot results such as OK-Robot [] are encouraging but remain far from the reliability a daily aide requires, and closing the gap depends on the open-vocabulary representations and sim-to-real transfer surveyed in Part III rather than on more in-domain data.

Long-horizon spatial memory. Because the assistant persists in one place, it must remember spatial state over days and weeks: where objects were last seen, which routines the user follows, what was already done. Real-time scene-graph memories [] and episodic-memory benchmarks [] begin to address this, but the general memory mechanisms are treated in Section ; the assistant-specific unsolved problem is maintaining a consistent, updatable, and forgetting-resistant model over long deployments in a private home.

Personalization and preference learning. The assistant’s geometric goals are user-specific, so it must learn an individual’s placement rules, comfort distances, and routines from sparse interaction. Few-shot preference summarization [] and learnable social cost functions are early steps, but acquiring rich preferences without burdening the user remains an open problem.

Social compliance and safety. Operating in continuous contact with people turns motion into a social and safety-critical act. Anticipatory, legible navigation and motion [] and shared-control safety zones [] mitigate risk, yet guaranteeing comfort and physical safety across the diversity of real human behavior is far from settled.

Privacy of persistent in-home perception. An assistant that continuously perceives a private home raises acute privacy concerns, the more so for assistive cameras worn by users who cannot themselves audit what is captured. The concern becomes sharper when assistance depends on remote operation or cloud annotation, because the raw spatial stream itself may reveal the user’s routines and vulnerabilities. Persistent spatial memory must be reconciled with selective perception, on-device processing, and user control over what is retained.

On-device compute and trust. Wearable and home platforms are power- and thermally constrained, forcing the heavy perception and reasoning stacks of Part III onto efficient, often on-device, inference. Compounding this, assistance for vulnerable users is safety-critical, so calibrated reliability and appropriate user trust, neither over- nor under-reliance, are prerequisites for deployment rather than refinements of it.

Other application domains of spatial intelligence are too numerous to enumerate, because spatial intelligence is a horizontal capability: any field that must perceive, reconstruct, localize within, or reason about the geometry of the physical world inherits the methods of Part III.

This chapter takes five further domains where that inheritance is already visible in deployed systems. Each stresses a capability the earlier chapters do not: registering a building site against its design, tracking many near-identical agents through occlusion, reconstructing fragile objects faithfully, working without clean light or satellite positioning underwater, and binding people to products across a network of cameras.

The architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) sector is built around a single spatial-intelligence problem: continuously registering the messy as-built reality of a site against the structured as-designed model that specifies what it should become. This is the same Building-Information-Modeling (BIM) substrate that anchors the city-scale digital twins of Section , but here the model is the working blueprint of an individual building under construction rather than a synchronized replica of a finished one, and the central task is detecting and acting on the discrepancy between plan and reality. Figure sketches this as-built versus as-designed loop. Scan-to-BIM is its perception front end: dense laser or photogrammetric scans of a structure are semantically parsed into walls, floors, columns, and components, building on the indoor point-cloud understanding of Chapter and its benchmarks S3DIS [] and ScanNet []. A specialized sub-problem is vectorizing a scan into an editable floorplan, where synthetic supervision such as Structured3D [] and transformer models that predict all room polygons in parallel [] now recover clean geometry from cluttered scans. Progress monitoring closes the loop in time: by registering an image-based or scanned as-built point cloud against a four-dimensional IFC-BIM model, deviations between planned and actual construction state can be recognized automatically [], the spatiotemporal core of the commercial reality-capture platforms now common on job sites. Construction robotics acts on the model directly, with mobile fabricators that localize against the design to print, place, or assemble structural elements at full scale []. Finally, structural inspection turns the same perception stack toward maintenance, localizing cracks and defects on concrete surfaces from imagery [], increasingly from a UAV-borne 3D reconstruction of a bridge or facade. Reality-capture and BIM tooling from Matterport, 1 footnote 1 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 1 footnote 1 https://matterport.com/ Autodesk, 2 footnote 2 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 2 footnote 2 https://www.autodesk.com/products/recap/overview and Leica, 3 footnote 3 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 3 footnote 3 https://leica-geosystems.com/products/laser-scanners progress-monitoring services such as OpenSpace 4 footnote 4 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 4 footnote 4 https://www.openspace.ai/ and Buildots, 5 footnote 5 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 5 footnote 5 https://buildots.com/ and on-site robots from Dusty Robotics 6 footnote 6 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 6 footnote 6 https://www.dustyrobotics.com/ and Built Robotics 7 footnote 7 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 7 footnote 7 https://www.builtrobotics.com/ are representative of the deployed layer.

para.p: Sports analytics lifts raw broadcast or arena video into a calibrated metric model of the playing surface, then reasons over the resulting positional field. What sets it apart is fine-grained, multi-agent spatiotemporal tracking under severe and persistent occlusion, where many near-identical players and a small fast ball must be followed and assigned consistent identities at sub-second resolution. Figure illustrates three linked capabilities: registered trajectories feed tactical analysis, while calibrated multi-view pose supports biomechanics. Tracking and registration form the geometric foundation: multi-object tracking benchmarks such as SoccerNet-Tracking [] and the multi-sport SportsMOT [] drive player and ball association, while sports-field registration estimates the homography from the broadcast frame to a metric pitch template so that pixel positions become field coordinates []. 3D pose and biomechanics recover athlete motion in three dimensions, with markerless capture systems estimating not only kinematics but joint dynamics from ordinary video, as in OpenCap [], typically by triangulating multi-view 2D pose into a 3D skeleton []. Tactical and team-space analysis then treats the positional field itself as the object of study, valuing the space each player controls and forecasting where players will move; deep models of expected possession value [] and multi-agent trajectory generation [] build directly on the spatial-reasoning methods of Chapter . The deployed layer is mature, spanning optical tracking and officiating from Hawk-Eye, 8 footnote 8 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 8 footnote 8 https://www.hawkeyeinnovations.com/ player-tracking data from Second Spectrum (now part of Genius Sports) 9 footnote 9 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 9 footnote 9 https://www.geniussports.com/ and Stats Perform, 10 footnote 10 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 10 footnote 10 https://www.statsperform.com/ and wearable spatial sensing from KINEXON 11 footnote 11 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 11 footnote 11 https://kinexon-sports.com/ and Catapult. 12 footnote 12 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 12 footnote 12 https://www.catapult.com/

para.p: Cultural heritage and archaeology apply spatial intelligence to the past, running from capture through recovery to discovery. What distinguishes it is high-fidelity, metrically accurate, and usually non-contact reconstruction, coupled to a preservation imperative: the artifact may be fragile, fragmentary, or buried, and the digital record must be faithful enough to stand in for an object that cannot be handled or that no longer exists intact. Figure organizes the field into three movements. Digitization captures artifacts and monuments in three dimensions, a lineage that runs from the landmark in-field laser scanning of the Digital Michelangelo Project [] through structure-from-motion photogrammetry [] to the neural radiance fields [] and 3D Gaussian splatting [] now used for photorealistic heritage capture, all drawing on the reconstruction methods of Chapter . Virtual restoration uses geometric AI to reassemble what time has broken, posing fragment reassembly as a 3D puzzle over fractured parts, with large benchmarks such as Breaking Bad [] and the real fresco-reassembly dataset RePAIR [] driving the methods. Archaeological prospection discovers sites at landscape scale, most strikingly through airborne LiDAR whose bare-earth models reveal structures hidden under forest canopy, as in the canopy-penetrating surveys of the Maya lowlands at Caracol [] and across northern Guatemala []. Organizations such as CyArk 13 footnote 13 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 13 footnote 13 https://www.cyark.org/ and the Factum Foundation, 14 footnote 14 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 14 footnote 14 https://www.factumfoundation.org/ together with photogrammetry tools including Agisoft Metashape 15 footnote 15 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 15 footnote 15 https://www.agisoft.com/ and the Open Heritage 3D archive, 16 footnote 16 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 16 footnote 16 https://openheritage3d.org/ anchor the practical layer.

para.p: Underwater spatial intelligence confronts a setting in which the two assumptions that anchor terrestrial methods both fail at once: light no longer propagates cleanly, since wavelength-dependent attenuation and scattering degrade vision with range, and satellite positioning does not penetrate water, so absolute position must be inferred from acoustics, inertia, or the structure being surveyed. Figure depicts the resulting perceive-localize-map-inspect loop. Navigation and SLAM solve the GPS-denied localization problem, surveyed comprehensively for autonomous underwater vehicles by Paull et al.[], with foundational deep-sea visual SLAM demonstrated on the wreck of the Titanic [] and modern visual-inertial-pressure localization benchmarked by datasets such as AQUALOC []. Perception and enhancement contend with the optical medium itself: physically grounded models remove the water from an image to recover true scene color and range [], learned enhancement restores contrast in real time for downstream perception [], and benchmarks such as UIEB standardize the evaluation [], while large annotated image databases like FathomNet [] enable ocean-scale detection. Mapping and inspection reconstruct the seafloor, habitats, and submerged structures, with structure-relative perception and coverage planning enabling autonomous inspection of complex ship hulls []. The operational layer spans low-cost platforms such as the BlueROV2, 17 footnote 17 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 17 footnote 17 https://bluerobotics.com/store/rov/bluerov2/ survey vehicles from Kongsberg 18 footnote 18 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 18 footnote 18 https://www.kongsberg.com/discovery/autonomous-and-uncrewed-solutions/auv/hugin/ and research institutions including WHOI 19 footnote 19 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 19 footnote 19 https://www.whoi.edu/ and MBARI. 20 footnote 20 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 20 footnote 20 https://www.mbari.org/

Dotted lines link scene details; the geometry and density are illustrative.

para.p: Retail and smart-space intelligence reduces to one persistent spatial problem: jointly associating, across a network of calibrated overlapping cameras and over time, which person is interacting with which product at which shelf location. Unlike the warehouse logistics of Section , where the environment is engineered for the robot, here the space is a crowded store full of untracked people, and its distinguishing challenge is dense multi-object tracking with reliable human-object association through frequent mutual occlusion. Figure shows how the major applications share this core. Multi-camera tracking provides the spatial backbone, with benchmarks such as WILDTRACK [] and MMPTRACK [] and methods that project per-camera features onto a shared ground plane to detect and track people across views []; this is the machinery behind cashierless checkout, where a shopper’s path and pickups must be reconstructed without a checkout line. Shelf monitoring turns perception toward the products, detecting densely packed items for inventory and planogram compliance, supported by the dense-detection benchmark SKU-110K [] and by methods that formulate compliance as matching the observed shelf layout against the ideal one as a sub-graph isomorphism []. In-store analytics aggregates the same tracks into shopper-flow heatmaps and layout insights, building on cross-camera re-identification [] to stitch one customer’s trajectory across non-overlapping views. The deployed layer includes cashierless systems such as Amazon’s Just Walk Out 21 footnote 21 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 21 footnote 21 https://www.justwalkout.com/ and platforms from Trigo, 22 footnote 22 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 22 footnote 22 https://www.trigoretail.com/ AiFi, 23 footnote 23 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 23 footnote 23 https://www.aifi.com/ and Zippin, 24 footnote 24 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 24 footnote 24 https://www.getzippin.com/ alongside shelf-analytics vendors such as Trax. 25 footnote 25 footnote Footnote footnotes Footnotes 25 footnote 25 https://traxretail.com/

para.p: The five domains above, whose benchmarks are collected in Table , are a sample, not a census. Spatial intelligence is equally at work in fields this survey does not treat at length: virtual try-on and 3D e-commerce, immersive education and high-fidelity training simulators, security and surveillance, energy and infrastructure inspection, precision agriculture beyond the remote-sensing view of Section , and many others. What unites them, and what unites them with the headline applications of the preceding chapters, is that each takes the perception, reasoning, and generation capabilities of Part III and specializes them to the geometry, sensing modality, and constraints of a particular slice of the physical world.
